Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) is the term used to refer to the standard framework of guidelines for financial accounting in the United States. GAAP includes the standards, conventions, and rules accountants follow in recording and summarizing transactions in the preparation of financial statements. In addition to reporting financial results in accordance with GAAP, we have provided certain non-GAAP financial measures, including adjusted revenue, adjusted segment revenue, adjusted operating income, adjusted segment income, adjusted cost of revenue, adjusted segment cost of revenue, adjusted operating expenses, adjusted operating margin, adjusted segment income margin, non-GAAP earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (non-GAAP EBITDA), free cash flow, free cash flow conversion,  net operating profit after tax return on invested capital (NOPAT ROIC), and non-GAAP adjusted net income. We also present key revenue, which is the sum of cloud services revenue and processing revenue, and non-key revenue, which is all other GAAP revenue. Key revenue and non-key revenue are components of GAAP revenue and are presented because management views key revenue as the strategic recurring revenue of the business most important for long-term growth.

We believe non-GAAP financial measures help investors better understand the underlying fundamentals and operating performance of our business. Adjusted revenue, adjusted segment revenue, adjusted operating income, adjusted operating margin, adjusted segment income, adjusted segment income margin, adjusted cost of revenue, adjusted segment cost of revenue, adjusted operating expenses, and adjusted net income eliminate deconversion revenue and associated costs, the gain on assets, net, and an acquisition, which management believes are not indicative of the Company's operating performance. Such adjustments give investors further insight into our performance. Non-GAAP EBITDA is defined as net income attributable to the Company before the effect of interest income, net, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, adjusted for net income before the effect of interest income, net, taxes, depreciation, and amortization attributable to eliminated deconversions, the gain on assets, net, and an acquisition. Free cash flow is defined as net cash from operating activities, less capitalized expenditures, internal use software, and capitalized software, plus proceeds from the sale of assets. NOPAT ROIC is defined as operating income for the trailing four quarters multiplied by one minus the average effective tax rate (ETR) for the trailing four quarters, with the result divided by average invested capital (average of the beginning and ending period balances). Free cash flow conversion is defined as free cash flow, less proceeds from sale of assets, divided by net income.  Management believes that non-GAAP EBITDA is an important measure of the Company's overall operating performance and excludes certain costs and other transactions that management does not consider indicative of the Company's ongoing operating performance; free cash flow is useful to measure the funds generated in a given period that are available for debt service requirements and strategic capital decisions; free cash flow conversion is useful to measure the efficiency with which operating results are converted into free cash flow; and NOPAT ROIC is a measure of the Company's allocation efficiency and effectiveness of its invested capital. For these reasons, management also uses these non-GAAP financial measures in its assessment and management of the Company's performance.

Non-GAAP financial measures used by the Company may not be comparable to similarly titled non-GAAP measures used by other companies. Non-GAAP financial measures have no standardized meaning prescribed by GAAP and therefore, are unlikely to be comparable with calculations of similar measures for other companies.

Any non-GAAP financial measures should be considered in context with the GAAP financial presentation and should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for GAAP measures. Reconciliations of the non-GAAP financial measures to related GAAP measures are included.

#5580. MSRs trade at richest levels in decades as lenders, funds pile in

Mortgage servicing rights are trading at their richest levels in decades, with pristine MSR multiples nearing 7x as more lenders choose to retain servicing and build recapture platforms.  AI Summary

Chicago-based Rate has recently changed its servicing strategy, retaining mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) instead of selling.

“We’ve been retaining all of our MSRs for the last 12 months, so we’re over $50 billion in MSR retention,” CEO Victor Ciardelli said in an exclusive interview with HousingWire. “We really believe in retaining the MSRs, staying close to the customer.”

Rate’s approach reflects a broader trend of mortgage lenders holding onto their portfolios or seeking to add MSRs as a way to recapture borrowers when rates eventually fall.

John Sullivan, managing director of MSR advisory services at Milliman, has seen that shift firsthand. Speaking during IMN’s Mortgage Servicing Rights Conference in New York on Monday, he said he’s having more conversations with clients about retaining their portfolios “unless liquidity is an issue,” and about monetizing them if they are not hedging.

Higher demand for MSRs is not limited to independent mortgage banks (IMBs). Depository institutions are also showing more interest, executives told HousingWire during the conference.

“Banks historically are not great at recapture, but we think that given some changes on the Basel capital front, we’re going to see more bank participation in this space on a go-forward basis, and I think banks will think about just customer acquisition in general, cross-selling in general,” said Larry Goldstone, president of capital markets and lending at BSI Financial Services.

Strategic investors are also willing to grow their portfolios. Rob Williams, co-founder and CEO at Grander Investment Management, a specialized asset manager focused on MSRs, said he’s tactical but sees MSRs as a “spectacular asset” that can reach double-digit returns.

“I can probably be more patient,” he said during the conference, when comparing his approach to the other buyers. “I can be more tactical.”

The buyer base views MSRs through different lenses.

Rich McRedmond, managing director at CrossCountry Mortgage, said that while banks see MSRs as part of their consumer banking strategy, real estate investment trusts (REITs) see them as a pure investment. And mortgage companies see them as a borrower recapture tool “from when they get the mortgage to when they get the next mortgage.”

Conventional, pristine MSRs are seeing 7x multiples amid high demand, a level not reached in more than two decades.

“We’ve seen some pretty extraordinary multiples of late,” Goldstone said. “This is usually an inexpensive asset, and therefore an asset that people want to be able to own. I think you could hedge MSR pretty effectively and still get low-double digits, high-single digit returns up until about the last year. That’s pretty attractive for an asset that really doesn’t have a whole lot of credit risk associated with it.”

Simon Aldrich, senior executive vice president at Freedom Mortgage, believes that at this point, “it’s very difficult to be in this market if you don’t have recapture.”

“In our model, we don’t hedge, so I’m not worried about rates going up or rates going down. Rates go up, I get the pickup at slower speeds. Rates go down, our call center kicks into gear.”

Bayview Asset Management, which acquires MSRs from the bulk and flow markets and uses five different subservicers, has also built out a full recapture strategy, including through its acquisition of Guild Mortgage. Managing director Michael Lau said Bayview has partnered with investors, including sovereign wealth funds and pension funds, that have long-duration strategies.

“MSRs are great because they’re not correlated to the equity or the bond market, and gives them something alternative that also, because we hedge out all the interest rate risk for them, delivers a very consistent return on their money, net of our fees,” Lau said.

Some companies have taken advantage of current pricing to sell MSRs for different reasons, including to pay back debt or raise funds.

In the third quarter, Rocket Companies sold $23 billion of unpaid principal balance (UPB) for $379 million in cash proceeds, retaining the subservicing and recapture services on nearly 70% of the MSRs sold. Analysts told HousingWire the company usually sells production in the wholesale channel due to lower recapture possibility.

Pennymac Financial Services entered into an agreement to sell $29 billion in UPB of low-coupon conventional MSRs, with $490 million of proceeds expected to pay down debt. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter.

Meanwhile United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) sold about $60 billion — at a roughly 6x multiple — to JPMorgan Chase, sources told HousingWire. The companies declined to comment. This is part of a plan to bring up to $80 billion of MSRs to market in the fourth quarter, with the expectation of being paid more than $1.8 billion in an attempt to reduce leverage.

Newrez President Baron Silverstein said his company is taking a disciplined approach. Across the Newrez portfolio, 60% of loans were originated before or during the COVID-19 pandemic.

“In today’s market, given where we are from a rate perspective, there’s pressure in a competitive environment where MSRs get created — where that gain on sale is from an all-in gain-on-sale perspective on loans that we originate or buy. And when we think about that, we get very selective and stay very disciplined about how we put that capital to work,” Silverstein said.

“When you think about hedging in a market like this, that also requires a lot of capital, and it’s very challenging in these markets today, regardless of the interest rate environment. This has been the case for the last year to year and a half.”

Looking ahead, servicing executives believe that multiples can stay higher as elevated mortgage rates reduce prepayment risks, which supports MSR cash flows. Some of them said multiples could move lower if there’s a liquidity issue due to large bulk sales hitting the market.

Regulation could also play a role. “If Basel III goes through and the banks decide to get back into the space, I think the high-six multiples could be relatively inexpensive,” Goldstone said. “You could see multiples in the 7x-8x category.”

#5579. Rhabdomyolysis: 3 warning-sign points the CDC makes on symptoms and tests

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The CDC flags muscle pain, dark urine, and weakness as rhabdo signs and says only repeated blood tests can confirm the condition.

A long shift on a hot job site or a punishing session at the gym tends to end the same way, with sore legs, heavy arms, and a body that wants to sit down. A person in that state may shrug off the discomfort and expect a night of sleep to erase it. In some cases, the ache signals something more serious unfolding inside the muscles. Rhabdomyolysis, a dangerous muscle condition that health officials shorten to rhabdo, can hide behind exhaustion that looks routine. Knowing its warning signs gives a person the tools to judge whether they, a coworker, or a training partner needs medical attention. The choice tends to fall to the person who feels the pain or to whoever stands nearby.

Rhabdo's warning signs can blur into the ordinary toll of hard work. Soreness after heavy labor counts as normal, and fatigue after a demanding week surprises no one. A person used to toughing it out may read every twinge as proof of effort. Coaches, supervisors, and coworkers can make the same mistake from the outside. The line between everyday strain and real muscle damage can stay invisible to the person living through it. Clear guidance on what the warning signs look like, how they behave, and how a clinician confirms them can narrow that gap. Without such guidance, a worker or athlete may wait out symptoms that call for a trip to a clinic.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidance on rhabdo comes from the agency's worker-safety research institute, which a 1970 federal law created to examine health and safety on the job. The advice sits on a single page aimed at a general audience. It explains which symptoms deserve attention, how soon they can emerge, when to seek care, and which tests a provider can use. It offers practical direction and draws on no survey, trial, or dataset. As a result, it gives no sample size, data period, or prevalence figures. Causes, risk factors, prevention, and treatment get their own pages elsewhere on the site. The three points below form a selection from the page's content and do not catalog every rhabdo warning sign.

Muscle pain, dark urine, and weakness or tiredness form the three main warning signs of rhabdo in the CDC guidance. Someone who develops the condition may notice one of these or several at once. The page names the trio twice, first among its key points and again in its detailed rundown, a repetition that marks them as the core signs to learn. The short list hands anyone coming off a demanding shift or gym session a set of cues to check against their own body.

Cramps, aches, or pains become a red flag once they hurt more than the activity should explain. The guidance folds all three kinds of discomfort into a single symptom, so the size of the hurt counts for more than its form. Hard work leaves some soreness behind, and the page draws its line at intensity. Pain that outstrips the exertion behind it belongs in a different category from routine stiffness.

Dark urine supplies the second clue, and the page describes its shade as tea-colored or cola-colored. Two everyday drinks give readers a concrete reference to hold against what they see. This marker stands apart from the other pair. A person can spot it without weighing how sore or drained they feel, and without recalling how much strain came before.

Weakness or tiredness rounds out the set, and the guidance defines it through lost ability. A person with this problem cannot finish tasks or workouts they once handled with ease. The page also labels the pattern exercise intolerance. The benchmark sits inside the individual's own history, with no outside standard required. A lift or a chore that felt easy last month and now stalls halfway illustrates the comparison the page has in mind.

Pain and fatigue in many cases outrun the effort that produced them, according to the page. The shared mismatch ties together the two complaints a person feels from the inside. Both depend on a person's own read of past effort, which makes dark urine the one signal on the list that needs no comparison at all.

Rhabdo symptoms can hold off for hours or days after the first muscle injury, and some people notice nothing until several days have passed. The damage and the first warning can land on different days. A person who feels sore or drained days later may not tie the feeling to the effort that caused it. The spread from hours to several days leaves no fixed point at which a person can declare the danger over. One or two nights of sleep settle nothing about the risk. The warning can arrive at home or on a day off, far from the job site or gym where the strain happened.

Creatine kinase, the muscle protein that climbs when rhabdo sets in, may take time to rise. Its slow climb mirrors the late arrival of symptoms. A blood test on the day of the strain can come back before the protein has gone up. In those first hours, neither the body's signals nor an initial lab result offers a final word.

Any symptom, at any point, calls for immediate medical care, according to the guidance. The instruction sets no waiting period and no cutoff. Dark urine on the third day after a hard shift deserves the same response as muscle pain that strikes within the hour. The rule extends to weakness or tiredness that takes hold midweek. A sign's timing does nothing to lower its urgency.

Early diagnosis buys time for treatment. Care that starts at an earlier stage improves the odds of recovering without lasting harm to health. The condition's lagging onset works against that goal. A person who dismisses a delayed symptom spends time that treatment could have used. Read together, the delay and the call for fast care stretch the period of vigilance past the day of the effort and into the days that follow.

Only a blood test that measures creatine kinase, a muscle protein that goes by CK or creatine phosphokinase (CPK), can confirm rhabdo, according to the CDC. Symptoms on their own settle nothing. Dehydration, heat cramps, and other conditions can produce the same signs. A person who feels sore and drained has no way to tell from the body alone which problem is at work.

Damaged muscle tissue releases CK into the bloodstream, and rhabdo pushes the protein's blood level higher. One draw captures a single moment. Providers need repeated samples to see whether the number is climbing or dropping, and the direction of travel tells more than any lone result.

Serial CK checks continue until two consecutive results show the level falling, the agency advises. The rule gives patients and clinicians a defined finish line. A single lower reading does not satisfy the standard, and monitoring ends once a second decline backs up the first.

Urine dipstick tests give inaccurate readings for rhabdo, the agency warns. The strips look for myoglobin, a component of muscle cells, and they detect it by indirect means. The body sheds myoglobin at a rapid pace, and a urine sample may show no trace of it. Elevated CK can persist in the blood for days. The mismatch in timing leaves the dipstick blind during a window when the blood test can register damage.

Patients share responsibility for getting the right workup. The guidance tells anyone with symptoms to ask for serial CK levels if a provider does not check them. It urges people who suspect rhabdo to request a CK blood test from a healthcare provider. A patient who knows which test counts can press for it at a visit that could end with a urine strip or a guess drawn from sore muscles.

A person whose symptoms appear several days after an injury may reach a clinic after the body has cleared its myoglobin, and the blood draw remains the check suited to that delay.

#5577. Novee’s External Surface Testing checks which exposed assets attackers can actually exploit

Artificial intelligence penetration testing startup Novee Cyber Security Ltd. today added External Surface Testing to its platform so its AI-driven attacks can reach a customer’s entire internet-facing footprint.

External Surface Testing is aimed at the scramble after a critical vulnerability is disclosed, when security teams have to work out which exposed assets are affected and whether any can actually be exploited. Novee argues that attackers see a target as a single environment with many ways in, including forgotten subdomains and staging servers someone left exposed.

Conventional external attack surface management products catalog a company’s exposed assets and score them by severity. Netta Rager Dan, vice president of product at Novee, said those products “show you what’s exposed, but don’t give you the full picture of real risk.” In the company’s telling, security staff are left to validate long lists of exposures on their own.

Novee’s version needs nothing more than a domain name to get started. From there the software works outward the way an outside attacker would, and it keeps track of what it learns about each asset and service as it goes. A newly disclosed vulnerability gets run against a customer’s live systems to see whether anyone could actually exploit it.

Findings exported from other vendors’ attack surface tools go through the same check. Novee says the testing also catches flaws nobody had logged, chained attack paths among them, and the customer ends up with a short, prioritized list of validated issues backed by evidence.

Until now Novee’s testing has stopped at the application layer. External Surface Testing runs on the same platform as the company’s Application Pentesting product, so a host found during external discovery can be promoted straight into a full gray-box or white-box pentest. Whatever the discovery phase learned carries over. Novee claims no other fully autonomous AI pentesting platform covers the external attack surface as well as web, mobile and AI applications.

Limits are built in to keep the testing safe. Customers approve the scope before anything runs, and the probes come from outside the perimeter without agents or customer-supplied credentials. Exploit attempts don’t use destructive payloads. Traffic is held under configured caps so testing doesn’t cause load spikes or bury the security operations center in noise.

Former national-level offensive security operators Ido Geffen, Gon Chalamish and Omer Ninburg founded Novee in May 2025. YL Ventures LP, Canaan Partners and Zeev Ventures LP backed the company when it launched in January with $51.5 million in funding.

External Surface Testing is available now as part of the Novee platform.

#5576. Finance of America grows origination volume but reports $110M loss in Q3

Finance of America reported a $110M net loss in Q3 2026, driven mainly by $125M in noncash fair value adjustments. Funded volume rose 24% year over year to $748M, while adjusted net income was $6M and adjusted EBITDA was $17M.   AI Summary

Finance of America (FOA) reported a net loss of $110 million in the third quarter of 2026, as noncash fair value adjustments weighed on results despite growth in the company’s home equity lending business.

The Plano, Texas-based company on Tuesday reported $748 million in funded volume for the quarter ending Sept. 30, up 24% from $603 million during the same period last year. Year-to-date funded volume reached $2.07 billion, a 17% increase from the first nine months of 2025.

FOA recorded a basic loss of $5.24 per share, compared with a loss of 98 cents per share in the third quarter of 2025. The quarterly net loss was primarily driven by $125 million in noncash fair value adjustments.

On an adjusted basis, FOA reported net income of $6 million, or 28 cents per share, compared with $33 million, or $1.33 per share, a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA totaled $17 million, down from $55 million in the third quarter of 2025.

“The third quarter of 2026 demonstrated the continued strength of our platform, with funded origination volume growing 24% year over year. While higher interest rates drove near-term pressure on earnings, we believe this impact is temporary,” CEO Graham Fleming said in a statement. “We have already taken steps to improve margins.”

During the company’s earnings call, Fleming said the company remains focused on production growth, operational efficiency and cash generation, and explained that margins compressed after the Federal Reserve shifted from cutting to raising interest rates.

“We have already made the necessary changes to product pricing, and we expect margins to return to historical levels in the first half of 2027,” Fleming told investors.

“Finance of America has grown volumes on average by 20% each year since 2023. The third quarter was a challenging rate environment, with the 10-year Treasury yields increasing over 75 basis points during the quarter, a reaction to the Fed’s pivot to raising rates and elevated inflation,” he added.

FOA’s retirement solutions segment, which originates home equity-based financing products, including reverse mortgages, recorded $748 million in funded volume during the quarter, up 24% year over year.

“Our retirement solutions revenue margin was impacted in the third quarter, decreasing to 9%, compared with 11.3% in the third quarter of 2025, and a historical average since the start of 2024 of 10.7%,” Fleming said during the call. “We believe these impacts are temporary and do not change the underlying fundamentals of our business.”

Revenue for the segment totaled $67 million, down 1% from the prior-year period and a decrease from Q2 2026‘s $74 million. Pretax income fell to $3 million, down from $10 million a year earlier, while adjusted net income declined to $9 million, down from $20 million.

The company attributed the decline in profitability primarily to pressure on origination margins as benchmark interest rates increased during the quarter. It said it implemented product and pricing adjustments to address the impact and expects margins to return to historical levels.

For the first nine months of 2026, the retirement solutions segment generated $2.07 billion in funded volume, up 17% year over year. Revenue increased 14% to $208 million.

“Since 2023, our submission volumes have increased by 21% annually, while our funded volume has grown by 20% annually. This is across our product suite, as HECM volume is up 14% year over year, HomeSafe first liens are up 15%, and HomeSafe seconds are up 63%,” FOA President Kristen Sieffert said during the call.

FOA’s portfolio management segment, which generates revenue through net interest income and fair value changes on portfolio assets, reported a pretax loss of $138 million, compared with an $11 million loss in the third quarter of 2025.

The company attributed the loss primarily to negative non-cash fair value adjustments on retained interests in securitizations. Portfolio management reported adjusted net income of $11 million, down from $30 million a year earlier.

Assets under management in the segment increased 23% year over year to $37.4 billion. The growth reflected new originations and the acquisition of Onity Mortgage Corp.‘s HECM servicing portfolio on July 1.

For the first nine months of 2026, portfolio management recorded a pretax loss of $128 million, compared with pretax income of $202 million in the same period last year. Adjusted net income totaled $57 million, down from $66 million.

FOA ended the third quarter with $118 million in cash and cash equivalents, up from $85 million at the end of June. The company attributed the increase to cash generation from originations and capital markets activity.

Total equity stood at $307 million as of Sept. 30, including $259 million attributable to common stock. Book value was $28.08 per common share.

The company said it expects to complete a $60 million paydown of senior secured notes in November. Looking ahead to the final quarter of 2026, chief financial officer Matt Engel said the company expects funded volume to reach $3.1 billion to $3.4 billion, a range “supported by consumer demographics, our product breadth, and ongoing conversion improvements.”

#5575. 5 snowy North American ski areas, from Alyeska to Little Cottonwood Canyon

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A regional snowfall roundup points to Alaska, British Columbia, Washington state, Utah, and California for deep powder.

Skiers start watching the forecast before the lifts begin turning, waiting for the first storm of the season to reset the mountains. A fresh powder day tops the wish list for many skiers, the sport's closest thing to a sacred prize. Snow decides whether a trip delivers soft, untracked turns or days on thin, worn cover, and no amount of planning can conjure it where the sky withholds it. Anyone picking a mountain for a vacation, a season pass, or a weekend drive has a stake in knowing where the flakes pile highest. The choice of destination sets the odds before anyone boards a chairlift.

Geography governs where those rare mornings arrive. Western North America collects the heaviest average totals on the continent. Still, conditions shift from one year to the next, and a resort that buries its slopes in one can run lean in the following. Two kinds of numbers capture the pattern. A long-run average shows what a visitor can expect in a typical year, while a one-year total reveals how high a peak can climb when the weather cooperates. Both matter to a traveler weighing where to spend money and time off. A resort with a strong average offers dependability. A resort with a towering record year marks the ceiling of what its terrain can hold. Together, the two figures sketch how much natural snowpack a place tends to supply and how wide its swings can grow.

OnTheSnow assembled a region-by-region tour of North American snowfall, moving from Alaska through Canada and the western U.S. before turning to the Midwest and the East. The roundup pairs historical annual means with standout single-winter accumulations, and it reports most values in inches, many of them as approximations or ranges. The piece offers no numbered ranking. It leaves out who took the measurements, which winters the means cover, and how anyone calculated them. The five entries below form a selection from that tour. Each one illustrates a separate way a region earns its standing in the hunt for new snow. Treat them as a field guide to reliable territory, and remember that any one winter can stray from the norm by a broad margin.

Alyeska collects around 670 inches of snow in a typical year, the heaviest average of any ski area in North America. The resort sits in Girdwood, 40 miles from Anchorage. The short distance turns the deepest snowfall on the continent into a day trip for Anchorage residents.

Alyeska's totals have climbed as high as 848 inches, a peak that outstrips its usual haul by a wide margin. The resort topped 700 inches during the 2023-24 ski season, a total the guide cautions Alyeska does not reach every year. Even that banner winter landed closer to the average than to the high-water mark. The top figure shows how far one exceptional season can stretch beyond a baseline that beats every other ski area on the continent. A visitor who plans around the norm stands on firmer ground than one chasing the peak.

Skiers who want natural snow they can count on, and plenty of it, should book a trip to Alyeska, the guide advises. The roundup delivers that advice alongside its caution about 700-inch years. The warning and the recommendation sit together without contradiction. The guide's endorsement leans on the long-run average. One quiet season does little to dent it. Other resorts may match Alyeska in a single big year, yet the guide reserves its promise of reliable snowfall for this one.

Alyeska offers 1,600 skiable acres, terrain the tour describes as rich in steep pitches and deep powder. Girdwood opens the way into Alaska's Chugach Mountains, which hold more than 700,000 acres of backcountry skiing. The lift-served ground forms a sliver of the wild country within reach of town. Skiers who outgrow the marked runs have a vast playground waiting in the surrounding peaks beyond the resort boundary. Girdwood functions as a base camp for an entire range, with Alyeska serving as its front door.

British Columbia owns Canada's single-season snowfall record, set when Revelstoke buried its slopes under 80 feet during the 1971-1972 ski season. The province's ordinary winters help explain how a mark of that size could form. Its snowiest resorts pile up hundreds of inches in a typical year. A heavy winter there builds on a high floor.

Revelstoke's normal season brings 400-500 inches. Converted to feet, the upper end of that range sits far below the 80 recorded in 1971-1972. A skier who books an average winter here meets a deep base. The record year marks how far past its usual haul the mountain can climb.

Whistler Blackcomb gathers 465 inches in an average season, a figure inside Revelstoke's range. Two of the province's resorts draw on similar supplies of powder. Snow totals give a visitor little reason to pick one over the other. Other priorities can settle the choice.

Revelstoke holds the record even though its range overlaps Whistler Blackcomb's figure. A national mark can emerge from one exceptional winter at a resort whose usual totals match its neighbor's. The 1971-1972 season shows British Columbia's ceiling towering over its norm.

The SkiBig3 resorts in Alberta receive about half the snow that British Columbia's snowiest mountains collect. The drop happens across a single provincial border. A skier who heads east trades the province's deepest terrain for a thinner supply. The province a skier picks shapes the snow outlook as much as the resort does.

Mt. Baker in Washington state piled up 1,140 inches of snow during the 1998-99 season, a world record for a single winter. The haul converts to 95 feet, and no ski area on the planet has matched it in one season. The total outstrips every annual average the roundup lists, including that of the continent's snowiest ski area.

Mt. Baker's summit tops out at 5,089 feet, a modest height for the holder of a global snowfall title. The peak stands less than a mile high, yet no taller mountain on Earth has topped its single-winter accumulation. The roundup cites that elevation as evidence that a mountain can amass enormous totals without soaring into the clouds. Altitude, by this measure, offers a weak forecast of how much snow a peak will catch. Skiers who equate tall summits with deep powder would overlook the place that set the mark.

Ocean air supplies what elevation does not. Moist currents drifting in from the Pacific run into the Cascade Range, which shoves them upward. The forced climb wrings heavy precipitation from the clouds over the Cascade Mountains of Washington state. Terrain in that path needs no great stature to gather a staggering load of snow. Its supply arrives from the sea.

Crystal Mountain and Stevens Pass in Washington state, along with Mt. Bachelor and Timberline in Oregon, each average well over 400 inches a season. Four separate resorts clearing that mark show the region's snowfall does not hinge on a single outlier. The depth spans two states and hands a powder hunter several targets in one stretch of the map. Mt. Baker's 1998-99 winter, set beside those neighbors, shows how far one season can overshoot a generous norm. A traveler who misses a banner year at one resort still lands in a corridor where deep seasonal averages are the rule.

Alta averages 548 inches of snow a season, and Snowbird, its next-door neighbor, takes in more than 500. Both figures describe a typical winter, before any record storms enter the picture. The two areas turn a single Utah canyon into a dependable source of deep powder.

The 2022-23 winter blew past those norms. Alta closed the season at 903 inches, and Snowbird broke its all-time record with 838. Several Utah resorts set new highs that year. The surge reached beyond one canyon, which points to heavy snowfall across much of the state.

Park City Mountain Resort and Deer Valley, both in Summit County, see 300-350 inches a year. Their totals trail Little Cottonwood Canyon by about 200 inches. The Summit County resorts sit about 1,500 feet lower, and that altitude difference accounts for part of the shortfall. A skier weighing Utah options can expect more snow by trading Summit County for the higher ground of Little Cottonwood Canyon.

Brighton and Solitude, two nearby Utah resorts, each receive about 500 inches a year. Both land close to the canyon's marks, putting four mountains at similar totals. Utah has long claimed the greatest snow on Earth, and a cluster of resorts near 500 inches gives that boast real weight.

Avalanche paths cross the most direct stretch of road between Snowbird and Alta and close the route more often than ice or collisions do. One slide broke loose from Mount Superior, crossed the canyon road, and reached Snowbird's Chickadee trail while skiers and snowboarders were on it. Ski patrol later declared that the slide had buried no one.

An interlodge at Alta confines everyone in an affected area to a permanent building, and no one may step outdoors until the order lifts. A day in Little Cottonwood Canyon can hinge on whether the road and the doors stay open.

Mammoth Mountain finished the 2022-23 season with close to 900 inches of snowfall at its summit, more than twice the 400 inches the resort gets in a typical winter. At the Main Lodge, the base tally reached 700 inches. Even the lower reading dwarfed the resort's usual total.

Only the summit measurement cleared the doubling mark. The base fell short of it, though 700 inches pushed the lodge area past its normal output by a wide margin. Skiers who stayed on lower runs saw a year beyond the norm, and those who rode to the top found a thicker pack.

Palisades Tahoe traced the same arc that year. The resort shares Mammoth's 400-inch baseline, and it topped 700 inches during 2022-23. Two California mountains that start from identical yearly expectations both cleared that mark in one season. The parallel totals suggest the storms behind them spread across more than a single corner of the state.

Sugar Bowl, a neighbor of Palisades Tahoe, collects 450 to 500 inches in an ordinary year. Even the low end of that range beats what Mammoth or Palisades Tahoe can expect from a standard winter. A traveler picking a California mountain by typical totals alone would lean toward Sugar Bowl.

Mammoth's Main Lodge and Palisades Tahoe each closed 2022-23 above the top of Sugar Bowl's yearly range. The two resorts with the smaller baseline posted figures that outstripped the best a normal year brings to their snowier neighbor. Mammoth's summit reading opened a wider lead over that benchmark.

Sugar Bowl's bigger yearly expectation makes it the stronger pick on paper for an average winter. Mammoth and Palisades Tahoe demonstrated in 2022-23 that a lower norm caps nothing once a heavy year rolls in. A smaller average sets a lower floor for an ordinary trip, and Mammoth's summit showed how little it limits the ceiling.

#5573. Groundcover turns its Wand acquisition into a Kubernetes rightsizing beta

Observability company groundcover Inc. today added Autonomous Infrastructure to its platform in beta to rightsize the processor and memory requests automatically on customers’ Kubernetes workloads based on how each workload behaves in production.

The technology comes from Kubernetes resource optimization startup Wand Cloud Ltd., which groundcover acquired in September.

The release is aimed at the processor and memory requests Kubernetes has engineers set for each workload up front, usually before it has handled any real traffic, and groundcover said most teams seldom return to those numbers. When one is set too low, the first sign is often a service throwing out-of-memory errors. Padding that goes unused ends up on the monthly cloud bill.

Because the groundcover sensor has been collecting production history all along, a customer on a supported version can open Autonomous Infrastructure for the first time without installing anything and find the data the feature needs already in place. Requested processor and memory for each workload appear next to actual usage. Estimated monthly savings sit beside a count of under-provisioned workloads, and a chart tracks over time how much of the potential saving has been realized.

Dollar figures in the beta are based on a price per processor and memory unit that customers enter themselves. Public cloud pricing is the next step, according to groundcover, and billing data such as the Cost and Usage Report from Amazon Web Services Inc. will come after that.

Most resource optimization tools size each workload in isolation, groundcover argues, so a request that looks right for one service can still starve its neighbors on a crowded node. Stability is the first constraint in groundcover’s own software. Before Autonomous Infrastructure raises a request, it checks how tightly the node is already packed so one workload’s increase does not leave the rest short of resources.

Shahar Azulay, groundcover’s co-founder and chief executive, said customers can check what their clusters stand to save, from data already held in their own cloud accounts, before they let Autonomous Infrastructure “change anything.” The feature stays off until an engineer turns it on and picks the deployments, namespaces or clusters it manages.

During the beta the software touches requests only and leaves limits where they are. Each policy carries minimum and maximum bounds for processor and memory, and an audit log records who assigned each workload to a policy and when. Groundcover suggests starting with lower-risk workloads such as development namespaces and leaving alone something like a production database that needs room to grow.

The beta is available now at no additional cost to every groundcover customer running its sensor on Kubernetes, and the company is also recruiting design partners to work with its product team while it runs. Demonstrations are scheduled for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City Nov. 9-12.

Groundcover is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised $160 million to date, including a $100 million Series C round led by One Peak in July.

#5572. 7 things to know about burnout, from symptoms to depression

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A psychologist explains in a Cleveland Clinic guide how burnout shows up in body and mood, how it differs from depression, and how to recover.

Plenty of people push through a heavy stretch at work and assume the drag they feel will lift after a good weekend. Psychologist Adam Borland, PsyD, offers an analogy for why the pattern escapes notice. Someone used to going 100 miles an hour who lifts a foot off the gas still moves at 85, yet that driver may feel the slower pace falls short because 100 has become normal. Those who like to stay busy can miss the moment they take on too much. Borland says many people overlook burnout at the start and recognize a serious problem only after it has set in. People tend to connect burnout with their jobs, yet it can grow out of many corners of life, seep into the rest, and take a toll on the body.

Long stretches of stress with too little room for recovery are a frequent driver of burnout. Four factors raise the risk: working long hours or being "on" around the clock, struggling to set or hold boundaries, carrying high personal expectations or perfectionism, and juggling ongoing life pressures on top of career demands. Borland says technology plays a major part in modern employment and makes limits harder to defend. A common expectation holds that employees stay reachable at any hour. Professional models describe anywhere from three to 12 stages, and Borland says they share one premise: burnout builds step by step instead of striking all at once. One 12-stage version carries the names Freudenberger and North. Many of today's mental health providers use a condensed sequence of five: the honeymoon phase, the onset of stress, chronic stress, burnout, and habitual burnout.

Cleveland Clinic published its patient-education guide to burnout on Jan. 27, 2026, with input from Borland. The piece explains what burnout is, who faces greater exposure, how it progresses, and what helps people recover. The guide offers explanation and advice and contains no survey, sample, data table, or ranking. It borrows its definition from the American Psychological Association's Dictionary of Psychology, which describes burnout as exhaustion of the body, the emotions, or the mind, arriving alongside weaker motivation, slipping performance, and a sour outlook on oneself and other people. The guide makes clear that burnout is not a medical condition and can resist easy description. Borland maintains that people can recognize burnout and take steps to climb out of it. The article names six common signs, and the list below covers each of them along with the ways burnout differs from depression.

Fatigue sits at the heart of burnout, and Cleveland Clinic calls exhaustion a key symptom. A person caught in burnout may feel a pull toward sleep at every hour of the day. Simple tasks drag on longer than they should. The drain surfaces in the most ordinary parts of a routine.

Duration separates garden-variety tiredness from burnout. Everyday fatigue brings a sense of being tired, lower energy, and a broad dip in attention and clear thinking, and it tends to fade within hours or weeks. The depletion tied to burnout runs deeper than common low energy. It counts as chronic, meaning it keeps coming back or never lifts.

Early weariness can look harmless. In the opening phase of burnout, a person feels driven and capable, may take pride in a packed schedule, and sees no cause for concern in being worn down. Occasional bouts of exhaustion and trouble concentrating surface as demands mount, yet the person keeps pushing.

The slide from a hard stretch into something worse can escape notice. Cleveland Clinic says a person may not recognize burnout until they have crossed from feeling run-down to being too spent to function. Rest does less good as stress hardens into a constant presence, and the figurative tank grows harder to refill. Burnout itself brings pronounced physical and emotional fatigue, and daily tasks can start to feel overwhelming.

Cleveland Clinic's first recovery step for burnout as a whole is to build breaks into the day. The practice means checking in with yourself throughout each day to notice overload and head it off. Borland boils the habit down to two questions. "Take a step back and ask: 'How am I doing emotionally? What about physically?'" he says. Tracking how long the fatigue lasts, and whether sleep and downtime relieve it, offers a practical way to tell a rough week from burnout.

Burnout converts the passing reluctance to start a workday into apathy and dissatisfaction that refuse to lift. Everyone has mornings when the job holds no appeal, and those scattered days count as part of ordinary working life. The difference with burnout lies in staying power. One flat afternoon says little, but the same indifference returning day after day signals a deeper problem.

Psychologist Adam Borland captures the questions that tend to surface once the feeling lingers. "You may feel like, 'What's the point? Is my work making a difference? Do I even enjoy what I'm doing, or am I just going through the motions?'" he says. Each question probes a separate layer. The first doubts purpose, the second doubts impact, and the third doubts whether any enjoyment survives the routine. Someone asking all three is weighing the worth of the job itself, beyond its daily tasks.

The World Health Organization counts mental distance from work among three defining dimensions of burnout, according to Gallup. The dimension covers cynicism toward a job and a growing negativity about employment in general. Workers caught in that state can turn skeptical or numb toward their roles and lose the drive and meaning they once drew from them. Managers may spot the shift when an employee withdraws from colleagues and loses interest in projects that used to matter.

Collapsing motivation marks the fourth step in the condensed sequence many providers use, the one labeled burnout itself, alongside pronounced exhaustion and everyday tasks that start to overwhelm. Left unaddressed, burnout hardens into a fifth stage in which detachment and exhaustion begin to feel normal. Escaping it at that point demands deliberate changes to routines and boundaries.

Lost drive runs through both of those final phases, which turns the misgivings Borland describes into more than passing gripes. Spotting them before indifference becomes habit leaves room for small, intentional adjustments to restore balance while burnout remains reversible.

Irritability and a persistent sense of being on edge become more likely once burnout takes hold, according to Cleveland Clinic's guidance. The fallout reaches past the individual. Burnout changes how a person feels, and that altered state can reshape how the same person treats the people nearby, from colleagues at work to family at home.

Small stressors carry outsized weight in this state. A minor annoyance can set off frustration, and in some cases an angry outburst. The reaction outgrows its trigger, and those on the other side of the exchange bear the excess.

Mood sits inside a wider pattern of damage. Burnout looks different in everyone, and its effects can turn serious on physical, mental, and emotional fronts. During the chronic stress stage, ongoing pressure wears on mood along with energy, sleep, and general well-being, and rest does less to refill the tank. Left unaddressed, burnout can settle into a habitual phase in which exhaustion and detachment start to feel normal. A short fuse that lingers that long risks passing for personality instead of a symptom.

Mindfulness offers one avenue among the seven recovery steps the article outlines for burnout as a whole. Deep breathing and meditation help keep attention fixed on the here and now, and Borland describes the goal as staying as present as possible with one's inner state. The article presents this step as general advice and does not match it to irritability or to any other single sign.

The article treats self-care as a key way to stay well enough to meet daily obligations, and supporting others sits among those obligations. In that framing, putting yourself first involves no selfishness. Applied to mood, the point carries an extra payoff. Someone who guards their own health also shields the coworkers, relatives, and friends who might absorb the brunt of a short temper.

Burnout can unsettle two of the body's most basic rhythms, pushing appetite up or down and knocking sleep off its normal length and schedule. Cleveland Clinic counts these shifts among the common signs of burnout, and they cut in both directions. One person starts eating more, and another loses interest in food. Some people slip away from the regular meals that once structured their day.

Stress can reshape hunger on several fronts, altering appetite, portion size, and the kinds of food a person reaches for, according to the American Psychiatric Association. Sudden, short-lived pressure tends to dull hunger as the body turns its attention to an immediate threat in fight-or-flight mode. Pressure that lingers can do the reverse. Stress hormones that stay high can fuel steady cravings for energy-dense foods loaded with sugar and fat. Some people under prolonged stress move the other way and eat less as their appetite fades. Drawn-out strain may also feed depression, a condition often tied to a smaller appetite.

Women tend to answer stress by eating, research indicates, while men more often turn to alcohol or cigarettes. A change at the dinner table may reveal strain in some people and leave little trace in others.

Sleep loses its footing too, running longer or shorter than a person's usual span or sliding to odd hours of the day or night. Cleveland Clinic's account of the chronic stress phase describes ongoing strain wearing on sleep, energy, and mood. Rest brings back less in that phase, and refilling the figurative tank grows harder. Extra hours in bed, then, offer no proof of recovery.

Cleveland Clinic's general recovery advice calls for a daily routine with set times for sleeping, eating, and seeing family and friends. The organization presents that schedule as a way to protect work/life boundaries and does not tie it to this sign. The routine still governs the same two habits this sign disrupts. A fixed bedtime and steady mealtimes give a person a baseline, and any swing in appetite or sleep stands out against it.

Tension headaches are common in burnout, according to Cleveland Clinic, and they tend to strike once long-term stress has begun to disrupt sleep and tighten muscles. The pain has a recognizable shape. People feel it as pressure spreading across the forehead and temples.

Two separate strains feed this headache, and burnout supplies both of them. Broken sleep is one. Muscles held tight by unrelenting demands are the other. Neither cause belongs to a single bad afternoon. Cleveland Clinic ties the headache to strain that drags on, which places it among the signs that build over time instead of appearing overnight.

Poor sleep shows up among the triggers NIH News in Health lists for tension-type headaches, along with too little fluid in the body and slouching or other bad posture. The outlet describes the pain as mild to moderate and notes that it can strike both sides of the head. Some people develop a chronic version, with headaches that recur and linger for hours, for days, or without letup. Dehydration and posture can produce the same ache with no burnout involved. A tension headache on its own has several possible explanations, and burnout becomes a stronger candidate once the headaches arrive alongside lost sleep and a long stretch of pressure.

Disrupted sleep is a hallmark of chronic stress, the stage in which ongoing strain wears on mood, energy, sleep, and overall well-being. Rest stops refilling the tank the way it once did. A headache rooted in lost sleep fits that picture. The rest that might relieve it no longer does much good.

Exercise appears among the seven recovery steps Cleveland Clinic offers for burnout in general, and the organization credits movement with lifting mood and improving sleep. The bar sits low. A gym membership counts, and so do a walk over lunch and a round of jumping jacks at the office. Small efforts add up, in Cleveland Clinic's view. Its guidance does not prescribe exercise as a headache remedy. Sleep links the cause Cleveland Clinic names for this sign to the benefit it assigns to exercise, which makes rest the place where this symptom and the wider recovery meet.

Back pain and gastrointestinal trouble, stretching from constipation at one end to diarrhea at the other, complete the bodily toll Cleveland Clinic attaches to burnout. The guide asserts that burnout can cause both complaints. The pair sits inside a broader warning in the piece that burnout can damage physical health and leave serious mental and emotional marks as well.

Muscle tension offers one route from prolonged strain to a sore back. Tightness that stress builds in the muscles can set off jaw pain along with aches in the back and shoulders. A stiff back carries no label naming its cause. Someone in the middle of a demanding stretch could write it off as an ordinary ache before connecting it to work.

Digestive complaints cover the full span of the bowel's range. Pressure can bring on stomach pain, bloating, and nausea, along with diarrhea or constipation. Under strain, the stomach and small intestine slow their movement while the large bowel speeds up, which in some cases sends a person rushing to the toilet. Opposite reactions in separate sections of the digestive tract help explain how a single stressor can push digestion in either direction.

Burnout surfaces differently from one person to the next, according to Cleveland Clinic. One worker might feel it as an aching back, while another registers it in the gut. The guide's seven recovery steps target burnout as a whole, and none pairs with a particular symptom. Firmer work/life boundaries appear among those steps. Job burnout runs so wide, the piece says, because people find it hard to say no. Borland adds that many struggle to set the limits that let them manage both personal life and career demands.

Unaddressed burnout can settle into what the guide calls habitual burnout, a stage in which symptoms such as exhaustion and detachment start to feel normal. Escaping that stage, the guide says, takes deliberate changes to routines and boundaries. A backache or unsettled stomach that keeps returning through a long run of heavy demands may point to the workload behind it before it fades into the background.

Burnout tends to grow out of one identifiable setting, such as a job, while depression can surface with no obvious trigger. The two remain separate conditions, yet they can resemble each other, and at times both strike the same person. The overlap makes the distinction easy to miss. Someone running on empty might blame every heavy morning on the office and never ask whether something deeper lies beneath.

Time away from the source of strain exposes a key difference between the two conditions. Stepping back from the situation behind burnout often brings relief, according to the Cleveland Clinic article. Depression is less likely to lift that way. The guide illustrates the contrast with a vacation. A person with burnout who escapes its cause can unwind and enjoy the trip. A person with depression most likely cannot. The depressive symptoms come along for the journey.

A getaway that fails to recharge someone carries a signal of its own. Ease that stays out of reach far from work points to a problem the person brings along. Depression matches that pattern in the piece's account. Its symptoms follow people wherever they go. The two can also coexist, so a pleasant break cannot rule out depression hiding under the burnout.

Seeing a therapist can serve as a good first step toward tackling burnout and learning coping strategies, according to Cleveland Clinic. Borland describes the therapist's focus as refilling the tank. He adds that a safe place to talk can change a person's life. The tank image echoes the article's portrait of chronic stress, a stage in which downtime restores less and refueling grows harder.

Putting yourself first is a key way to stay well enough to handle every obligation, including support for other people, in Cleveland Clinic's view. The guidance rejects the idea that such self-care is selfish. Burnout is common during long periods of pressure, and the piece says a person can reverse it. A condition rooted in one environment gives a person a specific place to start making changes, an opening depression's less obvious origins may not provide.

#5570. Microsoft earnings preview: Employee buyouts, AI spending and a new financial scorecard

by Todd Bishop on Oct 27, 2026 at 10:50 amOctober 28, 2026 at 3:02 pm

Update, 10/28: Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations. Read the full story.

Microsoft’s earnings report Wednesday will come two days after the company offered buyouts to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its employees. The call gives executives their first chance to say what the offer will cost, and to explain how it fits with the company’s long-term view of its workforce.

Whether or not they go into those details, it’s one of several issues to watch in Wednesday’s report, the first under Microsoft’s new reporting structure. Anthropic’s IPO filing on Monday adds another storyline, showing how much the Claude maker has agreed to spend on Microsoft’s cloud.

Coming into the report, Microsoft’s stock is near its high. Microsoft closed Monday at $532.60, about 2% below its record close of $543.45 on Oct. 13, after gaining roughly $1.4 trillion in market value since late June.

Here are the key numbers and issues heading into Microsoft’s results for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, ended Sept. 30.

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of $90.75 billion, up nearly 17% from a year ago, and earnings of $4.72 per share, up 14%, according to Yahoo Finance. Microsoft’s own forecast was $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion, so Wall Street is looking for a result near the top of that range.

In July, Microsoft reported $90 billion in revenue for the June quarter, well above the $87.7 billion analysts expected.

A new scorecard: Microsoft announced in September that it would sort its business into two groups instead of the three it had used since 2015. This is the first quarter under the new setup.

The first, dubbed Agents and Infra, includes Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics, LinkedIn’s recruiting and sales tools, and server and productivity licensing. It brought in 81% of Microsoft’s revenue and 88% of its operating income in fiscal 2026, based on figures Microsoft recast under the new structure.

Microsoft expects Agents and Infra revenue of $75.15 billion to $75.75 billion this quarter, which would be growth of about 22% to 23%, by GeekWire’s calculation.

The other group, Devices and Consumer, includes Windows, Xbox and search advertising. Microsoft expects it to bring in $14.7 billion to $15.2 billion, down 5% to 8% from a year earlier.

Azure, in dollars: Microsoft started disclosing Azure’s annual revenue last year, when it passed $75 billion, and topped $100 billion in fiscal 2026. Starting this quarter, it reports the figure every quarter. It also changed what counts as Azure: GitHub’s cloud business and Security Copilot now fall under Microsoft 365, and its healthcare cloud moved to a new industry unit.

Counted that way, Azure brought in $29.4 billion in the June quarter, up 42%. Microsoft expects growth of 44% to 45% this quarter, not counting currency fluctuations, which would put Azure at roughly $32 billion, by GeekWire’s calculation. That compares with the roughly 45% Microsoft projected in July, under the old definition.

Hitting that forecast may not be enough. Investors are looking for about 46%, BNP Paribas analyst Stefan Slowinski wrote in a note Monday. In January, Azure beat Microsoft’s own forecast and the stock still fell 10%, because investors had privately expected more.

“Azure moves the stock, but the read that matters is whether capacity is absorbed as fast as it lands,” wrote Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives in a note last week.

Capital spending: Microsoft expects capital expenditures of more than $50 billion for the quarter, which would be a record. That’s up from $41 billion in the June quarter and $34.9 billion a year earlier.

An accounting change reduces what Microsoft reports as capital spending, without reducing its planned investment. Microsoft now assumes its data center buildings will last 25 years instead of 15. As a result, more of its data center leases will be classified in a way that doesn’t count as capital spending, CFO Amy Hood said on the July earnings call.

That change alone lowered Microsoft’s capital spending estimate for calendar 2026 to about $175 billion, from the roughly $190 billion it projected in April. Hood said the company’s actual spending plans hadn’t changed.

Cloud margins: Microsoft Cloud gross margin came in at 65% last quarter, better than expected but down from a year earlier. Microsoft said it expects the figure to be relatively stable this quarter. It also expects operating margins to be roughly flat with a year ago.

Workforce: The new “voluntary exit” offer, announced Monday by Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, covers participating teams in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. It has no age or tenure requirement and extends to some vice presidents. Employees have until the first week of December to decide, and Microsoft hasn’t said how much the offer will cost or when it will record the charge.

For the spring retirement program, Hood disclosed the cost on the April earnings call: about $900 million, with roughly $350 million in cost of revenue and $550 million in operating expenses. The charge showed up in the following quarter. About 30% of the 8,750 eligible employees accepted.

The new offer is less generous. It matches Microsoft’s standard severance, without the extended healthcare of the spring program, and the company expects a much smaller share of people to take it. But the pool of eligible employees is nearly seven times larger.

Microsoft says the offer doesn’t mean it needs fewer people. Coleman said in July that the company was studying whether to make voluntary exits a regular part of managing its workforce. It has told investors to expect operating margins roughly flat this quarter and down less than a point for the full fiscal year, even with record capital spending.

Nadella has addressed this before. In a July 2025 memo to employees, after Microsoft laid off about 15,000 people, he acknowledged the “uncertainty and seeming incongruence” of thriving financially while cutting jobs. “This is the enigma of success in an industry that has no franchise value,” he wrote.

In his annual shareholder letter last week, he focused on Microsoft’s spending on AI infrastructure. “Based on the demand we see and the efficiencies we are driving, I am confident in the long-term returns on our investments,” Nadella wrote. “We are building against a growing book of business tied to this secular shift.”

Microsoft had about 223,000 employees as of June 30, before it cut 4,800 jobs in July and more in September. The Information reported this month that Azure President Girish Bablani told leaders in his group to find ways to cut costs by at least 20%. Microsoft called the report inaccurate and said Azure leadership had not directed teams to develop cost-cutting plans.

Copilot: Microsoft said in July that businesses were paying for more than 30 million Microsoft 365 Copilot seats, up from 20 million in April. That’s still only about 7% of the more than 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats.

The bigger change is in how Microsoft charges for Copilot and its other AI tools. In July it added usage-based billing alongside per-seat pricing. It’s also pushing customers toward E7, a new premium bundle that includes Copilot. Microsoft expects Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue to grow about 17% this quarter, not counting currency swings, a number that now includes GitHub.

The BNP Paribas analyst Slowinski, who attended Microsoft’s Frontier Tour event in London last week, wrote that partners are seeing more customers roll out Copilot company-wide. Partners also told him that Microsoft now ties 35% of E7 sales incentives to how much customers use features like Cowork.

Anthropic and OpenAI: Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows the company has committed to spend at least $44.9 billion with Microsoft from November 2026 to May 2033, up from the $30 billion Azure commitment announced last November. That’s well below its minimum commitments to Amazon ($110 billion) and Google ($114.5 billion).

Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic. Its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment.

OpenAI remains the bigger factor. Microsoft’s commercial remaining performance obligation (RPO), the measure of signed contracts it hasn’t yet delivered on, reached $678 billion last quarter, up 84% from a year earlier. Without OpenAI, the backlog grew 25%. OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue approached $50 billion at the end of September, The Information reported, lower than earlier reports of about $70 billion.

Windows: Microsoft expects revenue from Windows licenses sold to PC makers, along with its own devices, to fall a little more than 20%. Higher memory prices are making PCs more expensive, and PC makers are still working through extra inventory.

What’s next: Alphabet also reports Wednesday afternoon, and Amazon reports Thursday, setting up a side-by-side look at Azure, Google Cloud and AWS.

Anthropic is aiming to go public the week of Nov. 16, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Check back Wednesday afternoon for coverage.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.
