#5569. 10 things to know about medication recalls before you stop a pill, per AARP

Free daily briefing on global business news.

AARP's guide explains how to tell whether a recalled drug or supplement is yours and which steps to take before you stop it.

A news alert names a pill you swallow every morning, and the bottle on the bathroom shelf turns into a question mark. Plenty of people will face some version of this moment. A 2026 KFF poll found that about two-thirds of U.S. adults take at least one prescription drug, and nearly a third take four or more. Among people 65 and older, 6 in 10 take four or more medications, a tally that leaves out vitamins, minerals, and supplements. Every extra bottle in the cabinet adds another chance that a recall will name something you own. Older adults, who juggle the longest lists, face greater odds of landing in that situation.

A headline can name a drug without revealing whether the package in your hand came from an affected batch. The urge to act pulls in two directions. Some people toss the package on the spot. Others shrug and keep taking the medicine. Both reflexes skip the essential move of matching the bulletin against what you have at home. Quitting a needed treatment without advice carries its own risks, and brushing off a serious warning can keep a hazardous product in daily use. The distance between a broad news item and the fine print on your label imposes costs either way, and closing it requires no pharmacy degree. Confirming whether a recall applies to you takes a few minutes, time that can spare you a hasty decision you might regret.

AARP tackles this dilemma in a consumer guide that Sari Harrar and Aaron Kassraie wrote and Zachary Cox, PharmD, reviewed. The guide draws on expert input, comments an FDA spokesperson gave the publication, an FDA podcast, and statements from the FDA and USP. It explains the agency's three recall classes, a quick home check of whether a notice touches your own supply, and where to find official recall lists. Separate actions for prescriptions, over-the-counter remedies, and supplements follow, along with ways to report a problem and to vet those products before buying. A pair of lists rounds out the guide with recent drug and supplement recalls, current as of its Aug. 14, 2026, update.

A typical drug recall targets particular manufacturers, products, or lot numbers and leaves other versions of a same-named medication untouched. The guide's subtitle puts the point in everyday terms, telling readers that a recall does not always reach their own prescription or supplement. This limited scope reshapes the right response to recall news. A headline describes a family of medicines. A notice describes a narrow slice of one.

Companies pull a medication or supplement from the market when it turns out defective, contaminated, or capable of causing harm. Each of those failures arises in a specific product made by a specific company. Most recalls follow suit, naming the maker and the affected lots and leaving every other version sold under the same name outside their coverage. A contaminated batch from one company says nothing about tablets another firm produced, even when both labels carry the same name.

Two bottles bearing the identical drug name can sit side by side in a medicine cabinet, and a notice may apply to just one of them. A different manufacturer or a different production batch can place a product beyond a recall's boundaries even when the labels match. The name on the bottle opens the inquiry. The maker and the batch close it.

Alexander, one of the experts the guide quotes, warns readers against panic as their first response when a recall surfaces. His caution fits the guide's broader argument. Calm buys time to compare the notice with the package at home, and the details printed on each settle the question. A reader who reacts to the drug name alone can end up abandoning a medication the recall never touched. The same narrow reach works in both directions. A match on maker and lot turns a distant headline into a personal instruction, and the same check that clears one bottle can confirm the need to act on another.

The FDA sorts recalls into three classes according to the danger a product poses, and the class on a notice tells a reader how fast to act. Companies pull a medication or supplement when it proves defective or contaminated or poses a threat to users. The class pinpoints where a given problem falls on that scale.

Class I covers the gravest cases. A product in this tier has a reasonable chance of causing serious harm or death. The guide tells consumers to follow the notice's instructions without delay and to contact a pharmacist or health care provider with any questions.

Class III sits at the other extreme. Products in this group are unlikely to hurt anyone, and the flaw tends to involve a label, the packaging, or an expiration date. The guide advises people to keep using a Class III product unless someone directs them otherwise. A recall in this category can arrive with an alarming headline yet leave a person's daily routine untouched.

Class II fills the middle ground and accounts for most drug recalls, according to the guide. The overall number of recalls has changed little in recent years. The odds favor a Class II label on any new drug alert a reader spots, a designation that places the issue between an urgent hazard and a packaging slip.

Either the manufacturer or the FDA can set a recall in motion. A company may act on its own, and the agency may request one after it decides consumers need protection. Ileana Elder, a branch chief in the Incidents, Recalls, and Shortages Branch within the Office of Compliance at the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, said on an FDA podcast that most recalls are voluntary and start with the company. Her account suggests a typical notice reflects a firm flagging trouble in its own products, with the class telling patients how much that trouble matters.

Most generic medicines in the U.S. supply come out of overseas factories, one expert in the AARP guide warns. The active ingredients inside those drugs originate abroad at a still higher rate, he adds. The FDA makes few inspection visits to those foreign sites, according to the same specialist.

The guide calls the country's drug supply dependable as a whole, and the expert's caution stands beside that verdict without overturning it. His concern targets oversight inside the factories where pills and their raw components take shape.

Distance separates the plants that turn out generics from the agency charged with policing them. Raw materials trace back to offshore facilities at a higher rate than finished tablets do, which pushes the gap further up the production chain. Sparse FDA visits to those plants give the agency fewer chances to spot a flaw where it starts. A generic's dependability, in the expert's telling, rests on manufacturing the FDA observes from far away.

Dietary supplements, unlike prescription and over-the-counter medicines, can reach buyers in most cases without FDA approval. The agency does the bulk of its supervising after a product goes on sale. Its usual trigger for action is a problem that has surfaced. Skipping a premarket review removes the chance for regulators to catch a contaminant before the first bottle ships.

The FDA can act against a contaminated or mislabeled supplement only once buyers can purchase it. A finding that a supplement is unsafe lets the FDA pull it from sale or ask its maker for a voluntary recall. Both tools kick in after someone discovers a defect. By then, a flawed product may sit in shoppers' homes.

The FDA treats supplements as a type of food, and that category determines where their recalls appear. Most supplement notices land on the agency's food and dietary supplement recall page instead of its drug recall page. Someone who searches only the drug list could miss a warning about a capsule or powder sitting in the medicine cabinet.

The food and dietary supplement page collects recent recall announcements for both product types in one place. AARP's own roundup of supplement recalls directs readers to the FDA's dietary supplements page for the newest entries. The agency posts recall notices on its website and lets people sign up for alerts about recalls, market withdrawals, and safety issues. An alert can deliver a supplement notice that a person would never think to seek out on a food page.

Oversight that begins after purchase shifts much of the work of spotting a recall onto the consumer. A capsule stored beside a prescription bottle answers to food rules, and news of its defect travels a separate route. Anyone who takes supplements alongside prescriptions needs to monitor both FDA lists to catch every relevant warning.

A recall notice reaches the medicine in your cabinet only when the manufacturer it names matches the company behind your product. AARP's guide makes this comparison the second stage of its three-part home check. Several firms produce many of the same medications, and a single recall often hits one of those makers and spares the rest.

A shared drug name proves less than it seems to. Two bottles of an identical medication can come from different producers, and an alert aimed at one of them leaves its competitors' versions outside its scope. The guide advises setting the notice beside the package at home and reading the manufacturer listed on each.

Each entry in the guide's lists of recent recalls pairs a product with its manufacturer or distributor, and some name two businesses. A reader comparing labels should hold the package up against every name on the bulletin.

A matching maker narrows the question without settling it, and the step that follows turns to lot numbers. A mismatch, by contrast, shows that a headline about a familiar drug does not touch the product in hand.

A pharmacy that repackages medication into an orange prescription bottle may leave the lot number off the label, erasing the detail that settles many recall checks. Many recalls reach certain lots or batches and no others, so the missing code can strand a reader one step short of an answer. Two bottles of the same drug from the same company can fall on opposite sides of a notice, separated by nothing more than the production run each came from.

The lot comparison comes last in AARP's three-part home check, after the product name and the manufacturer both line up with the notice. Clearing those first two matches narrows the question to one company's version of one drug. The batch code then shows whether the bottle came from the affected run or from one the recall left alone. A notice drawn around specific lots makes this final comparison the deciding one, and a narrower recall leans harder on it.

Mogo Moringa LLC confined its May 25, 2026, recall of moringa capsules to two lots, according to the CDC. The agency identifies them as Lot #15525AA, with a June 2027 expiration, and Lot #00926AA, with a January 2028 expiration. Each code appears beside its own expiration date in the notice. A bottle of the same capsules stamped with any other code sits beyond the recall's reach, even though the brand and product match.

Repackaging severs the procedure at its last link. A bottle can clear the name and maker comparisons and still leave its owner guessing when the pharmacy label lacks the code. A matching name and manufacturer cannot place a product inside a notice on their own, because other lots of the identical item may sit outside it. The gap lands on the reader who has done everything else right, holding a bottle that passes two tests and cannot take the third.

Pharmacy customers should expect an orange bottle to answer two of the home check's three questions. The third rests on whether the pharmacy carried the lot number onto the label. AARP's guide notes that the code tends to appear near the expiration date, which gives readers a place to start looking. Without the code, the bottle in hand can show that a recall might apply but cannot confirm that it does. The guide's answer to a missing number is a phone call to the pharmacy that filled the prescription.

Stopping a recalled prescription without guidance can carry more risk than staying on it until a patient and clinician arrange a replacement, according to the key takeaways in AARP's guide. The advice cuts against a common reflex. A recall notice can feel like an order to empty the bottle at once. The guide treats an unsupervised halt as a hazard in its own right.

AARP applies this caution to many prescription drug recalls and stops short of a blanket rule. The wording leaves room for notices that carry different instructions. A reader holding a recalled drug still has to read the notice itself before changing anything.

Product type determines the next move. Once the drug name, manufacturer, and lot number on a notice match the package at home, the guide splits its advice three ways, covering prescription, over-the-counter, and supplement products. Each category follows its own path.

Prescriptions stand apart in that three-way split. The takeaway names two people, the patient and the clinician, as partners in setting up a replacement. Swapping out a prescribed medicine becomes a joint decision, and the guide's advice favors keeping the current supply in use until the switch takes place.

A confirmed match on a prescription recall calls for a conversation with the prescriber, and in many cases the medicine stays in the daily routine until that conversation produces a replacement.

Possible cross-contamination with ranitidine prompted a July 18, 2026, recall of cetirizine hydrochloride tablets, USP, 5 mg, which Unique Pharmaceutical Laboratories made and Rising Pharma Holdings Inc. distributed. A pharmacy technician caught the problem while counting out tablets to dispense, spotting red dots and discoloration on some of them. The manufacturer reported no adverse events tied to the affected pills.

A potency shortfall sits behind the July 13, 2026, recall of Levothyroxine Sodium Tablets, USP, in strengths from 25 to 150 mcg, from Major Pharmaceuticals and Cardinal Health $CAH. The tablets hold less active ingredient than their labels state. Every other drug recall on the guide's list cites a contaminant, so this entry stands alone as a dosing problem.

Yeast above acceptable microbiological limits pushed Beekeeper's Naturals to recall its saline nasal spray on June 11, 2026. The notice adds that the spray may contain aspergillus. Haleon pulled Gas-X $TWTR Extra Strength Softgels, 125 mg, in 120-count and 72-count packages on June 4, 2026, citing potential chemical contamination. The two notices arrived seven days apart and involve a spray and a softgel, which shows contamination can strike very different product types.

Possible salmonella contamination triggered both moringa recalls on the supplement list. Relay Peak Research LLC (Zen Principle Naturals) recalled Zen Principle moringa leaf powder capsules on July 19, 2026. Total Nutrition Inc. had recalled TNVitamins organic moringa products on June 26, 2026, over the same suspected pathogen. Two separate companies flagged one threat in the same botanical 23 days apart. The CDC told anyone holding recalled moringa leaf products at home to throw them away or return them to the place of purchase. Its guidance extends to washing anything the products may have touched, including surfaces, with hot soapy water or in a dishwasher.

Undeclared mitragynine and other substances led Better Weather Actives LLC to recall its Better Weather Fix elixir on May 28, 2026. Here the defect sits in what the label omits. A buyer scanning the ingredient list would find no mention of mitragynine. The moringa recalls involve a possible contaminant, while this one involves an ingredient the label never disclosed.

Both lists carry a note marking them as the latest at publication, and each points readers to an FDA page for newer entries, the drug recall page for medicines and the dietary supplements page for supplements. People who want notices sent to them can sign up for FDA alerts about recalls, market withdrawals, and safety issues. The dated entries span 69 days, from May 11 to July 19, 2026. Any recall issued after that stretch falls outside a roundup frozen at publication. The FDA pages remain the place to confirm a match.

A medicine or supplement that made you sick, or one with a quality defect, belongs in a report to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting system. The guide frames the trigger around your own experience with a product. A bad reaction or a flawed product qualifies whether or not any recall notice has named the item.

Filing online keeps the whole process on a screen. You complete the report and submit it through the site, with no envelope or fax machine involved. The web form offers one way around paper, and the FDA runs others. Adverse event reports also reach the agency by phone at 1-800-332-1088, according to NCATS. The FDA Safety Reporting Portal gives filers another route.

Paper remains an option for people who skip the web. You can download the form, or call 800-332-1088 and ask for a copy. The finished sheet goes back by regular mail to the address printed on the preaddressed form, or by fax to 800-332-0178. In the guide's telling, the phone line serves to request a blank form, and a caller who takes that path must complete and return the sheet. The preaddressed design spares a filer from hunting down a mailing address.

MedWatch serves as the FDA's program for raising safety concerns about therapies, and it accepts reports from health professionals, patients and families, and consumers. Its online voluntary form spans unexpected adverse effects, quality problems with a therapy, and preventable therapy use or medication errors. The form's categories line up with the guide's two triggers. Adverse effects match a product that made someone sick, and quality problems match a faulty one.

Medication errors widen the net beyond defective products. A preventable mistake in taking or giving a therapy also counts as a reportable event.

Patients and relatives sit on the same intake list as health professionals. The person who notices a reaction at home can bring it to the agency without a go-between. Someone who matches a recalled product to the bottle in the cabinet and suspects it caused harm has a direct channel to tell the FDA.

A third-party certification seal can help a supplement buyer verify what the bottle holds, according to Cohen, one of the experts the AARP guide consults. Most supplements hit the market without the FDA approval that prescription and over-the-counter drugs must earn. The guide calls extra checking before purchase worth the effort, and much of that work lands on the shopper. Buyers who spot a seal gain some assurance that the capsules or powder inside match the ingredient list printed outside.

Cohen draws a firm line around what the seal proves. Certification says nothing about whether a supplement delivers the results its marketing promises. A product can contain every ingredient on its label and fail to produce the benefits its packaging advertises. Shoppers who treat a seal as proof of effectiveness read more into it than it offers.

Labels can stray from what sits inside the bottle. The FDA has turned up prescription drugs in products sold as supplements, among them the anticoagulant warfarin and the anticonvulsant phenytoin. The agency concedes it cannot test every supplement that might carry a harmful hidden ingredient. A maker's own claim that a product is "standardized," "verified," or "certified" can promise quality and consistency without guaranteeing either. The federal Office of Dietary Supplements names ConsumerLab.com, NSF International, and U.S. Pharmacopeia in its discussion of supplement quality, adding that the mention is no endorsement.

FDA oversight picks up where the seal leaves off and centers on products already in circulation. The agency can move against a contaminated or mislabeled supplement after it goes on sale, not before. The FDA can pull an unsafe supplement off store shelves or ask its maker for a voluntary recall. It publishes recall notices on its website, and consumers can sign up for agency alerts about recalls, market withdrawals, and safety issues.

Timing separates the two safeguards. A seal answers the contents question before money changes hands. Alerts flag the hazards that surface later, after a bottle has sat in a kitchen cabinet. A buyer who leans on one of them alone leaves a blind spot on one side of the checkout.

#5568. Tech Moves: Xbox COO’s sudden departure; SeekOut leadership shakeup; Fred Hutch names VP

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 2:08 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 1:05 pm

— Xbox Chief Operating Officer Helen Chiang has suddenly left Microsoft after 21 years with the company, just months after landing the role in July. Her past roles include leading Mojang and the Minecraft franchise.

Verge first reported the news on Friday, citing a memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma that did not disclose the reason for her departure.

An Xbox spokesperson was likewise mum on details. “We don’t discuss individual personnel matters. We’re grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well,” the company said in an email to GeekWire.

In response to speculation around her departure, Chiang offered a LinkedIn post on Nov. 2 refuting rumors that she left because of leaks to the media, to take a role with a competitor, for poor behavior or because she was passed over for a larger role.

“My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind,” Chiang wrote, without providing specifics.

Xbox has undergone a massive reorganization that included Chiang’s appointment, roughly 3,200 job cuts through the fiscal year — about 20% of the Xbox workforce — the spinoff of four game studios and a plan to dramatically flatten management.

— Seattle-based tech leader Philip Su has joined Anthropic as a member of technical staff on beneficial deployments. The management role focuses on AI applications in global health, life sciences, economic mobility and education.

Su started his tech career with 12 years at Microsoft and later worked for Facebook. He has launched multiple ventures, including Audere, a global health software nonprofit, and Superphonic, a podcast player. In 2021, he worked at an Amazon fulfillment center to experience the holiday rush.

Su also created and leads an annual course for University of Washington computer science students on how to maximize their personal and professional growth.

— More leadership changes are underway at SeekOut, a Bellevue-based recruiting startup launched in 2017. The company announced Monday that co-founder John Tippett is now president, moving from his role as chief client officer.

In April, SeekOut CEO and co-founder Anoop Gupta retired and passed the reins to enterprise software veteran Sean Thompson. In August, co-founder and chief technology officer Aravind Bala took over as CEO. Thompson is now listed as an adviser to the board.

Tippett will lead day-to-day operations and work with Bala “on the company’s direction,” according to a press release. SeekOut said it wants to integrate AI tools into customers’ operations to reduce recruiters’ workload.

SeekOut is No. 68 on the GeekWire 200, a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Fred Hutch Cancer Center has appointed Michael (Mick) Merritt as vice president of strategy and partnerships, effective Dec. 7.

Merritt joins from Penn Medicine, where he was chief operating officer of Penn Signature Services. He has more than 25 years of experience in academic medicine, consulting, strategy, business development and operations.

— Industrial wastewater treatment startup Membrion has named Alexander Demihovsky as director of applications engineering. He joins the Seattle-based company from Xylem. His past employers include Evoqua Water Technologies and Bechtel National.

“Alex helps turn customer needs into viable project plans, mitigate execution risks and develop competitive proposals,” the company said.

— Marine geothermal energy startup Endurance Energy has named Marty Calvert as the director of turbomachinery. Calvert joins the Seattle startup from Blue Origin. He was previously a turbomachinery engineer at NASA for more than 13 years.

Endurance completed its fifth deployment to the ocean floor last month, testing Adélie, a 100-kilowatt geothermal generator named for a penguin.

#5567. Snowflake expands agentic AI platform with business context and governance tools

Snowflake Inc. today announced a sweeping collection of artificial intelligence capabilities designed to bring business context, governance and autonomous development into the same environment, as enterprises increasingly hand over software engineering and everyday operations to AI agents.

The announcements, during the company’s Expedition 2026 virtual conference, include a new Business Ontology framework, expanded agent governance through Cortex AI Gateway, and autonomous data engineering capabilities that allow AI agents to build, monitor and troubleshoot data pipelines with less human intervention.

The company is betting that more coders and engineers will use AI throughout the software development lifecycle as creation moves even faster, while other back-end departments begin to adopt agents in their day-to-day work. For example, sales operations are creating agents that can analyze sales risks and prepare customer outreach without writing code.

“AI is industrializing software creation. Actually, it’s industrializing intelligence,” Chief Executive Sridhar Ramaswamy said. “What once took months can now take hours, days, or even minutes.”

Ramaswamy noted that while AI is changing the economics of software development, as agents take over tasks usually relegated to specialized developers, business users become developers. This is changing the competitive landscape, meaning that the advantage no longer goes to specialists, but to proprietary knowledge.

Snowflake is taking the field by helping ordinary AI models understand and contextualize that business knowledge. It does this with Business Ontology, an extension of its existing semantic views that lets organizations establish approved definitions used across the organization. Without a standard definition, two agents could respond to the same business-related question with incompatible answers, even when both agents have accurate underlying data.

Using information from Business Ontology, Snowflake CoCo, the coding agent for data teams, and Snowflake CoWork, the personal work agent for knowledge workers, use these approved business concepts to ground their responses.

This new feature is currently in private preview, but is headed to public preview soon.

Cortex AI Gateway arrives to become a single front door for agents within an organization. It is not entirely new; Snowflake introduced it in July 2026 as a centralized way to govern and monitor agents.

Today’s announcement expands its capabilities rather than introducing the gateway for the first time. The new updates include agent abuse detection, observability and tracing, Cortex sandboxes, AI cost governance, dynamic model routing and tools integration using technology from Snowflake’s Natoma acquisition.

“An agent that acts on your business has to be trusted, and it has to know three important things: what the data means, which data to trust, and what it’s allowed to do,” said Ramaswamy.

The platform most importantly applies existing security mechanisms, including data masking and access restrictions, to agent-driven operations while adding capabilities to monitor activity, detect potential abuse and maintain records of what agents do. The information technology and security teams can also apply cost controls, select models based on efficiency or accuracy and restrict which external tools agents can access granularly.

The underlying role of this governance, control and transparency is aligned with giving agents the same sort of role observation granted to employees. Treating them similarly in terms of autonomy.

Snowflake’s push comes amid a broader industry race to establish the control layer for enterprise AI agents. SAP has been expanding its Autonomous Enterprise architecture and governed Joule agents, while Salesforce has introduced its Enterprise AI Harness and AI Control Plane to secure autonomous workflows. Snowflake is approaching the same problem from the data platform side, seeking to become the foundation through which agents access trusted business information and operate under enterprise policies.

Snowflake also announced the public preview of Cortex Training, which will allow customers to tailor open-weight AI models with their own proprietary information.

The service is designed to make it simpler to create specialized models using post-training without needing vast arrays of graphics processing units. Snowflake lets them train models without managing the underlying infrastructure.

“Specialized, smaller models that come with more efficient responses, faster responses, and frequently cost benefits in terms of tokens,” Executive Vice President of Product Christian Kleinerman said.

Many enterprise companies will require sovereign control of their own AI models as increasing restrictions on foreign open-weight AI or regulations on handling sensitive information. It’s easier to audit what passes through an AI model on your own hardware than in a third-party vendor’s cloud.

Separately, Snowflake announced an expanded partnership with Oracle Corp. to make its platform available as a first-party service on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The integration will give customers easier access to Snowflake’s analytics and AI capabilities while allowing them to work directly through Oracle databases and applications.

#5565. 10 essential desk stretches and movement habits for office workers

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A selection of 10 items from a medically reviewed deskercise routine: chair-based stretches, a breathing cue, and ways to move at work.

Hours into a desk shift, a worker's body can settle into one shape and keep it until the day ends. Nothing about the scene looks dangerous. Construction sites and heavy manufacturing floors may come to mind first, yet they hold no monopoly on work-related health problems. Any industry can produce them, and offices belong on that list. A quiet room with a monitor and a keyboard still makes physical demands on the people who spend their working hours inside it.

Desk jobs tend to fix workers in a single posture while they repeat the same motions for hours. The arrangement may feel uncomfortable, and over long periods it may not serve their health. Those habits can contribute to a long list of problems, from neck and shoulder pain and lower back pain to musculoskeletal disorders, carpal tunnel, stress, and obesity. The response can start small. Moving and stretching function as habits a person can build over time. A timer offers an easy entry point, a nudge to get up for a short walk or a quick stretch. Getting up through the day also helps keep repetitive stress injuries at bay. Workers with crowded schedules can do certain stretches at the desk itself, with no need to leave the chair.

Healthline published its deskercise routine as Day 2 of its 30 Days of Movement Challenge, a program that uses quick, accessible workouts to help readers make fitness a lasting part of their lives. Gregory Minnis, DPT, medically reviewed the guide, which carries an update date of July 1, 2026. The piece offers editorial advice. It scores nothing, ranks nothing, and reports no percentages, participant counts, or study results of its own. Its reference list includes a 2022 systematic review by Tersa-Miralles and colleagues on workplace exercise interventions for musculoskeletal disorders in office workers, along with a 2023 "Editors' Desk" column by Whitsel and colleagues on creating a movement for healthy physical activity at work. The guide sorts its seated stretches by body area, covering the arms, the torso, the legs and knees, and the head and shoulders, then adds breathing tips and ways to move beyond the chair. The 10 items below form a selection from that material and carry no order of merit.

The triceps stretch asks for a hold of 10 to 30 seconds on each arm, and the chair a worker occupies supplies all the equipment it requires. Raise one arm and bend it at the elbow so the hand reaches toward the opposite shoulder. The free hand draws the bent elbow in toward the head. Once the hold ends, switch arms and repeat the full sequence on the other side.

Healthline files the move under its arm stretches, paired with the overhead reach, and the pair comes ahead of the routine's torso moves. The triceps stretch reappears in the guide's key takeaways, on a short roster of moves a person can complete from a seated position. Its presence in both places puts it among the handful of moves the guide singled out for its summary.

The motion divides its labor between two hands. The bend sets the working arm in position, and the tug from the opposite hand supplies the stretch. The pulling hand governs how far the elbow travels toward the head. Healthline's steps stop short of saying where a person should feel the effect. A comparable stretching guide describes pulling the right arm during the bend so the sensation travels from the elbow through the upper arm and upper torso. The same guide then sends the reader to the left arm for a matching round. Both sets of instructions treat the arms as a matched pair that takes turns.

Covering both arms adds 20 to 60 seconds of stretch time per round. The gap between the shortest and longest hold lets a worker scale the effort to the moment, from a brief pause on a crowded day to a fuller hold when the schedule loosens. A round that short slips between tasks at the desk, so the stretch asks little of a working day.

The overhead reach calls for a 10- to 30-second hold, with one arm raised above the head and angled toward the opposite side of the body. The routine files it beside the triceps stretch in the section devoted to the arms, and a worker can finish it without standing up. The two arm moves part ways on one practical point. The triceps stretch recruits the free hand to draw the elbow toward the head. The overhead reach assigns the other hand no task and relies on the raised arm alone.

Each side gets its own turn. After the first reach ends, the instructions send the worker through the same motion with the other arm. Two holds at the top of the range add up to a full minute of stretching. Two at the bottom take 20 seconds in all. The threefold gap between those totals lets a worker scale the move to the moment, a brief version between tasks or the longer one during a natural pause. Even the full version claims a sliver of each hour at the desk.

A walking and stretching handout describes a side reach that carries one arm over the head and out to the side. The handout asks readers to keep the hips steady as the arm travels. It wants the shoulders straight to the side. The deskercise steps name where the arm should go and stop there, with no word on the hips or shoulders. The handout's pair of cues points toward a stretch that originates along the arm and flank while the base of the body stays put.

A companion edition of the handout warns against bouncing during any stretch. It calls for each one to unfold at an unhurried pace and to go no farther than feels comfortable. Most experts, the handout notes, prefer to save stretching for after a warm-up. Its suggested starter is a few minutes of slow walking.

The shoulder, or pectoralis, stretch takes three movements and a hold of 10 to 30 seconds, and a worker can finish it without leaving the chair. The routine's key takeaways name shoulder stretches among the simple moves a person can complete from a seated position.

Laced fingers behind the back start the sequence. The chest presses forward and out, and the chin lifts, tilting the head up while the clasped hands stay low behind the body. Each step involves a different region, so one hold puts the hands, chest, and head to work in the same pose.

The routine files the pose in its torso section, apart from the shrug and the upper trap stretch, which sit under head and shoulders. The grouping suggests the guide treats the chest push as the core of the move, whatever the name implies.

Its partner in the torso group, the forward stretch, reverses the grip by clasping the hands in front of the body. One pose pushes the chest out with the hands behind, and the other presses forward with them out front. A worker can pair the two to cover both directions without standing up.

The instructions end after one hold. Several other seated moves in the routine tell the reader to switch sides or alternate legs. Both arms join in this pose, so neither works alone, and the steps call for no second round on an opposite side. The routine sets no repetition count either, so one hold completes the assignment, while the moves that switch sides take two.

A standing variant, the doorway pectoral stretch, staggers the feet and has the person lean forward a little to stretch the chest muscles. The seated version asks for no doorway and no change in stance. It can fit into a brief pause between tasks at the desk.

A single 10- to 30-second hold completes the forward stretch, and the move requires a seat and two clasped hands. The worker links the hands out in front, drops the head until it lines up with the arms, and presses forward. The routine builds every stretch around the chair, and this one asks no one to rise. The instructions include no step for switching sides. Both arms travel forward together, so one hold covers the work that the triceps and overhead reach stretches split into two separate holds.

Healthline's instructions attach two other names to the move, the rhomboid upper stretch and the upper back stretch. Both labels direct attention to the upper back. Healthline leaves the forward stretch out of its key takeaways, where the summary of chair stretches names the triceps, overhead reach, shoulder, hip and knee flexion, hamstring, and neck stretches. The move surfaces in the full step-by-step instructions alone.

Two muscles share the rhomboid name. The rhomboid major and rhomboid minor cooperate to pull each shoulder blade toward the spine and upward, a motion that squares the shoulders. The minor is the smaller of the pair and sits higher on the back than the major. The rhomboids join the trapezius to draw the shoulder blade back toward the midline of the back, which steadies the shoulders as they move.

The forward stretch mirrors its torso-group partner, the shoulder, or pectoralis, stretch, move for move. The two make up the whole torso group in Healthline's routine. The pectoralis version clasps the hands behind the back, pushes the chest outward, and lifts the chin. The forward version clasps them in front, lowers the head, and presses the arms away from the body. Someone who runs them back to back reverses the position of the hands and the tilt of the head without standing up.

A seated worker can give the legs attention by bringing one knee toward the chest and holding it there for 10 to 30 seconds. The routine files this move under its legs-and-knees group, which shifts the focus away from the arms, shoulders, and torso that the earlier groups cover.

Each knee gets its own hug. The worker draws one leg up, keeps it close through the count, sets it down, and repeats the sequence with the opposite leg. The instructions name only the hug and the motion toward the chest, leaving the grip to the worker.

Alternating legs doubles the time on the clock. A worker who gives each side the full 30 seconds spends a minute on the move. The briefest version adds up to 20 seconds across both legs, a window small enough to slot between other desk tasks. A complete round at the bottom of the range runs shorter than a single side at the top of it. The chosen hold length governs how much of the day the move consumes.

A floor-based cousin of the stretch appears in separate exercise guidance under the name quad and gluteus stretch. A person lies on the back with the head and shoulders down, keeps one leg extended, and bends the other at the knee and hip. Both hands clasp the lower thigh behind the bent knee and ease it toward the chest before the person switches sides.

The floor guidance spells out what the seated move's name implies, with the knee and the hip bending together. The floor version places both hands behind the knee, a detail the desk instructions leave open. Both versions share the same core action and the same switch between legs.

The desk edition swaps the floor for an office chair, which brings that knee-to-chest action within reach of anyone in the middle of a workday.

The seated hamstring stretch carries a single-leg rule, and the routine spells out the reason. Extending both legs at once can cause back issues. The move belongs to the legs and knees group, and it is the only stretch in the routine that calls for a second chair. It shares that group with the hip and knee flexion stretch, which alternates legs as well. Both lower-body moves in the routine switch sides one leg at a time, but only the hamstring stretch attaches a safety warning to that pattern. Healthline names hamstring stretches in its summary list of moves a worker can do without leaving the chair.

A worker stays seated through every step. Extend one leg and prop that foot on the spare chair. Fold forward from the waist and hold the position for 10 to 30 seconds. Bring the leg back down and give the other side the same treatment. Each hamstring gets a separate turn.

The one-leg approach carries over to floor versions of the stretch. A single leg hamstring stretch in one set of exercise guidance has the person sit upright on the floor and tuck the sole of one foot near the inner upper thigh. The bent knee relaxes toward the ground. From there the person leans forward from the hips over the extended leg, holds the back straight, and stops at a mild stretch. The same steps repeat on the opposite side. A related upper hamstring and hip stretch has the person grip the outside of the ankle or knee along with the foot. The person draws the whole leg toward the torso until a slight stretch registers in the back of the upper leg.

Both floor versions require room on the ground. The desk version replaces that floor space with a second chair, which lets an office worker stretch one leg at a time without standing up or leaving the workstation.

The shoulder shrug runs on a count of 10 repetitions in each direction, which sets it apart from the timed holds that govern the rest of the deskercise stretches. Both shoulders rise in unison toward the ears and then sink back to their resting height. A worker can run through the full set without getting up from the desk.

Healthline files the shrug under its head and shoulders group, beside the upper trap stretch. The pairing gives one region of the body two kinds of work. The trap stretch asks a worker to settle into a position and keep it, while the shrug cycles through lift and release. The trap stretch also moves one side at a time, and the shrug works both shoulders together. Anyone who reaches this section trades a stopwatch for a tally.

Two motions make up the whole exercise. Raise both shoulders at once, lower them, and repeat until the reps run out. The guide sets no tempo and says nothing about how high the shoulders should travel. Each worker decides the pace and the height. The length of a set follows from those choices. A brisk round ends in moments, and a deliberate one takes longer.

Few moves in the routine demand less preparation. The shrug calls for no clasped hands, no free hand drawing an elbow toward the head, and no spare chair to prop a foot on. Healthline's key-takeaways summary also leaves it off the list of chair stretches, so a reader who skims the top of the guide could miss it.

An ergonomics exercise sheet builds the same motion into a longer sequence. It calls for an unhurried lift toward the ears followed by a rotation of the shoulders backward and downward. The deskercise guide leaves out the rotation and keeps the shrug to a plain rise and drop.

A set of fixed reps carries its own finish line, and a worker can close it out without a glance at a clock.

The upper trap stretch calls for a hold of 10 to 15 seconds per side, half the 30-second upper limit set for most of the other timed moves. A worker who completes both sides at the full count spends 30 seconds on the whole move, the same ceiling those other stretches set for a single side.

A light stretch marks the finish line. Seated at the desk, the worker eases the head toward one shoulder, holds once a mild pull registers, and then repeats the move on the other side. The instructions name no target angle and no distance to cover. The body's own signal decides how far the head travels.

CNBC reports that the traps occupy the upper back, spanning the space between the shoulders and the neck. Rounded shoulders pull those muscles taut, according to CNBC.

A fitness trainer in the same piece loosens the traps with a myofascial release ball. She sets it on top of the opposite shoulder near the neck, presses it onto a knot, and lets the hanging arm's weight work the ball in. The deskercise version needs no gear at all. A slight pull and a quick hold carry the whole effort from the chair.

The shoulder shrug and the neck stretches share the head and shoulders heading with this move. The guide's summary lists neck stretches among its chair-friendly options, and the step-by-step section gives them their own instructions apart from the trap stretch. The three moves divide the labor by motion. The shrug raises both shoulders together and counts repetitions. The neck stretch leans the head forward, rolls it toward one side, and holds for 10 seconds before switching. The trap stretch draws the head toward one shoulder at a time and keeps the clock running a little longer, up to 15 seconds.

Its short clock makes it easy to slip between tasks at the desk.

Exhaling during the lean earns top-tip status in Healthline's deskercise routine, and the payoff it names is a greater range of motion. The cue ties the out-breath to the instant the body settles deeper into a position. Breathing turns into an active tool inside each hold, beyond a rhythm running in the background.

A normal breathing pace underpins every move in the set. The guidance forbids holding your breath at any point in a stretch. Steady breathing and the timed exhale function as partners. The first keeps the rhythm even, and the second adds reach as the lean begins.

Comfort sets the outer boundary for every pose. The routine warns against pushing past that point, so any extra ground gained from an exhale has to stay within it. The advice gives no breath count and no target angle. Each worker's own sense of ease decides where a pose stops, which lets the same cues fit a stiff back and a loose one.

Flexibility gains come with a hedge. Healthline suggests you may notice yourself loosening up with each stretch, and the wording stops short of a promise. The breathing cues hand that possibility a lever the worker controls. Each exhale opens a little more room, and the limit of ease keeps any gain within bounds the worker sets.

Breathing travels into every seated stretch in the routine, which makes it the one cue a worker can practice from the first move of a desk session to the last.

Shifting into a new position several times a day can make repetitive stress injuries less likely. The habits in this final item chase that goal away from the chair, and none of them involves a hold time, a repetition count, or a posture to master.

Phone calls and lunch give an employee two chances to get up without adding a task to the day. Standing through either one turns an ordinary activity into a break from the seat. The routine's summary goes a step further and suggests walking during calls, which converts the same conversation into steady motion.

An adjustable standing desk carries the idea across an entire shift. With one, a person can trade sitting for standing as the work changes, and the switch can happen as often as the day demands. The desk is the only option on the list that calls for new furniture. The rest work with whatever office a person has.

Brief meetings can turn into walking laps. Covering ground during a short check-in keeps the discussion going while the legs get some work. The routine pins the suggestion to quick gatherings, so a long session can stay at the table.

Rising once an hour for a stroll around the office asks the least of the worker. It needs no equipment, no reserved space, and no planning beyond a glance at the clock. No other suggestion ties itself to a set interval. Across a full shift, the hourly lap by itself delivers the several daily position changes the routine recommends.

Every habit here borrows time from something the job includes — calls, meals, meetings, or the passing hour — so a full calendar need not block a break from a fixed stance. The earlier stretches work inside the chair, and these habits cut into the time spent in it.

#5564. Etzioni on AI: Is Anthropic worth $2 trillion? Do the napkin math with this handy calculator

by Oren Etzioni on Oct 27, 2026 at 4:45 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 4:45 pm

Anthropic filed to go public on Monday under the ticker ANT, and you may end up owning the stock soon even if you never buy it directly, because index funds and ETFs will be required to buy it within weeks of its debut.

Anthropic’s bankers are reportedly valuing Anthropic between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. Below is a simple, interactive tool to help you form your own opinion of what’s an appropriate valuation for Anthropic.

Disclaimer: this is highly simplified, and I’m not an investment advisor.

The whole IPO debate comes down to two numbers nobody knows: how much revenue Anthropic will have in 2028, and how much of it will be profit. Pick yours.

Your number = revenue × margin × profit multiple. The IPO valuation is $2 trillion, the top of the reported range. The arithmetic ignores two things that roughly cancel: a 2028 profit is worth about 17% less today than the same profit earned now, and Anthropic’s $132 billion in cash adds about 7% to any result. Big Tech multiples are market value divided by the latest quarter’s operating profit, annualized; margins are operating margins from the latest quarter. Anthropic’s figures are from its S-1 and the forecast it gave investors. This is arithmetic, not investment advice.

#5563. Verra Mobility Announces Inducement Grant under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4)

MESA, Ariz., Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Verra Mobility Corporation (NASDAQ: VRRM) (the "Company"), a leading provider of smart mobility technology solutions, announced today that it granted an inducement award to Jon Newhard on November 2, 2026, in connection with Mr. Newhard's  appointment as President and Chief Executive Officer of the Company, effective November 1, 2026 (the "CEO Commencement Date"), pursuant to the employment agreement entered into between the Company and Mr. Newhard on October 1, 2026. The award was granted as an inducement material to Mr. Newhard's employment with the Company and was approved by the Company's Compensation Committee, in accordance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4).

The inducement award consists of a one-time grant of 1,583,333 time-vested restricted stock units covering shares of the Company's Class A common stock, par value $0.0001 per share, valued at $4,750,000 on the date of grant, vesting in three (3) equal annual installments of one-third (1/3) each on each of the first three (3) anniversaries of the CEO Commencement Date, subject to Mr. Newhard's continued service as the Company's Chief Executive Officer through and including each such vesting date.

This award was granted pursuant to a stand-alone inducement award agreement outside of the Verra Mobility Corporation Amended and Restated 2018 Equity Incentive Plan, as amended, and is subject to the terms and conditions of the applicable award agreement.

Verra Mobility Corporation (NASDAQ: VRRM) is a leading provider of smart mobility technology solutions that make transportation safer, smarter and more connected. The company sits at the center of the mobility ecosystem, bringing together vehicles, hardware, software, data and people to enable safe, efficient solutions for customers globally. Verra Mobility's transportation safety systems and parking management solutions protect lives, improve urban and motorway mobility and support healthier communities. The company also solves complex payment, utilization and compliance challenges for fleet owners and rental car companies. Headquartered in Arizona, Verra Mobility operates in North America, Europe, and Australia. For more information, please visit www.verramobility.com.

#5562. From the 1935 act to Medicare: 10 milestones in the history of Social Security

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Trace the history of Social Security through 10 turning points, from Roosevelt's 1935 law and the first checks to Medicare, the 1983 reforms and today's trust fund outlook

Social Security began as a narrow answer to old-age poverty during the Great Depression. The Social Security Act of 1935 created federal old-age benefits for retired workers, paid for by a tax on wages. Over the following decades, Congress turned that retirement program into something much broader. It came to cover spouses, young children, survivors and disabled workers. It also became the legal home of Medicare.

The idea was not new. Germany had adopted a national old-age insurance system in the 1880s under Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. That system served as a precedent for the American program, which arrived decades later.

The history of Social Security explains much of how the program works now. Many of the rules that workers and retirees deal with today trace back to a specific law passed in a specific year. The payroll tax on wages took effect in 1937. Benefits for spouses, children and survivors arrived with the 1939 amendments. Disability insurance followed in 1956. Automatic inflation adjustments were written into law in 1972 and began in 1975.

Each of those changes filled a gap in the original design. The 1935 law paid no monthly benefits to the spouses or survivors of workers. It offered no insurance for workers who became disabled before retirement age. Until the mid-1970s, any increase in benefits depended on Congress passing a new law.

The 10 slides that follow trace that arc in order. They begin with Franklin D. Roosevelt's signature on the 1935 act and the committee chaired by Labor Secretary Frances Perkins that drafted it. They move through the first lump-sum payment to Ernest Ackerman of Cleveland and the first monthly check to Ida May Fuller of Vermont. Next come the family and disability expansions, the creation of Medicare in 1965 and the launch of Supplemental Security Income under the 1972 amendments. The series closes with the 1983 law that raised the full retirement age and with the program's current funding and trust fund outlook.

Each slide covers one turning point and can be read on its own. Taken together, they form a Social Security timeline that runs from the first checks to today.

President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act on August 14, 1935. The law created federal old-age benefits for retired workers and became the legal foundation of today's Social Security program.

Roosevelt signed the bill during the Great Depression. Mass unemployment had cut off wages for millions of workers, and bank failures had erased many families' savings. Before this law, older Americans who could no longer work had no national retirement benefit to fall back on.

Retirement income was only one part of the act. The law also set up an unemployment insurance system run jointly by the federal government and the states. Under that structure, states operated their own programs within a national framework. Unemployment insurance gave laid-off workers temporary income, a direct response to the joblessness of the era.

A third piece of the law sent federal grants to the states. That money supported aid to dependent children, aid to the blind and public health programs. It also funded old-age assistance, a separate need-based program for older people with little or no income. The mix of insurance and grants made the act a broad social welfare law, not just a pension bill.

The old-age program was designed around work. Benefits were reserved for retired workers who had earned wages in jobs the law covered. Payroll taxes paid by workers and their employers would fund them. The self-employed were among the groups left outside the system at first.

The law created a three-member Social Security Board to administer the new programs. John G. Winant, a former Republican governor of New Hampshire, became its first chairman. The board was the forerunner of today's Social Security Administration.

The act set 65 as the age when retirement benefits could begin. That age remained the full retirement age for decades, until later legislation raised it in stages.

The 1935 statute remains in force today. Each major expansion since then has come as an amendment to it rather than as a separate law.

Labor Secretary Frances Perkins chaired the Committee on Economic Security, the panel that drafted the proposals behind the Social Security Act of 1935. President Franklin D. Roosevelt created the committee in 1934.

Perkins was the first woman to serve in a U.S. cabinet. She led the committee while holding the post of labor secretary.

The committee's job was to turn the Roosevelt administration's policy goals into specific legislative proposals. Those proposals became the basis of the law Congress passed in 1935.

The committee's work is the link between the administration's plans and the statute that created Social Security. Its drafts shaped the program in the form that took effect.

Social Security payroll taxes took effect in January 1937. Workers and employers each paid 1% on the first $3,000 of a worker's annual wages.

The cost was split evenly between the employee and the employer. That shared arrangement became the program's basic funding model.

The $3,000 figure worked as a ceiling. Wages above that amount in a given year were not taxed. A worker who earned more than $3,000 paid the same tax as one who earned exactly $3,000.

The tax depended on a way to track each person's wages. The government issued Social Security account numbers so employers could report every worker's covered earnings. Those earnings records later determined who qualified for benefits and how much each person received.

Collection began before regular benefits did. Payroll deductions came out of workers' wages starting in 1937. Monthly retirement checks did not go out until 1940.

Lump-sum payments filled that gap. The original 1935 law provided one-time payments to covered workers who reached 65 before they could qualify for monthly benefits. It also provided them to the estates of covered workers who died. In both cases, the payment gave something back for the taxes the worker had already paid.

Ernest Ackerman of Cleveland received the first of these lump-sum payments. It marked the first time the new system paid money out instead of only taking it in.

The lump-sum stage was temporary. Monthly benefits replaced it as the program's main form of payment.

Ida May Fuller of Vermont received the first ongoing monthly Social Security retirement check on January 31, 1940. Her payment marked the program's shift from one-time lump sums to the regular monthly income it pays today.

Fuller lived in Ludlow, Vermont, and worked as a legal secretary. Her employer was a law practice that included John G. Sargent, who later served as U.S. attorney general under President Calvin Coolidge.

She retired in November 1939. Around that time, she stopped by the Social Security office in Rutland, Vermont, to ask about benefits while she was in town on an errand.

Her claim put her among the first retirees to collect monthly benefits, which the 1939 amendments had moved up to 1940.

Her record as a contributor was short. Payroll taxes for the program began in January 1937. Fuller paid them for only a few years before she stopped working.

Her time as a beneficiary was far longer. Fuller lived to age 100 and collected a monthly check for the rest of her life. She died in January 1975.

Her payment did not stay fixed over those decades. Congress raised benefits a number of times starting in 1950. Those increases applied to retirees already on the rolls, including Fuller.

The gap between her brief contributions and her long years of benefits made her a frequently cited example of how the early program worked. The first generation of retirees received far more in benefits than they had paid in through payroll taxes.

Fuller was not unusual in that respect. Workers who were already near retirement age in 1937 had little time to build a long contribution record. They could still qualify for monthly checks once payments began.

Her benefit was not capped at the taxes she had paid. It was set by a formula in the law based on her covered earnings, not by the balance of a personal account. That design let the program pay monthly income to people with short work records under the system.

The 1939 amendments to the Social Security Act extended benefits beyond the retired worker. They added monthly payments for the wives and young children of retirees and for the families of insured workers who died.

That change turned Social Security into protection for households, not just individuals. Before 1939, the monthly retirement benefit belonged to the worker alone. A family that had depended on that worker's wages lost the income entirely once the worker died.

Congress addressed that gap in two ways. The first was a set of dependent benefits. A retired worker's wife and young children could now draw monthly payments based on the worker's earnings record.

The second was survivor protection. When an insured worker died, eligible family members could receive monthly benefits that replaced part of the lost income. Those provisions covered widows who had reached retirement age. They also covered younger widows caring for the worker's children, along with the children themselves. A deceased worker's dependent parents could qualify when no widow or child was eligible.

The amendments also changed the timetable. The 1935 law had scheduled monthly retirement payments to begin in 1942. The 1939 legislation moved that start to 1940.

The benefit formula changed as well. The 1935 law had based benefits on a worker's total lifetime covered wages. The 1939 version based them on average monthly wages instead. That shift allowed larger payments for people who retired in the program's early years.

The financing structure gained a formal home too. The amendments created the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund to hold payroll tax revenue not needed for current benefits. The retirement program itself took the name Old-Age and Survivors Insurance, often shortened to OASI. The label reflected the program's wider purpose. It insured a worker against the loss of earnings in old age. It also insured a family against the loss of a breadwinner.

The family-based design from 1939 still shapes Social Security. Benefits for spouses, children and survivors continue to be calculated from one worker's earnings record. The relatives collecting them did not pay into the system on that record. Later laws widened eligibility, but they built on this structure rather than replacing it.

The 1956 amendments created Social Security Disability Insurance, which paid monthly benefits to disabled workers aged 50 to 64. A 1960 law removed that age floor. It opened disability benefits to disabled workers of any age.

The disability program changed what Social Security insured against. Until 1956, the system paid out when a worker reached the benefit age of 65 or died. A worker forced out of the labor force by a disability before 65 had no monthly benefit of their own.

The 1956 law closed that gap, but only for older workers at first. Someone disabled at 45 still fell outside the program. The 1960 law ended that cutoff. A younger worker with a qualifying disability could now draw benefits too.

The 1956 amendments made a second change to eligibility. Women workers and wives could claim reduced benefits as early as age 62.

President Dwight D. Eisenhower was in office for both disability laws. He also held office for the coverage expansion of 1954.

The decade opened under President Harry S. Truman with the 1950 amendments. That law brought a cost-of-living adjustment to benefits. It was the first increase since monthly payments began in 1940.

That 1950 increase was the first of several ad hoc adjustments. Each one was a separate decision by Congress rather than an automatic formula. Retirees had no guarantee that their checks would keep pace with prices from one year to the next.

The 1954 amendments widened the program in a different direction. They extended coverage to groups of workers the original law had left out.

Coverage decides who pays Social Security payroll taxes and who earns credit toward benefits. Workers outside covered jobs could not build a record for retirement, survivor or disability protection. Bringing more occupations into the system enlarged both its tax base and the number of families it protected.

By 1960, the program reached a wider share of the workforce. It also protected against disability at any age, alongside retirement and death.

President Lyndon B. Johnson signed Medicare into law on July 30, 1965, as amendments to the Social Security Act. The law gave Americans aged 65 and older federal health insurance tied to the same system that paid their retirement benefits.

Johnson held the signing ceremony at the Harry S. Truman Library in Independence, Missouri, rather than in Washington, D.C. He picked the site to honor Truman, who had backed national health insurance as president.

Truman sent Congress a proposal for a national health program in 1945. It stalled and never passed during his time in office. At the 1965 ceremony, Truman and his wife, Bess, received the first Medicare cards.

The 1965 law built Medicare in two main parts. Part A, hospital insurance, covers inpatient hospital stays and related care. Part B, medical insurance, covers doctor visits and other outpatient services. Enrollees pay a monthly premium for Part B. Benefits began on July 1, 1966.

The same legislation also created Medicaid. That program is run jointly by the federal government and the states. It covers people with low incomes rather than people defined by age.

Medicare's hospital coverage borrows the payroll tax model that funds Social Security retirement benefits. Workers and employers each pay 1.45% of wages toward Medicare's hospital insurance trust fund. Unlike the Social Security portion of the payroll tax, the Medicare tax has no annual wage cap.

Coverage later reached beyond older Americans. In 1972, Congress extended Medicare to some younger people with disabilities, including those who had received Social Security disability benefits for two years. People with end-stage kidney disease became eligible at the same time.

The program has kept adding benefits since then. The Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 created Part D, a prescription drug benefit that took effect in 2006. Today the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services runs the program. The Social Security Administration still handles much of the enrollment for Parts A and B.

The 1972 amendments to the Social Security Act tied benefit increases automatically to inflation, and the first automatic adjustments took effect in 1975. The same legislation created Supplemental Security Income, a needs-based program for elderly, blind and disabled Americans.

The automatic cost-of-living adjustment, usually shortened to COLA, replaced raises that each required a separate act of Congress. Benefits now rise with consumer prices without a new vote.

The adjustment is based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as the CPI-W. The percentage increase in the CPI-W's average for July through September sets the size of the raise. The agency announces each year's COLA in October, and it first appears in benefits paid in January. If the index does not rise, benefits stay the same rather than falling.

President Richard Nixon signed the 1972 amendments into law. The original indexing formula contained a technical flaw that could push benefits up faster than intended. Congress corrected it in the 1977 amendments.

SSI payments began in January 1974. The new program replaced a patchwork of state-run assistance programs for older, blind and disabled adults, which the federal government had helped fund. SSI set a national minimum payment level, and many states add their own supplements on top of it.

SSI differs from Social Security retirement benefits in how it is paid for. It draws on general tax revenues from the U.S. Treasury, not on payroll taxes or the Social Security trust funds. Eligibility depends on income and assets rather than work history. A person who never held a job covered by Social Security can still qualify. Adults must be 65 or older, blind or disabled, and fall under the program's financial limits. Children with disabilities can qualify as well.

The Social Security Administration runs both programs. A person can receive SSI alongside Social Security retirement or disability benefits if their total income stays low enough. Federal SSI payments rise each year by the same COLA percentage as Social Security benefits.

President Ronald Reagan signed the Social Security Amendments of 1983 on April 20, 1983. The law raised the full retirement age in stages from 65 to 67 for people born in 1960 or later.

The changes came from a bipartisan commission chaired by Alan Greenspan. The panel's formal name was the National Commission on Social Security Reform. Its job was to propose fixes for a short-term funding shortfall in the program. Its recommendations became the basis of the bill Congress sent to Reagan that spring.

Greenspan was an economist who had chaired the Council of Economic Advisers under President Gerald Ford $F. He became chair of the Federal Reserve in 1987.

The retirement age increase was phased in gradually. It did not affect anyone who was already close to retirement in 1983. The first affected group was people born in 1938, whose full retirement age rose to 65 and two months. The age then rose by two months for each later birth year. It reached 66 for people born from 1943 through 1954. A second phase brought back the two-month steps for people born in 1955 and later. It ended at 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later.

Full retirement age is the age at which a worker can claim an unreduced retirement benefit. Raising it meant that a worker who claims at a given age before 67 receives a smaller monthly benefit than under the old rules. Workers can still start retirement benefits as early as 62, but at a reduced rate.

The law also made part of Social Security benefits subject to federal income tax for the first time. The tax applied only to higher-income recipients. Under the 1983 rules, up to half of benefits could be taxed once a recipient's income passed a threshold. That threshold was $25,000 for single filers and $32,000 for married couples filing jointly. The revenue from the tax is credited to the Social Security trust funds.

A third major change widened the program's coverage. New federal employees hired after 1983 were brought into Social Security. Before that, most federal workers had been covered by the separate Civil Service Retirement System.

Social Security is paid for mainly through a payroll tax of 12.4% on wages. Workers and employers each contribute 6.2%, and the tax applies only to earnings up to an annual cap.

That structure follows the program's original design, in which both sides of the paycheck shared the cost. The rate and the wage ceiling are far higher now. The even split between worker and employer has not changed.

Self-employed people pay both halves themselves. Under the Self-Employment Contributions Act, they owe the full 12.4% on net self-employment earnings up to the same cap.

The cap is formally called the contribution and benefit base. It is adjusted each year to track growth in average wages across the economy. Earnings above it are not subject to the Social Security tax. Those earnings also do not count when a worker's future benefit is calculated.

Medicare's hospital insurance tax is collected separately from the Social Security tax. Workers and employers each pay 1.45% toward it. Unlike the Social Security tax, it has no wage cap.

Payroll tax revenue flows into two trust funds. One pays retirement and survivor benefits. The other pays disability benefits.

The Social Security Board of Trustees reviews the finances of both funds. Each year it publishes a report projecting how long the funds can keep paying scheduled benefits in full. Those projections shape the debate in Congress over the program's future.

Depletion of a trust fund would not end benefit payments. Payroll taxes would keep arriving from current workers. That revenue would cover a portion of scheduled benefits rather than the full amount.

The main options lawmakers discuss fall into a few categories. They include raising the payroll tax rate, lifting or removing the wage cap and changing the benefit formula. Each choice shifts the cost among current workers, employers and future retirees.

#5561. LiveX brings engaging, AI-powered intelligent human-sized avatar kiosks to retail and airport sites

Palo Alto-based LiveX AI Inc., a company building interactive experience artificial intelligence agents for retail and hospitality environments, today announced AI City, its kiosk-driven, life-size, human-like AI hosts.

The company’s products, currently deployed in more than 100 sites, engage guests through life-sized human avatars across retail, technology, hospitality and entertainment. Customer sites include PUMA stores, San José Mineta International Airport, SAP Center, the San Jose Sharks stadium, El Camino Hospital, and Marriott and Hilton hotels.

“We believe intelligence of this nature should meet people wherever they are, live and in person, where life happens,” said President and Chief AI Officer Jia Li. “AI should be greeting travelers at the airport, guiding a grandmother through the hospital, helping every shopper like the best employee in the building or answering sixty thousand fans at once.”

A traditional interactive kiosk relies on rigid menus and doesn’t converse with the user; it also doesn’t automatically translate into the user’s native language by simply listening to them speak. An AI City kiosk can see and hear the other person and react almost like another person, using real-time discovery to provide personalized help.

The company added that these kiosks are coming as companies try to bring other physical AI products, such as general-purpose robotics, to market, but these are still years away from widespread deployment.

As a kiosk, a user could walk up and see a projected AI person who can assist with navigation, product recommendations, event guidance or answer questions about the venue. According to LiveX, the City kiosk products have been expanded with interactive 3D maps for location-aware navigation and discovery, 3D products and multilingual translation.

LiveX said such a system could assist customers with product, venue and event questions, enabling staff to walk around with more customers at the site and handle more complex problems requiring deeper oversight.

“AI that can understand people and their surroundings is opening new ways to make everyday spaces more helpful and accessible,” said Madison Huang, senior director of product marketing for physical AI at Nvidia Corp.

The LiveX Interactive Intelligence platform runs on Nvidia RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell Server Edition graphics processing units and uses the Metropolis VSS Blueprint to build visual AI agents powered by Nvidia Cosmos, an open world model builder. Nvidia also provided a surface for supplying libraries from Omniverse, which delivers digital twins for location-aware applications.

LiveX said its platform brings together proprietary models it developed and trained for human interaction, shaped on real-world interaction data and experience through live deployments. Its Omni Model provides multimodal understanding and responses, while a noise management model lets it assist users even with significant background noise.
