#5559. A new pal for Pluto? Rubin Observatory finds its first dwarf planet candidate

by Alan Boyle on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:54 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 8:23 pm

Astronomers sorting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile have found an icy world that has a good chance of joining Pluto in the solar system’s retinue of dwarf planets.

University of Washington astronomer Mario Jurić joined the astronomer who made the discovery, Matthew Holman of the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, to announce the findings today at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division for Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Jurić, the Rubin team’s solar system lead scientist, said the observatory’s capabilities made it possible to detect and characterize the new dwarf planet candidate, known as 2026 ED138.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Jurić said in a news release. “And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and ‘precover’ objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.”

2026 ED138 traces a tilted orbital path that takes it well beyond Pluto, the solar system’s best-known dwarf planet. It’s currently at a distance of 46 astronomical units, where 1 AU equals the average distance between Earth and the sun. Pluto, by comparison, is currently about 40 AU from the sun.

Astronomers suspect ED138 formed billions of years ago closer to the sun before being flung into a wider orbit by gravitational interactions with Neptune.

Based on an analysis of its distance, brightness and assumed composition, ED138 is thought to be somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (373 to 932 miles) in diameter. At that size, an icy object should possess enough gravity to pull itself into a round shape — satisfying the primary physical criterion for a dwarf planet.

ED138 may be Rubin’s first dwarf planet candidate, but it almost certainly won’t be the last. Thanks to the observatory’s Simonyi Survey Telescope — named after the family of Seattle software billionaire Charles Simonyi — the Rubin team detected more than 11,000 new asteroids even before June’s official start of a 10-year survey of the southern sky.

Rubin’s researchers analyze the data from those scans to find objects of interest — ranging from asteroids to gamma-ray bursts — and track them over time. On Oct. 13, Holman was running data through a search code that he developed with Kevin Napier, a colleague at the Center for Astrophysics. ED138 stood out due to its exceptional size and brightness.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”

To confirm the discovery, Holman, Jurić and their colleagues found 30 archived observations of ED138 dating back to March 4. The Asteroid Institute’s ADAM Precovery service found still more images of the object, going back to 2016, in the archives of a different astronomical survey.

The precovery data confirmed that ED138 was a special case.

“Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation,” Jurić said. “It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.”

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined dwarf planets as planetary objects that are big enough to crush themselves into a roundish shape — technically speaking, into a state of hydrostatic equilibrium — but not big enough to clear their orbital neighborhood.

So far, the IAU has classified five solar system objects as dwarf planets — including Ceres in the main asteroid belt, plus Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake in the region beyond Neptune. 2026 ED138 joins a host of other celestial objects that are thought to be dwarf planets but haven’t yet been added to the IAU’s official list.

“The official list hasn’t moved since 2008,” Jurić told GeekWire in an email. “I’m not sure if there’s an active process that reviews candidates, and what are the timelines.”

Jurić and his colleagues hope additional observations will boost ED138’s chances of attaining true dwarf planethood.

“The next step in building the case would be to prove it’s round (in hydrostatic equilibrium),” he wrote. “The means to do that would be directly through occultations (and there’s a good chance of that, given it’s in a dense stellar field), and then thermal measurements plus modeling and light curves (or the absence of variability).”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5558. WhiteFiber Completes Acquisition of Two North Carolina Data Center Development Sites and Provides NC-1 Update

NEW YORK, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- WhiteFiber, Inc. (Nasdaq: WYFI) ("WhiteFiber" or the "Company"), a provider of artificial intelligence infrastructure solutions, today announced that, through its wholly owned subsidiary Enovum Data Centers Corp., it has completed the previously announced acquisition of two industrial properties in Yadkin County, North Carolina, designated NC-2 and NC-3. The purchase price for the properties was $60 million, paid in cash.

Located approximately 55 miles from WhiteFiber's NC-1 campus in Madison, North Carolina, the properties comprise approximately 120 acres of land and 500,000 square feet of existing warehouse space. The properties are expected to provide a combined minimum of 60 megawatts ("MW") of initial gross utility capacity, with the potential to support up to approximately 200 MW within seven years following closing, subject to confirmation and power availability. WhiteFiber intends to retrofit the properties into data center campuses, building on its regional development experience and operating capabilities.

WhiteFiber has received non-binding letters of intent from a broad range of prospective customers for capacity at NC-2 and NC-3 and expansion capacity at NC-1. These include proposals from investment-grade counterparties and proposals incorporating investment-grade credit support. The Company is engaged in advanced discussions with prospective customers across these opportunities.

WhiteFiber is targeting initial ready-for-service capacity at NC-2 and NC-3 in late 2027, subject to customary development conditions. WhiteFiber's development spending plans are expected to be aligned with definitive customer agreements and financing.

In connection with the acquisition, the seller will continue to occupy portions of the properties under occupancy and partial leaseback arrangements. These arrangements are expected to offset a portion of property carrying costs as WhiteFiber advances its development plans.

Switchgear-related commissioning issues interrupted service and billing for the first 20 MW IT data hall and delayed NC-1's ramp to full contracted run-rate billing beyond the previously anticipated August timeframe. Approximately 35 MW of the contracted 40 MW IT deployment is now operational, with work ongoing to bring the remaining 5 MW online.

Capital investment required to deliver the initial contracted deployment is substantially complete, with total development costs currently expected to remain within the Company's initial budget.

WhiteFiber continues to advance financing for the initial contracted deployment at NC-1 with the previously disclosed prospective lending group. The parties are working through the remaining documentation and closing requirements. There can be no assurance that the financing will be completed.

"We are encouraged by the breadth of customer demand, including proposals from investment-grade counterparties and proposals with investment-grade credit support," said Sam Tabar, Chief Executive Officer of WhiteFiber. "We are building on our development and operating experience in North Carolina to meet strong customer demand across our portfolio. Our priority is to turn that demand into long-term contracts and develop capacity with the right customer and financing commitments in place. We look forward to working closely with local stakeholders as we develop these sites and being a responsible long-term partner to the community."

WhiteFiber will report its third-quarter 2026 financial results on November 10, 2026, and provide further financial and operating updates at that time.

WhiteFiber is a provider of artificial intelligence ("AI") infrastructure solutions. WhiteFiber owns high-performance computing data centers and provides cloud services to customers. Our vertically integrated model combines specialized colocation, hosting, and cloud services engineered to maximize performance, efficiency, and margin for generative AI workloads. For more information, visit www.whitefiber.com. Follow us on LinkedIn and X @WhiteFiber.

#5557. Connecticut's average Social Security check beats Mississippi's by $418.64 a month

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Average Social Security check by state compared for 10 states at either end of a ranking of all 50 states and D.C., using December 2025 retired-worker data

Retirees in Connecticut and Mississippi receive checks calculated by the same federal formula. The typical payment in each state still lands far apart. Connecticut's average retired-worker benefit was $2,308.36 in December 2025. Mississippi's was $1,889.72. That is a gap of $418.64 a month.

The figures come from Table 5.J6 of the Social Security Administration's Annual Statistical Supplement, 2026. The table reports the average Social Security check by state for retired workers as of December 2025. It has 51 rows, one for each of the 50 states and one for the District of Columbia.

At that point, 53,624,664 retired workers were collecting benefits nationwide. Their average monthly payment was $2,071.30. The national median was $1,991.90. The median marks the midpoint, with half of beneficiaries above it and half below. It can order states differently than the average does, and at the top of this table it does.

This article covers 10 of those 51 rows: the five states with the highest averages and the five with the lowest. The high group is Connecticut, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Delaware and Maryland. All five sit in the Northeast or Mid-Atlantic. The low group is New Mexico, Kentucky, Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi. Four of those five are in the South.

The selection leaves out the states with the most retired-worker beneficiaries. California had 5,341,103. Florida had 4,191,491, Texas had 3,710,457, New York had 3,000,986 and Pennsylvania had 2,319,503. Together those five states account for 18,563,540 people, or 34.6% of the national total. None of them falls among the five highest or five lowest averages.

Each state slide that follows gives the average monthly payment, the median and the number of retired workers receiving benefits. It compares those figures with the national numbers from the same month. An individual check depends on lifetime earnings and the age at which a person starts claiming. The table itself does not explain why any one state lands where it does.

A separate, later figure tracks the national average. The average retired-worker check was $2,087.52 in August 2026. That figure covers a different month. The state comparisons here use December 2025 throughout.

Connecticut retirees collected an average Social Security retired-worker benefit of $2,308.36 in December 2025, the highest of any state or the District of Columbia. Connecticut is also the only state in the table with an average above $2,300.

Connecticut's lead at the top is narrow. Kiplinger points out that its average sits just $10.66 above New Hampshire, the second-highest state, at $2,297.70. Over a full year of checks, that monthly edge adds up to $127.92. Maryland, the fifth-highest state at $2,257.51, trails Connecticut by $50.85.

The gap with the country as a whole is far wider. Kiplinger also notes that Connecticut's average is $237.06 above the national average of $2,071.30. Over 12 months, a check at Connecticut's average totals $27,700.32. A check at the national average totals $24,855.60 over the same stretch. The annual difference comes to $2,844.72.

The median ranks Connecticut one spot lower. Its median retired-worker benefit was $2,248.90, second in the country behind New Jersey's $2,255.90. New Jersey's median edges Connecticut's by $7.00. Connecticut's median runs $59.46 below its average. When an average sits above the median, the largest checks in the group pull the average upward.

Against the national median of $1,991.90, Connecticut's median is $257.00 higher. On that measure, the state's margin over the country is wider than its lead on the average.

Connecticut had 606,612 retired-worker beneficiaries in December 2025. That is about 1.1% of the 53,624,664 retired workers receiving benefits nationwide. Among the five states with the highest averages, Connecticut's count trails New Jersey's 1,406,793 and Maryland's 892,917. It exceeds New Hampshire's 277,320 and Delaware's 206,680. Connecticut's total is about 2.2 times New Hampshire's.

State tax rules also affect how much of each payment a retiree keeps. Connecticut taxpayers whose federal adjusted gross income reaches the cutoff for a full exemption on Social Security income may still qualify for a partial exemption.

New Hampshire retirees collected an average Social Security check of $2,297.70 in December 2025. That was the second-highest average among the 50 states and D.C. Only Connecticut's average was higher, by $10.66.

The gap below New Hampshire was even narrower. New Jersey ranked third with an average of $2,287.75, which left it $9.95 behind. Just $20.61 a month separated first place from third.

New Hampshire's average sat $226.40 above the national average retired-worker benefit of $2,071.30. Its median of $2,214.90 was $223.00 above the national median of $1,991.90. The state's average was also $407.98 higher than Mississippi's, the lowest in the country.

New Hampshire has a small retiree population compared with the other two states at the top. It had 277,320 retired-worker beneficiaries, the fewest among the three states with the highest averages. Connecticut had 606,612, more than twice as many. New Jersey had 1,406,793, about five times New Hampshire's count. New Hampshire's beneficiaries made up about 0.5% of the 53,624,664 retired workers nationwide.

Measured by median, New Hampshire slips from second to fourth within the top-five group. Its median trailed New Jersey, Connecticut and Delaware. Only Maryland, at $2,180.90, had a lower median among the five states with the highest averages.

The two measures can rank states differently because they respond to different parts of the distribution. An average adds up every check and divides the total by the number of beneficiaries. Every dollar counts toward it. A relatively small number of large checks can pull it upward. The median depends only on which check sits in the middle. Larger checks at the top do not move it in the same way.

In New Hampshire, the average ran $82.80 above the median. Across the U.S., the national average exceeded the national median by $79.40. New Hampshire's spread was $3.40 wider than the national one. The table does not break down which checks produced that spread.

New Jersey has the highest median Social Security retired-worker benefit in the U.S., at $2,255.90 a month in December 2025. Its average check, $2,287.75, ranks third among the 50 states and D.C.

On the median, New Jersey edges out Connecticut, whose midpoint benefit is $2,248.90. The gap is $7.00. Connecticut leads the average ranking at $2,308.36, which is $20.61 above New Jersey's figure. New Hampshire sits between them on averages, in second place at $2,297.70.

Delaware, New Hampshire and Maryland complete the top five by median, at $2,224.90, $2,214.90 and $2,180.90, respectively. New Jersey climbs two places from its average rank to its median rank. No other state in the high group moves up more than one place.

New Jersey's median sits $264.00 above the national median. Its average runs $216.45 above the national average. Its median is also $465.00 higher than Mississippi's $1,790.90, the lowest median in the country.

The distance between New Jersey's own average and median is $31.85. The national average exceeds the national median by $79.40. New Jersey's narrower spread means its average sits closer to what the retiree in the middle of its distribution receives.

New Jersey's gap is the narrowest in the high group. Connecticut's spread is $59.46, Delaware's is $48.87, Maryland's is $76.61 and New Hampshire's is $82.80.

New Jersey also has the most retired-worker beneficiaries among the five states with the highest averages, at 1,406,793. That exceeds the combined 1,090,612 in Connecticut, New Hampshire and Delaware. Maryland is next in the group, with 892,917. New Jersey's count equals about 2.6% of all retired workers receiving benefits nationwide.

The state had a net exodus of retirees, according to Hire a Helper's report The New Retirement Map: Where Retirement-Age Americans Moved in 2025 and Why. The report examines where retirement-age Americans relocated during 2025 and why.

Delaware's retired workers received an average Social Security check of $2,273.77 in December 2025. That ranked fourth among the 50 states and D.C., $202.47 a month above the national average.

A year of checks at Delaware's December 2025 average would total $27,285.24. The same 12 checks at the national average would total $24,855.60. That is a difference of $2,429.64, assuming payments held steady all year.

Delaware had 206,680 retired-worker beneficiaries, the fewest of the 10 states in this selection. That is about 0.39% of all retired-worker beneficiaries in the U.S. New Hampshire, the next-smallest of the 10, had 277,320. Maryland, fifth in the high group, had 892,917, more than four times Delaware's count.

Delaware moves up one place on the median measure. Its median benefit of $2,224.90 ranks third in the country, behind New Jersey and Connecticut. Connecticut's median, second in the country, is $24.00 higher. Delaware's is $233.00 above the national median. New Hampshire, which edges Delaware on the average, falls behind it on the median.

Delaware's average exceeds its median by $48.87. The national gap between the two measures was $79.40. Delaware's pair of figures sits closer together than the national pair.

Delaware's average falls within a tight band at the top of the table. It trails New Jersey's $2,287.75 by $13.98 and leads Maryland's $2,257.51 by $16.26. Connecticut, in first place, is $34.59 ahead. Mississippi, at the bottom of the table, averages $384.05 less per month.

Delaware's checks are set by the same national rules that apply in every state. The calculation begins with a primary insurance amount, the benefit payable at full retirement age. That age falls between 66 and 67, depending on birth year. A retiree who claims at full retirement age receives 100% of that amount. These rules describe how any check is calculated. They do not explain Delaware's position in the ranking.

Maryland has the fifth-highest average Social Security check among the 50 states and D.C., at $2,257.51 a month for retired workers in December 2025. That puts the state $186.21 above the national average of $2,071.30.

Maryland's median benefit was $2,180.90. It beat the national median of $1,991.90 by $189.00. That is a slightly wider margin than the state's lead on the average.

The Maryland median also cleared the national average, by $109.60. Within the state, the average and the median sat $76.61 apart. That gap is wider than Connecticut's, where the two figures differ by $59.46.

By median, Maryland also ranks last among the five states with the highest averages. The other four reshuffle when that group is sorted by median. Maryland is the only one whose position within the group does not change.

The spread among the leading states is narrow. Maryland's average trails Delaware's $2,273.77 by $16.26. It sits $40.19 below New Hampshire's $2,297.70. It falls $50.85 short of Connecticut's $2,308.36, the highest average in the table. At the other end of the ranking, Maryland's figure is $367.79 above Mississippi's $1,889.72, the lowest. It also sits $302.84 above New Mexico's $1,954.67, the fifth-lowest average.

Maryland also has a large retiree base. The state counted 892,917 retired-worker beneficiaries, about 1.7% of the 53,624,664 nationwide. That count is more than four times Delaware's 206,680. Among the five highest-average states, only New Jersey had more beneficiaries, with 1,406,793.

At Maryland's December 2025 average, 12 monthly checks would total $27,090.12. The same 12 checks at the national average would come to $24,855.60. The difference is $2,234.52 over a year. That is an illustration at a fixed monthly rate, not a reported annual figure.

Maryland's position fits a regional pattern. Kiplinger reports that average benefits run highest in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic. Maryland and its neighbor Delaware are both Mid-Atlantic states, and both rank among the five highest averages. The source does not tie Maryland's rank to any state-specific cause.

New Mexico retirees received an average Social Security retired-worker benefit of $1,954.67 a month in December 2025, the fifth-lowest figure among the 50 states and D.C. The state's median benefit was $1,825.90.

That average sits $116.63 below the national average for the same month. The gap widens at the midpoint. New Mexico's median trails the national median by $166.

Over a full year, the difference adds up. Twelve checks at New Mexico's December average would come to $23,456.04. The same 12 checks at the national average would total $24,855.60. That is $1,399.56 more.

The distance grows against the top of the ranking. Connecticut's average check, the highest in the table, is $353.69 larger than New Mexico's.

New Mexico had 366,403 retired-worker beneficiaries in December 2025. That is the smallest count among the five states with the lowest averages. Kentucky, Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi each had more retired workers drawing benefits. Kentucky's total of 719,046 is nearly twice New Mexico's.

The state's average runs $128.77 above its median. That is the widest average-to-median spread among the five lowest-ranked states. Louisiana comes closest at $119.25, while Kentucky's spread is $77.23. The national spread in December 2025 was $79.40.

A mean that sits well above the median points to a smaller group of larger checks pulling the average up. Half of New Mexico's retired workers received $1,825.90 or less. For a typical payment in the state, the median is the closer measure.

That spread also shifts New Mexico's place within the low group. Its median ranks below Kentucky's $1,875.90 and Arkansas's $1,841.90, even though both of those states have lower averages. Only Louisiana and Mississippi post lower medians than New Mexico among the five.

New Mexico is the one state in the bottom five located outside the South. It sits in the Southwest. That fits a low group that is mostly, but not entirely, Southern.

Kentucky retirees collected an average Social Security retired-worker benefit of $1,953.13 in December 2025. That figure ranks fourth-lowest among the 50 states and the District of Columbia.

Kentucky sits just behind New Mexico, the fifth-lowest state, whose average was $1,954.67. The difference between the two is $1.54 a month. In the ranking, the two states are nearly level.

The gap with the national average is far wider. Kentucky's average falls $118.17 short of the U.S. average for the same month. Over 12 months, that adds up to $1,418.04 less than a check at the national average would pay.

Kentucky places higher on the median than on the average within its group. Its median benefit was $1,875.90, the highest among the five states with the lowest averages. Arkansas came next at $1,841.90, $34.00 behind Kentucky. New Mexico's median was $1,825.90, Louisiana's was $1,807.90 and Mississippi's was $1,790.90. Kentucky's median still sits $116.00 below the national median.

Kentucky's own average runs $77.23 above its median. When an average exceeds the median, the larger checks in a state's distribution lift the mean above the midpoint.

The state also has the largest pool of retired-worker beneficiaries in the low group. In December 2025, 719,046 retired workers in Kentucky drew benefits. That is more than Louisiana's 661,928, the next-largest count among the five lowest-average states. It is also 352,643 more than New Mexico, the state just above Kentucky in the average ranking.

Kentucky checks are sized under the same national rules that apply in every state. A person born in 1960 or later who starts benefits at 62 receives 30% less than the benefit payable at full retirement age. Waiting until full retirement age pays 100% of that amount.

The December 2025 table does not show how many Kentucky retirees claimed early. The rules explain how individual checks are sized, not why the state's average lands where it does.

Arkansas has the third-lowest average Social Security retired-worker check in the country, at $1,932.29 a month in December 2025. That places it 49th among the 50 states and the District of Columbia.

The state's median benefit was lower, at $1,841.90. That leaves a gap of $90.39 between the two measures.

A median below the average means the higher checks in the state pull the average above the midpoint. For a typical retiree in Arkansas, the median is the closer guide to a monthly deposit.

Both measures trail the national figures for the same month. Arkansas falls $139.01 a month short of the U.S. average retired-worker benefit. Its median sits exactly $150 below the national median.

The monthly shortfall equals about 6.7% of the national average. Over a full year, the gap in averages adds up. Twelve months at the Arkansas average comes to $23,187.48. The same 12 months at the national average comes to $24,855.60. The difference is $1,668.12.

Arkansas sits in a tight cluster near the bottom of the table. Its average is $5.14 above Louisiana's, which ranks second-lowest. It is $42.57 above Mississippi, the lowest in the country. Kentucky, one spot higher, averages $20.84 more.

The distance to the top is wider. Connecticut's average, the highest in the table, runs $376.07 a month above the Arkansas figure.

Arkansas had 513,912 retired-worker beneficiaries in December 2025. That is just under 1% of all retired workers collecting benefits nationwide. Among the five lowest-average states, that count trails Kentucky and Louisiana but tops Mississippi and New Mexico.

Social Security sets each retiree's check from that person's own work history. Lifetime earnings are a central input in the calculation. Higher earnings over a career generally lead to a larger monthly benefit.

Those rules work the same way in every state. A state's average is the total of its retirees' individual checks divided by the number of retirees.

Louisiana retirees collected an average Social Security retired-worker benefit of $1,927.15 a month in December 2025. That is the second-lowest average among the 50 states and D.C., ahead of only Mississippi.

The state's figure sits $144.15 below the national average for the same month. Over a full year, a $1,927.15 monthly check adds up to $23,125.80 before any deductions.

Louisiana's nearest neighbors in the ranking sit close by. Arkansas, with the third-lowest average, comes in just $5.14 higher at $1,932.29. Mississippi's average trails Louisiana's by $37.43. The distance to the top is far wider. Connecticut, the highest-average state, paid retired workers $381.21 more a month on average.

Louisiana's median benefit was $1,807.90, which is $119.25 below the state's own average. When a mean sits above the median, a smaller number of larger checks pulls the average above the typical payment.

Louisiana's midpoint is $184.00 below the national median. Among the 10 states covered in this list, only Mississippi posts a lower median, at $1,790.90.

The state counted 661,928 retired-worker beneficiaries in December 2025. That is the second-largest total among the five lowest-average states, behind Kentucky's 719,046. It is more than Mississippi's 493,663 and Arkansas's 513,912.

A state average blends hundreds of thousands of individual records into one number. Two retirees in the same state can collect very different amounts.

Claiming age is one factor a worker controls. For each month a person waits past full retirement age, the benefit grows by two-thirds of 1%. That works out to 8% for each full year of delay. The credits stop growing at age 70.

Full retirement age is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. Waiting from 67 to 70 adds three years of credits, or 24% on top of the full benefit. A worker due $1,000 a month at full retirement age would collect $1,240 by claiming at 70. The table does not show how many Louisiana retirees chose that route.

Mississippi ranked last in the nation for retired-worker Social Security benefits in December 2025. Its average check was $1,889.72 and its median was $1,790.90. Both were the lowest figures among the 50 states and D.C.

The average falls $181.58 short of the national average for the same month. Across 12 monthly payments, that shortfall comes to $2,178.96. The gap on the median is larger. Mississippi's midpoint benefit sits $201.00 below the national median.

Finishing last on both measures sets Mississippi apart from the top of the table, where the leader changes. Connecticut has the highest average, while New Jersey has the highest median. New Jersey's median sits $465.00 above Mississippi's.

Louisiana comes closest on the median. Its figure of $1,807.90 is $17.00 higher than Mississippi's.

On the average, Mississippi sits a clear step below its nearest neighbor. Louisiana, the second-lowest state, averaged $1,927.15. That is $37.43 more than Mississippi. No other pair of adjacent states in the bottom five is separated by as much. The next-widest gap, between Arkansas and Kentucky, is $20.84.

The state had 493,663 retired-worker beneficiaries. That is about 0.92% of the national total. Among the bottom five, only New Mexico has fewer.

Mississippi's median sits $98.82 below its average. At least half of the state's retired workers therefore receive less than the state average. A smaller share of larger checks pulls the mean upward. That spread is narrower than Louisiana's $119.25 and New Mexico's $128.77. It is wider than Kentucky's $77.23.

Louisiana, Arkansas and Kentucky join Mississippi in the bottom five, and all three are in the South. New Mexico is the one state in that group outside the South.

Mississippi does not tax Social Security benefits. CNBC reports that eight states do: Colorado, Connecticut, Minnesota, Montana, New Mexico, Rhode Island, Vermont and Utah.

Mississippi does levy an income tax. It exempts retirement income, provided the taxpayer meets retirement plan requirements. Pension income is not taxed by the state either.

#5556. Amazon earnings preview: AWS is booked up, and Wall Street wants to know what comes next

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:11 amOctober 28, 2026 at 8:11 am

Amazon reports third-quarter earnings Thursday afternoon with more demand for its cloud services than it can serve, driven by AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI along with growth in its traditional cloud business.

One big question for Wall Street going into the report is what Amazon might signal about next year’s spending as it tries to keep up with that demand.

CEO Andy Jassy said on an Andreessen Horowitz podcast last week that AWS capacity is largely booked for this year and next, along with “a good chunk of ’28.”

Amazon has said it expects to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditures this year, largely on AI and cloud infrastructure, up from its earlier plan of $200 billion. Even at that level, Jassy said, Amazon is “leaving a meaningful amount of demand on the table.”

Past spending pushed Amazon’s free cash flow to negative $7.6 billion for the 12 months ending in June, as the cost to add data centers, chips and other equipment exceeded the cash its operations brought in. Jassy gave no indication of slowing down, saying the company “could invest a lot more and it wouldn’t be a bad use of capital.”

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of about $202 billion, up 12% from a year ago, according to Yahoo Finance. That’s at the top of Amazon’s own forecast of $197 billion to $202 billion.

Analysts expect earnings of $1.96 per share, about the same as a year ago.

Amazon’s sales growth will likely look slower this time, about 12%, down from 20% last quarter. A big reason is timing. Prime Day, the company’s biggest sales event of the year, fell in the second quarter this year, rather than the third quarter as it did last year, so this quarter is up against a tougher comparison.

Amazon estimated in July that the shift would take nearly 4 percentage points off its growth rate this quarter. It hits online store sales hardest: analysts expect them to grow only about 3%, according to Zacks.

AWS: Amazon Web Services, the company’s cloud business, generates the majority of its operating profit. AWS revenue grew 37% to $42.2 billion in the second quarter, its fastest pace since 2021 and the fifth straight quarter of faster growth.

Analysts expect AWS revenue of about $45.4 billion this time, up 37.5%, according to Zacks. Wedbush is more optimistic, projecting growth of about 41%.

AWS had $496 billion in signed contracts it hadn’t yet delivered as of June, more than double the year before. That means its growth depends largely on how quickly Amazon can bring new data centers online.

“Capacity, not demand, is the constraint,” Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote of the industry in a note Sunday.

Jassy said on the a16z podcast that running AI models is still “an order of magnitude too expensive” for businesses to use them widely, and that Amazon’s custom chips, including its Trainium AI processors, are a big piece of bringing that cost down. Amazon said in July that its chip business was on pace for more than $25 billion in annual revenue.

Anthropic stake: Amazon’s reported earnings could look very different. That’s because its profit fluctuates significantly depending on the value of its stake in Anthropic.

Last quarter, $53.4 billion in pre-tax gains, mostly on Anthropic, pushed Amazon’s earnings to $5.75 per share, against expectations of $1.82.

Anthropic filed paperwork Monday for a planned IPO on the Nasdaq. Amazon’s stake in the AI company was valued at about $190 billion as of June 30, according to Amazon’s latest quarterly filing. That includes about $92 billion in gains on convertible notes, a form of loan that turns into stock, which haven’t yet been counted in Amazon’s profit. Those notes would convert to Anthropic stock when it goes public.

Anthropic is also one of Amazon’s biggest cloud customers. Its IPO filing shows commitments to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon’s computing capacity into the 2030s, behind the $114.5 billion it committed to Google, as GeekWire reported Tuesday. Anthropic also said in the filing that it has asked its cloud providers for more computing power than they were willing to supply.

Shopping agents: Amazon blocked Meta’s new Muse AI agent from its store last month, escalating a fight over who controls the customer relationship when software does the buying. Amazon said Muse broke its rule requiring agents to identify themselves.

Agents that shop on a customer’s behalf could bypass Amazon’s advertising business, which depends on people browsing its pages. Ad revenue grew 26% to $19.8 billion last quarter, and analysts expect about $20.8 billion this time, up 18%, according to Zacks.

“Investor questions remain on agentic commerce risk, particularly to advertising, but we see limited risk,” Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian wrote in an Oct. 16 note, citing Amazon’s logistics advantage and its role connecting shoppers with sellers.

Amazon is trying to give shoppers fewer reasons to look elsewhere. It now lists 250 million products sold on other retailers’ sites, about 2.5 times as many as in March, The Information reported Wednesday. On the seller side, Amazon opened its tools to outside AI agents in September, starting with Anthropic’s Claude.

Cloud rivals: Microsoft and Alphabet report quarterly results Wednesday afternoon, a day before Amazon. Microsoft’s report is its first under a new structure that breaks out Azure cloud revenue every quarter.

Check back with GeekWire on Thursday afternoon for coverage.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5554. IBM puts agentic workloads at the heart of its AI operating model

Agentic workloads present a new operating challenge for enterprises putting artificial intelligence into production. As autonomous systems take on ongoing responsibilities, organizations must support decisions and actions across their data, applications and infrastructure.

IBM Corp.’s approach draws on the experiences of clients scaling AI across their organizations. That work helped identify the requirements underpinning its AI operating model, according to Ritika Gunnar (pictured), chief performance marketing officer of IBM.

“As you’re more successful in using AI, especially as AI is taking action, you now have workloads that are continuously being utilized,” she said. “You are incented to be always on because those agents are always taking action for you.”

Gunnar spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier for IBM’s AI Operating Model interview series in an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed enterprise integration, data governance, human oversight and evaluating AI against business outcomes in preparation for IBM TechXchange 2026. (* Disclosure below.)

IBM’s AI operating model brings together four components that enterprises may already obtain from different providers. Applying them means accounting for established applications and business processes alongside emerging AI systems, Gunnar explained.

“You need to be able to integrate with your existing systems,” she said. “People aren’t going to run away from their SAP systems that exist, from their Salesforce systems that exist. What does it mean to integrate with those and have workloads that are representative of your past and your future together?”

The components have distinct roles: Data supplies current enterprise knowledge, workloads encompass applications and workflows, automation supports oversight and optimization, and hybrid cloud accommodates distributed operations. Their effectiveness depends on how they function together across agentic workloads, according to Gunnar.

“If you have your data and that data is feeding your systems, but you’re not really taking care of automation in a way where you have complete observability of all of your workloads with that AI infused, then you’re not necessarily having an optimal way of picking the right model or picking the right agents for those kinds of workloads,” she said.

The information supporting an agent’s decision may span operational systems, edge devices and context generated by other agents. Providing governed context requires enterprises to consider both the completeness of that information and how permissions travel with it, Gunnar explained.

“Our belief is if you can take data and if you can shift left a lot of the governance — a lot of the who has the right access to the right data at the right time — it becomes important because you flow that data in real time with the context and provenance of who actually has ownership of that data,” she said. “Therefore, the agents make much better decisions.”

Enterprises also depend on knowledge employees develop through experience rather than explicitly recording it in their systems. Prompts and other context can help convey that judgment, but capturing it remains an ongoing challenge, Gunnar pointed out.

“When you think about workloads today … there is a lot of it that will be autonomous in nature,” she said. “But in most cases, if you’re talking about your essential systems, you do have humans in the loop to be able to bring some of that tacit knowledge in place where the AI has not yet matured to be able to even get there.”

Agent activity generates logs of decisions and actions, while prompts record the instructions supplied to those systems. Together, that information supports an ongoing feedback loop between enterprise data and AI workloads, Gunnar explained.

“You can actually have multiple different permutations of that agent making a decision and having another set of eval loops actually doing an evaluation of, ‘Did that agent actually make the decisions?’” she said. “Would there have been a more performant way, a more accurate way, a more cost-effective way to be able to do that?”

Performance encompasses accuracy, timeliness and cost, with the intended business result guiding how those measures are assessed. Putting AI into production therefore requires organizations to examine the work itself alongside the technology supporting it, according to Gunnar.

“Make sure that you have all of these elements and that you’re really thinking about the outcomes, and you’re willing to start with what it means to take a look at the business process transformation,” she said. “That’s really where it’s at.”

#5553. Social Security tax cap history: 10 milestones from $3,000 in 1937 to $184,500 in 2026

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Social Security tax cap history in 10 milestones, from a $3,000 wage base in 1937 to the $184,500 limit the SSA announced for 2026

In 1937, the most any American worker could owe in Social Security tax for a full year was $30. That ceiling came from two numbers set under the 1935 Social Security Act. Workers paid a one percent tax, and only the first $3,000 of annual earnings counted. Employers paid a matching one percent. For 2026, the Social Security Administration has announced a cap of $184,500.

That cap goes by several names, including the Social Security wage base, the taxable maximum and the payroll tax cap. Each describes the same line: the highest amount of yearly earnings subject to the Social Security portion of payroll tax. A worker who earns more than the cap pays that tax only on earnings up to it.

For decades, the climb between those two figures depended on Congress. The cap stayed at $3,000 every year from 1937 through 1950. When it began rising in the 1950s, each increase needed a new act of Congress. Lawmakers kept setting new figures through legislation into the early 1970s.

The 1972 amendments changed the mechanism. They tied the cap to growth in average wages. Indexing took effect with the 1975 cap of $14,100. That link answers a common question about why the cap rises most years. When average wages grow, the cap follows by formula, with no vote required. Congress has still passed some one-time increases since then.

The tax rate has its own history. The one percent charged in 1937 later rose. In 1990, the rate reached 6.2 percent each for workers and employers. That is 12.4 percent combined, the same rate in place today. Medicare follows different rules. Its separate payroll tax has applied to all wages, with no cap, since 1994.

This slideshow traces Social Security tax cap history through 10 milestones. They run from the long freeze at $3,000 to the jumps from 1978 to 1981, the flat years from 2009 to 2011 and the recent run of increases. The 10 slides are a selection of turning points, not a year-by-year ledger. Each slide covers its own stretch of years and stands alone. A reader can start with whichever period matters most.

The first Social Security wage base was $3,000. When payroll taxes began in 1937, only the first $3,000 of a worker's annual earnings was taxed. That ceiling meant no worker could owe more than $30 for the year.

The tax traces to the Social Security Act of 1935. Congress passed that law two years before payroll tax collection began.

The 1937 rate was one percent for the employee. The employer paid a matching one percent on the same wages. Together, the two shares came to two percent of covered pay.

The wage base, also known as the taxable maximum, set the upper limit on earnings subject to that tax. Every dollar a worker earned up to $3,000 in a year faced the one percent rate. Every dollar earned beyond $3,000 went untouched by the Social Security tax.

The $30 limit follows directly from those two numbers. One percent of $3,000 is $30, the most any single worker could owe in 1937. The employer's matching share for that worker topped out at the same $30. The combined payroll tax on one employee's wages therefore could not exceed $60 for the year.

The cap shaped tax bills differently depending on pay. A worker who earned $2,000 in 1937 sat below the ceiling and owed one percent of the full amount, or $20. A worker who earned $5,000 paid tax on only the first $3,000. That worker's bill was $30, the same as someone who earned exactly $3,000.

Above the ceiling, the tax took a shrinking share of total pay as income rose. For the $5,000 earner, $30 equaled 0.6 percent of wages. A worker earning $10,000 also owed $30, which worked out to 0.3 percent.

The $3,000 ceiling was written as a fixed dollar amount. The 1937 rules did not tie it to wages. Raising it would take a new act of Congress.

The Social Security tax cap stayed at $3,000 in every year from 1937 through 1950. For 14 straight years, earnings above that amount were not subject to Social Security payroll tax, however much a worker made.

The cap, also known as the taxable maximum or the wage base, is the most a worker can earn in a year that still counts toward the Social Security payroll tax. Pay up to that line is taxed. Pay beyond it is not.

The $3,000 limit was set under the 1935 Social Security Act, and payroll taxes under that law began in 1937. In this era, the cap had no way to move on its own. Automatic adjustment tied to wages came decades later. Any change had to come from Congress, and none took effect before 1951.

Wages did not stand still over the same stretch. As pay rose, more of the earnings paid across the economy landed above $3,000. A growing share of total earnings therefore fell outside the reach of the tax.

A worker whose pay crossed $3,000 during these years moved from paying on every dollar to paying on only part of it.

The fixed dollar line also put a clear limit on each worker's tax bill. For a worker earning less than $3,000 a year, the tax applied to every dollar of wages. For a worker earning more, it applied only to the first $3,000. A raise above that line added nothing to the worker's Social Security tax. With the bill capped, a higher earner's Social Security tax shrank as a share of total pay each time that pay grew.

The same ceiling applied to employers. Their matching tax also stopped at the first $3,000 a worker earned. Payroll above the line carried no Social Security cost for the employer either.

The freeze ended when Congress raised the cap to $3,600 for 1951. That $600 step was the first change to the wage base since payroll taxes began.

Congress lifted the Social Security taxable maximum three times in the 1950s: to $3,600 for 1951, $4,200 for 1955 and $4,800 for 1959. Each step required a new act of Congress.

The taxable maximum is the ceiling on yearly pay subject to the Social Security payroll tax. Pay above that ceiling owes no Social Security tax.

The 1951 increase was the first change to the cap since payroll taxes began. It replaced the original $3,000 ceiling with $3,600. For anyone earning $3,600 or more, an extra $600 of yearly pay became taxable.

The next two steps followed the same pattern. Each added another $600. The increase for 1955 set the cap at $4,200. The increase for 1959 raised it to $4,800.

The steps came four years apart. By 1959 the cap stood $1,800 above its starting level, a 60 percent rise from $3,000.

In dollar terms, the three increases were identical. In relative terms, they were not. Each $600 step was added to a larger base than the one before. As a result, each raised the cap by a smaller share than the last. The 1951 increase was the largest of the three in proportional terms.

No formula produced these numbers. Each was a fixed dollar amount written into law. Moving the cap meant lawmakers had to agree on a new figure and pass it. Until the next act, the cap stayed put regardless of what happened to pay.

That design put the timing of every change in the hands of Congress. Taxable earnings for higher-paid workers could grow only when lawmakers chose to act. A worker earning $3,000 or less saw no change in taxable pay from any of the three increases. The cap rose only for earnings above the old line.

The 1950s established the legislated approach that the next two decades would continue.

Lawmakers doubled the Social Security wage base in eight years, raising it from $6,600 in 1966 to $13,200 in 1974. Every figure in that stretch came from legislation rather than a formula.

The wage base, also called the taxable maximum, is the most of a worker's annual earnings that can count toward Social Security payroll tax. Pay above that line is not subject to the tax. In this period, the line moved only when Congress wrote a new figure into law.

The cap stood at $6,600 in 1966. That was $1,800 higher than the $4,800 limit that applied for 1959. By 1968, the ceiling had reached $7,800, or $1,200 more than the 1966 level.

The next figure was $9,000 for 1972. It sat another $1,200 above the 1968 cap. As a share, though, that step was smaller. The move from 1966 to 1968 equaled about 18 percent, while the move from 1968 to 1972 came to about 15 percent.

Increases then grew larger and came faster. The cap rose to $10,800 in 1973, which was $1,800 above the 1972 amount and a 20 percent gain. It climbed again to $13,200 in 1974. That added $2,400 in one year, an increase of about 22 percent.

The cap was different in each of 1972, 1973 and 1974. The 1974 step was the largest dollar increase from 1966 through 1974.

A higher ceiling brought more earnings under the payroll tax for anyone paid above the old limit. Workers who earned no more than the old cap saw no change in how much of their pay was taxed.

The 1974 level also shows how far the cap moved in 15 years. At $13,200, it was 2.75 times the $4,800 limit that applied for 1959.

The $13,200 cap for 1974 was the last one set before automatic wage indexing took effect with the following year's limit.

Automatic wage indexing of the Social Security cap began with the 1975 taxable maximum of $14,100. From that year on, the ceiling on earnings subject to Social Security payroll tax rose by formula. The adjustment followed growth in average wages instead of waiting for a vote in Congress.

The mechanism came from the 1972 amendments to the Social Security Act. Those amendments created automatic adjustments to the wage base, linked to how much average wages grew.

Before indexing, the cap moved only when lawmakers passed new legislation. Every increase from the 1950s through 1974 worked that way, ending with a legislated cap of $13,200. The first indexed cap of $14,100 was $900 higher than that final legislated figure. That works out to an increase of about 6.8 percent.

The formula is the reason the Social Security wage cap usually changes from one year to the next. The ceiling tracks average pay. When average pay grows, the taxable maximum grows with it, and no new law is needed.

The first years under the formula show how it worked in practice. The cap reached $15,300 in 1976, an increase of $1,200 over 1975. It rose to $16,500 in 1977, another step of $1,200.

In percentage terms, those steps were about 8.5 percent and 7.8 percent. Identical dollar increases produced smaller percentage gains as the base grew.

Between 1975 and 1977, the wage base climbed $2,400, from $14,100 to $16,500. Measured from the last legislated cap of 1974, the total gain by 1977 was $3,300. The 1977 cap was 5.5 times the $3,000 limit in place when payroll taxes began in 1937.

Indexing did not remove Congress from the process entirely. Lawmakers have still passed some one-time increases to the cap. The automatic formula has continued alongside those legislated changes.

For a worker with earnings above the cap, the indexed figure sets the point each year at which Social Security payroll tax stops applying to further pay.

The Social Security wage cap rose from $17,700 in 1978 to $29,700 in 1981, a gain of $12,000 over three years. The 1977 amendments lifted the cap above the level that automatic wage indexing alone would have produced.

The cap marks the most a worker can earn in a year and still owe Social Security payroll tax on every dollar. Earnings past that line are not taxed for Social Security.

The 1978 cap of $17,700 was $1,200 above the $16,500 limit for 1977. That step matched the size of the yearly increases in 1976 and 1977, which were also $1,200 each.

The step into 1979 broke that pattern. The cap climbed to $22,900, up $5,200 from 1978. That one-year increase was more than four times the $1,200 rise of the year before. Measured as a share, the 1979 cap was about 29 percent higher than the 1978 cap.

The cap kept rising in 1980, reaching $25,900. That was $3,000 above the 1979 figure, an increase of about 13 percent.

In 1981 the cap rose again, to $29,700. The gain from 1980 was $3,800, or about 15 percent. That increase was larger than the 1980 step but smaller than the 1979 jump.

Taken together, the two steps after 1979 added $6,800. That is more than the 1979 increase alone, though it took two years rather than one.

Across the three years from 1978 to 1981, the cap grew by an average of $4,000 a year. The 1981 figure was about 68 percent higher than the 1978 figure. The 1979 increase alone accounted for $5,200 of the $12,000 total, or about 43 percent of the growth across the stretch.

The 1981 cap was also more than double the $14,100 limit of 1975, the first year the cap was set by wage indexing. It was nearly 10 times the $3,000 ceiling of 1937.

The Social Security taxable maximum climbed from $51,300 in 1990 to $72,600 in 1999. The same decade set the payroll tax rate at its current level and removed any wage limit from the Medicare tax.

The taxable maximum is the highest amount of yearly earnings subject to Social Security payroll tax. A worker pays the tax on every dollar up to that line. Earnings above it owe nothing more to Social Security for that year.

In 1990, the employee rate reached 6.2 percent. Employers paid a matching 6.2 percent, for a combined 12.4 percent. Both rates still apply today.

At the 1990 cap, a worker earning $51,300 or more owed at most $3,180.60 in Social Security tax. The employer owed the same amount. Together, the maximum combined payment on one worker's wages came to $6,361.20.

The cap reached $60,600 in 1994, up $9,300 from the 1990 level. A worker at or above that ceiling paid up to $3,757.20 in Social Security tax that year. With the employer's matching share, the combined maximum that year was $7,514.40.

The year 1994 also marked a change for Medicare. Since then, the separate Medicare payroll tax has applied to all wages, with no upper limit.

That split means a high earner stops owing one payroll tax once earnings pass the cap but keeps paying the other on every dollar. Both taxes come out of the same paycheck. They follow different rules on how much income they reach.

By 1999, the cap stood at $72,600, another $12,000 above the 1994 figure. That ceiling put the maximum employee contribution at $4,501.20. The combined employee and employer maximum reached $9,002.40.

Across the decade, the wage base rose by $21,300. That is an increase of about 42 percent from the 1990 level. The maximum employee contribution grew by $1,320.60 over the same span. The combined maximum on one worker's wages grew by $2,641.20.

The Social Security wage base sat at $106,800 for three straight years, from 2009 through 2011, because the automatic wage-indexing formula produced no increase. Before that pause, the cap climbed from $76,200 in 2000 to $102,000 in 2008.

The wage base marks the most a worker can earn in a year before Social Security payroll tax stops applying. No Social Security tax is due on earnings above that line. During the 2000s, a formula linked to average wage growth set the line.

Over the eight years from 2000 to 2008, the cap rose by $25,800, an increase of about one-third. By 2008, the taxable maximum had passed $100,000.

At the 6.2 percent employee rate, the most a worker could owe rose from $4,724.40 in 2000 to $6,324 in 2008. Employers paid a matching amount on the same wages.

The step into 2009 added $4,800, lifting the cap from $102,000 to $106,800. At that level, a worker's maximum Social Security tax at 6.2 percent came to $6,621.60 for 2009.

Then the figure stopped moving. The 2010 cap matched the 2009 cap exactly, and the 2011 cap matched both. Indexing yielded no increase for either year. The taxable maximum stayed at its 2009 level.

For higher earners, the ceiling on taxable pay held still for three years. A worker earning above $106,800 in each of those years had the same amount of pay subject to Social Security tax in 2011 as in 2009.

Increases resumed in 2012, when the cap rose to $110,100. That increase of $3,300 was smaller than the $4,800 step into 2009.

Measured across the whole stretch, the wage base grew from $76,200 in 2000 to $110,100 in 2012. That is a rise of $33,900 over 12 years, or about 44 percent. For a quarter of that span, from 2009 through 2011, the cap stood at a single figure.

The Social Security wage base rose from $118,500 in 2015 to $137,700 in 2020, an increase of $19,200 over five years. The cap stayed flat for 2015 and 2016 before resuming its climb in 2017.

The wage base, also called the taxable maximum, is the most a worker can earn in a year and still have every dollar taxed for Social Security. Earnings above that ceiling are not subject to Social Security tax for the year.

The 2015 ceiling of $118,500 carried over unchanged into 2016. For two straight years, the earnings limit sat at the same dollar figure. A worker earning well above the cap faced the same maximum Social Security tax bill in both years. At the 6.2 percent employee rate, that maximum was $7,347.

The cap moved again in 2017, rising to $127,200. That was an $8,700 increase in a single year, about 7.3 percent above the 2016 level. It was the largest one-year dollar gain in this stretch. The maximum employee tax rose to $7,886.40, which was $539.40 more than in 2016.

Later figures kept rising. The taxable maximum stood at $132,900 in 2019, which was $5,700 higher than the 2017 level. At the 2019 cap, the maximum employee tax was $8,239.80. By 2020, the cap reached $137,700, another $4,800 in one year.

At the 2020 cap, the most a worker could owe in Social Security tax was $8,537.40. Employers paid a matching amount on the same earnings. Combined, the maximum came to $17,074.80 for one employee earning $137,700 or more.

Across the full stretch from 2015 to 2020, the payroll tax cap grew by about 16.2 percent. The maximum employee tax rose by $1,190.40 over the same period, from $7,347 to $8,537.40. Those figures cover only earnings up to the ceiling. Pay above $137,700 in 2020 added nothing to a worker's Social Security tax.

The Social Security Administration announced a taxable maximum of $184,500 for 2026. That is the wage cap in effect for the 2026 tax year, $41,700 above the 2021 level of $142,800.

The cap marks the top of the earnings range that owes Social Security payroll tax. A worker's pay up to that amount is taxed. Earnings above it owe no Social Security tax for the rest of the calendar year.

In 2021, the limit stood at $142,800. It rose to $147,000 in 2022. That was an increase of $4,200, or about three percent.

The largest single-year move in this stretch came next. The wage base climbed to $160,200 in 2023, up $13,200 from 2022. That was a gain of about nine percent. It was more than three times the size of the previous year's increase.

Smaller annual gains followed. The cap reached $168,600 in 2024, up $8,400, or about five percent. It rose to $176,100 in 2025, a gain of $7,500, or about four percent. The 2026 level of $184,500 adds another $8,400, about five percent. Between 2021 and 2026, the taxable maximum rose about 29 percent.

The cap also sets the most a high earner pays in Social Security tax. At the 2026 limit, the maximum employee contribution is $11,439. The employer pays a matching $11,439, for a combined maximum of $22,878. That compares with a combined maximum of $17,707.20 in 2021.

The employee maximum was $8,853.60 in 2021, $9,114 in 2022, $9,932.40 in 2023 and $10,453.20 in 2024. It reached $10,918.20 in 2025. The largest yearly jump came in 2023, when the top employee contribution rose $818.40. Over the full stretch from 2021 to 2026, it climbed $2,585.40.

Ideas to raise the cap sharply or to remove it altogether have been debated. None has replaced the current limit, and the $184,500 figure applies to 2026 earnings.

#5552. Blue Origin leases former Bartell Drugs warehouse south of Seattle for new manufacturing site

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:25 amOctober 28, 2026 at 12:33 pm

Blue Origin is taking over an industrial building in Des Moines, Wash., where the Jeff Bezos-founded space company plans a mix of lab, development and light production work, the company confirmed to GeekWire.

The 265,922-square-foot facility, known as Prologis Park SeaTac 3, was previously a Bartell Drugs distribution center just south of Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Blue Origin said that at full capacity over the long term, the site is expected to support hundreds of employees.

KING 5 first reported the news Tuesday, citing a state environmental application filed in September that lists Blue Origin Manufacturing LLC at the building’s address, 21202 24th Ave. S. A pre-application under review by the city indicates the property could be used for research and development of commercial satellites, the station reported.

Commercial real estate firm Newmark announced a lease for the entire building last week without naming the tenant.

“The manufacturing project that will be using this property is cutting-edge and we are excited about the job growth and possibilities that it represents for our region,” Newmark Executive Vice Chairman Thad Mallory said in a news release.

With roughly 33,000 residents, the small city of Des Moines is becoming something of an aerospace hub.

Blue Origin’s new location is around the corner from where Shield AI is building X-Forge 3, a 420,000-square-foot facility that will make the company’s X-BAT autonomous fighter jet. Shield AI said last month it expects to have 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s, and that it’s looking for another 1 million square feet.

“It’s all about labor and access to power,” Mallory told KING 5, referring to the advanced manufacturing projects coming to the area.

Blue Origin is headquartered in nearby Kent, Wash., about 5 miles from the Des Moines site.

The company is working to get its New Glenn rocket flying again after one exploded during a ground engine test in May, which damaged its Florida launch pad. New Glenn is slated to carry Blue’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander on NASA’s Artemis 3 mission, a test in Earth orbit planned for mid-2027 ahead of a crewed moon landing targeted for 2028.

#5550. Norway tops the 2026 retirement index — the U.S. ranks 24th of 44

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The 2026 Natixis Global Retirement Index ranks 44 countries — see how Norway, Ireland, the Netherlands and Denmark score and why the U.S. slipped to 24th

No country spends more on health per person than the U.S. Yet the U.S. finished 24th of 44 countries in the 2026 Natixis Global Retirement Index. That result sits well below its best showing of the past decade — 14th, in 2016.

The index comes from Natixis Investment Managers, which builds it with CoreData Research and publishes a new edition each September. Scott Staton reported the 2026 results for Boldin on October 13, 2026. Each country receives an overall percentage score drawn from four categories: health, finances in retirement, material wellbeing and quality of life. A country can lead one category and trail in another. Its overall rank reflects the balance across all four.

European countries fill most of the upper end of the list. Nine of the top 10 countries are European. Australia, at 77%, is the only top-10 entry from outside the continent. Norway holds first place at 83% for the second year running. Ireland is second at 81%, and the Netherlands is third at 79%. Switzerland is fourth, also at 79%, and Denmark is fifth at 78%.

Category leadership is spread across several countries. Luxembourg posts the highest health score, at 94%. Finland leads on quality of life. Ireland ranks first on finances in retirement, and Denmark tops material wellbeing.

The U.S. result points in the other direction. Its overall score slipped from 70% to 68%, and its rank fell from 21st. It now sits between Cyprus and Japan. In finances in retirement, the country fell eight places to 18th. Its material wellbeing ranking also dropped as unemployment and income equality got worse.

The slides that follow are a selection from the full ranking, not a complete list. Four cover European systems that finished near the top — Norway, Ireland, the Netherlands and Denmark. Each was chosen for a specific result, from first place overall to a leading category score. The fifth looks at the U.S. and breaks down where it lost ground, where it held steady and where it improved. For readers comparing national retirement systems, the category scores show where each country gains and loses points.

Norway is the top-ranked country in the 2026 Natixis Global Retirement Index, with an overall score of 83%. It also finished first in the previous edition, which makes 2026 its second straight year at No. 1.

Boldin reported the 2026 results, which show a narrow margin at the top. Ireland, in second place at 81%, sits two points behind Norway.

Norway's overall score rests on strong results in three of the index's four categories. It scores 92 for health, 90 for quality of life and 81 for material wellbeing.

None of those marks is the highest in its category. Norway reaches first place overall without leading any single category. Its rank comes from consistent scores across the board rather than one standout result.

On health, Norway's 92 matches Ireland's score, sits just below Switzerland's 93 and is higher than the Netherlands' 88 and Denmark's 86. On quality of life, its 90 is higher than Denmark's 87 and the 82 that Ireland and Switzerland each record. On material wellbeing, its 81 edges the Netherlands' 80 and Ireland's 77 but trails Denmark's 83.

Finances in retirement is Norway's lowest category score, at 70. Ireland, at 76, and Switzerland, at 74, both rank above it on that measure. Norway still finishes ahead of the Netherlands, at 67, and Denmark, at 61.

Norway's retirement system includes a public reserve fund called the Government Pension Fund. Pensions there are linked to the Social Security Base Amount, known in Norwegian as Grunnbeløpet, or G. The country also pays a special supplement to people whose pension is low.

The U.S., 24th overall at 68%, trails Norway in all four categories. Its health score is 80 against Norway's 92. On material wellbeing the U.S. scores 55, and on quality of life it scores 72. Finances in retirement is where the U.S. comes closest, at 67 against Norway's 70.

Ireland ranks second in the 2026 Natixis Global Retirement Index with an overall score of 81%. It also places first in the finances in retirement category with a score of 76, a position it has held for two years running.

Finances in retirement takes in measures such as inflation, government debt and tax pressure. No country in the 2026 index posts a higher score in this category than Ireland. Holding that top spot in consecutive editions means the lead is not a single-year result.

Other high-ranked countries trail Ireland on this measure. Switzerland, fourth overall, scores 74. Norway, the overall leader, scores 70. The Netherlands scores 67, and Denmark scores 61. Norway's lead in the overall table does not carry over to this category.

Ireland's other category results run higher than its finance score. It scores 92 on health, level with Norway. Its quality of life score is 82, the same as Switzerland's. Material wellbeing comes in at 77.

That spread means the category Ireland leads is also its lowest score of the four. Its finance score of 76 sits just below its material wellbeing result. The pattern shows that a first-place category finish measures Ireland against other countries. It does not mark the country's strongest area in absolute terms.

In the overall standings, Ireland finishes two points behind Norway. Its finance lead does not close that gap. Norway posts higher scores on material wellbeing and quality of life.

Ireland's position marks a long climb. In 2013, the country placed 25th overall. Today only Norway ranks above it.

In Ireland, benefits from the mandatory pension scheme are not tied to how much a person earns. A self-employed worker can expect the same benefits as an employee with a contribution record of the same length.

The country also has a means-tested State Pension (Non-Contributory). It can be paid as an alternative to the contributory pension.

The Netherlands ranks third in the 2026 Natixis Global Retirement Index, with an overall score of 79%. It moved up three places in this edition, reaching its best position since the index began.

The index scores each of its 44 countries in four categories: health, finances in retirement, material wellbeing and quality of life. The Dutch results are 88 for health, 67 for finances in retirement, 80 for material wellbeing and 81 for quality of life.

The Netherlands leads none of the four categories. It reaches third place with three scores in the 80s and no first-place result.

Health is the highest Dutch score, at 88. Norway and Ireland each post 92 on health, and Denmark, fifth overall, posts 86.

Finances in retirement is the lowest of the four Dutch scores, at 67. Ireland leads that category at 76. Switzerland scores 74 and Norway scores 70. Denmark is lower than the Netherlands on this measure, at 61.

Material wellbeing is a stronger area for the Dutch. Denmark leads that category at 83. Norway scores 81, and the Netherlands follows at 80.

The Dutch quality of life score of 81 sits just below Ireland and Switzerland, which each post 82. Norway scores 90 in that category, and Denmark scores 87.

Switzerland, fourth in the ranking, posts the same overall score of 79%. The two countries reach that total by different routes. Switzerland is stronger on health, at 93, and on finances in retirement. The Netherlands is stronger on material wellbeing, where Switzerland scores 68.

The U.S. posts the same finances in retirement score as the Netherlands, at 67%. The gap between the two countries shows up in the other three categories, where every Dutch score is higher.

Part of the Dutch retirement setup is decided at the workplace. Employees in the Netherlands are typically required to take part in the pension scheme their employer offers.

Denmark places fifth overall in the 2026 Natixis Global Retirement Index, with a score of 78%. It leads all 44 countries in the index on material wellbeing, with a category score of 83.

Material wellbeing is one of four categories that Natixis Investment Managers and CoreData Research combine into each country's overall result.

The other countries in the index's top five all score lower in this category. Norway, first overall, scores 81 on material wellbeing. The Netherlands, third overall, scores 80. Ireland, in second place, scores 77. Switzerland, ranked fourth, scores 68, the lowest material wellbeing result among the index's top five.

Denmark outscores Norway in this category, even though Norway finishes higher overall.

Quality of life is Denmark's other strong category. Its score of 87 is the second highest among the index's top five countries. Norway, at 90, is the only one of the five to score higher. Switzerland and Ireland each post 82 on quality of life, and the Netherlands posts 81.

Health is a weaker area for Denmark. Its health score is 86, the lowest among the five top-ranked countries. Switzerland scores 93 on health, Norway and Ireland each score 92, and the Netherlands scores 88.

Finances in retirement is Denmark's weakest category. Its score of 61 is the lowest of any country in the index's top five. Norway scores 70 on finances, and the Netherlands scores 67. Switzerland scores 74, and Ireland leads the whole index in this category at 76.

The pattern shows how the index's categories offset one another. Denmark holds the top material wellbeing score of any country, yet it has the lowest health and finance scores among the top five.

Some basic services in Denmark come from the state. Older people in Denmark receive a state pension as well as help with care. The country's health system is funded through taxes. Patients pay nothing for it.

The U.S. ranks 24th of 44 countries in the 2026 Natixis Global Retirement Index, down from 21st a year earlier. Its overall score fell 2 points, from 70% to 68%.

That is a three-place drop in a single edition. Three of the four category rankings moved down, and only one improved.

Finances in retirement produced the steepest fall. The U.S. now ranks 18th in that category, with a score of 67%. Inflation was one weak point, and the country slid to 30th on that measure. Government debt was another. The U.S. ranks 40th of 44 on debt, near the bottom of the index.

Tax pressure moved the other way. The U.S. climbed one place on that measure, to 11th.

Health also slipped. The U.S. fell one place to 25th in the health category, with a score of 80%. That leaves its health ranking one spot below its overall position.

Material wellbeing is the weakest of the four U.S. category scores, at 55%. The country dropped four places in that category to 28th. Income per person held steady at sixth. That leaves a 22-place gap between the country's income ranking and its material wellbeing ranking.

Quality of life was the one category where the U.S. gained ground. It rose three places to 22nd, with a score of 72%. Environmental scores drove most of that improvement.

Natixis survey data shows how American investors view some of these pressures. The firm's 2025 Global Survey of Individual Investors covered 7,050 investors in 21 countries, each with at least $100,000 to invest. Among U.S. respondents, 76% said they expect public debt to cut their retirement benefits. Health costs were a bigger worry in the U.S. than elsewhere. In the survey, 35% of U.S. investors said they worry about going broke paying for health and long-term care, against a global average of 24%.

Natixis's 2026 advisor survey pointed to a separate risk, one that sits with savers. Advisors named unrealistic return expectations as the biggest mistake investors make. Investors expected returns of 10.7% a year above inflation. Advisors put a more realistic figure at 8.8%.

#5549. Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert exits board of directors, wraps up his run at the wireless giant

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 9:51 amOctober 28, 2026 at 10:17 am

Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert is hanging up his magenta hat, leaving the wireless giant’s board of directors and vice chair role effective Nov. 1.

Sievert will also leave the board’s Transaction Committee, according to a federal filing. His departure comes a year after he handed the CEO job to Srini Gopalan.

A company spokesperson said via email that the vice chair role was structured as a one-year term, adding that Sievert has “been a valued strategic advisor throughout the leadership transition, and we’re incredibly grateful for his contributions.”

T-Mobile said in the filing that his departure “is not the result of any disagreement with the Company on any matter relating to its operations, policies or practices.”

Sievert joined T-Mobile in 2012 as executive vice president and chief marketing officer, the same year John Legere became CEO. He later became president and chief operating officer and was mentored by Legere before succeeding him as chief executive in 2020. He served as CEO for about five and a half years.

Sievert was a central figure in T-Mobile’s campaign to brand itself the “Un-carrier.” During his time at the company, T-Mobile grew from fewer than 30 million customers to more than 130 million by September 2025, a period that included its merger with Sprint.

Once the scrappy outsider, Bellevue, Wash.-based T-Mobile currently ranks second among U.S. telecom companies by market capitalization, behind Verizon and ahead of AT&T.

Sievert previously worked at Microsoft, AT&T Wireless, E-Trade, IBM and Procter & Gamble.
