#5547. Salesforce to buy customer service automation startup Cresta for reported $2.7B

Salesforce Inc. has agreed to buy Cresta Intelligence Inc., a venture-backed provider of customer service software.

The cloud giant didn’t disclose the financial terms in its late Monday announcement of the deal. The Information reported that Salesforce is paying $2.7 billion.

Cresta’s platform uses artificial intelligence to answer customer inquiries. It can also perform more advanced tasks such as scheduling doctor’s appointments. The platform personalizes its output based on each customer’s preferences, past interactions with the support team and related data.

Companies can customize Cresta by creating AI voice agents optimized for specific support request categories. For example, an electronics retailer could develop an agent focused on processing device returns. Cresta makes it possible to customize details such as the AI model that powers an agent and its regulatory compliance guardrails.

The platform can split complex support requests into smaller tasks to ease processing. A company could use one agent to interpret a ticket, another to find relevant help desk articles and a third to scan those articles for troubleshooting advice. Such agent ensembles often provide faster response times than a single multi-purpose agent. They save time by parallelizing tasks that would usually have to be carried out after one another.

Cresta ships its platform with an agent called Deputy. It’s geared toward particularly complex support tickets that require multiple employees to process. Deputy automatically collects the information needed to fulfill the user’s request and then loops in the relevant workers. From there, it manages follow-up tasks such as sending reminders about outstanding tasks.

Another agent provides human support representatives with real-time guidance during customer conversations. Cresta can, for example, point out potential upselling opportunities. It can also pull relevant information from external systems.

The company offers its core support automation features alongside various related tools. A feature called Opera enables organizations to fine-tune AI models for specific customer service use cases. Another tool, Synthetic Customers, provides AI-generated support conversations. Companies teams can use that data to test the reliability of newly created AI agents.

“By uniting our platform with Salesforce, we will realize our full vision at scale, embedding real-time conversation intelligence and agentic experiences directly into Salesforce’s first-class customer service Platform,” said Cresta Chief Executive Officer Ping Wu.

The deal is the second multibillion-dollar acquisition that Salesforce has made in the customer service market this year. It previously agreed to buy Fin Inc., formerly Intercom Inc, for $3.6 billion. Like Cresta, the company developed an AI platform capable of automatically answering support requests.

Salesforce’s largest acquisition this year is the $5.66 billion purchase of Braze Inc. it signed last month. The deal will buy it an AI marketing platform that can automatically deliver personalized promotions to customers.

Salesforce expects to close both the Braze and Cresta deals in its 2028 fiscal year, which starts next February.

#5546. 15 things to know about 401(k) balances, savings targets and habits

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The average 401(k) balance by age climbs from $7,259 under 25 to $330,186 at 65 and older, while medians and savings habits show where typical savers stand

A typical 401(k) holds far less than the overall average suggests. A 2026 Vanguard analysis put the overall average 401(k) balance at $167,970, while the median came in at $44,115. The median marks the midpoint of all accounts, with half holding more and half holding less. That makes it a closer picture of where an ordinary saver stands. The average gets pulled higher. A relatively smaller number of high-balance accounts could be causing that gap.

That distinction matters for anyone checking their own progress. Comparing a personal balance with the average alone can make a normal account look small. Looking at both numbers side by side gives a more grounded benchmark.

Not everyone saves through a workplace plan. As of 2025, 56% of Americans took part in workplace retirement savings plans. A separate figure shows that 45% of workers took part in retirement plans outside the workplace. The two numbers cover different groups and should be read on their own.

This guide looks at the average 401(k) balance by age alongside the median for each age band, using figures from a 2026 analysis. The average climbs at every step, from $7,259 for savers under 25 to $330,186 for those 65 and older. The median rises through ages 55 to 64, then dips for the 65-and-older group.

The numbers alone don't say what to do next. After the age bands, the slides turn to targets and habits. Those include saving a multiple of annual income by certain ages, setting aside 5% to 15% of each paycheck and raising contributions a little each year. Collecting the full employer match gets its own slide. Later slides cover catch-up contributions at 50, turning a 401(k) into retirement income and keeping fees and early withdrawals in check.

Each slide stands on its own. Readers can jump straight to their own decade. Targets vary with retirement goals and lifestyle. The information here is general and is not investment or tax advice.

The average 401(k) balance across all ages is $167,970, and the median is $44,115, according to a 2026 Vanguard analysis cited by Ally. Both numbers describe the same pool of savers, but each one answers a different question.

The average is the mean. It comes from adding every account balance together and dividing the total by the number of accounts. Every dollar in every account counts toward the result.

The median works differently. It is the balance in the middle once all accounts are sorted from smallest to largest. Making the largest account bigger or the smallest account smaller does not change it.

That difference shapes how each figure moves over time. A sharp gain in a handful of very large accounts can lift the mean on its own. The median shifts only when enough accounts cross from one side of the midpoint to the other.

Each figure gives a different yardstick for a personal balance. A saver who compares an account with $167,970 is measuring against a figure that every account helps set, large or small. A saver who compares an account with $44,115 is measuring against the account at the exact midpoint.

The average shows how much money the accounts would hold if the total were split evenly among savers. The median shows where a typical account actually lands.

Both figures combine all age groups. A worker in their first job and a worker close to retirement are counted in the same totals. Neither number is a benchmark for any single stage of a career.

Each figure is also a single snapshot from 2026. They show where balances stood, not how quickly any individual account grew to reach that level. A saver's own balance reflects years of contributions, market performance and withdrawals that the snapshot does not capture.

The figures cover 401(k) accounts only. They do not capture savings held in IRAs, taxable brokerage accounts or other retirement plans. A household with money spread across several account types may have more set aside than its 401(k) balance alone shows.

A relatively smaller number of high-balance accounts could be what lifts the overall average 401(k) balance to $167,970, well above the median of $44,115. Ally presents those large accounts as a possible cause of the gap, not a proven one.

Both figures come from a 2026 Vanguard analysis and describe the same set of accounts. Each one answers a different question about that set.

An average, or mean, adds every balance together and divides the total by the number of accounts. Every dollar in every account feeds into that result. A single very large balance raises the figure for the whole group. A handful of them can move it a long way.

A median ignores how big the biggest accounts are. It sorts every balance from smallest to largest and reports the one in the middle. If the largest account in a group doubled overnight, the median would not budge. The average would rise.

Statisticians describe the median as robust, or resistant to outliers. That is why it is often the preferred figure for measures with a few extreme values, such as household income or home prices.

Data with this shape is called right-skewed, or positively skewed. Most values cluster toward the low end, while a long tail of large values stretches toward the high end. In that kind of distribution, the mean typically lands above the median.

Retirement account balances fit that shape. A balance cannot fall below zero, but there is no ceiling on how large it can grow. That leaves room for a long upper tail and none for a matching lower one.

The pattern repeats across age groups. A 2026 analysis that breaks balances down by age shows the average above the median in every band. That holds from savers under 25 through those 65 and older.

For a saver measuring a personal balance against national numbers, the median offers the more realistic yardstick. The average still measures total assets spread across all accounts, but it says less about where most individual savers sit.

Savers under 25 hold an average 401(k) balance of $7,259 and a median balance of $2,234, according to a 2026 analysis. Both are the lowest figures for any age band in that data.

The spread between the two numbers is already wide at this age. Most savers in this group hold far less than the average suggests. For someone under 25 checking their progress, the $2,234 median is the more realistic comparison point.

The first goal in this decade is to make regular contributions a habit. In a 401(k), contributions come straight out of each paycheck. Saving then continues without a fresh decision every month.

Choosing an amount that fits the budget helps the habit last. A manageable contribution is easier to keep up than one that strains each paycheck.

Collecting the full employer match is the other early priority. A worker who contributes at least enough to qualify for the whole match leaves none of the employer's matching money unclaimed.

Two setup steps are easy to miss in a first job with a retirement plan. One is choosing the investments the contributions go into. The other is naming beneficiaries, the people who would receive the account if the saver dies.

Starting early gives compounding more time to work. Money contributed before 25 has more years to grow than money added later. Any returns it earns can then produce returns of their own.

Savers aged 25 to 34 hold an average 401(k) balance of $50,261 and a median balance of $18,732, according to a 2026 analysis. For a typical early-career saver, the median is the closer reference point.

In this band, the average lands well above the median. A balance near $18,732 is ordinary for savers in this age range.

The band covers the late 20s and the early 30s. The 30s are a decade to speed up retirement saving as careers advance and incomes grow.

A 401(k) is seldom the only claim on a paycheck at this stage. Buying a house, paying down debt, starting a family and investing in an IRA all compete for the same income. Each of those goals draws on money that could otherwise go into a workplace plan.

An IRA is a retirement account opened outside the workplace, separate from an employer's 401(k). Money put into one still adds to a saver's retirement savings. It does not appear in a 401(k) balance, though. The figures for this band may therefore not capture everything a saver in this age range has set aside for retirement.

Savers ages 35 to 44 hold an average 401(k) balance of $120,742 and a median balance of $46,919, according to a 2026 analysis. The median is the figure closer to what a typical account in this age band holds.

The gap between those two numbers is wide for this group. A saver in their late 30s with a balance well under the average may still sit near the middle of their peers. Checking an account against both figures gives a clearer sense of standing than the average alone.

The 30s are a decade for speeding up retirement saving as careers and incomes grow. Rising pay can create room to put more toward a 401(k).

A raise or a promotion offers a clear moment to act. Increasing the share of each paycheck that goes into the plan at the same time as a pay increase means the higher contribution arrives alongside more income. Raising the rate later, without a pay increase, lowers take-home pay. Pairing the two changes ties the decision to an event that already alters the paycheck.

Some workplace plans offer auto-escalation. The feature raises the contribution rate automatically over time. The saver does not have to remember to make each change. Workers can check their plan documents or benefits portal to see whether their plan includes it.

The investment mix deserves a fresh look during these years too. A portfolio chosen early in a career may no longer match how far away retirement is. It may also no longer match how much market risk the saver is willing to accept.

A review should test the current allocation against both measures. One is the time left before retirement. The other is the saver's comfort with swings in the account's value. An allocation that fails either test is a reason to adjust it.

Savers ages 45 to 54 hold an average 401(k) balance of $214,991 and a median balance of $78,730, according to a 2026 analysis. The typical account in this band sits well below the average figure.

For a saver in this decade, the median is the more practical yardstick. An account near $78,730 sits around the middle of its age group, even though it trails the average by a wide margin.

The contribution rate should keep pace with salary growth through these years. Pay often rises in this stretch of a career. If the percentage stays flat, each raise lifts the dollar amount saved but not the share of income going to retirement. Raising the rate along with salary keeps saving in step with earnings.

Asset allocation needs a fresh look in the mid-40s and early 50s. The bigger the balance, the more the investment mix shapes how the account performs.

Two items specific to 401(k) plans also call for review at this stage. The first is how much of the account sits in the employer's own company stock. That holding ties part of a saver's retirement money to the same company that pays the saver's salary.

The second is any decision about borrowing from the 401(k) through a plan loan. Money taken out as a loan is no longer invested in the account until it is paid back.

An IRA is a possible additional account for savers in this group. It is opened and held separately from the workplace plan.

Savers aged 55 to 64 hold an average 401(k) balance of $305,006 and a median balance of $107,269, according to a 2026 analysis cited by Ally. At this stage, the main goal shifts from growing retirement savings to protecting them.

For a saver checking progress in this band, the median is the closer benchmark. Half the accounts hold more than $107,269 and half hold less.

These years usually fall near the end of a working career. That timing changes which questions matter most. Ally treats the period as a turning point and centers its guidance on three tasks.

The first is reviewing investment risk. An allocation picked decades earlier was built for a long horizon. A saver a few years from needing the money has a much shorter one. A review checks whether the current level of risk still fits the time left before withdrawals begin.

The second is planning future withdrawals. Savers in this band are nearing the point where the account stops mainly taking in contributions and starts paying money out. Ally advises mapping out that plan before the first withdrawal comes due. The plan and the risk review are linked. The expected timing of withdrawals sets how long each part of the balance has left to stay invested.

The third is watching for early-withdrawal penalties. Pulling money out of a 401(k) too soon can trigger them. Ally flags these charges for savers at this stage. The same caution applies to anyone weighing the account as a source of cash for expenses before retirement.

Savers aged 65 and older hold an average 401(k) balance of $330,186 and a median balance of $103,202, according to a 2026 analysis cited by Ally. That average is the highest of any age group in the data, while the median sits below the one for the group just before it.

Savers aged 55 to 64 have a median balance of $107,269 in the same analysis. For the 65-and-older group, that midpoint slips to $103,202. No other age band in the data shows the median falling.

The average moves the other way. It climbs from $305,006 for ages 55 to 64 to $330,186 for savers 65 and older. With one measure rising and the other falling, the distance between them is wider in this band than in the one before it.

The analysis gives no reason for the split. The figures record where each age group stood, not what drove the change.

The band itself is built differently from most of the others. The middle groups each span 10 years, from 25 to 34 through 55 to 64. The 65-and-older group has no upper age limit. That means one pair of figures covers savers at every age from 65 upward. The under-25 band is the only other open-ended group, at the opposite end of the table.

Even after the dip, the median for this group remains above the medians for every age band younger than 55. Only the 55-to-64 group posts a higher midpoint.

For a saver at or past 65 who wants to compare a personal balance with the middle of this group, the median of $103,202 is the closer benchmark. The average of $330,186 sits well above what a typical account in this band holds.

Many people in their early 60s still contribute to a 401(k). At that stage, they are also deciding when and how to start drawing money out.

A salary-multiple benchmark sets retirement savings goals as a share of pay. The targets are one times annual income saved by age 30, three times by 40, five times by 50 and seven times by 60.

Ally lays out these milestones in its guide to 401(k) balances by age. The guide does not name the research behind them. It offers the multiples as suggested targets rather than fixed rules.

The yardstick ties savings to income instead of a set dollar amount. The goal moves with earnings. A higher salary means a higher target, and a lower salary means a lower one. Two savers of the same age can be on track with very different balances.

Checking progress takes one step. A saver divides the current retirement balance by annual pay and compares the result with the multiple for the nearest milestone age. The answer is a ratio, not a dollar figure. That makes it usable at any income level.

The milestones rise by two times annual income each decade after 30. The first checkpoint asks for one year of pay. Each later one adds two more years of pay to the total. The target grows by the same amount from one decade to the next.

The multiples measure the whole balance, not yearly contributions. Contribution rates are a separate question. A saver can reach a milestone through steady saving, investment growth or both.

The right number for any one saver depends on that person's retirement goals and expected lifestyle, according to the guide. A saver who expects to spend more in retirement may need more than the benchmark suggests.

Debt repayment is part of the picture for many savers. For people paying down loans, Ally's guidance is to handle both at once. That means continuing to save for retirement while staying on the loan repayment schedule. Under that approach, retirement saving does not wait until the debt is paid off.

Set aside 5% to 15% of every paycheck in a tax-advantaged retirement account. A 401(k), a traditional IRA and a Roth IRA all fit that description.

The guideline is a share of pay, not a dollar amount. Two savers at the same rate put away different sums if they earn different salaries. A raise lifts the dollar contribution even when the percentage stays the same.

The range is wide enough to fit very different household budgets. Rent, childcare, loan payments and other bills all draw on the same paycheck. A saver with heavy fixed costs may sit near the bottom of the range. One with more room may sit near the top. Either end meets the guideline.

Because it is stated as a percentage, the range applies at any age and income. A worker in a first job and one nearing retirement can use the same yardstick. What changes over a career is the number of dollars the percentage produces.

The guideline is not tied to one type of account. A 401(k) is sponsored by an employer, and contributions usually come out of each paycheck automatically. A traditional IRA and a Roth IRA are individual accounts opened outside the workplace. A worker whose employer offers no plan can still aim for the same range through an IRA.

The three accounts handle taxes differently. Traditional accounts generally defer income tax until money is withdrawn. Roth accounts take after-tax contributions, and qualified withdrawals come out tax-free. Which treatment fits better depends on each saver's own tax situation.

Savers who can't yet set aside 5% to 15% of each paycheck can start with a smaller share and raise it by 1% every year. The increases keep going until contributions land inside that range.

The approach fits a 401(k), a traditional IRA or a Roth IRA. All three are tax-advantaged accounts, and the yearly step works the same way in each.

Starting small lets a saver begin at a level the current budget can handle. The alternative is waiting until the full range feels affordable, with nothing going into the account in the meantime.

Even a modest first contribution builds the account and the habit together. In a 401(k), contributions come out of each paycheck through payroll deduction. The money reaches the plan before the saver can spend it. Saving becomes routine from the first pay period.

Some workplace plans can handle the yearly increase on their own through a feature called auto-escalation. Once it is turned on, the plan lifts the contribution rate on a set schedule. The saver does not need to submit a new contribution election each year.

Not every plan offers auto-escalation. The plan's own materials show whether the feature is available, how often the rate rises and whether the increases stop at a set level.

Without the feature, the saver makes the change by hand. That means updating the 401(k) contribution rate through the plan once a year. In an IRA, the same step means raising the amount sent into the account.

When an employer offers a 401(k) match, contribute at least enough of your own pay to collect all of it. That contribution level serves as a floor for anyone whose plan includes a match.

A match is money an employer adds to a worker's account based on what the worker contributes. The formula differs from plan to plan. Each plan's own documents set out the terms, including how much a worker must put in to receive the full amount.

The match is tied directly to the worker's own contributions. A worker who contributes below the match level leaves part of the employer's offered money unclaimed. Contributing at or above that level captures all of it.

The matched money also adds to the account without coming out of the worker's paycheck. Only the worker's own contribution reduces take-home pay.

The advice to capture the full match applies at every age. It is among the first steps for savers in their 20s, when the habit of regular contributions is just forming. It also appears among the general steps for improving a 401(k) balance at any point in a career.

Capturing the full match is a separate goal from a broader savings-rate target. A saver can keep contributions at or above the match level while working toward a higher overall rate. The two goals run side by side, with the match level as the minimum.

Workers become eligible for catch-up contributions at age 50. A catch-up contribution is money added to a retirement plan on top of the regular yearly contribution amount.

Eligibility begins at 50 and does not end when a saver leaves their 50s. It gives workers in the years before retirement a separate way to add to an account beyond the standard amount.

Timing affects how far that money can go. A dollar contributed at 50 has fewer years to grow before retirement than a dollar contributed in a person's 20s or 30s.

The Thrift Savings Plan, the retirement savings plan for federal employees, attaches a specific condition to catch-up contributions. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's National Finance Center describes the rule. A federal employee must expect to contribute the full yearly maximum of regular contributions, either to the TSP or to a comparable tax-deferred employer plan.

TSP catch-up contributions come out of the employee's pay. Under that requirement, catch-up money is added on top of a full regular contribution rather than replacing part of it.

That condition is a TSP rule for federal employees. It should not be read as a general 401(k) rule. Workers saving through a 401(k) can check the plan's documents or ask the plan administrator about catch-up eligibility and the current limits for that account.

In your 60s, a 401(k) shifts from building savings to paying for retirement. Ally recommends reviewing four decisions at this stage: withdrawal timing, rollovers, consolidation options and required minimum distributions.

The change rarely happens all at once. Many people in their early 60s are still putting money into their plans. At the same time, they are working out when and how to start drawing it down.

That overlap is why withdrawal timing comes first. The date of the first withdrawal marks when the account stops serving only as savings and starts serving as a source of income. The other three decisions all depend on it.

Rollovers and consolidation come next. Both concern where the money sits once it starts paying out. A saver with plans at several former employers can check whether combining them makes a withdrawal plan easier to manage.

Required minimum distributions are withdrawals the tax code requires from tax-deferred retirement accounts such as a traditional 401(k). Their timing has tax consequences. Putting off the first required minimum distribution means two distributions land in the same year, according to CNBC. Taking both in one year could push a retiree into a higher tax bracket.

Keeping costs low and leaving the money untouched help a 401(k) hold on to the balance it has built. Fees may come down when a saver consolidates accounts or chooses certain funds. Avoiding early withdrawals, where possible, keeps the savings in place for retirement.

Consolidation is one way to address fees. A worker who changes jobs can end up with retirement money spread across more than one account. Bringing those accounts together may lower the fees the saver pays. It also leaves fewer statements and investment mixes to track.

Fund selection is a second way. The funds inside a plan do not all carry the same costs. Choosing certain funds over others may reduce fees. How much a saver can cut this way depends on the plan and the options it offers.

The other half of protecting a balance is leaving it alone. The general guidance is to avoid taking money out before retirement whenever possible. An early withdrawal shrinks the balance. It can also bring early-withdrawal penalties.

Staying invested for the long haul works alongside that rule. Money left in the account keeps its full time to grow. Pulling out of investments early cuts that time short.

A periodic look at the account's asset allocation rounds out the routine. The check confirms the investment mix still fits the saver's goals.

Plan rules, fund costs and penalty terms differ from plan to plan. The right choices depend on each saver's circumstances. This information is general and is not investment or tax advice.

#5545. PicoBrew’s patents are back on the market, six years after the Seattle homebrew startup’s collapse

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:36 amOctober 28, 2026 at 3:08 pm

The patents behind PicoBrew, the Seattle startup that once promised to do for home beer what Keurig did for coffee, are up for sale again — six years after the company collapsed into receivership and after two changes of ownership.

Hilco Global, an Illinois-based diversified financial services company, announced this week that its Intellectual Property Services group has been retained by PicoBrew’s current owner to market the startup’s technology to potential buyers.

The sale includes 17 patents and patent applications, two of them pending, along with engineering and design files and product concepts. Buyers can bid on all or part of the portfolio, and non-binding indications of interest are due Nov. 18. Hilco is pitching the assets to companies in coffee, tea, kombucha, spirits, beverage appliances and housewares.

The seller is Pico Craft Group, which Hilco described as led by a former PicoBrew investor. After PicoBrew’s 2020 collapse, its bridge lender took over the assets. That lender, PB Funding Group, was managed by former Microsoft software developer Greg Whitten, The Seattle Times reported at the time. Pico Craft Group bought the assets from the lender in 2024 for an undisclosed amount, according to Hilco, which did not say who runs the group.

“PicoBrew was a true innovator in the consumer and commercial craft beverage space, and its portfolio has applications well beyond beer,” Eric Hurwitz, a senior director at Hilco, said in a news release.

The portfolio covers technology from PicoBrew’s full product line, according to the release, including the Pico Pro and Pico C home brewing appliances, the PicoStill accessory for spirits, the Pico U Multibrew platform for beer, coffee, tea and kombucha, and Z-Series brewing machines and KegSmarts kegerators for commercial use.

Bill Mitchell, a former Microsoft vice president and longtime homebrewer, founded PicoBrew in 2010 with his brother Jim Mitchell, a food scientist, and Avi Geiger, an engineer who also worked at Microsoft. Their countertop machines automated the brewing process using PicoPaks, ingredient packs based on recipes from craft breweries.

The startup became a Kickstarter regular. Its 2017 campaign for the Pico Model C raised $1.93 million from 4,301 backers, a record at the time in the site’s food category, and the $549 machine landed at retailers including Best Buy, Williams-Sonoma and Amazon. A 2018 campaign for the Pico U pushed PicoBrew into coffee, tea and kombucha.

But the company struggled to land more funding. In February 2020, after failing to close a new round, PicoBrew entered receivership. It had raised more than $15 million and cut its staff to fewer than 40, down from a peak of more than 80.

PicoBrew ceased operations in 2020, and no one has supported existing devices since, according to Hilco. Any decision about future support would be up to a buyer. The King County Superior Court approved the 2020 sale, which freed PicoBrew’s bridge lender from the company’s liabilities and from responsibility to past customers, The Seattle Times previously reported.

Some owners kept their machines brewing without the company’s servers by using a workaround developed by a Facebook group of PicoBrew users, The Spoon reported in 2020. The founders were let go after the receivership, according to the site.

When PicoBrew went up for sale in 2020, Mitchell told GeekWire that hardware takes time and multiple funding rounds backed by firm investor commitment.

He shared advice he’d gotten from Dan Leviton of Maveron: “Startups only fail for one of two reasons — they run out of heart, or they run out of money.”

#5544. Transfer Online Partners with OnchainTA, a Digital Transfer Agent, to Expand Tokenized Securities Services

The partnership establishes a framework for OnchainTA to provide tokenized securities capabilities to Transfer Online

FULLERTON, Calif., Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Akemona, Inc., a capital markets infrastructure provider for tokenized securities, today announced a partnership between its wholly owned subsidiary, Akemona TA Services, LLC, doing business as OnchainTA, and Transfer Online, Inc. (TOL). OnchainTA is an SEC-registered Digital Transfer Agent focused exclusively on tokenized securities, while TOL is a full-service, SEC-registered transfer agent. Under the signed agreement, OnchainTA will provide digital transfer agent services powered by Akemona's tokenization platform to TOL, enabling TOL to expand its services for tokenized securities.

Since 1999, TOL has provided transfer agent services to private and public companies, combining experienced human support with a technology-forward shareholder management platform, compliance-focused operations, and real-time reporting.

The relationship is designed to allow TOL to extend its issuer-facing transfer agent services to tokenized securities. TOL will remain the transfer agent of record and the primary point of contact for participating issuers, while OnchainTA will provide assigned tokenization and digital securities services through TOL-approved workflows.

"Transfer Online has always invested in its own technology, and that commitment keeps us at the forefront of the transfer agent industry," said Bryan Cochran, Director of Operations at Transfer Online. "For tokenization, we chose to partner with proven experts in the space to complement the platform we've built in-house. OnchainTA's digital securities capabilities let us offer issuers what's next in capital markets, while TOL remains their transfer agent of record and the team they already trust."

OnchainTA's Digital Transfer Agent services may include token setup, digital security recordkeeping, transfer and corporate action support, and reconciliation reporting. The scope of services for each issuer or offering will be mutually agreed by the parties.

"Rather than reinvent what specialists already do well, we brought in a leading tokenization partner and integrated their capabilities into our existing operations," added Cochran. "Every engagement runs through TOL-defined workflows, with full oversight and real-time visibility. Our team will support issuers from token setup through transfers, corporate actions, and reconciliation, and we plan to begin offering tokenization to Transfer Online clients early next year."

The agreement reflects a model developed for established transfer agents that want to add tokenized securities capabilities seamlessly alongside their existing operations. Services will be delivered through TOL-approved workflows and mutually agreed operating procedures.

"Transfer Online brings decades of transfer agent experience, a strong issuer-service model, and a practical commitment to technology," said Alex de Lorraine, Chief Executive Officer of Akemona. "Winning TOL's RFP and completing the partnership agreement are important validations of our approach. OnchainTA gives established transfer agents a way to add digital securities capabilities directly within their existing operating and compliance frameworks."

The relationship comes as OnchainTA prepares to introduce OnchainTA Release 2 shortly. Built on Akemona's tokenization infrastructure, the release will expand self-service capabilities across the Issuer Hub, Investor Portal, Admin Console, and related tokenization workflows. TOL personnel will receive training and support on the platform so they can obtain the records, reports, transaction information, and exception data needed to oversee each engagement and serve participating issuers.

OnchainTA Release 2 will include peer-to-peer Direct Transfer capabilities for compliant bilateral transfers of tokenized securities, subject to investor eligibility, identity verification, applicable transfer restrictions, and transfer agent controls. It will also include Cap Table Tokenization (CTT), which will enable verified issuer cap table positions to be converted into administered digital securities through a controlled process, and Digital Cap Table (DCT) capabilities designed to record, reconcile, and present digital security ownership information across complex ownership structures.

Akemona TA Services, LLC, doing business as OnchainTA, has operated as an SEC-registered Digital Transfer Agent for tokenized securities since 2021. OnchainTA combines registered transfer agent functions with Akemona's tokenization technology to support the administration of digital securities throughout their lifecycle.

"OnchainTA Release 2 brings together capabilities that issuers, transfer agents, and investors need as digital securities move into practical use," said Ravi Srivastava, Founder and Chief Product Officer of Akemona. #5542. 401(k) deferral limit projected to rise $1,000 to $25,500 in 2027

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Projected 2027 401(k) contribution limits from Milliman's final estimates show 10 deferral, catch-up and other employer plan thresholds rising ahead of official IRS figures

Inflation sets the pace for how much Americans can save in workplace retirement plans each year. The consumer price index rose 3.7% over the 12 months ended September 30, 2026. That figure comes from the CPI report the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics published October 14, 2026. It was faster than the 3.0% increase for the 12 months ended September 30, 2025.

The latest reading also ran above longer-term trends. The 10-year average annual change through September 30, 2025 was 3.2%. The 20-year average through the same date was 2.5%.

Those inflation readings feed into the annual cost-of-living adjustments for retirement plan limits. Milliman, the actuarial and consulting firm, used the September data to produce its final forecast of 2027 IRS limits. It puts the annual increase factor for those limits at about 3.5%.

The result is a set of estimated 2027 401(k) contribution limits that sit above 2026 levels. The employee deferral cap for 401(k), 403(b) and 457 plans would climb by $1,000. That cap governs how much a worker can steer from pay into a plan through elective deferrals in a year. Catch-up amounts, the maximum annual addition to defined contribution plans and several compensation thresholds would also move higher.

Every 2027 number in this list is a projection. The IRS had not published its official 2027 limits when Milliman released the forecast. The firm said only that publication was expected in the coming weeks. The official figures could differ from these estimates.

The 10 slides that follow cover 10 of the 11 items in Milliman's forecast table. Some are limits that shape what individual workers can put away, such as the deferral and catch-up caps. Others are thresholds employers use to test and administer their plans, such as the compensation limit and the highly compensated employee dollar amount. One covers defined benefit pensions, and another covers withdrawals tied to domestic abuse. Each slide gives the 2026 figure, the estimated 2027 figure and the change between them.

IRA limits are not part of this forecast. The estimates include no individual retirement account contribution caps, IRA catch-up amounts or IRA income phase-outs. None of those figures appear in this list.

The employee deferral limit for 401(k), 403(b) and 457 plans is projected to rise to $25,500 in 2027, up $1,000 from $24,500 in 2026. The estimate comes from Milliman, and the IRS has not yet published its official figure.

An elective deferral is the share of salary a worker chooses to send into a workplace retirement plan instead of receiving it as pay. The money moves through payroll, a set amount or percentage at a time. This annual cap governs the employee's own contributions.

Deferrals can go in before taxes, which lowers taxable income in the year the money is contributed. Many plans also offer a Roth option. Roth deferrals use after-tax dollars, and qualified withdrawals in retirement come out tax-free. Pre-tax and Roth deferrals both count toward the same annual limit.

Contributing the full estimated $25,500 evenly over a year works out to $2,125 a month. A worker paid every two weeks would need to defer a little under $981 per paycheck to get there.

The cap applies to the person, not to each plan. A worker who changes jobs midyear and joins a second 401(k) must keep combined deferrals across both employers under one annual limit. The new employer's payroll system may not know what went in earlier in the year. Keeping track of that running total falls to the employee.

Governmental 457(b) plans follow a different rule. Their deferral limit is separate from the shared 401(k) and 403(b) limit. A worker offered both a 403(b) and a governmental 457(b) can defer up to the full limit in each plan. Some public school districts and state and local governments offer that pairing.

Employer matching and profit-sharing contributions do not count against this cap. They fall under a separate, higher limit on total annual additions to an account.

The IRS adjusts the deferral limit for inflation in $500 steps, rounding down to the nearest step. The projected $1,000 increase equals two of those increments.

Workers age 50 and older could contribute an estimated $8,500 in catch-up contributions to defined contribution plans in 2027. Milliman projects this as a $500 increase from the $8,000 limit in effect for 2026.

Like every 2027 figure in Milliman's forecast, it is a projection, not an IRS-published limit.

Catch-up contributions sit on top of the standard employee deferral limit. They let older participants in 401(k), 403(b) and governmental 457(b) plans put away more as retirement approaches. Eligibility begins in the calendar year a participant turns 50, regardless of the month of the birthday.

Adding the two limits together shows the full amount an older saver could defer. In 2026, a worker age 50 or older could defer $32,500 by combining the standard deferral limit with the $8,000 catch-up. Under Milliman's estimates, that combined total would rise to an estimated $34,000 in 2027.

The $500 step reflects how the tax code adjusts this limit. The catch-up amount is indexed to inflation and then rounded down to the nearest multiple of $500. Inflation must push the unrounded figure past the next $500 mark before the published limit changes. In some low-inflation years, the catch-up limit has stayed flat as a result.

Employers decide whether to offer catch-up contributions. Federal rules permit the feature but do not require plan sponsors to include it. A participant whose plan does not allow catch-ups cannot make them through that plan, even if old enough to qualify.

Catch-up contributions also get different treatment under the overall plan limits. They do not count toward the cap on total annual additions from employee and employer sources. As a result, they can push a participant's total contributions above that cap.

Two separate figures apply to some older savers. Participants ages 60 to 63 have their own, higher catch-up limit. A prior-year wage threshold determines when catch-up contributions must be made as Roth contributions. Milliman gives each its own 2027 estimate.

Workers ages 60 to 63 could contribute up to an estimated $11,750 in catch-up money to their workplace retirement plans in 2027, according to Milliman's final forecast. That would be $500 above the 2026 limit of $11,250. Milliman's 2027 figure is a forecast, and the IRS sets the official limit.

This age band has its own catch-up tier, set above the standard catch-up limit for defined contribution plans. The SECURE 2.0 Act, a retirement law Congress passed in December 2022, created the higher tier. It first took effect in 2025.

The tier covers only four ages: 60, 61, 62 and 63. A saver who turns 64 during the year drops back to the standard catch-up amount. Catch-up savers ages 50 to 59 use the standard limit. A saver in the 60-to-63 band uses the higher limit in place of the standard one, not in addition to it.

Like regular deferrals, catch-up contributions come out of a worker's paycheck through the employer's plan. Plans are not required to offer them. Whether a worker can use the higher tier depends on whether the employer's plan permits catch-up contributions.

Milliman projects the standard catch-up limit at $8,500 for 2027, up from $8,000 in 2026. Under those estimates, the 60-to-63 tier would sit $3,250 above the standard limit. That gap matches 2026. Both limits are projected to rise by the same $500.

Catch-up contributions sit on top of the regular employee deferral limit for 401(k), 403(b) and 457 plans. Milliman also projects a $1,000 rise in that deferral limit for 2027. If both estimates hold, a saver aged 60 to 63 could defer as much as $37,250 in 2027. Under the 2026 limits, the same combination came to $35,750.

That combined ceiling would rise by $1,500 from one year to the next. The regular deferral limit would supply $1,000 of the increase, and the catch-up tier the other $500.

The prior-year wage threshold that triggers Roth catch-up contributions is estimated to rise to $155,000 in 2027. That is up $5,000 from $150,000 in 2026. The 2027 figure is a Milliman projection, not a limit the IRS has published.

The threshold determines how some older workers can make catch-up contributions to an employer retirement plan. Workers whose wages from the previous year exceed the line must put their catch-up money into a Roth account. Workers at or below it keep the choice between pre-tax and Roth catch-ups, where their plan offers both.

The requirement comes from the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022, the retirement law Congress passed in December of that year. The law set the original threshold at $145,000 and tied it to inflation. That indexing is why the line moves from year to year along with other plan limits.

The test looks at wages, not income in general. It uses wages as defined for Federal Insurance Contributions Act, or FICA, payroll taxes. It counts only wages paid by the employer that sponsors the plan. Investment income does not count, and neither does pay from a different, unrelated employer.

The test also looks backward. It uses the previous calendar year, so pay earned in 2026 determines who falls above the 2027 threshold. A worker who crosses the line in one year faces the Roth requirement in the following year.

The difference between the two account types comes down to when tax is paid. Pre-tax catch-up contributions reduce taxable income in the year they are made. Withdrawals of that money are taxed later. Roth contributions go in after tax, and qualified Roth withdrawals, including earnings, come out tax-free.

For workers above the threshold, the rule removes the upfront tax break on catch-up money. It does not reduce how much they are allowed to contribute. The catch-up dollar limits themselves are set separately from this wage test.

Plan design also affects the outcome. A plan that offers no Roth option cannot accept catch-up contributions from employees above the threshold. A plan administrator can confirm whether a particular plan includes a Roth feature and how the rule applies to its participants.

The maximum annual addition to a defined contribution (DC) plan is projected at $75,000 for 2027, according to Milliman. That estimate is $3,000 above the 2026 limit of $72,000.

This cap sets the total amount that can go into one participant's DC account in a single year. It counts money from the worker and the employer together. That makes it a different measure from the employee deferral limit, which covers only what a worker chooses to set aside from pay.

Several types of contributions count toward the annual addition. Employee elective deferrals, both pretax and Roth, are included. So are employer matching contributions and employer profit-sharing or nonelective contributions. Voluntary after-tax employee contributions also count. Forfeitures reallocated to a participant's account count too.

Some money falls outside the cap. Catch-up contributions are not counted toward the annual addition limit. Rollovers from another plan or an IRA do not count either. Neither do investment earnings on money already in the account.

The dollar figure is not the only ceiling. A participant's annual additions also cannot exceed that person's compensation for the year. Whichever amount is lower applies. For a worker with modest pay, the compensation test can bind well before the dollar cap does.

The gap between this cap and the estimated 2027 deferral limit shows how much room remains for other money. For a worker who maxes out deferrals, up to $49,500 could come from employer contributions or after-tax savings. Plans that allow after-tax contributions and in-plan Roth conversions let some workers use that room. The approach is known as the mega backdoor Roth.

The annual addition limit generally applies per employer rather than per person. A worker in plans at two unrelated employers may have a separate annual addition limit at each one. Plans of related employers in the same controlled group are combined for this purpose. The employee deferral limit, by contrast, applies across all of a person's 401(k) and 403(b) plans combined.

Employer retirement plans could count up to an estimated $375,000 of a worker's annual pay in 2027, according to Milliman. That projection is $15,000 above the 2026 compensation limit of $360,000.

Milliman's figure is a projection, and the official IRS number could differ.

The compensation limit sets a ceiling on how much of an employee's pay a qualified plan may take into account in a given year. It comes from Section 401(a)(17) of the Internal Revenue Code. Earnings above the cap are disregarded for plan purposes.

The limit does not restrict what a person can earn. It restricts how much of that pay can feed into plan calculations. That distinction matters most for contributions and benefits tied to salary.

Employer contributions are often calculated with reference to pay. When a plan uses a pay-based formula for matching or profit-sharing contributions, it must stop counting at the compensation limit. A worker paid well above the cap receives contributions figured on the capped amount, not on full salary.

Defined benefit pensions follow the same rule. Many traditional pension formulas combine years of service with a measure of average pay. The pay used in that measure cannot exceed the limit for each year counted.

The cap also feeds into the nondiscrimination tests that qualified plans must pass. Those tests compare how a plan treats higher-paid and lower-paid workers. Capping compensation keeps very large salaries from skewing the results.

Most workers never reach the threshold. The limit is aimed at executives and other high earners. It shapes plan design at the companies that employ them. Some employers offer nonqualified deferred compensation plans to provide retirement savings on pay above the cap.

The tax code indexes the limit to inflation and adjusts it in increments of $5,000. The estimated $15,000 rise is the largest dollar increase in Milliman's forecast table for 2027.

The pay threshold that identifies a highly compensated employee is projected to rise from $160,000 in 2026 to $170,000 in 2027, according to Milliman's final estimates. That $10,000 increase is a forecast, not an announced IRS figure.

The HCE label shapes how employer retirement plans are tested. It does not set how much any single worker can contribute. Federal tax law bars 401(k) and similar plans from favoring higher earners over the rest of the workforce. The HCE definition sorts employees into two groups so that comparison can be made.

An employee generally counts as an HCE in one of two ways. The first is owning a significant stake in the business, either in the current year or the year before. The second is earning more than the dollar threshold in the prior year. Employers may also elect to limit the pay-based group to the top-paid slice of their workforce.

The threshold works on a one-year lookback. Pay earned during a given year determines who is treated as an HCE in the following plan year. Under that structure, the estimated 2027 figure would generally shape which employees are classified as HCEs for 2028 plan testing.

The classification feeds into annual nondiscrimination tests. The actual deferral percentage test compares the average salary deferral rates of HCEs with those of everyone else. The actual contribution percentage test does the same for employer matching and after-tax contributions.

When a plan fails one of these tests, a common fix is refunding excess contributions to HCEs. Those refunds are taxable income for the employees who receive them. Another option is an additional employer contribution to non-highly compensated workers. That contribution raises their average and narrows the gap.

Many employers sidestep these tests by adopting a safe harbor 401(k) design. Those plans commit to a required employer contribution. In exchange, they get relief from the deferral test and, for qualifying matches, the matching test.

A higher threshold can change who falls on each side of the line. Some non-owner employees paid between $160,000 and $170,000 could be classified as non-HCEs once the new figure applies. The IRS rounds the HCE amount down to a $5,000 increment. As a result, the figure can stay flat from one year to the next.

Milliman estimates the compensation threshold for officers who count as key employees will rise to $245,000 in 2027. That would be $10,000 above the $235,000 figure for 2026.

The figure matters for one part of federal retirement plan law. The Internal Revenue Code uses the term "key employee" for a small group of an employer's most senior people. Certain business owners fall into that group. So do officers whose annual pay exceeds the dollar threshold. An officer paid below it does not become a key employee through officer status alone.

The code also caps how many officers can count. No more than 50 officers are treated as key employees. Smaller employers face a lower cap tied to their headcount.

The classification feeds into the top-heavy rules in Section 416 of the Internal Revenue Code. Those rules test whether the share of plan benefits held by key employees exceeds a limit set in the code. A plan that crosses that line is considered top-heavy. The employer must then generally provide minimum contributions or benefits to employees who are not key employees.

Small businesses are the employers most likely to run into these rules. In a company with a few owners and officers, a large share of plan assets can sit in those people's accounts. For those employers, the officer pay threshold helps determine whose balances count on the key employee side of the top-heavy test.

The key employee threshold is separate from the highly compensated employee dollar amount, which applies to different nondiscrimination tests. An officer can be a highly compensated employee without being a key employee. The two figures are adjusted separately.

The officer threshold has its own rounding rule. The tax code rounds its inflation adjustment down to the next lowest multiple of $5,000. A modest rise in prices can leave the figure unchanged from one year to the next. A larger rise lifts it by $5,000 or more.

Employers check top-heavy status each plan year. The official 2027 officer threshold will come from the IRS, and it could differ from Milliman's estimate.

The maximum annual pension a defined benefit plan can pay is estimated to rise to $300,000 in 2027, up $10,000 from $290,000 in 2026. The projection comes from Milliman's final estimates for 2027. The IRS had not published the official figure when Milliman released its forecast.

A defined benefit plan is the traditional pension. Instead of building an account balance, the plan promises a specific payment in retirement. That payment is usually set by a formula tied to an employee's pay and years of service.

The employer generally funds the plan and carries the investment risk. If plan assets earn less than expected, the employer typically has to contribute more to cover the promised benefits. Participants do not pick investments the way 401(k) savers do.

This cap works differently from most retirement plan limits. It does not restrict how much goes into the plan each year. It restricts how much comes out, measured as the yearly benefit a participant can receive.

The limit comes from Section 415(b) of the Internal Revenue Code. A separate provision of the same section, Section 415(c), governs annual additions to defined contribution accounts.

The dollar figure is stated as a straight life annuity. That is a payment made every year for the retiree's lifetime, with nothing continuing to a beneficiary after death. A plan may pay a benefit in another form, such as a lump sum. In that case, the amount is converted to an equivalent annual figure for testing against the cap.

The dollar cap is not the only constraint. Section 415(b) also ties the maximum benefit to the participant's own average pay over their highest-paid consecutive years. For many people, that pay-based test produces a lower ceiling than $300,000.

Few workers approach the dollar ceiling. A $300,000 annual pension generally requires high pay, long service and a generous benefit formula. The limit matters most for highly paid participants, including owners of small businesses that sponsor their own pension plans.

Savers who have experienced domestic abuse may be able to take up to an estimated $10,900 from an eligible workplace retirement plan in 2027 without the usual early-withdrawal penalty. Milliman projects that cap will rise $400 from the $10,500 limit in place for 2026.

The official 2027 cap could differ once the IRS publishes its limits.

This withdrawal option is a recent addition to retirement plan rules. Congress created it in the SECURE 2.0 Act, which was signed into law in December 2022. The provision applies to distributions made after December 31, 2023. Lawmakers set the starting cap at $10,000 and indexed it to inflation.

The option is available in defined contribution plans, including 401(k), 403(b) and governmental 457(b) plans. Employers are not required to offer it. Each plan sponsor decides whether to add the feature. Access therefore depends on the terms of a specific plan. A participant can check the summary plan description or ask the plan administrator whether it is offered.

The law defines domestic abuse broadly. It covers physical, psychological, sexual, emotional and economic abuse by a spouse or domestic partner. That includes efforts to control, isolate, humiliate or intimidate the victim. It also includes efforts to undermine the victim's ability to reason independently.

A participant must take the distribution within one year after the abuse occurs. The plan can rely on the participant's own written self-certification that they qualify. The law does not require the participant to hand the plan a police report or court order.

The penalty waiver does not make the money tax-free. Pre-tax savings withdrawn this way generally still count as taxable income for the year. Participants may repay the amount to the plan within three years. A repayment is treated like a rollover, which can let the saver recover income tax paid on the withdrawal.

The $400 increase is the smallest dollar change among the 10 estimated limits in this list.

#5541. F5 stock suffers worst day in more than a decade as AI spending shakes investors

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:56 amOctober 28, 2026 at 11:05 am

Shares of F5 fell about 20% on Wednesday, a day after the Seattle-based company beat Wall Street’s estimates and said it would boost spending to capitalize on expected growth in the AI security market.

The application security and delivery company’s stock was trading around $368 late Wednesday morning, down from $459 at Tuesday’s close, wiping out about $5 billion in market value. That put F5 on pace for its biggest one-day drop in more than 13 years, according to Barron’s. Before the drop, F5’s shares had climbed nearly 80% this year.

F5’s revenue for its fiscal fourth quarter rose 13% to $917 million, and product revenue jumped 23%. Adjusted earnings of $4.42 a share beat estimates of about $4.30.

Slower growth ahead: Investors seem to be focused on the outlook. F5 expects revenue to grow 8% to 9% in fiscal 2027, down from 11% this year, and adjusted earnings per share to grow 3% to 5%. It’s also projecting lower margins as memory and storage components get more expensive, and as it doubles its team of AI security sellers.

F5’s hardware business is also cooling off. Systems revenue jumped 29% in the quarter as customers replaced aging equipment, but F5 Chief Financial Officer Cooper Werner said on the earnings call that those replacements will taper off in the second half of fiscal 2027.

The AI bet: F5 is spending more to go after AI security. CEO François Locoh-Donou said on the call that the company will double its team of specialist AI security sellers in fiscal 2027 and more than double its marketing in that area. It’s also adding compensation incentives for all of its field sellers to discuss AI security with customers.

F5’s adjusted operating margin fell to 33.7% in the quarter, from 37% a year earlier.

Locoh-Donou said F5’s AI-related bookings topped $100 million in fiscal 2026, up about 300%. Most of that came from AI data delivery, which moves data to and from AI systems, rather than security. More than 300 customers are using an AI-powered web application firewall that F5 launched in March.

The company estimates the AI market it sells into will grow from about $1 billion this year to $11 billion by 2030.

Wall Street reaction: Piper Sandler downgraded the stock to neutral, according to The Motley Fool. Analysts at William Blair, which rates F5 “market perform,” wrote in a research note that “the AI opportunity has yet to contribute meaningfully to the top line.”

We’ve contacted F5 for comment on the stock decline.

F5 has been building out its AI security business, including its acquisition of SurePath AI. Locoh-Donou talked about the company’s path from the early web to AI security on a GeekWire Podcast episode marking F5’s 30th anniversary. He said companies adopting AI are losing track of what those systems can access, and that juggling separate tools to manage it is a burden, which is why F5 is building a single AI security platform.

This week, F5’s board authorized an additional $1.5 billion in stock buybacks, on top of $322 million remaining in its existing program.

#5540. Generative media inference startup fal raises $1.3B at a $16B valuation

Generative media inference startup fal today announced it has raised $1.3 billion in new funding at a valuation of $16 billion, according to Bloomberg.

The company will spend the money on computing power and on hiring beyond its current 185 employees.

Fal provides a cloud platform for running image, video and audio generation models, and developers reach all of them through a single application programming interface. Entertainment studios, advertising agencies and game developers are among the customers using those models in production, according to the company.

In-house researchers also post-train some of those models to run faster. Over the past year that work has centered on video, in partnership with the open- and closed-source developers that build the models. Some of the deals pay fal licensing fees or a share of revenue, Bloomberg reported.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Burkay Gur told the outlet the round is as large as it is because demand has surged and serving it takes more compute. “We hit a point in summer where we were not able to serve our customers and had to rate-limit them,” he said. Pretraining a model of fal’s own is not on the near-term agenda, said Gur, who did not rule it out for later.

Annualized revenue at fal passed $800 million earlier this year, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. The valuation puts fal just behind rival inference provider Fireworks AI Inc., which closed $1.5 billion in funding at a $17.5 billion valuation in July. Several people familiar with the finances of inference companies told TechCrunch that gross margins across the sector remain thin because compute is expensive to buy or lease.

Gur started the company in 2021 with Chief Technology Officer Gorkem Yurtseven. His resume includes leading machine learning work at Coinbase Global Inc. and an engineering role at Oracle Corp. Yurtseven was previously a developer at Amazon.com Inc.

Bessemer Venture Partners led the Series F round, and its partner Talia Goldberg is joining the board of Features & Labels Inc., as fal is formally known. Nvidia Corp., Sound Ventures, HOF Capital and T. Rowe Price Group Inc. also participated. Fal described Nvidia as a strategic investor.

Today’s announcement also covered an April round led by Sequoia Capital. That Series E round raised $350 million at an $8 billion valuation, per Bloomberg, and fal said the two rounds come to $1.65 billion combined. Last December, the company raised $140 million at a $4.5 billion valuation.

Investors have now put more than $1.9 billion into the company.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- I AM ALS and its national force of advocates are celebrating as the President signed the ACT for ALS reauthorization bill into law. #5538. PNC Bank, T-Mobile, and HPE: 3 large employers that list pensions as a perk

Free daily briefing on global business news.

PNC Bank, T-Mobile, and Hewlett Packard Enterprise appear among 2,492 companies that list a pension as a workplace perk.

Picture a job offer sitting in your inbox, with the salary settled and only the benefits page left to read. Dental coverage, commuter stipends, and wellness credits blur together on a first pass. Then one word stands out: pension. The term suggests income that keeps arriving after the last paycheck, and it carries weight for anyone choosing between two large employers. A higher starting wage shows up on payday. A retirement benefit pays off later, across a future a worker has not seen. Weighing the two forces a job seeker to picture life at 40, 55, and beyond. A single line on a perks page can tip that choice.

A benefits tag leaves out most of what an applicant needs to judge a pension. The tag tells a candidate that some plan exists on paper. It says nothing about what the plan pays, which employees qualify, or how many years someone must stay before the benefit vests. Plan terms decide whether a listed pension delivers real security or amounts to a footnote in an offer letter. A candidate has to put those questions to the employer. The window to ask closes once competing offers expire or a start date arrives. Company listings narrow the search by flagging which employers mention a pension at all. No listing can close the gap between a posted benefit and a guaranteed one. Readers should treat every entry as a starting point for questions.

Built In maintains a directory of 2,492 companies that list a pension among their perks. Each profile card shows the employer's industry tags, its number of offices and employees, how many benefits it carries, and its open positions, along with the four departments hiring most. The page sets out no criteria for inclusion and no logic behind the order of its cards. It carries no date and gives no pension terms, plan types, or eligibility rules for any company. This article looks at three employers from the directory whose profiles each report tens of thousands of workers. All three sit among the largest employers shown on the page, but they are not the only ones at that scale. Ericsson, for one, lists 88,000 employees and falls outside this selection. The choice of these three makes no claim about which companies provide the strongest retirement benefits.

PNC Bank lists a pension among the perks it offers a workforce of 55,000 employees, who work out of six offices. The bank's profile counts 55 benefits in all, which sets the pension inside a broad package of workplace extras. By its own account, PNC belongs to one of the largest diversified financial services institutions in the U.S., with branches stretching from one coast to the other.

Six offices and a coast-to-coast branch network make an uneven pair on the page. The card does not say which sites its office count covers. A job seeker cannot tell from the listing where most of the bank's staff report for work.

Technology dominates the bank's industry labels. PNC's card pairs Financial Services with Machine Learning, Payments, Security, and Software. Four of its five tags point to the digital systems that move and protect money. The mix reads closer to a software firm's than a neighborhood lender's.

Recruiting tilts the same way. PNC shows 76 open positions, and its four busiest departments are Product Management with 24, Engineering with 20, AI & Machine Learning with 11, and Cybersecurity with eight. AI & Machine Learning and Cybersecurity combine for 19 roles, which points to demand for specialists in automated systems and digital defense. The four groups together account for 63 openings, or about 83% of the total. The remaining 13 fall in departments the listing does not break out. None of the leading four names teller, lending, or branch work.

PNC carries about one vacancy for every 724 employees, the thinnest hiring ratio of the three companies in this article. Product Management and Engineering supply 44 of the bank's posted openings, more than half its total. A "See Our Teams" link lets visitors browse individual groups, and the bank's recruiting tagline invites applicants to build a brilliant career there. The most direct path to the pension perk at PNC, on this evidence, runs through building and securing digital products.

T-Mobile $TMUS reports 89,016 employees on a profile that counts a pension among its perks, the largest stated workforce of the three companies here. The firm spreads its staff across four offices, an average of 22,254 people per location. Its card tallies 43 benefits, the shortest list among the three despite the biggest headcount. A pension, by this measure, is one item in a package of more than 40 offerings.

The company identifies itself as T-Mobile U.S. Inc., which trades on the Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker TMUS. It brands itself America's Un-carrier and says it provides a 4G LTE network alongside a nationwide 5G network. The directory files T-Mobile under two industry tags, Other and Utilities. Neither label names wireless service, the business at the center of the carrier's own pitch. Both other employers in this group carry technology tags, such as software at PNC Bank and cloud at Hewlett Packard Enterprise. T-Mobile alone among the three sits outside a technology category.

Sales drives the company's hiring, with 153 of its 436 open positions, or about 35% of the total. Product management follows with 25 openings, engineering with 22, and finance with 14. The three departments account for 61 roles. Sales postings outnumber that group by a ratio of 2.5-to-1. Engineering trails sales by about 7-to-1 in openings, a mix that tilts toward customer-facing jobs. The four biggest teams claim 214 openings between them, which leaves 222 positions in departments left unnamed. Combined, the remaining departments hold about 51% of all openings.

Vacancies look modest against the company's size. The 436 listings amount to less than 1% of T-Mobile's roster, or one for every 204 people on its payroll. Sales postings alone work out to one for every 582 people. Candidates outside sales compete for the other 283 slots, a narrow door into a pension-listing employer of this scale.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise advertises 2,773 open positions, and a pension appears among the 45 benefits on its profile. The company reports 85,422 employees across 25 offices. Hiring at this volume works out to about one vacancy for every 31 people on the payroll, or close to 111 openings per office. The ratios point to an employer recruiting in bulk across its entire footprint.

Engineering claims the largest share of those listings, with 897 posts, and sales follows at 804. Together, the two groups hold 1,701 jobs, or about 61% of the total. Program & Project Management, at 149, and Operations & Support, at 141, trail by a wide margin. The narrow 93-position gap between engineers and sellers suggests the company wants people who build its products about as much as people who sell them.

The four named departments account for 1,991 roles between them, and the top pair outnumbers the next two by more than five to one. Another 782 positions fall outside those four categories. More than a quarter of the demand sits with smaller teams the profile does not break out. The smallest of the named groups caps any unlisted team at 141 slots.

The company's industry tags cover artificial intelligence, cloud, information technology, and consulting. The engineering-heavy demand matches a tag list built around technology. Its own account of its history starts in 1939, with Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard setting up shop in a rented Palo Alto garage. Audio oscillators were their first products. The company says those devices laid the foundation for its growth into what it calls a global leader in enterprise technology.

Candidates drawn to the company by its listed pension have the best odds of entering through engineering or sales, the two teams with the most doors open. Outside those fields, prospects thin out. Program & Project Management, the next-largest group, offers about one-sixth as many roles as engineering.

#5537. Seattle farmworker payroll startup Ganaz acquired as CEO Hannah Freeman steps away

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:38 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 1:47 pm

Seattle startup Ganaz, which provides payroll and HR tech for agricultural workers and employers, has been acquired by Beacon Holdings.

Ganaz co-founder and CEO Hannah Freeman announced the deal Wednesday on LinkedIn, saying the public benefit corporation “is in great hands” at Beacon, which “is building momentum for our next exciting season.”

Freeman indicated she is stepping away from the company to “catch my breath, spend more time with my daughter, and dream about what’s next,” she wrote. “I’ll miss our team & customers, but will be cheering you on from the sidelines.”

Ganaz launched in 2017 and has raised more than $10 million, with its last disclosed funding round in June 2021. That financing valued the company at $26 million, according to PitchBook. Terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Beacon, based in Toronto, buys software businesses serving traditional industries and provides shared technology and operational resources. The company said in September that its portfolio included 45 software businesses.

Ganaz’s platform provides employee onboarding, training, communication and analytics tools. It also offers a Mastercard payroll card that gives unbanked workers access to digital banking. Employers save time and money by skipping paper checks, while workers keep more of their pay by avoiding check-cashing and high remittance fees.

Ganaz received GeekWire’s 2023 Geeks Give Back Award. “We founded Ganaz to make life better for farm workers, and we do that by building technology that agricultural employers love and can’t live without,” Freeman told GeekWire in 2023. “We build our tools to help both workers and employers prosper, and that kicks off a virtuous cycle that helps agricultural communities prosper as well.”

At that time, the startup was serving more than 250,000 agricultural workers in the U.S. and Mexico and 100 employers in the sector.

The company has about 17 employees, according to LinkedIn. Freeman did not say in her post whether Ganaz will continue as a subsidiary or whether its employees will receive job offers from Beacon. GeekWire has reached out to Freeman for comment and will update the story with any reply.

#5536. Atomic Mobile unveils multi-carrier IoT service connecting devices across the globe

SPRING LAKE, N.J., Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Atomic Mobile today introduced Atomic Orbit , a cellular internet service designed to maintain connectivity for IoT devices by utilizing multiple carrier networks. The service addresses the critical need for reliable data access in scanners, tablets, POS terminals, and smart meters that frequently move across varying signal environments. Atomic Orbit offers global reach across hundreds of operators worldwide.

Relying on a single carrier often leads to coverage gaps, especially for mobile assets or devices deployed in diverse geographic regions. Atomic Orbit solves this by providing access to three national carriers and 18 regional carriers within the United States, alongside global multi-carrier support. This architecture ensures that devices automatically switch to the strongest available signal, maintaining uptime for essential business operations. By eliminating the limitations of a single-provider model, the platform enables enterprises to deploy devices globally without the risk of localized dead zones.

Aaron Ogden, VP of of Customer Success, says "Over the years, I've worked across finance, energy, education, logistics, and healthcare, and I've seen how much day-to-day operations depend on reliable connectivity. Whether it's a payment terminal processing a sale, a remote utility sensor reporting a reading, a fleet tracker sending its location, a field technician pulling up a work order on a tablet, or a backup solution, the connection matters wherever the work happens. A multi-carrier SIM gives organizations access to more than one network, helping keep devices connected as they move between locations or when coverage varies or fails."

The implementation of eSIM technology further simplifies logistics, allowing enterprises to manage profits by reducing the operational complexity of physical hardware swaps when changing service plans or carriers. This flexibility is critical for organizations looking to scale their IoT footprint without increasing administrative overhead.

Learn more about Atomic Orbit at https://atomicmobile.com/products/orbit .

Atomic Mobile developed the product in response to direct requests from customers seeking a reliable multi-carrier service for connected devices both in domestic and international markets. The service is available now for enterprises requiring high-availability mobile connectivity.
