#5535. Block shares rise after third-quarter beat and a third straight guidance raise

Shares of Block Inc. rose more than 7% in late trading today after the payments and financial services company beat third-quarter expectations and raised its full-year guidance for the third straight time.

For the quarter that ended on Sept. 30, Block reported adjusted earnings of $1.13 per share, up from 54 cents in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $6.72 billion, up nearly 10% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting $1.03 per share on revenue of $6.58 billion.

Gross profit grew 22% to $3.24 billion and finished ahead of the company’s own guidance. Adjusted operating income almost doubled to a record $923 million, and the adjusted operating margin rose to 29% of gross profit. Product development spending fell 11% from a year earlier, reflecting the workforce cut Block made in February.

Operating income on an unadjusted basis rose a more modest 5% to $428 million, held back by $435 million in contingencies, restructuring and other charges. Net income attributable to common stockholders came to $566 million, compared with $462 million a year earlier.

Cash App gross profit grew 27% to $2.07 billion. Monthly transacting actives reached 60 million in September, and Block named Neighborhoods as a key driver after the loyalty network auto-enrolled more than 30,000 Square seller locations in August. Consumer lending originations rose 40% to $19 billion, led by Cash App Borrow and Afterpay Post-Purchase. Transaction, loan and consumer receivable losses climbed 66% as that lending grew.

Square gross payment volume grew 14% to $76.4 billion, the fastest rate since the first quarter of 2023, with U.S. growth accelerating to 10.4%. Square’s gross profit kept pace at $1.16 billion. Block’s bitcoin business shrank again, as gross profit there halved to $52 million after the company cut fees on certain bitcoin transactions in Cash App.

Business highlights in the quarter included the July alpha release of Buzz, an open-source workspace for people and AI agents that has since had more than two dozen updates. General availability of Cash App Tags tap-to-pay hardware followed in August. In September, Block said it would open Cash App Score, its in-house credit score, to outside lenders through Nova Credit Inc.

Much of Chief Executive Jack Dorsey’s shareholder letter dealt with AI. Block, he wrote, has “meaningfully crossed the chasm” in turning itself into a company that “streams intelligence as people need it.” Pilots of Buzz with prospective customers began in October, and Block expects to book its first machine intelligence revenue in the fourth quarter. Builderlab, the ecosystem Block created to sell Buzz and related tools to other companies, will be formally introduced at a San Francisco event on Nov. 10.

Fourth-quarter guidance calls for gross profit to grow 15% to $3.32 billion. Adjusted earnings are forecast at $1.15 per share, a cent below the $1.16 analysts had expected. For the full year, Block now projects gross profit of $12.63 billion, up from the $12.51 billion it forecast in August, and adjusted earnings of $4.15 per share, up from $4.02. The consensus estimate was $4.06.

A preliminary outlook for 2027 calls for gross profit to grow at least 15% to $14.52 billion. Adjusted operating income is expected to rise 30% next year to $4.58 billion, well above the $3.51 billion target Block set at its investor day in November 2025.

#5534. How migration shapes 9 U.S. states with older populations

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These nine states with older populations show how retirement migration, young-adult out-migration and aging in place shape the U.S. age profile, state by state

A state's median age is a record of who is born there, who arrives, who leaves and who stays put. When retirees move in and young adults move out, the midpoint of a population's age distribution climbs. Lower birth rates push it up as well. When families with children settle and older residents depart, it falls. Each state's figure is the sum of those shifts over decades.

The U.S. Census Bureau is the main source for this picture. It publishes median age by state, along with the share of residents 65 and older, through its population estimates and the American Community Survey. Median age is the age that splits a population into two equal halves. Half of residents are older, and half are younger. The share of residents 65 and older measures something different. It counts how much of a state's population has reached the traditional retirement age.

Those figures change with every release. A state's position can shift from one year to the next, and the order depends on which measure and which year a reader looks at. For that reason, this list does not rank anything. It is a selection of nine states with older populations, drawn from New England, the Mid-Atlantic, the South and the Mountain West.

Some names recur. Maine, Vermont and West Virginia have repeatedly appeared near the top of Census Bureau median-age rankings. Florida has the largest share of residents 65 and older among large states. The other states in this selection — Delaware, Pennsylvania, Montana, New Hampshire and Connecticut — round out a picture that spans small rural states and larger ones with major cities.

Two forces run through the slides that follow. The first is the migration of retirees into a state, which is central to Florida's age profile. The second is young adults leaving for other states, a pattern that shapes places such as West Virginia and Maine.

The age of a state's population affects how it plans. An older population changes the size of the local workforce. It shifts demand toward health care and long-term care. It also influences what a state collects in taxes and what it spends. Each slide below looks at one state's age profile and the factors behind it.

Maine has repeatedly appeared near the top of U.S. Census Bureau median-age rankings. Young adults leaving the state is one of the forces behind that older age profile.

The pattern has held across more than one Census Bureau release. Maine's exact median age and its position on the list belong to the reporting year of each release. No single figure describes the state permanently.

A high median age means a population leans toward middle and later life. In Maine, that tilt reflects decisions made over many years by residents of every age.

Young-adult out-migration is part of the explanation. When young adults move to other states, the residents who remain skew older. That shift raises the median age even when nobody else in the state moves.

Out-migration is one factor in Maine's age profile, not the whole story. The residents who stay and age in place also shape where the state lands in each release. So do the people who move in.

Florida has the largest share of residents aged 65 and older among large U.S. states. Its standing rests on that share of seniors rather than on median age. This sets it apart from the smaller states that tend to lead median-age lists.

A high share of older residents does not mean a state lacks younger people. Florida is also home to large numbers of children and working-age adults. Its retiree population stands out because of how much of the total it represents.

Size changes what that share means. In a small state, a high proportion of seniors can still add up to a modest number of people. In a state as populous as Florida, a similar proportion describes a large group in absolute terms.

Retirement migration is a defining feature of Florida's demographics. The state sits in the Sun Belt, the band of states across the southern U.S. Many people move there after leaving the workforce. They spend their later years somewhere other than the place where they built their careers.

That pattern differs from states where an older age profile builds up mainly because younger residents leave and longtime residents stay. In Florida, the older population grows partly through arrivals from other states.

The two routes leave different marks. An aging profile driven by departures reflects a smaller pool of younger residents. One driven by arrivals reflects a state that draws newcomers in later life.

Age 65 is also the point at which most Americans become eligible for Medicare. That makes the 65-and-older share a common reference point for health care planning at the state level.

Vermont, like Maine and West Virginia, has repeatedly appeared near the top of U.S. Census Bureau rankings of median age by state. That recurring position places it among the U.S. states with older populations.

Vermont's exact median age is not fixed, and neither is its precise place in those rankings. Both can move when the Census Bureau publishes new estimates. What recurs is Vermont's presence near the top across releases.

Vermont is a small, largely rural state in northern New England. It is one of the least populous states in the U.S. It borders the Canadian province of Quebec to the north and New Hampshire to the east. Massachusetts lies to the south, and New York lies to the west.

Vermont shares its northern New England setting with Maine. Maine is another state that recurs near the top of Census Bureau median-age rankings.

West Virginia has repeatedly ranked near the top of U.S. Census Bureau median-age rankings. Younger adults moving to other states are one factor behind that older age profile.

This pattern does not require older people to move in. When residents in their 20s and 30s relocate, they take their age bracket with them. The people who stay behind skew older as a group, even though no individual resident has aged any faster.

That sets West Virginia apart from a state whose older profile comes mainly from retirees arriving. In West Virginia's case, the older skew can build through departures alone.

The effect can compound over time. Children born to adults who have already left are counted in their new home states, not in West Virginia. That keeps the younger end of the state's age distribution smaller than it would otherwise be.

West Virginia's exact spot in the median-age rankings is not fixed. Its recurring place near the top is the consistent part of the record.

Delaware is one of the nine states in this selection of states with older populations. It represents the Mid-Atlantic coast in a group drawn mostly from New England and other regions.

Delaware is a small state on the Atlantic coast. Only Rhode Island covers less land. Delaware shares borders with Maryland, Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

Pennsylvania is part of this selection of states with older populations, and it differs from most of the others in one basic way: size. It is one of the most populous states in the Northeast. Its age profile covers millions of residents rather than a small, mostly rural population.

Those residents live in very different places. Philadelphia, the state's largest city, sits in the east. Pittsburgh, its second-largest city, sits in the west. Smaller cities, towns and rural counties fill the territory between them.

That spread shapes how a statewide figure should be read. A single median age or 65-and-older share for Pennsylvania folds big-city neighborhoods and rural counties into one number. The result describes the state as a whole, not any one community within it.

Montana is the Mountain West state in this selection of states with older populations. Its inclusion shows that an older age profile is not limited to New England, the Mid-Atlantic or Florida.

Montana is a large, mostly rural state. Its residents are spread thinly across long distances, with wide gaps between towns.

That geography separates Montana from the smaller, more compact states in this selection, such as Delaware and Connecticut. Montana's older residents live across open country rather than in a densely settled region.

New Hampshire is one of the nine states in this selection with older populations. It sits in northern New England, between two neighbors that have repeatedly appeared near the top of U.S. Census Bureau median-age rankings: Maine and Vermont.

Maine lies to the east and Vermont to the west. Massachusetts borders New Hampshire to the south. The Canadian province of Quebec lies to the north.

The state also has a short stretch of Atlantic coastline between Maine and Massachusetts. That gives it both an inland, mountainous north and a southern edge that faces the Boston area.

This slide does not give New Hampshire a median age, a share of residents 65 and older or a rank position. No dated Census Bureau figure for the state was available for this article.

Connecticut places this selection of states with older populations firmly in the Northeast. It is one of five states here from the U.S. Census Bureau's Northeast region, which is the largest regional group among the nine.

The bureau sorts the 50 states into four regions: the Northeast, the Midwest, the South and the West. It then splits each region into smaller divisions. The Northeast has two of them, New England and the Middle Atlantic.

Connecticut sits in New England, a division of six states. Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont are also in this selection, and all three share that division. Pennsylvania is the fifth Northeastern state here. It belongs to the Middle Atlantic division.

The other four states come from two regions. Delaware, Florida and West Virginia fall in the South. Montana falls in the West. The Midwest contributes no states to this selection.

The New England states on this list are not alike. Connecticut is more densely populated than Maine, New Hampshire or Vermont, which are largely rural. Its place alongside them shows that, within this selection, an older population in New England is not limited to rural states.

The regional grouping describes where Connecticut sits in the bureau's framework. It is a matter of geography, not a measurement. Membership in the Northeast does not by itself set a state's median age or the share of its residents who have reached retirement age.

#5533. Microsoft Azure revenue surges 48% to $33.2B, beating expectations as cloud and AI demand grows

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:47 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:30 pm

Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations.

The growth suggests that Microsoft is selling cloud and AI computing about as fast as it can install it. Azure revenue rose $10.8 billion from a year earlier, driven by demand for services across the platform, Microsoft said in its quarterly filing. That came even as some new data center capacity arrived late.

For investors worried about Microsoft’s record capital spending, it’s a sign that the company’s massive AI and cloud infrastructure buildout is turning into sales. Microsoft’s shares rose nearly 4% in after-hours trading following the earnings report.

Overall, Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, up 19% and above the $90.75 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance. Earnings were $4.89 per share excluding the impact of its OpenAI investment, compared with expectations of $4.72.

It’s the first time Microsoft has reported Azure’s quarterly revenue figure, not just its growth. The disclosure is part of a new financial structure that took effect this quarter, splitting the company into two segments: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.

Capital spending came in below Microsoft’s forecast. The company spent $45.2 billion, including finance leases, short of the more than $50 billion it expected. Some data center capacity that third parties were supposed to deliver in the quarter was delayed, the company said.

Google Cloud, which includes Google’s Workspace productivity apps, brought in $30.7 billion in revenue in the quarter, up 103% from a year earlier, Alphabet reported Wednesday afternoon.

Amazon reports earnings Thursday afternoon, including AWS results.

Update, 3:05 p.m.:Microsoft expects Azure growth to accelerate again this quarter, to 49% to 50% excluding currency changes, CFO Amy Hood said on the earnings call. “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply,” she said.

Hood said Azure’s growth came from Foundry, Microsoft’s service for building AI apps and agents, and from engineering work that let Microsoft sell unused capacity on its existing servers. That helped make up for delays in new data center capacity that outside providers were supposed to deliver.

Those delays pushed some spending later into the fiscal year. Microsoft now expects to spend about $170 billion on capital expenditures in calendar 2026, down from about $175 billion. It expects to spend more than $50 billion this quarter, and Hood said spending will accelerate in the first half of calendar 2027.

Hood also said Microsoft may tap additional sources of financing to help pay for the buildout, “when we believe it is attractive to do so.” The company still expects to bring in more cash than it spends this fiscal year.

Microsoft’s expense forecast for the December quarter includes an estimate for the buyout offer it announced Monday, Hood said, though she didn’t give the amount.

The company expects total revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion for the December quarter, above the $95.7 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance.

#5532. Bigger than Bing or Xbox: Microsoft’s OpenAI haul reaches $10B in quarterly revenue

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 4:28 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:33 pm

OpenAI generated $10 billion in revenue for Microsoft in the quarter ended Sept. 30, about 11% of the Redmond company’s total revenue, according to its quarterly filing Wednesday.

The amount is up sharply. In the fiscal year that ended in June, Microsoft recorded $24.1 billion in revenue from its business with OpenAI, or about $6 billion a quarter on average.

That $10 billion surpasses some of Microsoft’s longest-running businesses. Xbox brought in $5.4 billion in the quarter. Search and advertising, which includes its Bing search engine, generated $6.6 billion. Windows licenses sold through PC makers, along with Surface and other Microsoft devices, brought in $3.6 billion.

The total covers revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI, as well as other business between the companies, such as OpenAI’s use of Azure to train and run its AI models. Microsoft didn’t say how much came from each, or how much of Azure’s growth came from OpenAI.

Azure revenue rose 48% to $33.2 billion in the quarter, beating Wall Street’s expectations and the company’s own forecast of 44% to 45% growth.

Microsoft has begun disclosing its revenue from OpenAI because its stake of about 24% makes OpenAI a “related party” under accounting rules, requiring it to report the business they do with each other.

Microsoft first reported the number in its annual report in July, as a full-year total. This is the first time it has given a quarterly figure.

The original AI alliance: Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019, eventually committing $13 billion, and became its exclusive cloud provider. ChatGPT ran on Azure when it launched in late 2022.

The companies have loosened their ties since then. OpenAI restructured as a public benefit corporation in October 2025, and Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal to supply OpenAI’s computing capacity. OpenAI committed to buy an additional $250 billion in Azure services. An April 2026 agreement gave OpenAI broader freedom to use other cloud providers.

OpenAI has also agreed to keep sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030.

In addition, Microsoft sells access to OpenAI’s models to business customers through its Azure OpenAI Service, and the models became the foundation for its Copilot products, putting Microsoft at the front of the generative AI boom. That revenue comes from Microsoft’s own customers, so it isn’t part of the $10 billion.

Microsoft, for its part, now builds its own AI models and offers models from Anthropic and others.

Many customers, not a few: Asked by Bernstein Research analyst Mark Moerdler whether AI growth on Azure was coming from big businesses or AI-native companies, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella didn’t mention OpenAI.

He said he doesn’t want Azure’s AI business to depend on a few big customers, and that broad adoption by businesses is just getting started.

Nadella described it as “a decade-long thing,” and contrasted it with relying on “four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you” to show a few quarters of growth. That, he said, is “not a business as far as I’m concerned.”

He added that Microsoft has large customers who want to buy capacity, “and as long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some. If not, we will be patient.”

Later in the call, Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges brought up the fact that OpenAI made up 11% of revenue. Nadella didn’t address the number but praised OpenAI’s latest models and said customers are increasingly mixing models from different companies, or training their own.

He cited Microsoft’s tools for routing each task to whichever AI model handles it best. If you use AI coding agents, Nadella said, you want Anthropic and OpenAI “to compete for your workload, not like once a quarter, but for every task.”

New risk language: Microsoft also expanded a warning in its quarterly filing about the risks of depending on outside AI providers. The company builds products such as Copilot on AI models from outside companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. It now says it has “limited visibility into or control over” how those models are designed, trained, secured and tested.

Without naming OpenAI or Anthropic, the same section notes that some of these AI partners are also “significant customers of Azure,” and that the benefits Microsoft expects from those relationships “may not be realized or sustained.” It says those partners could change how much they buy, and that Microsoft itself may change how it allocates scarce data center capacity or prices it.

Microsoft is an investor in both companies. According to its latest filing, it owns about 24% of OpenAI, down from about 25% in June and about 27% after OpenAI’s restructuring a year ago, and has put $12.0 billion of a promised $13.0 billion into the company.

In addition, Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, and its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment. Microsoft hasn’t disclosed the size of its Anthropic stake, and Anthropic’s IPO filing earlier this week didn’t specify it either.

#5531. 10 retirement destinations for Americans, from Thailand to Italy, and how residence works

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Thailand, Panama, Colombia, and seven more countries draw U.S. retirees. Here is how residence routes compare.

Picture a retiree at a kitchen table, a beach-town listing open on one screen and a retirement budget on the other. The daydream feels close, and the math behind it can hold up. Many eligible U.S. citizens can keep collecting Social Security payments after they settle in another country, though limits differ by benefit and by location. The Social Security Administration runs a Payments Abroad Screening Tool so people can review their own case before they pack. A steady federal payment turns a vague wish into a plan someone can price. A plan built on one pleasant week of vacation can unravel once ordinary routines set in. Sunsets and sidewalk cafes reveal little about visa paperwork, pharmacy access, or the hours a flight home takes.

Medicare stops covering most care once a retiree leaves the U.S. The program lists a handful of narrow exceptions. Most people who relocate need a separate policy for routine visits and emergencies. Residence rules pile on more variables, from income or asset tests and age floors to renewal schedules and minimum-stay conditions. Americans carry U.S. filing obligations with them, along with questions about how a new home taxes pensions and investments and whether foreign tax credits apply. Currency swings can shrink a fixed income measured in dollars. Distance from children and grandchildren adds a cost no spreadsheet captures. Each of these pressures argues for an exit strategy a retiree sketches before departure.

Wise compares 10 destinations that U.S. citizens weigh for retirement and presents them in no universal order. Each country entry cites an official government or consular page for its visa terms and outlines popular places, a common route, and the kind of retiree it suits. The guide walks through practical checks on Social Security, Medicare, residence permits, and foreign-account reporting. It urges readers to judge every destination against one scorecard covering the residence route, healthcare, tax position, daily life, and long-term resilience. The guide assigns no scores and offers no cost-of-living data for individual countries. It warns that immigration rules can change and tells readers to confirm details with the relevant government or consulate. The 10 countries below form a selection from a wider field. The guide names Mexico, Spain, and Uruguay as worth comparing, too.

Thailand opens its retirement visa options to applicants aged 50 or older, and a financial test sits beside the age requirement. Applicants can satisfy that test with pension income or with qualifying funds. The funds route gives savers who never earned a pension a workable path into the country. A floor set at 50 puts the visa within reach of people who leave work in their early 50s. Applicants should confirm the exact financial amount with Thai authorities before they build a monthly plan around it. Thailand runs an electronic visa process called THAI E-VISA, which foreign nationals can reach through www.thaievisa.go.th.

Chiang Mai, Bangkok, and Phuket draw steady interest from American retirees, and the three settings point toward different budgets. Spending shifts from the capital to the resort areas to the northern cities. A monthly plan drafted around one of those settings can fall apart in another. A trial stay in only one of the three tells a retiree little about the other two.

Private health insurance needs a side-by-side comparison with local care before any move. Retirees with an existing condition face the highest stakes. The way a policy treats a prior diagnosis can decide whether coverage protects a household or leaves it exposed. Prescriptions belong on the same checklist. A retiree on regular medication needs to know how to obtain it in a new city.

Picking a city and choosing a policy work as linked decisions. A retiree's address shapes both living expenses and which clinics sit close by. A resort town and a capital can yield different answers to both questions. Settling on Bangkok before comparing insurers, or the reverse, risks a mismatch between the two.

The real price of a Thai retirement belongs to a specific city and a specific policy. Retirees who settle both questions before applying will know whether the move fits their income.

Panama's Pensionado residence asks retirees to prove a verifiable pension of at least $1,000 a month, plus $250 for each dependent. Panama designed the route with retirees in mind, and its test centers on steady monthly income. The threshold climbs in fixed steps as a household grows. A household with one dependent needs $1,250 a month, and one with two needs $1,500. Each dependent adds 25% to the base figure. A retiree supporting three dependents must document $1,750 a month. Across a full year, the base requirement equals $12,000 in pension payments.

Paperwork carries as much weight as income. A Panamanian attorney files the application inside the country, which puts the process in the hands of local counsel. Each foreign document needs authentication or an apostille before it counts toward the file. Applicants in the U.S. should leave time to gather records, certify them, and ship them to the lawyer. Hiring that attorney belongs near the start of any timeline.

Panama lets newcomers budget in U.S. dollars, so a pension lands in the same currency the landlord and grocer expect. Panama City, Boquete, and a string of coastal communities draw much of the interest. The short distance to the U.S. eases trips home to see family. Dollar pricing does not guarantee bargains. Housing in favored neighborhoods and private medical care can run high. A sound plan starts with prices in the specific town a retiree wants.

Program membership has also trimmed several everyday bills. CNBC reported in 2019 that Pensionado holders received half off entertainment, along with cheaper airfare, discounted hotel rates, and reduced energy costs. The discounts reached leisure, travel, and utilities. None of the listed perks touched rent or private insurance. Panamanian officials can confirm which of those breaks remain in force, a necessary step for a report from 2019. Meeting the $1,000 test settles legal status, but it says nothing about whether that sum covers a home in Boquete or a coastal town.

Greece puts four places in front of American retirees: Athens, Thessaloniki, Crete, and Corfu. Each name marks a separate setting a retiree can visit and compare before committing to one.

Greece's residence terms for retirees call for firsthand confirmation. Anyone drawn to the four locations should check the current income, age, and stay requirements with the Greek government or a consulate before building a budget around a move.

Costa Rica gives U.S. retirees three residence categories to weigh: Pensionado, Rentista, and Inversionista. Three separate doors into one country leave room to maneuver. A retiree who finds one category a poor fit can study the other two before crossing Costa Rica off a shortlist.

The guide attaches no income or asset threshold to any of the three categories. Applicants must get those numbers from Costa Rican officials before they can tell which door suits their finances. A household should bring a full picture of its pension, savings, and other income to that conversation.

Retiree categories make up one part of the country's legal framework. Costa Rica extends legal status to temporary residents and to people on foreign government missions. Pensioner status appears on that broader list, too. Retirees form one group among several that Costa Rica's residency system accommodates.

Costa Rica shares the Pensionado name with Panama, yet a common label guarantees no common rulebook. The guide spells out a pension floor for Panama's version and lists none for Costa Rica's. The shared name tells a retiree nothing about the price of entry. A retiree weighing the two countries needs both sets of requirements side by side before treating them as interchangeable options.

Nature sits at the center of Costa Rica's appeal. A large international community and reasonable access to the U.S. round out the picture. An established expatriate population can hand newcomers a social circle during their first months abroad. Expatriates who hold one of the three categories can offer firsthand accounts of the filing process. Costa Rican officials still set the rules that decide eligibility. Manageable flights home keep family members within reach for holidays, milestones, and emergencies.

Scenery and expatriate networks pull Americans toward Costa Rica, but a confirmed category alone lets them stay.

Malaysia gives American retirees a residence route with its purpose written into the title: the Malaysia My Second Home program, known as MM2H. The program serves as the common entry point for U.S. citizens who retire in the country. Its name casts Malaysia as a place to stay for the long haul. The title omits pensions and age, unlike Panama's Pensionado or Colombia's pensioner visa. The label alone tells an applicant little about who qualifies.

Kuala Lumpur, Penang, and Kota Kinabalu draw many of the Americans who make the move. Scouting all three lets a retiree compare housing, transport, and community before committing to one address. A short list of established destinations narrows the search for someone sizing up an unfamiliar country from thousands of miles away.

Modern city infrastructure gives Malaysia much of its appeal, and English turns up in many everyday settings. Language governs routine errands such as a pharmacy visit or a lease signing. Wide use of English lowers the hurdle a newcomer faces at those moments. Malaysia's modern infrastructure is an urban asset, which steers a retiree who values it toward a metro area such as Kuala Lumpur.

The country works as a Southeast Asian base for retirees who want the surrounding region within reach. Panama, Colombia, and Costa Rica each offer proximity to the U.S., a quality absent from Malaysia's profile. Retirees with family visits in mind may weigh that difference before picking Malaysia over a closer option.

Malaysia's pitch rests on urban amenities and a familiar language, and the MM2H terms decide whether a retiree can act on it.

Portugal gives American retirees a European base, a mild climate, and five popular destinations in Lisbon, Porto, Cascais, the Algarve, and Madeira. The five span urban and seaside settings. A newcomer can pick a city routine or a home near the water without crossing a border.

Temperatures and rainfall shift from region to region. The Algarve occupies the country's southern tip and holds Portugal's hottest, driest weather. Porto, in the north, gets sunny and breezy summers. Snow and skiing arrive in the Serra de Estrella mountains of central Portugal.

Such range lets one country suit retirees with opposite tastes. Someone chasing heat and dry days would look south toward the Algarve. A person who favors breezier summers could weigh Porto. A skier finds slopes inside the same borders.

The national label of a mild climate masks sharp regional contrasts. The region a retiree picks inside Portugal will set the weather of everyday life.

Colombia's pensioner visa asks applicants to prove a pension worth at least three current Colombian minimum monthly wages. The benchmark rests on the local wage scale and carries no fixed dollar amount. A retiree paid in dollars must measure that income against a yardstick set in Colombian currency. The gap between pension and threshold shifts whenever the minimum wage or the exchange rate moves. Anyone near the line should look up the current wage figure before filing.

Colombia rewards retirees who want options: a choice of cities, regional climates that shift from one area to the next, and a short trip back to the U.S. Proximity shrinks one cost the wage test never captures: the distance from children and grandchildren.

Cartagena de Indias puts the coastal end of that range on the Caribbean Sea in the Bolívar department. Its Walled City and Getsemaní are areas people can explore on foot. Boats carry residents and visitors out to nearby islands and beaches. The shoreline location lets a retiree pair a historic city base with nearby Caribbean destinations.

Healthcare quality, safety, and living costs swing from city to city and from one neighborhood to the next. The visa bar stays the same whatever city a retiree chooses, but the price of daily life does not. An income that clears it can buy more in one district than in another. Two retirees with identical incomes could end up with different access to care and different risks depending on where they settle.

Groundwork for Colombia begins with the calendar. Retirees should visit in more than one season, compare insurance networks, and draw up a security plan built for the exact spot they have in mind before committing. The three-wage test governs who qualifies, and the address a retiree picks determines what that pension buys after arrival.

France's common route for retirees is the long-stay visitor visa. Most people planning to remain in France beyond 90 days need a long-stay visa, and the length and purpose of the stay decide which type applies. The visitor category is one option within that family, not a blanket pass for every longer stay. The cutoff divides an extended holiday from a relocation. A retiree who intends to spend most of the year in France falls on the long side of it from the start. The habits of a short-trip vacationer offer little guidance for a move of that length.

Culture, transport links, and access to city, coastal, and countryside lifestyles define France's draw for retirees. The three settings give a newcomer distinct daily rhythms, and a single visa covers all of them. A retiree can weigh urban streets, a seaside town, and rural quiet and still pursue the same application. Good transport links mean a home in one setting need not shut out the other two.

Paperwork for a French move begins before the flight. Most travelers to France need a visa, and anyone outside the exempt groups must secure it ahead of departure through the French embassy or consulate serving the place where they live. An American retiree applies from the U.S. and cannot settle the question after landing.

Border officers run a second check. Every foreign national arriving in France must be ready to show documents covering the purpose of the visit, the means to pay for it, and the address where the traveler will stay. Each of those three items reflects a decision a retiree makes at home. The visit's purpose matches the long-stay visa the consulate issued. Applicants need records showing how a pension or savings will fund life in France. The address requirement pulls the choice among city, coast, and countryside forward. A newcomer cannot land first and shop for a region later. France favors the retiree who settles housing and gathers financial proof in the U.S. before boarding a flight.

Ecuador sets aside a temporary residence visa for retirees, and the newcomers who use it gravitate toward Cuenca, Quito, and a string of coastal communities. The word temporary in the visa's title signals a permit with an end date. Any status that expires comes with renewal conditions. A retiree should learn how long the permit lasts and what renewing it requires before shipping furniture south. The guide lists no income or asset threshold for the visa. Applicants should get the current financial test from Ecuador's government or consulate before they apply.

Smaller-city options give Ecuador its distinct appeal. Retirees who would trade a large metro for a more manageable town can find one here. Climates also vary across Ecuador's regions. The town a newcomer picks shapes the weather outside the window as much as the pace of daily life.

Ecuador's use of the U.S. dollar strips currency conversion out of the monthly budget. Retirees can plan spending in the same currency their Social Security deposits or U.S. pension payments arrive in. A swing in the exchange rate cannot shrink a check its owner spends in the money it arrived in. Shoppers can read local price tags without doing mental math.

Older Ecuadorians have drawn tangible perks beyond the visa. CNBC reported in 2017 that Ecuadorian retirees received half off utility bills, lower property taxes, and refunds of value-added tax on most purchases. Ecuador refers to its retirees as Third Agers, according to CNBC. Custom lets them move ahead of others in line at government offices, supermarkets, banks, and other businesses. Line priority shortens routine errands such as banking and government paperwork.

Utility and property tax discounts trim bills that recur for as long as a retiree stays. Ecuadorian officials can confirm whether those benefits remain in force, a necessary step for a 2017 report.

Italy steers American retirees toward one named path, the Elective Residence visa. The word "elective" frames relocation as a decision a person makes freely, which suits a retiree who arrives by choice and without a job offer.

Newcomers on the visa must also sign up with their local Comune, the municipal office that confirms their residency and unlocks local services. Registration binds a retiree to one specific municipality. The choice of town therefore carries administrative weight on top of its everyday appeal.

Renewal brings the original conditions back into view. Applicants must demonstrate that they still hold enough financial resources, valid accommodation, and adequate health coverage. None of the three tests comes with a stated sum in the requirements as described, so the exact bar remains something to pin down with the consulate.

The renewal terms turn a one-time application into an ongoing audit. A lease that ends without a replacement, an insurance policy that expires, or savings that dwindle could each put an extension at risk. Italy's route favors retirees whose money, housing, and coverage stay stable from one renewal to the next.

No further supported fact was available without padding or repeating the introduction.

#5530. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI Predicts an XRP Explosion as Binance Resumes Withdrawals Following Hack

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Something potentially massive could be coming for Ripple XRP, according to Mark Zuckerberg’s AI bot. Meta AI predicts that XRP could be the market leader across Q4 and into 2027, with an explosive move into double digits, but only if an over-the-top scenario built around a hypothetical landmark catalyst lands.

The idea centers on a major global payments consortium and several large commercial banks formally adopting the XRP Ledger as a preferred liquidity and settlement layer for next-generation cross-border corporate treasury and trade-finance flows.

In this framework, significant volumes of institutional payment activity would migrate onto the XRP Ledger, creating structural demand for XRP as a bridge asset at a scale far beyond previous cycles.

On the higher timeframes, XRP has been consolidating in the $1.20–$1.30 region following recent market volatility. Price continues to hold above key intermediate supports while facing resistance around the $1.35–$1.45 zone.

In a standard bull market, a sustained breakout above $1.60–$1.80 would confirm intermediate strength and open the path toward a retest of the prior all-time high near $3.65–$3.66.

Under the extreme corporate treasury and trade-finance adoption scenario outlined above, clearing that previous high would likely trigger powerful measured-move extensions and multi-cycle Fibonacci projections from the long-term base.

#5529. Zillow agrees to pay $212.5M to settle investor lawsuit over failed home-flipping business

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 6:40 pmOctober 29, 2026 at 7:46 am

Zillow Group will pay $212.5 million to settle a shareholder class action lawsuit over its handling of Zillow Offers, the home-flipping business it shut down in 2021.

The lawsuit alleged that Zillow executives painted an overly positive picture of Zillow Offers in the months before the shutdown, without disclosing how poorly the company was able to predict home prices. That kept the stock artificially high until Zillow revealed the problems and announced the shutdown in November 2021, according to the complaint.

The Seattle-based company disclosed the settlement Wednesday in an SEC filing. About $48 million of the payment is expected to come from insurance. The deal requires court approval and includes no admission of wrongdoing.

In a statement, a Zillow spokesperson said, “We are pleased that the parties have reached a resolution on the matter.”

The settlement comes about three weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear Zillow’s challenge to the case’s class status. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups backed Zillow’s petition.

Steve Berman, managing partner of Seattle law firm Hagens Berman, the court-appointed class counsel, told Real Estate News he believes it’s the largest single securities settlement in the history of the Western District of Washington, the federal court district that includes Seattle.

Separate shareholder lawsuits filed on the company’s behalf against its leaders, known as derivative suits, remain pending, according to the filing.

Zillow bet its future on buying and selling homes in 2019, when co-founder Rich Barton returned as CEO and projected the business would reach $20 billion in annual revenue within three to five years. The company used its pricing algorithms to buy houses, fix them up and resell them.

The effort unraveled in the fall of 2021. An analyst report found that two-thirds of 650 homes it sampled from Zillow’s inventory were listed for less than the company paid.

Days later, Zillow shut down the business, cut about 2,000 jobs and took a $304 million inventory writedown, with Barton citing the unpredictability of its home-price forecasts. Zillow’s stock fell 32% over two days, according to Reuters.

The original lawsuit, filed that month in federal court in Seattle, cited upbeat statements executives made in the months before the shutdown.

They included a September 2021 remark by Jeremy Wacksman, then Zillow’s chief operating officer and now its CEO, that “the strength and the appeal for Zillow Offers just continues to grow.” Investor Jeremy Jaeger later became the lead plaintiff.

The class covers investors who bought Zillow Class A or Class C shares between Aug. 5 and Nov. 2, 2021. If the judge grants preliminary approval, Zillow will pay the money into a settlement fund within 20 business days.

#5528. Seattle-area startup Group14 raises $169M, plans battery materials factory in Spain

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 29, 2026 at 5:00 amNovember 2, 2026 at 1:32 pm

Next-generation battery materials startup Group14 Technologies today announced $169 million in new funding and plans to build a manufacturing facility in Spain, expanding a production network that includes Washington state and South Korea.

“In order to be a global player in a global industry, we need a global footprint, which means it’s not about picking one specific region and going all in,” Group14 CEO Rick Luebbe told GeekWire. “We really need to grow all regions.”

The startup has developed a silicon-carbon material that replaces graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes, enabling higher energy density and faster charging, according to the company. The material already ships primarily to consumer-electronics customers, while the company pursues automotive and data center applications.

The funding came from a European investor, Luebbe said, but he did not name the firm. It extends the company’s $463 million Series D round and brings Group14’s total funding to nearly $1.5 billion.

The new facility will be located in Sagunto, near Valencia, with production targeted for mid-2029. The site offers clean energy, skilled labor from the chemical industry and proximity to automotive customers, given that Spain is the second-largest vehicle producer in Europe after Germany.

Group14 already has a presence on the continent, acquiring Germany’s Schmid Silicon Technology Holding GmbH in 2023 to secure a European source of silane gas, a key ingredient in its battery material.

Just as the U.S. has been working to bolster its domestic battery manufacturing and reduce its reliance on Chinese supplies, Europe is doing the same, Luebbe said. The company wants to be part of that solution and is eager to make its move.

“Building chemical plants takes a long time, and so you’ve got to think ahead and be able to establish that global footprint and development strategy,” Luebbe said. “We’ve learned a lot in the lifetime of Group14.”

Group14 was founded in 2015 and six years later began operating its first commercial-scale factory, called Battery Active Materials-1, or BAM-1, at its headquarters in Woodinville, Wash.

In 2023, it broke ground on BAM-2 in central Washington’s Moses Lake with funding that included $100 million from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. The site has two modules that at full capacity will be able to produce up to 4,000 tons of silicon-carbon battery material annually, enough for at least 200,000 electric vehicles.

The company originally aimed to start production by late 2024, a target later pushed to early 2026. Group14 laid off an undisclosed number of Washington workers in July 2025 and furloughed additional employees at Moses Lake in January as it shifted resources toward South Korea. The company’s total headcount is approximately 383 employees.

Luebbe said this week that the company is now targeting mid-2027 to bring the first module online, following equipment installation and commissioning. The second module does not yet have a firm completion date.

“It’s a very complicated infrastructure, and it takes a lot longer than we had anticipated to do the final installation and commissioning,” he added.

The company has at least secured the power it needs. It previously contracted sufficient clean energy to run the site, as well as a planned silane gas facility. Since Group14 began its development, data center deployments have accelerated in the region and projects are competing for clean electricity from hydropower dams.

While BAM-2 has been delayed, Group14’s BAM-3 site in South Korea — which originally began as a joint venture with SK materials — has been producing anode material since 2024. The facility has been scaling up and expects to reach its 2,000-ton annual capacity within about six months.

Group14 is shipping primarily to consumer-electronics customers, which qualify new materials faster than automakers. Luebbe also sees a growing opportunity in data-center battery backup units, where silicon-anode batteries could help smooth rapid spikes in AI-server power demand.

“I’m anticipating data center batteries, battery backup units, to be the second biggest market for us behind EVs,” he said.

#5527. Super Micro Computer stock pops after quarterly sales more than tripled

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Supermicro expects net sales of $72.0 billion to $82.0 billion for fiscal 2027 and $19.5 billion to $21.5 billion next quarter

Super Micro Computer reported first-quarter net sales of $19.9 billion for the quarter ended Sept. 30, up from $5.0 billion a year earlier, and its stock gained 6.4% in extended trading on Tuesday.

Net sales in the prior quarter were $11.1 billion. Net income was $1.59 billion, compared with $168 million a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share were $1.75, versus $0.26 a year earlier, and non-GAAP diluted earnings per share were $1.81, versus $0.35.

Gross margin was 12.7%, up from 9.3% a year earlier and down from 17.5% in the prior quarter.

"Supermicro's transformation into a Total AI and IT Datacenter Solution provider continues to accelerate, delivering record revenue of $19.9 billion for the first quarter fiscal 2027," Charles Liang, the company's founder, president and CEO, said in a statement.

Chief Financial Officer Mark Long told MarketWatch that a "high-quality customer base" is behind the company's revenue growth.

For the second quarter, which ends Dec. 31, the company expects net sales of $19.5 billion to $21.5 billion. It expects GAAP net income of $1.59 to $1.83 per diluted share and non-GAAP net income of $1.66 to $1.90 per diluted share.

For fiscal 2027, the company expects net sales of $72.0 billion to $82.0 billion.

Operations used $434 million in cash in the quarter. As of Sept. 30, the company held $6.9 billion in cash and cash equivalents and had $8.6 billion in total bank debt and convertible notes.

The company said the figures are unaudited and preliminary because its financial closing procedures for the quarter are not complete.

Supermicro will hold a live audio webcast to review the results at 5 p.m. ET on Tuesday.

#5526. Coding Dojo co-founder unveils ‘Idea to Launch,’ a 30-day program to help aspiring founders build with AI

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 29, 2026 at 8:00 amOctober 29, 2026 at 7:47 am

Richard Wang, co-founder and former CEO of coding bootcamp Coding Dojo, is launching Idea to Launch, a 30-day program that helps would-be founders turn a startup idea into a working product using AI coding tools and hands-on engineering help.

Nearly four years after selling Coding Dojo to Perdoceo for $70 million, Wang was looking for a way to keep doing work that had a measurable impact on people’s lives. He found it in mentoring aspiring founders.

Wang thinks AI is about to do for software what smartphones did for video. Cheap cameras and cloud platforms gave rise to the influencer economy, and he believes AI will push the cost of building a product close to zero.

“We’re going to create this whole new builder economy that’s about to come in the next three to five years,” he said. “Baby boomers are gifted with cheap housing. I think Gen Z is going to be gifted with a cheap price to build.”

He sees plenty of demand. Citing a Shopify-Gallup study and a Zapier/Harris poll, Idea to Launch says 60% of Americans have a business idea but only 9% launch one. Wang said the reasons people hold back include fear of failure, not knowing how to get started, and not wanting to give up a paycheck or benefits.

Unlike accelerators such as Techstars or Y Combinator, Idea to Launch doesn’t take equity, and participants don’t have to quit their jobs. Over 10 evening sessions, founders get coaching, run customer interviews, build a product with AI tools such as Lovable, Replit and Cursor, and plan a launch. Each founder also gets 10 hours of one-on-one help from professional engineers.

Wang said people without technical backgrounds can now vibe-code 80% to 90% of a product on their own. The hard part, he said, is connecting it to other services, setting up the database correctly and making it secure.

“We’ll provide that type of knowledge with real engineering support,” he said. For engineers who have never done customer discovery or marketing, the program fills in the business side.

Security researchers have found serious vulnerabilities in apps built on vibe-coding platforms. A 2025 scan found 170 of 1,645 apps built with Lovable exposing user data, and another case this year exposed nearly 19,000 user records. Wang said the program’s engineers will make sure security holes are fixed “before they launch or before they get onto the first customer.”

The first cohort starts Jan. 11, followed by three more through April. Each is capped at 15 to 20 founders. Tuition is $3,500 for the inaugural cohort, down from the normal $5,000. Sessions will be held in person in Seattle or Bellevue, and Wang said he expects to pick a space within the next month. He is self-funding the venture.

Wang, who immigrated from China at 13 and was the first in his family to attend college, became Coding Dojo’s CEO in 2015. He left in 2017 for Trupanion and returned in 2019. The company grew to $50 million in peak annual revenue, according to Wang, and had 194 employees at the time of the sale, according to GeekWire’s earlier reporting. It operated campuses in several states before shifting online during the pandemic.

Wang sees Idea to Launch expanding to other tech hubs, then online, and eventually licensing the program globally, much as Coding Dojo grew to multiple campuses. If the first cohorts go well, he can envision a follow-up program, Launch to Traction, to help founders find more customers.

He doesn’t plan to invest in participants’ companies. Having spent years building and selling Coding Dojo, Wang said he knows how hard that road is and would rather “cheer them on from the sidelines.” He said taking VC money at Coding Dojo created pressure to grow 100% a year, something he calls “startup steroids.”

For Wang, the point isn’t to find the next unicorn. It’s to give more people a shot at building something now that AI has made it cheaper and easier.

“I think everyone should try at least once just to bring their idea to reality,” he said.

#5525. AMD beat earnings estimates as data center revenue nearly doubled

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The chipmaker forecast fourth-quarter revenue of about $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, and its stock rose in extended trading

AMD $AMD reported third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45% from a year earlier, as Data Center segment revenue rose 97% to a record $8.5 billion. Adjusted earnings were $2.09 a share, up from $1.20 a year earlier, the company said.

Analysts had expected revenue of $13.1 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal. They had expected adjusted earnings of $1.95 a share, according to CNBC, or $1.97, according to Bloomberg. Bloomberg said analysts had predicted data center revenue of $8.2 billion.

AMD stock rose in extended trading on Tuesday.

"We delivered a record quarter with revenue exceeding the high end of our guidance as Data Center segment sales nearly doubled year-over-year," AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su said in a statement. She said the company expects growth to accelerate in the fourth quarter as it scales production of its Helios rack-scale systems and "Venice" processors.

On a GAAP basis, net income was $2.4 billion, or $1.46 a diluted share, compared with $0.75 a year earlier. The results included a $1.1 billion charge from the change in fair value of warrants issued to certain customers. The charge stems from AMD's agreement with OpenAI, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Client and Gaming segment revenue fell 8% to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue dropped 40% to $773 million on lower semi-custom and graphics sales, while Client revenue rose 7% to $2.9 billion. Embedded segment revenue rose 29% to $1.1 billion.

Anthropic, Meta $META, Microsoft $MSFT, OpenAI and Oracle $ORCL Cloud Infrastructure are running models and workloads on the first Helios systems, which use AMD Instinct MI450 Series GPUs and 6th Gen AMD EPYC CPUs, the company said.

For the fourth quarter, AMD expects revenue of about $17 billion, plus or minus 3%. The midpoint implies growth of about 66% from a year earlier and 27% from the third quarter. The company expects non-GAAP gross margin of about 55%, compared with 56% in the third quarter.

Analysts had expected fourth-quarter revenue of $16.2 billion, according to CNBC, or $16.3 billion, according to Bloomberg.

AMD stock slid last week as investors reacted to Intel $INTC's results, which pointed to weak PC sales and a shortage of server chips. Intel reported that data center and AI revenue rose 78% to $7.3 billion. Its stock dropped more than 22% in after-hours trading Thursday.

The higher cost of memory chips has hampered PC manufacturing and sapped buyer interest, according to Bloomberg.

#5524. Jupiter's Q3 Staking Rewards For All Wallets Opens Today, See Who Clears the 50 JUP Bar

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

50 JUP sounds like a threshold almost anyone can meet. It isn't, and today is when many stakers will find that out.

Jupiter's Active Staking Rewards (ASR) for July to September 2026 are now open to every wallet. That means a 50 million JUP pool can be claimed by anyone who qualified. The problem is that "qualified" doesn't mean what most people think. The rule isn't "have 50 JUP staked." It's "average 50 JUP across the whole quarter." Running the numbers this morning and a lot of wallets that look eligible at a glance aren't.

The round started quietly. According to the official Q3 campaign page, the campaign ran from July 1 until earning closed on September 30, and claims opened on October 12. That first week was reserved for Jupiter's own apps. Early access was limited to Jupiter Wallet and the Jupiter Mobile app, and other wallets can claim from 20 October 2026.

So if you stake from Phantom, Solflare, Backpack or a hardware wallet, today is your first real opportunity. Jupiter's documentation explains why the wallet matters. Rewards are linked to the wallet you staked from. If that wallet lives in another app, you either wait for the general opening or import the same recovery phrase into Jupiter Wallet or Jupiter Mobile.

There's no rush to the finish line yet. Reports put the claim deadline at January 12, 2027. Still, I wouldn't leave it to the holidays.

The campaign page states the rules plainly. 50M JUP will be distributed to stakers this period, ASR is calculated on a time-weighted average of your stake, and an average of 50 JUP or more staked during the quarter qualifies.

The words that matter are "time-weighted average." A wallet that held 50 JUP for all 92 days of Q3 averages exactly 50. A wallet that held 500 JUP for only a few days might average less than that. Jupiter designed it this way on purpose. The 7-day unstaking cooldown stops users from staking briefly around distribution periods to collect rewards without sustained participation.

One more detail surprised me, given the program's name. Voting has no effect on ASR, and you do not need to vote to be eligible. The "Active" in Active Staking Rewards now refers to keeping tokens staked, not to governance turnout.

Here's the simple math. It assumes the average is weighted day by day across the 92 days from July 1 to September 30. Jupiter hasn't published its exact snapshot schedule, so treat these figures as close estimates, not guarantees.

The edge cases are where people get caught. Suppose a wallet held 60 JUP from July 1 but started unstaking at the end of August. Its average comes to only about 40 JUP, so it misses. Another wallet held 40 JUP all quarter and added 30 more on September 1. It ends up at roughly 49.8 JUP, just under the line. Adding 31 instead of 30 would have qualified it.

The simplest check is to connect your wallet at Jupiter Rewards. The page will show the amount of ASR you're eligible to claim. If it shows nothing for an older address, the time-weighting is the most likely reason.

Now for the payout. As of mid-October 2026, total staked JUP topped 1.1 billion tokens, roughly 33% of circulating supply, spread across more than 357,000 wallets.

If you divide 50 million JUP by about 1.1 billion staked, you get roughly 4.5% for the quarter. A wallet that just clears the 50 JUP average would receive about 2.3 JUP. An average of 1,000 JUP works out to about 45, and 10,000 to around 455. The quarter's average total stake may have been a bit below the October figure, so actual allocations could come in slightly higher. Your campaign page shows the real number.

Don't expect the tokens to show up as spendable JUP. ASR is paid in JUP and added to your staked balance, which increases your governance power over time.

Three problems come up again and again in Jupiter's support notes:

Squads multisig users have a more manual process. The ASR documentation covers it in detail, including checking that the claim uses the Jupiter Merkle Distributor program, DiS3nNjFVMieMgmiQFm6wgJL7nevk4NrhXKLbtEH1Z2R before you approve anything.

Missing the deadline has real consequences. According to the Jupiter DAO portal, unclaimed ASR goes back to the community treasury once the claim period ends. Jupiter also says that no transfer is made on your behalf after the support deadline.

The bigger picture is a pool that's getting more crowded. Every quarter, 50M JUP goes to eligible stakers, and that figure doesn't change. With staked JUP now above 1.1 billion, each new staker gets a smaller slice of the same pie.

ASR is also the main reward Jupiter is still paying out. The Jupiter DAO voted in February 2026 to postpone Jupuary and send its 700 million JUP back to a community multisig. That leaves this quarterly distribution as the core reason to keep JUP staked.

My advice is to claim this round now and then look ahead. The October to December period is already more than halfway through. The same math applies, and each week you wait raises how much JUP you need to reach a 50 JUP average.

#5523. She Won 8 Olympic Medals, Then Retired at Age 25. Here’s How She’s Changing Her ‘Super Intense’ Mindset.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Former Olympic athlete Ariarne Titmus is reconsidering the all-or-nothing thinking that shaped her life in the pool.

After winning eight Olympic medals and retiring last year at age 25, Ariarne Titmus is done with competitive swimming. Now the 26-year-old Australian athlete is rethinking a life built around winning or failing.

According to a recent report from The Guardian, Titmus acknowledged that she looks at “a lot of things” in her life as “pretty black and white” and it is “not a good way to be sometimes.”

“In my swimming career, I was all or nothing,” she said. “I was win or lose. I was achieve it, or fail. And I guess that’s not a great way to be in life.”

Titmus, 26, earned four gold, three silver and a bronze medal at Olympic events, making her one of the world’s most accomplished athletes. She left competitive swimming after the 2024 Paris Olympics.

Titmus had to reorient herself to a new normal after realizing that an all-or-nothing mindset didn’t work for life after retirement from competitive sports. She knew how to win Olympic medals. Then she had to learn to live beyond them.

Titmus said undergoing a surgery in 2023 to remove an ovarian growth prompted her to reconsider her priorities and make room for life after swimming.

“I’ve definitely tried to change my outlook on a few areas of my life and not live with that super intense mindset that I had to have to be successful in the pool,” she said. “Because I don’t have to be like that any more.”

For other elite athletes besides Titmus, retiring has required them to reconsider how they structure their days and measure success.

Record-breaking U.S. swimmer Michael Phelps, who retired from the sport in 2016 after taking home 28 Olympic medals, told CNBC in 2021 that his competitive career had revolved around controlling everything he could to achieve near-perfection. When he retired, he had to learn to slow down, take deep breaths during stressful situations and seek support rather than manage everything himself. During the pandemic, that meant speaking more frequently with his therapist, friends and family.

Phelps did not abandon every familiar habit. He said he still exercised six or seven times a week, including weightlifting sessions.

Meanwhile, competitive Australian tennis player Ashleigh Barty took a different approach. When she retired, she focused on separating happiness from results.

Barty announced her retirement at age 25 in March 2022, explaining that her tennis career had resulted in a change in perspective. For her, success meant knowing that she had given everything and felt fulfilled. She would not allow results of a match to determine her happiness.

Barty achieved her childhood dream of winning Wimbledon, an annual tennis tournament held in London, in 2021. She said the accomplishment changed her perspective. She decided that her ambition had delivered enough results in tennis and chose to retire instead of chasing another title.

“There’s no right way, there’s no wrong way, it’s just my way,” Barty said in her retirement announcement video.

After winning eight Olympic medals and retiring last year at age 25, Ariarne Titmus is done with competitive swimming. Now the 26-year-old Australian athlete is rethinking a life built around winning or failing.

According to a recent report from The Guardian, Titmus acknowledged that she looks at “a lot of things” in her life as “pretty black and white” and it is “not a good way to be sometimes.”

“In my swimming career, I was all or nothing,” she said. “I was win or lose. I was achieve it, or fail. And I guess that’s not a great way to be in life.”

#5522. AWS growth hits 39%, its fastest in nearly five years, as Amazon misses on earnings

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 1:37 pmOctober 30, 2026 at 10:35 am

Amazon Web Services revenue grew 39% to $46 billion in the third quarter, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said he expects the cloud unit to top 40% growth in both 2027 and 2028.

That wasn’t enough for investors. Amazon posted earnings of $1.89 per share, well short of the $1.97 analysts expected, as higher interest costs on its growing debt and other losses ate into its profit.

Operating income beat expectations at $28.1 billion, above the high end of Amazon’s own guidance, and the 13.9% operating margin for the quarter was the highest in the company’s history.

Revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12%, came in just under analyst estimates but at the top of Amazon’s forecast range. Shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading, after closing down 4% during the regular session.

Update: On the earnings call, Jassy said AWS has a backlog of $578 billion in contracted future revenue, more than double a year earlier. He also said Amazon expects to spend “meaningfully more” on capital projects in 2027 than the roughly $220 billion it plans for this year.

Amazon may need to count on its legendary willingness to be “misunderstood for long periods of time,” as it asks investors to look past the costs to where its biggest businesses are headed.

In the company’s earnings release, Jassy said Amazon’s retail business is gaining market share with improving margins. Retail sales, including online stores, physical stores and third-party seller services, totaled nearly $500 billion over the past 12 months, and AWS is now at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate.

“There has never been a trillion dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years,” he said.

On the earnings call, Jassy said those two businesses are AWS and Amazon’s stores business.

Advertising grew 11% to $19.6 billion, or 12% excluding currency changes, down from 22% on that basis a year earlier. Amazon blamed the timing of Prime Day and a few other factors, and said it expects ad growth to return to the high teens in the fourth quarter.

Online stores grew 2% to $68.5 billion, held back by Prime Day moving into the second quarter this year. Amazon said overall revenue growth would have been about 4 percentage points higher without the shift.

Third-party seller services, the fees Amazon collects from merchants on its site, grew 9% to $46.5 billion. AWS came within about $500 million of it.

Subscription services, which includes Prime memberships, grew 11% to $14 billion.

Physical stores, mostly Whole Foods, grew 2% to $5.7 billion.

Outlook: Amazon expects fourth-quarter revenue of $240 billion to $247 billion, up 12% to 16%, and operating income of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion.

Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky said on the earnings call that costs for Amazon Leo, the company’s satellite internet service, are weighing on its fourth-quarter profit forecast as the service gets ready to launch later this year.

Wall Street had expected fourth-quarter operating income of $33.2 billion, near the top of that range, according to analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives. It still expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year.

Amazon’s free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier, mostly because of its AI investments.

#5521. SEO or PPC? How to Choose Between Long-Term Growth and Instant Traffic on Your Website

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Every business owner eventually faces the same marketing crossroads: invest in search engine optimization (SEO) or spend money into pay-per-click (PPC) ads.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Every business owner eventually faces the same marketing crossroads: invest in search engine optimization (SEO) or spend money into pay-per-click (PPC) ads. Both strategies aim to get your business in front of potential customers on search engines, but they work in fundamentally different ways.

SEO builds long-term, cost-effective organic traffic through content and keyword optimization, while PPC delivers immediate, measurable results through paid campaigns. Choose SEO if you have time to invest and want sustainable growth. Choose PPC if you need fast visibility or compete in a crowded market. Many businesses combine both for balanced results.

SEO focuses on earning organic (unpaid) rankings by optimizing your website’s content, structure, and authority. PPC, on the other hand, involves paying for ad placements that appear above organic results, charging you each time someone clicks.

Choosing the right approach, or the right blend of both, can significantly affect your marketing budget, timeline, and overall business growth. This guide breaks down how each strategy works, compares their key differences, and helps you decide which fits your goals.

SEO is a long game. By optimizing your website for relevant keywords and producing high-quality, valuable content, you build sustainable visibility in search engine results pages (SERPs) over time.

One of SEO’s biggest advantages is cost efficiency. While it requires an upfront investment in content creation, technical optimization and link building, the cost per click decreases significantly as your organic traffic grows. You’re not paying for every visitor, you’re earning them through relevance and authority.

The tradeoff? Patience. SEO results typically take three to six months to materialize, and competitive industries may take even longer. Search engine algorithms also evolve constantly, meaning your rankings can shift based on factors outside your direct control.

PPC campaigns offer what SEO can’t: speed. Launch a campaign today, and you can start driving traffic and conversions within hours. This makes PPC an attractive option for product launches, seasonal promotions or businesses that need quick wins.

PPC also gives you granular control. You decide your budget, target audience, ad messaging and even the specific times your ads appear. This level of precision allows for rapid testing and optimization based on real performance data.

The downside is cost. PPC requires ongoing spend, and in competitive industries, cost-per-click rates can climb quickly. The moment you stop paying, your traffic stops too—there’s no lasting equity built the way there is with organic rankings.

When deciding between SEO and PPC, four factors matter most:

The right choice depends on your business goals, timeline and budget.

Choose SEO if you have the patience to invest in long-term growth and want a cost-effective strategy that keeps paying off after the initial work is complete. This approach suits businesses planning for sustained visibility rather than quick wins.

Choose PPC if you need immediate traffic, are launching a new product, or operate in a highly competitive market where organic rankings are difficult to achieve quickly. PPC is also useful for testing messaging and offers before committing to a long-term content strategy.

Consider combining both strategies if you want comprehensive coverage. Many businesses use PPC to generate quick wins while building their organic presence through SEO, creating a balanced approach that captures both immediate and long-term opportunities.

Neither SEO nor PPC is universally better, the right choice depends on your budget, timeline and business goals. SEO rewards patience with cost-effective, lasting visibility, while PPC delivers speed and control at a higher ongoing cost.

Most successful businesses don’t choose one over the other. Instead, they use a hybrid approach, leveraging PPC for immediate visibility while building long-term equity through SEO. Start by evaluating your current resources and goals, then test which strategy — or combination — moves the needle for your business.

Is SEO cheaper than PPC?Yes, it can be, over the long term. SEO requires upfront investment in content and optimization, but once rankings improve, you don’t pay per click. PPC requires continuous spending to maintain visibility.

How long does it take to see results from SEO?SEO typically can take three to six months to show meaningful results, depending on your industry’s competitiveness and the quality of your optimization efforts.

Can I use SEO and PPC together?Yes. Many businesses combine both strategies, using PPC for immediate traffic while building long-term organic visibility through SEO.

Which is better for a small business with a limited budget?SEO often makes more sense for limited budgets since it doesn’t require ongoing ad spend. However, a small, targeted PPC campaign can help generate quick traction while your SEO strategy develops.

What happens if I stop paying for PPC ads?Your traffic and visibility from those ads stop almost immediately. Unlike SEO, PPC doesn’t build lasting equity — it only works while you’re actively paying for it.

Every business owner eventually faces the same marketing crossroads: invest in search engine optimization (SEO) or spend money into pay-per-click (PPC) ads. Both strategies aim to get your business in front of potential customers on search engines, but they work in fundamentally different ways.

SEO builds long-term, cost-effective organic traffic through content and keyword optimization, while PPC delivers immediate, measurable results through paid campaigns. Choose SEO if you have time to invest and want sustainable growth. Choose PPC if you need fast visibility or compete in a crowded market. Many businesses combine both for balanced results.

SEO focuses on earning organic (unpaid) rankings by optimizing your website’s content, structure, and authority. PPC, on the other hand, involves paying for ad placements that appear above organic results, charging you each time someone clicks.
