#5519. Binance Withdrawals Top FTX Levels in November, but Crypto Liquidity Defies Panic

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Binance withdrawals surged into the billions after a record-breaking $6.3 billion hack, bringing back memories of FTX’s November 2022 collapse. Yet the world’s largest crypto exchange is showing a resilience that could barricade the industry from its darkest chapter.

Binance processed $4.65 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits during the first nine and a half hours after reopening services on November 1, resulting in $3.64 billion in net outflows. According to its October 28 Proof of Reserves data, the exchange held $171 billion in total assets, so the withdrawal wave accounted for just 2.1% of its reported holdings.

Binance withdrawals are BACK!BTC, ETH, BNB, XRP, DOGE, USDT, USDC and more are being re-enabled across supported networks.Binance also says 95% of the stolen assets have already been replaced.Bears were screaming FTX 2.0, desperately hoping for another collapse.

This puts the outflows in perspective: despite the initial rush following the $6.3 billion hack, Binance retained assets worth 47 times the net amount withdrawn. The exchange said withdrawals had begun stabilizing, while deposits remained substantial.

The figures initially look alarming, especially against the backdrop of FTX. The failed exchange suffered $6 billion in net withdrawals over 72 hours before suspending customer withdrawals in November 2022.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

“98% choose to stay. Trust isn’t earned by what you say in good times. It’s earned by what you do in hard times.” – Changpeng Zhao, Binance Founder

Binance has previously said that it had set aside more than $6.34 billion to cover the incident, including $5 billion in the affected token assets. It also reported that partners had frozen approximately $3 billion linked to the attack.

So how does this compare to FTX? This current crisis is fundamentally different from FTX’s collapse. FTX’s withdrawal run exposed a liquidity shortfall tied to customer funds and its relationship with Alameda Research. Binance, by contrast, says it will cover the stolen assets rather than pass the losses to users.

Bitcoin’s reaction offers one of the clearest signs of crypto’s resilience compared with the FTX collapse. Following the $6.3 billion Binance hack, BTC briefly slipped toward $76,700 but held above the closely watched $75,000 support level before recovering toward $79,000. The contrast with November 2022 is stark. Bitcoin fell nearly 10% on November 8 as FTX’s withdrawal crisis intensified, then plunged another 14.4% on November 9 to close near $15,877, after briefly hitting $15,632.

While Binance’s hack triggered billions in withdrawals and market-wide liquidations, Bitcoin has so far avoided the cascading selloff that followed FTX’s implosion. Its ability to defend $75,000 suggests investors are treating the incident as a major exchange security failure rather than evidence of a systemic liquidity crisis across crypto.

Binance has already faced a major financial and regulatory reckoning. In November 2023, the exchange agreed to pay more than $4 billion to resolve U.S. investigations into anti-money laundering and sanctions violations. Founder Changpeng Zhao also pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program. He resigned as CEO and paid a separate $50 million fine.

Despite that enormous settlement, Binance continued operating as the world’s largest crypto exchange. The latest hack now presents another test of its financial strength, operational resilience, and ability to maintain customer confidence.

Crypto markets have still felt the shock. Bitcoin and Ethereum fell following the breach, while spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded huge outflows and leveraged positions faced heavy liquidations. However, both major cryptocurrencies partly recovered after hitting lows.

Now, can Binance withdrawals continue to ease? The exchange publishes updated Proof of Reserves data and completes its security review. The comparison with FTX shows the scale of investor concern, but not necessarily the same outcome. Binance has absorbed a major hack, committed to covering customer losses, and resumed withdrawals after billions left the platform.

November has brought back memories of 2022. Binance’s response shows crypto’s largest exchange is determined to keep this crisis from becoming another industry-wide collapse.

#5518. Musk says Grok Bot’s costs are ‘unsustainably high,’ while OpenAI admits Dots are ‘compute heavy.’ Is the personal AI agent push dead on arrival?

The success of Meta’s Muse personal assistant has convinced the AI industry that personal agents that proactively complete tasks are the next logical evolution of the technology, but it’s unclear if there is enough compute to power them—at least in the timeframe that these companies are betting on.

This week, Elon Musk said the cost of running Grok Bot, the personal AI assistant SpaceX introduced in August, is “unsustainably high relative to revenue.” He suggested the company was throttling back the compute allocation for the technology, causing users to hit their limits faster.

Last night, at an intimate dinner with reporters in New York City, the head of ChatGPT’s consumer business Adam Fry said that OpenAI’s Dots assistants are “on the compute heavy side.” Each Dot assistant has its own cloud computer, which it uses to execute tasks on the user’s behalf, accessing any accounts and services it has been given access to.

Dots are helping people read and respond to emails, find and book tickets to events, and a far range of other assistant-like tasks. Through new features like “background mode,” Fry said, Dots plan to become an always-available presence, quietly changing how we go about our daily lives.

The company is moving all the right chess pieces to make this possible—as long as it gets enough compute. OpenAI has invested heavily in voice AI models, whose humanlike responses make interacting with the technology more seamless. ChatGPT’s voice mode now has 250 million weekly active users, Fry said. OpenAI also claims that ChatGPT search volume, measured by queries with search intent, is now one-fifth of Google’s volume. Paired with its forthcoming consumer devices designed by legendary iPhone architect Jony Ive, set to debut this year, all of these pieces could come together in a powerful consumer experience.

The success of these initiatives hinges on whether OpenAI can find enough compute in the couch cushions. The availability of Dots is limited today to those with a Pro subscription, which costs a whopping $100 per month. Bringing Dots to the masses would require a breakthrough in compute efficiency, which Fry said he expects will happen, causing costs to fall rapidly, even as model performance improves. At the same time, the more powerful—and constantly running—personal AI agents become, the more compute they consume. Will OpenAI ever be able to catch up with itself?

Today, OpenAI announced it is introducing a system by which Dots will route different tasks to different underlying AI models, including its GPT-6.1 Terra model. Terra is smaller and uses less computing power than GPT-6 Astra, the larger model that originally powered all Dots tasks. This new automatic task router will allow OpenAI to reduce how compute intensive Dots is.Meanwhile, the nationwide, bipartisan backlash to data centers has become so undeniable that OpenAI this week kicked off efforts to rebrand them “compute campuses.” Community pushback could cause permits to slow, or even kill facilities entirely, if the benefit to the community is not clear enough when it comes to job creation, environmental protection, and a host of other issues. In OpenAI’s inaugural post for the “compute campuses” lingo, it promised to reduce strain on local electrical grids and not take the limited supply of power from local families.

Anthropic’s S-1 filing gives us a sense of the astronomical sums the frontier labs are spending on compute. Anthropic has reportedly entered into various long-term and short-term purchase agreements, totalling $895.4 billion, “substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure,” an updated amendment to its S-1 from this week reads. Yet it may not be enough. Inability to secure even more compute is listed as a major risk factor that could cause Anthropic to be unsuccessful.

Although OpenAI has not yet filed its S-1, or confirmed IPO timing, sources tell us it almost certainly faces similar compute challenges, although it has some unique ones of its own. Unlike Anthropic, whose infrastructure includes four different types of chips, OpenAI’s fleet is largely dependent on Nvidia GPUs. The company is working on developing its own in-house chip, which it’s calling Jalapeno, set to scale up production in 2027.

OpenAI is also still searching for more funding, given that the company—like Anthropic—does not yet make a profit. Yet private funding may be nearing its end after OpenAI’s latest round fell short of its $30 billion target, landing at $11 billion, the Wall Street Journal reports. But even $30 billion would likely be a drop in the bucket when it comes to compute spending. The only option to fund the personal AI agent boom might be to go public, and even then success is not guaranteed.

#5517. Andy Jassy’s prediction: Amazon could have two $1 trillion businesses within a decade

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 6:08 pmOctober 31, 2026 at 8:51 am

No company has ever had a business with $1 trillion in annual revenue. Andy Jassy says Amazon is on a path to have two.

Amazon Web Services and the company’s stores business could both reach that milestone in the next five to 10 years, the Amazon CEO said Thursday in the company’s third-quarter earnings release and on its call with analysts.

It’s “pretty rare” for Jassy to make a projection that far out, Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak observed on the call, asking how he gets there.

Jassy’s answer started with AWS, which is at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate after growing 39% in the third quarter. He expects growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028, and pointed to a $578 billion backlog of contracted AWS revenue.

The largest customers reserve capacity in huge blocks, sometimes as much as a gigawatt at a time, giving Amazon “very good visibility” into 2027, 2028 and part of 2029, he said.

Beyond that, he said, businesses are still early in using AI, the cost of running AI models keeps falling, and new uses keep emerging, such as AI models finding and fixing security flaws.

“You can’t predict with any certainty five to 10 years from now, especially at these types of growth rates,” Jassy said of AWS. “But it’s not a stretch for us to imagine that this could be over a trillion dollar business.”

Jassy’s forecast is a big jump from seven months ago. In March, Jassy told employees that AWS had a chance to reach at least $600 billion in annual revenue within about a decade, double his earlier expectation, according to Reuters.

Amazon’s stores business is bigger than AWS. Sales from Amazon’s online and physical stores totaled $309 billion over the past 12 months, or about $575 billion if Jassy is including third-party seller services and advertising in his trillion-dollar projection. We’ve asked Amazon to clarify.

For comparison, Walmart, the world’s largest retailer, had $713 billion in revenue in its most recent fiscal year.

Whichever numbers he’s using, Jassy said “some folks are sleeping a bit” on how much progress the stores business has made.

Jassy argued that Amazon’s stores business is gaining ground on competitors. Amazon added more than $90 billion in gross sales over the past 12 months, he said, and is adding about twice as much per quarter as its next-largest U.S. competitor.

Units sold are up nearly 15% so far this year, Jassy said. He noted that nearly 80% of retail sales still happen in physical stores, which he expects to shift online over time.

The bold prediction came on a rough day for the company. Amazon shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading after its profit fell short of Wall Street’s expectations.

It’s not going to be cheap to get there. Amazon expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year, mostly for AWS, and Jassy said the company will spend “meaningfully more” in 2027. He said Amazon has “a clear line of sight to attractive financial returns” and is earning back its capital spending faster than before.

The impact is showing up in Amazon’s finances. Its free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier.

With its spending running ahead of the cash its businesses bring in, Amazon has raised $115 billion through long-term debt this year. Its interest expense more than tripled in the third quarter to $1.7 billion, cutting into its profit.

“We’re in the very early days of this inflection,” Jassy said. “Our strategy is working, and I expect it will for the foreseeable future.”

#5516. ‘We were wrong’: From Dewey to Trump, the polling misses hanging over the 2026 midterm forecasts

One of the most iconic images in 20th-century American political history shows a beaming President Harry Truman holding up a copy of the Chicago Daily Tribune emblazoned with the headline “DEWEY DEFEATS TRUMAN.”

In fact, Truman had just resoundingly defeated his Republican challenger, New York Gov. Thomas Dewey, winning 303 electoral votes to Dewey’s 189. The Tribune had gone to press before the race was called, but its editors can be given a measure of grace: just about every major poll put Dewey ahead.

That includes the one this magazine published. Elmo Roper’s final survey for Fortune gave Dewey 44% to Truman’s 31%, and the editors wrote, “So decisive are the figures given here this month,” that no further detailed reports were planned, according to historian David Greenberg’s account in Politico.

Seventy-eight years later, as Americans vote in the 2026 midterms, the major forecasters point to a strong night for Democrats. For companies and investors that plan around which party controls Congress, the question is how much weight those forecasts can bear. History says less than their precision suggests: presidential polls have underestimated Donald Trump in three straight elections, and the people who answer pollsters are a shrinking, skewed slice of the electorate.

The 1948 miss was not close. Gallup and Crossley both gave Dewey about a five-point edge in their final polls, FiveThirtyEight found, and Roper stopped polling weeks before Election Day. Newsweek asked 50 political writers to pick the winner; all 50 chose Dewey. Afterward, George Gallup offered a blunt verdict: “We were wrong,” the Deseret News recounted.

Polls that seemed staid and reliable have since proved flagrantly inaccurate. In 1960, Roper’s election-eve poll had Richard Nixon edging out John F. Kennedy by two points, Time reported. Kennedy won, clinching 303 electoral votes to Nixon’s 219, though his popular-vote margin was razor thin.

A generation later, most polls saw the 1980 race between Republican Ronald Reagan and President Jimmy Carter as harrowingly close; Gallup’s final survey had Reagan up just three points, according to Gallup. Reagan won 489 electoral votes and carried 44 states. Carter took 49 electoral votes, six states, and the District of Columbia.

Hillary Clinton was favored to beat Trump in 2016 but lost 304 electoral votes to 227, even as she won the popular vote. In 2020, polls correctly pointed to a Joe Biden win, but Trump ran well ahead of them; Biden won 306 electoral votes to 232, a striking parallel to 2016. The American Association for Public Opinion Research later found that 2020’s national polling error was the highest in 40 years.

The error shrank in 2024, but surveys still underestimated Trump for a third straight presidential race, 538 found. As historian W. Joseph Campbell wrote for Fortune that year, election polls have kept their popular appeal despite a checkered record.

If the major forecasts hold, Democrats will take the House and have a real shot at the Senate. As of Election Day, the Cook Political Report rated 204 House seats Solid or Likely Democratic and 178 Solid or Likely Republican, with 18 leaning Democratic, 17 leaning Republican, and 18 toss-ups, according to Newsweek’s tally.

An NBC News poll conducted Oct. 28–30 found 52% of registered voters preferred Democratic control of Congress, versus 45% for Republican control.

The 270toWin consensus forecast, which aggregates several forecasters, leans Democratic in 220 House seats and Republican in 196, with 19 toss-ups. Its Senate map is less settled: Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, and Texas sit in the toss-up column, and Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip a chamber Republicans hold 53–47.

We won’t know how accurate this year’s polls were until the votes are counted. Polling has never been an exact science, and even as text-based surveys and AI-driven modeling have become commonplace, the raw material pollsters depend on keeps getting harder to collect.

The biggest reason is falling response rates. In generations past, pollsters called voters on landlines, and people almost always answered. Now it’s easy to screen calls or ignore texts. Pew Research Center’s telephone response rate fell from 36% in 1997 to 6% in 2018, NBC News reported.

Those who do respond often don’t represent the electorate. Andreas Philippou, a professor emeritus of probability and statistics at Greece’s University of Patras, has traced several major polling failures to nonresponse.

In the U.S., the problem has a partisan tilt. AAPOR’s review of the 2016 polls found that better-educated Americans were significantly more likely to answer surveys than voters without degrees, who lean Republican.

Most pollsters now weight their samples by education. Yet AAPOR concluded that the 2020 miss wasn’t caused by a failure to do so, leaving the industry to chase a harder-to-measure gap between the people who answer and the people who don’t.

Midterms have been kinder to pollsters. In 2022, the RealClearPolitics generic-ballot average showed Republicans ahead by 2.5 points; they won the national House vote by 2.8.

That makes tonight a clean test. If Republicans outrun their polling in the toss-up House districts and the five Senate races the consensus can’t call, the nonresponse problem will have surfaced in a year without Trump on the ballot. If the results land near the averages, as they did in 2022, pollsters will have their strongest case yet that they’ve learned the lessons of 1948.

#5515. CertiK Verified 40.68M TPS for Sui, Here Is What It Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The biggest throughput figure a blockchain security firm has ever signed off on is sitting on CertiK's homepage right now: 40.68 million transactions per second.

It isn't CertiK's own number, and it isn't an on-chain number either. If you read the 2,000-word report behind it, you'll come to become more interested in what CertiK chose not to verify than in what it did.

Scroll past the client logos and media mentions on CertiK and you'll find it in the "Latest Research And Market Insights" strip. One card says CertiK independently verified Sui's Mainnet Tunnel performance campaign, which recorded more than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions across 7,680 tunnels at a peak of 40.68 million TPS.

Most readers will see "CertiK" next to "40.68 million TPS" and stop there. Crypto social media mostly did the same. Sui's own post described the figure as set live on stage at Sui Basecamp 2026 and certified by CertiK, and added that the network now clears in under 20 seconds what Visa processes in a day.Walking through CertiK's verification method when the report first came out. Now that the number has been promoted to CertiK's front page, it's worth looking at exactly what it represents.

According to CertiK's announcement, Sui ran a live Mainnet performance campaign on October 7, 2026, during Sui Basecamp Day. It recorded 15,241,348,297 tunnel transactions across 7,680 tunnels, and every tunnel was opened and settled on chain.

A Sui Tunnel works roughly like a private room. A small group of participants carries out many application actions without sending each one to the blockchain. Sui records the starting terms when the tunnel opens and the final result when it closes. Everything in between happens off-chain as signed receipts. CertiK compares the design to Bitcoin's Lightning Network but notes that tunnels can handle more than payments.

The test was more varied than a single payment loop. The campaign ran 10 runs across five workload types: simple payments, flash, blackjack, tic-tac-toe and battleship. Payments still made up most of the activity. Its 6,144 tunnels committed more than 12 billion transactions, or 78.98% of the total.

This is the part of the report I respect most. The peak came from the busiest complete second, between 08:46:17 and 08:46:18 UTC, when 40,682,328 qualifying tunnel transactions were committed. The highest 60-second rolling average was 40,339,143.65 TPS.

Doing the math on the gap between those two figures. It's about 343,000 transactions, or roughly 0.84%. In other words, the network held near-peak throughput for a full minute rather than spiking for one second.

CertiK also avoided the easiest way to inflate a number like this. For concurrent tunnels sharing the same time window, it added up their transaction counts once and divided by a single shared duration. It did not add individual per-tunnel rates together or multiply one tunnel's rate by the number of tunnels.

The checking itself was thorough. All 7,680 executions and all 960 slots reached VERIFIED status, and the 15.24 billion committed transactions matched the full-history admitted receipts exactly. The work ran on dedicated AWS infrastructure with 128 vCPUs and 247 GiB of RAM.

There's also a small correction in the story. Sui's first announcement reported 40,614,180 TPS. CertiK's audited peak came in about 68,000 higher, a 0.17% difference. A verifier landing slightly above the project's own claim is unusual, and I think it reflects well on the method.

The homepage card doesn't mention any of this, but the full report is clear about its limits.

First, this isn't on-chain throughput. CertiK states that Tunnel TPS measures off-chain tunnel transactions and is not a measurement of Sui's on-chain capacity.

Second, the data came from the project being tested. The Sui team supplied the campaign data and executed all test scenarios, and CertiK examined the retained evidence and recalculated the totals.

Third, the cryptographic checks were not exhaustive. CertiK reconciled the arithmetic, receipt counts and timestamps, but it did not re-run individual signatures or do a fresh cryptographic replay of every receipt.

Fourth, the report can't speak to how the system would behave in normal use. The records don't establish clock accuracy, failure rates, latency percentiles or results across repeated runs. The sustained figure is the best 60-second window observed, not a guaranteed minimum.

Put simply, CertiK verified that the accounting is correct. It did not verify that Sui can handle 40 million real users' actions every second.

The number that's most telling isn't the TPS figure. More than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions were anchored to Sui through just 1,920 on-chain lifecycle transactions: 960 openings and 960 settlements.

By simple calculation, that's about 7.9 million off-chain actions for every on-chain transaction. That ratio is what the tunnel design is built to achieve. It's an impressive engineering result, but it measures how well Sui compresses activity, not how fast its base layer runs.

This isn't the first speed record CertiK has signed off on, and the earlier ones show why comparisons are tricky. In its earlier TON verification, CertiK worked from per-minute transaction count data and arrived at 104,715 TPS for TON's testnet. In April 2025, Qubic announced 15.52 million TPS verified by CertiK, measured over 10 peak ticks on its Layer 1 mainnet.

On paper, Sui's tunnel figure is about 2.6 times Qubic's and nearly 390 times TON's. But these were three different kinds of tests: a sharded testnet, a base-layer burst and an off-chain channel network. They don't belong on the same leaderboard.

My view is that the 40.68 million figure is real, well documented and carefully bounded. It's also a measure of what an off-chain system can process, not what Sui's blockchain itself handles. CertiK's report is honest about that, even if the one-line homepage card isn't.

#5514. Power outage takes down KEXP streaming for Seattle radio station’s worldwide audience

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 2, 2026 at 8:22 am

KEXP’s website and online streaming were down Friday morning after a power outage hit the Seattle radio station, though its over-the-air broadcast was back and running.

The outage started around midnight, and the station was on and off for a while before it was “knocked offline by a major power outage” between 2 and 3 a.m., said Dashel Schueler, KEXP’s director of marketing and communications. Schueler didn’t know the cause of the outage.

The station’s backup power system, known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS), also failed.

“There’s no power to the server room infrastructure because the UPS that is supposed to protect all of that gear has failed,” Schueler said. Staff are trying to power critical devices to restore services while they wait for the UPS to be repaired or for a workaround that bypasses it.

There’s no estimate yet for when streaming will return.

Listeners in the Seattle area can tune in at 90.3 FM. The outage affects the KEXP.org stream and the station’s mobile app. KEXP estimates about 175,000 people stream its live broadcast each week, and another 85,000 listen to its shows on-demand.

The outage also took down 92.7 KREV, the station KEXP now owns in the San Francisco Bay Area, which relies on KEXP’s Seattle-based digital infrastructure. Because KEXP’s DJs pick songs live rather than playing a preset playlist, underwriting breaks vary in timing and length, Schueler said. DJs fire the separate Seattle and Bay Area spots manually and at the same time.

KREV was back by around 8:30 to 8:45 a.m., running on a barebones setup KEXP typically uses for remote broadcasts, Schueler said. Listeners may notice some issues while the station gets everything put back together.

Around 7:30 a.m., KEXP DJ John Richards read messages on air from listeners across Seattle who were happy to have the station back — terrestrially at least.

A few posts from listeners on X and Bluesky referenced the streaming outage.

Update: Late Friday afternoon KEXP said it was still working to restore services, but it did manage to put up a temporary livestream on its site.

Update: KEXP CEO Ethan Raup details what went wrong and how it was fixed in this post on LinkedIn.

#5513. Anthropic’s third-quarter results mean IPO math and history are not on its side, analysts say

Anthropic’s IPO is looking like an increasingly expensive and risky bet after the company released third-quarter financial results yesterday that showed its rate of revenue growth slowing and its expenses climbing at a faster pace compared to prior quarters.Several analysts Fortune spoke to said math and past experience are not in favor of Anthropic producing stellar returns for investors. That may explain why institutional investors are reportedly pushing the company and its IPO advisors to price Anthropic’s shares at the lower end of a $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation range that the company is seeking in its public stock offering.

Even that may be too pricey, according to analysts. Any IPO valuation above about $1.41 trillion would ask Anthropic’s buyers to pay more than $40 for every dollar the company generated in revenue over the past year—a price level achieved by just 14 of the 4,110 IPOs that took place between 1980 through 2024, according to a study from Jay Ritter, director of the University of Florida’s IPO Initiative. What’s more, those IPOs delivered lower average returns than the broader market, Ritter said.

Against the roughly $35.3 billion in revenue Anthropic booked over the past four quarters, a valuation range of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion would mean investors paying between $43 and $57 for every dollar of sales the company generated in the past 12 months.

To justify a valuation north of $1.4 trillion, Anthropic needs a path toward annual after-tax profits of at least $100 billion, Ritter told Fortune. Only a handful of companies have ever earned that much in a year, he said, including Alphabet, Nvidia, Apple, and Microsoft.

In the third quarter, Anthropic’s revenue rose nearly 47% from the previous quarter, while compute and infrastructure expenses climbed about 77% to $9.9 billion. About half of that compute bill, roughly $5 billion, came from the company purchasing short-term capacity. Anthropic typically orders compute 12 to 18 months ahead but is forced to buy more expensive short-term capacity when customer demand or research needs exceed what it has secured. The company attributed the decline in its adjusted operating margin to 15% from 19%, primarily to those short-term costs.

Tomasz Tunguz, founder and general partner of Theory Ventures, told Fortune that higher compute costs would put increasing pressure on Anthropic’s margins, although he noted that the company’s implied gross margin was still a healthy 85%. Gross margin counts only the cost of serving customers. It excludes the far larger sums Anthropic spends training models and on research, which are booked as separate operating expenses.

The pressure on adjusted operating margins arrived sooner than Tony Trzcinka, an investment-grade portfolio manager at Impax Asset Management, said he expected. “The key question is whether revenue can compound fast enough to absorb the future commitments and outpace compute cost,” he told Fortune. He expects the company’s existing obligations and interconnected relationships to limit its ability to borrow at the kinds of low interest rates available to investment-grade companies. This means if Anthropic does need to take on debt to fund its compute capacity, that money will be expensive, further weighing on margins.

But paying more for compute can also help an AI company generate future revenue, Campbell Hutcheson, a senior researcher at Epoch AI, said. Frontier models, such as those Anthropic builds, can command premium prices and help improve the training and inference efficiency of other models, he told Fortune. Because revenue growth often depends on reaching a capability or product threshold first, as with ChatGPT and Claude Code, he said it can be rational for labs to pay a premium to get there first. Hutcheson said Anthropic continued to show “very strong growth, high gross margins” while investing heavily in AI research.

With about $131.8 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments at Sept. 30, Anthropic has resources to keep investing while it works to improve those economics. Its operations generated $6.6 billion in cash during the first nine months of the year. Ritter said those reserves, combined with IPO proceeds, would allow considerable investment. Trzcinka also views liquidity as a positive for bondholders, while watching for further spending commitments and any borrowing under the company’s revolving credit facility.

In estimating what Anthropic could be worth to shareholders, Aswath Damodaran, a finance professor at New York University’s Stern School of Business, looked a decade ahead. His Oct. 28 valuation—which was produced prior to Anthropic releasing its third-quarter results—assumed annual revenue reaching $1 trillion by 2036, a target operating margin of 27.5%, and an estimated $100 billion in IPO proceeds. Those assumptions produced an equity value of about $1.475 trillion, which he described as at the lower end of the $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion range.

Damodaran told Fortune that Anthropic’s third-quarter figures gave him little reason to revise his valuation, calling them “the most telegraphed 3rd quarter number of all time.” His earlier post had already discussed slowing revenue growth and continued margin volatility, he said. “If my intrinsic value changed significantly based on this news story, it would be neither intrinsic nor value, just a pricing chase.”

Ritter likewise saw no big surprises in the third-quarter numbers, but his research highlights the risk of paying for exceptional growth in advance. In Ritter’s study, the 14 IPOs that commanded the kind of price-to-sales ratio that Anthropic is asking investors to swallow delivered returns averaging 15.4% below the broader stock market, measured from their offer prices over holding periods of up to three years, although some companies outperformed. Each company had at least $100 million in revenue over the 12 months before listing, adjusted for inflation to 2025 dollars.

Anthropic has substantial upside potential, Ritter said, but “a lot of things have to go right” for its revenue and profits to grow enough to support such a high valuation.

Wen Shao is a reporting fellow at Fortune covering AI, with a focus on the companies, economics, and infrastructure shaping the industry.

#5512. Metal fabricator NIC Global to cut 103 jobs near Seattle, move production to Eastern Washington

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:24 amOctober 30, 2026 at 10:25 am

Metal fabricator NIC Global plans to close its Woodinville, Wash., plant, eliminating 103 jobs. Declining business from local customers is prompting the company to shift production primarily to Eastern Washington to meet data center-related growth.

The layoffs are scheduled to begin Jan. 18, 2027, with final departures Aug. 31, 2028, according to a notice filed with the Washington Employment Security Department. Affected jobs include assembly, engineering, quality assurance, metal fabrication specialists, and forklift positions.

The building will be returned to its landlord when the lease ends in September 2028.

“This is a sad day for our company. Woodinville is where NIC was formed — three Seattle-area sheet-metal shops brought together under one roof in 2001 — and the people in that building built the foundation of everything NIC is today,” Troy Wood, company president and CEO, said via email.

The 100,000-square-foot site mostly served energy and medical device customers. Wood said the volume of work at the plant has declined while demand has increased in Eastern Washington for customers building power distribution technology needed by data centers.

“NIC is a supplier of sheet-metal fabrications and assemblies, and in our business, being close to our customers is what keeps us competitive,” Wood said.

While most of the work from Woodinville will go to Spokane, and a smaller portion will go to NIC’s Gallatin, Tenn., facility. The company also has manufacturing in Pullman; Chillicothe, Ohio; and Denton, Texas. The work outside of Washington is focused on the heavy truck sector. The company’s headcount is nearly 600.

Laid-off workers will be encouraged to apply for openings at other plants.

There are smaller fabricators remaining in the Seattle area, including JEMCO Components & Fabrications, which provides precision machining and sheet-metal fabrication for customers in medical, aerospace and defense sectors, and QUAL-FAB serving medical and dental customers.

NIC’s legal and financial headquarters will stay in the Woodinville area, where the company plans a new office for its finance, IT, sales and West Coast support teams.

Wood praised the quality and reliability of the Woodinville employees’ work.

“I am grateful to every one of them,” he said, “and especially to those who chose to stay with us through two and a half years of uncertainty and kept doing their jobs with integrity.”

#5511. What Clients Need Before They Trust You With Sensitive Work

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Your clients, and potential clients, need to know that they can trust you with their confidential information.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Confidentiality is essential. Without proper protection, sensitive personal or business information can become public. Cybersecurity tools and practical safeguards are critical for protecting confidential data. What assurances do your clients need before trusting you with sensitive work?

Every company seeks credibility. Building a strong reputation takes years, but a data breach or employee error can erase it instantly.

Business plans are drafted with intricate details on how a service or product will be offered. Features and benefits are discussed at length, alongside profit projections. However, few business proposals address building and protecting the company’s reputation. Why? Because entrepreneurs assume if they provide a quality product or service, that consumer trust will follow.

When I started my transcription company, I quickly realized protecting sensitive data would be our top priority. Our service is not a simple transaction. Clients entrust us with audio or video files containing sensitive information. Whether the content is for a select audience or public release, we safeguard every file as if it were confidential.

Handling sensitive data requires safeguards both inside and outside the company. Companies often require new hires to sign non-disclosure agreements (NDAs), but reputations can still be damaged if employees violate these agreements and share confidential information.

Recent headlines report charges against a foreign national accused of planting listening devices in a corporate boardroom. This case involves unauthorized recording of confidential information at a major AI company planning to go public. Both executives and future shareholders need assurance that sensitive information will remain secure.

Clients need assurance that their information will be protected. While some businesses still accept cash, most rely on electronic payments, and customers expect trusted vendors to handle their data securely.

The same applies to transcription. Secure file upload and transfer are essential. I frequently remind clients not to email files. Work for legal and medical clients must comply with CJIS and HIPAA requirements to protect sensitive data. Any breach would harm our reputation.

Industries like legal, medical and technology must protect sensitive data, but every business should prioritize customer data protection. Safeguarding information, from credit card transactions to medical histories, matters just as much across all sectors.

No matter your industry, reassure customers and clients that protecting sensitive data is a top priority. Here are a few ways to convey the importance of safeguarding customer info:

Clients and customers lose trust in companies for various reasons. Often, companies don’t realize this erosion until sales decline or complaints rise, making recovery harder. Key reasons for lost trust include:

Unfortunately, many customers are skeptical of marketing claims because products or services sometimes fail to meet expectations. When this happens, customers incur extra costs to resolve issues, and companies lose revenue through replacements or additional service.

Ethical decline is another concern. Clients become frustrated when companies fail to deliver on their promises, which underscores the importance of consistent, honest communication.

When discussing service commitments, I strive for clarity in writing, email and phone conversations. However, clients may sometimes overlook or misunderstand service details, either by not listening or reading disclosures. Following up and confirming information by email helps protect both parties.

The greatest cost of a data breach is reputational damage. While ransom payments and IT expenses are straightforward to calculate, the long-term reputational impact can cost millions over several years.

Minimizing data breach risk should be a top priority for every company. For this reason, my company employs only U.S.-based individuals who undergo comprehensive criminal background checks.

Many hackers and scammers who obtain confidential information operate overseas. I am often surprised when competitors use contractors abroad to transcribe files. Clients should know who can access their data and where those individuals are located.

Every company, regardless of size, should maintain an up-to-date data breach plan. Hackers often target small businesses as entry points to larger networks. I recommend a six-step plan:

Developing a comprehensive data breach plan requires specialized expertise. However, I recognize the importance of data security and take extensive measures to protect the sensitive information our clients entrust to us. Ultimately, all data is important to your clients and customers.

Regardless of the cause, how your company responds to failure is crucial. Mistakes happen, and even the most diligent employees or companies can “drop the ball.”

When mistakes are made, transparency matters. Be honest and admit your mistakes. Even the most irritated customer can moderate their views when a company admits its errors.

Recently, I was dining at a restaurant with high ratings for its food and service. Nonetheless, four- and five-star reviews aren’t worth much when your experience is going south. From the moment I entered the restaurant, nothing went well.

First, the host could not find my reservation, even after I provided the confirmation number. After being seated, we waited 10 minutes for our server. To speed things up, we ordered all courses at once, and the server assured us he would pace the meal appropriately.

Despite these efforts, the dining experience did not improve. When the server noticed my frustration, he brought the manager, and both apologized. The manager comped our meal, offered a premium bottle of wine and gave me a $100 gift certificate. This response changed my perspective, and when I returned the following week, the manager personally thanked me for giving them another chance.

A disappointing restaurant experience is minor compared to a multi-million-dollar mistake or data breach. However, the fundamentals of response remain the same.

Transparency and honesty are essential, but customers will only give companies a second chance if they believe their mistakes can, and will be corrected. Most importantly, customers want to feel that your company genuinely cares about them.

#5510. ‘You have to be willing to make those hard choices’: Freshworks CEO on crossing $1 billion in ARR with 30% fewer employees in the AI software age

Freshworks has passed $1 billion in annual recurring revenue, CEO Dennis Woodside told Fortune. The software company, which started about 15 years ago in Chennai, India, as a help-desk tool for small businesses, ended its third quarter on Sept. 30 with about $992 million in annual recurring revenue. It crossed $1 billion in October after closing its acquisitions of Torii and Robusta, the company said. Freshworks doesn’t disclose how much of its ARR came from acquisitions.

“$1 billion in ARR is a really important milestone for any software business,” Woodside said in an interview ahead of the results. “It’s a good indication of scale.”

Woodside took over as CEO in May 2024 from founder Girish Mathrubootham. “I think we’ve added about $250 million in ARR in that time period,” he said. ARR measures contracted subscription revenue over the next 12 months, so it runs ahead of reported sales. Earlier today, Freshworks reported $18.3 million in GAAP net income for the third quarter, its second straight profitable quarter, along with adjusted free cash flow of $73.9 million, a record. “We’ll be GAAP profitable this quarter and going forward,” Woodside said. The company has described sustained GAAP profitability as a goal.

Getting there meant deciding what Freshworks would stop doing. “We wound up stopping a bunch of smaller projects,” Woodside said, to “really focus on the business that had the biggest potential, has the biggest market, where we have the most distinctive competitive advantage.”

“You have to be willing to make those hard choices of what’s not going to be important in two years, in five years,” Woodside argued. “And then invest in those areas that are going to be important,” he said. “I think that can be hard to do.”

Some of this is standard management theory, skating to where the puck is moving and seeing around the corner, but it has a counterintuitive element that thought leaders in the space argue isn’t appreciated by enough companies.

In an interview at McKinsey’s global headquarters at 3 World Trade Center, two senior partners echoed Woodside’s advice. “AI is everywhere except in the EBIT line,” Alex Panas, who leads McKinsey’s industry practices globally, joked, describing what’s around boardrooms and echoing the famous Robert Solow paradox about the computer age appearing everywhere except in the productivity statistics.

Michael Park, a senior partner in Singapore who co-leads the firm’s technology, media and telecom practice, chimed in. “The number of companies that have really rethought how they’re doing work today, and then changing it to be whatever it should be or could be with AI, is very small.” He shared the example of product development. In the old way, an idea moved down a line: marketing built a business case and PowerPoints, then HR weighed in, then operations. In the new way, a cross-functional team works separately with an AI agent and after a few weeks, Park said, the agent tells them, “There’s like 20 things you guys agree on. But there’s five things that you disagree on.” Then the team meets about those five things.

This is unsettling to people used to the old way of working, because the agent is suddenly the store of knowledge for the enterprise, not the management layer for each silo. Panas noted that org charts have barely changed since McKinsey’s Gilbert Clee wrote the 1959 paper behind the matrix organization in the 1950s. “That’s the last time somebody’s actually thought about organizational structure,” he said. Panas said he thinks the best book about AI was written in 1993: Reengineering the Corporation, the Hammer and Champy management bestseller. Its argument is that technology only pays off once you change the people and the processes around it.

Woodside said the reason people don’t do this is because it’s essentially really unpleasant. Shutting down products meant telling people their work was over. “When you wind down a product, to some degree, you’re saying to somebody that your baby’s ugly,” he said. “And a real person is a product manager of that. You have to say, ‘No, I’m sorry, we’re not going to do that.’”

When Woodside took over, he was already a Silicon Valley veteran. He had run Motorola Mobility and was chief operating officer at Dropbox when it went public. The first thing the board asked him to do, he said, was “really revisit this strategy” because AI was coming. The company had started as Freshdesk, and its founder had built it around customer support, “and there’s a lot of passion around that,” Woodside said, but still, it was an inflection point.

He decided IT software for bigger companies, “the EX business,” was the future for Freshworks and they had to shift resources into that business, “literally in the first couple of months of being the CEO.”

About a month into his tenure, on June 6, 2024, Freshworks closed its purchase of Device42, an IT asset-management company. It has since bought FireHydrant, Torii and Robusta. EX made up 59% of ARR, or $588 million, as of Sept. 30, up from 35% at the 2021 IPO, and grew 22% from a year earlier, according to the company. The customer-service business it was founded on, CX, accounted for $404 million.

Then he started cutting. “We had a lot of entrepreneurial, you know, $5 million ideas,” he said. “We need $100 million ideas, right, if we’re going to get to a billion [dollars in ARR].” Woodside cited the examples of Freshping, Freshteams, and Freshsurvey as things he deemphasized, focusing on Freshservice, which was already generating several hundred million dollars in ARR when he took over as CEO.

It also meant getting smaller, Woodside said, noting Freshworks now has roughly 3,800 full-time employees, down from a peak of about 5,400 in 2022, roughly a 30% reduction. (That includes an 11% cut announced in May.) “That was hard for the company,” Woodside said. “It was also hard because we wound up reducing the staffing pretty significantly over time.”

He has been on the other end of that call. At Motorola, Woodside engineered the 2014 sale to Lenovo. “We sold it — which meant I sold it — which meant I sold myself out of a job,” he told Fortune’s Diane Brady at the COO Summit in June.

Wharton professor Ethan Mollick, who popularized the phrase “jagged frontier” as he emerged as a thought leader on the topic of AI adoption, puts this as a question. “That’s one of the big questions I ask,” he told Fortune, echoing comments he made on a recent appearance on Peter Kafka’s Channels podcast. “Have you stopped doing anything? With that being attested, almost every company has failed.”

The “micro version” of this is that “there’s just some stuff you stopped doing,” Mollick said, citing hand-written messages of compliance forms. “Then there’s the bigger question about what larger projects in your organization are now obsolete.”

When I put Mollick’s question to Woodside, he responded that “a lot of work that used to be done by kind of early-tenure employees, we are doing with AI.” Designers now build prototypes in Figma that get turned directly into code, and testing that code “is mostly done by AI today as well.” What’s left for people? “The humans get to think at a higher level about: what’s the business problem that I need to go solve.”

He said it wasn’t optional. “If we hadn’t done that very fast, we would simply not be competitive in what we’re putting out there in the market,” he said. “So, for us, it was not a choice.”

Mollick has been vocal in saying he worries most about the bottom of the ladder: the old apprenticeship deal “all broke down because interns are doing work with AI, and middle managers would rather turn to AI than interns,” he told Charter this month. Well, that’s the other worrying outcome, right? Is like, in some ways, the least ambitious way of the well-worn path to using automation is replacing people.”I think that there’s some danger in that,” Mollick told Fortune. He said he worries about too many companies heading down a path of being aggressive at cutting headcount while productivity stays the same; this is not the case with the strategy Woodside laid out, and Mollick was not commenting directly on any particular company.

Woodside emphasized that “early-career talent remains essential to our business,” but it won’t continue to be the kind of “repetitive, mechanical work” that it has been historically. He said early-career workers are being asked to do more “problem-solving and product development.”

Just as most companies are not evaluating what to stop doing, they also haven’t acted on significant headcount reductions. In McKinsey’s State of AI survey, 39% of respondents expected AI to shrink their headcount over the next year, while only 14% said it already had.

Investors have rewarded the change so far. Software stocks were hit hard early this year as AI-native startups went after the incumbents’ customers, and Freshworks fell with them. In late March its shares were down about 31% for the year, trading under $8. By late October they were around $15. In a year marked by the so-called “Saaspocalypse” coming for companies a lot like Freshworks, it has returned more than 25% year-to-date.

Woodside told Fortune in general terms that he thinks software’s bottom was in February. Since then, he argued, investors have sorted the sector. “Businesses that are more focused on SMB in particular have been hurt,” he said, referring to small and medium-sized businesses. “Software companies with simpler products, which are perceived to be more easily replicated with AI, they haven’t come back.” Small business is exactly the market Freshworks started in and the strategy the board asked him to revise years ago.

Park argued that the old moats are shrinking because too many executives still think about AI “like enterprise software,” where a system, once installed and customized, “is very difficult to get it out.” Now a company can ask an AI model to help migrate it from one system to another, he noted. He said he thinks companies should move past an idea that AI is “just like automation 2.0,” saying it’s less about costs and efficiencies and more about “doing more things.” That cuts both ways for Freshworks: it’s how an attacker takes share, and it’s how the next attacker could take it back.

From Woodside’s perspective, Freshworks is positioned for that kind of disruption. He said it’s now aiming at what he calls the “agile enterprise”: companies with up to 20,000 employees. “We are absolutely taking share from our larger competitors” in that segment, he told Fortune. Customers paying more than $100,000 a year rose 25% in Freshworks’ third quarter, while those paying more than $5,000 rose 6%.

The pressure comes from both directions. AI-first startups are going after the help desk, the layer Freshworks was built on, while investors fear the model of pricing per seat being hollowed out by AI. Freshworks now prices by usage, by the number of assets managed and by problems resolved. “We’re seeing more and more of our growth coming from the elements that are not seat-based,” Woodside said, although customers still want seats for budgeting. “Our customers want predictability. Seats offer a predictable element.”

Woodside said he doesn’t think the big software players should be counted out in this moment. Startups, he said, find it “always a smart strategy … to throw dirt at the incumbent because you get attention.” But “it doesn’t mean that you can take a business that’s generating, you know, tens of millions of dollars and turn it into tens of billions of dollars. That’s actually really hard.” He gave the incumbents more credit, saying they’re “filled with incredibly ambitious, incredibly smart people. And they’re competitive as hell.”

Panas cited lessons learned from the dot-com era: “We overestimated the short term. We underestimated the long term.”

Woodside used the same logic about his own company. “It’s very easy to overestimate the short-term impact on some of these larger successful organizations, such as us,” he said. “And it’s easy to underestimate how successful the company could continue to be if they get the shift right. In this case, the shift to AI.”

The next number is already on the whiteboard, according to Woodside. “We’re now talking internally about, okay, well, what’s the path to $2 billion and multiple billions?”

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5509. Filing: Chip startup Powerlattice raises $86M to ease AI’s power crunch

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 11:30 amOctober 30, 2026 at 3:35 pm

Powerlattice, a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday.

The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing also lists Wen Hsieh, founding managing partner of Matter Venture Partners, as a director.

The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment.

AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling.

“AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A.

Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators.

CEO Peng Zou, Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan.

Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon.

In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors.

“Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.

#5508. OpenAI’s hiring of former Army Secretary just 2 months after Pentagon resignation is part of a ‘trend’ of it pivoting resources to defense projects

OpenAI’s hiring of a recently departed Pentagon official points to the frontier lab’s growing interests in defense and expanding roster of former military officials in its ranks.

OpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll to the bespoke role of senior counselor for national security modernization, the company announced on Monday. The new job comes two months after Driscoll left the Trump administration after reportedly clashing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

In the role, Driscoll will advise OpenAI’s public and private sector partners on how to modernize policy and strategy in support of improving national security with AI, according to OpenAI. The focus of his work will be on how AI can be used responsibly to improve security among the U.S. and its allies.

Gwanhoo Lee, the chair of the Department of Information Technology and Analytics at American University’s Kogod School of Business, said that by tapping Driscoll, OpenAI is continuing in its strategy of pouring resources into the defense sector, where it sees high demand for AI systems to bolster national security.

“This hire is a continuation of their trend to see the opportunity in hiring significant government officials to strengthen their relationship with the government and strengthen their business in dealing with the government agencies,” Lee told Fortune.

In June 2024, OpenAI appointed retired U.S. Army General Paul Nakasone, former National Security Agency director, to its board of directors. Later that year, it partnered with American defense firm Anduril to integrate OpenAI’s systems with Anduril’s database of unmanned drone threats.

Driscoll did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Within the federal government, Driscoll pushed modernization efforts such as low-cost battlefield drones, cutting red tape for defense contractors for drone development, and switching the Pentagon to commercial software—a departure from its practice of purchasing custom-built software specifically for the military. He also became an unlikely negotiator in working to end the war between Russia and Ukraine by making several trips across Europe to broker talks between Ukrainian and European officials. He also made a secret trip to the Middle East to meet with Russian officials.

“The U.S. has an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI” following Driscoll’s hire, Altman said in a statement in the press release.

“This technology will help them keep pace by cutting through paperwork, making sense of more information, and getting the right answer to the right person faster,” Driscoll said. “I’m joining OpenAI to help the United States and our allies put this technology to work responsibly, for the people who keep us safe.”

The former Army secretary stepped down from his role in the Pentagon in September after just 18 months on the job following widely reported tensions between him and Hegseth—particularly disagreements over promotions and the scale of the Pentagon’s modernization efforts. Driscoll’s exit followed a series of departures from other senior military officials, including the ousting of Gen. Randy George, the agency’s top uniformed official, in April and the resignation of Gen. Christopher Donahue, a champion of unmanned drone-use in Ukraine, in June.

Before his time in the Trump administration, Driscoll was involved in several investment and advisory firms, working as the chief operating officer at venture capital firm Flex Capital and partner at private equity firm 100watt. He served in the U.S. military from 2007 to 2011, and was deployed to Baghdad, Iran, in 2009.

Driscoll’s new private-sector role is likely to raise questions about a “revolving door problem” of the company’s access to government officials, according to Lee. He noted that potential conflicts of interest could impact the government’s procurement process, or how it decides with private entities from which to buy goods and services.

“If AI companies can take high-level officers from the Pentagon or any other important government agencies right after they’ve left their organizations, in terms of procurement process, I don’t know how fair the government procurement process will be when AI companies have significant individuals from that organization,” Lee said.

As countries depend more on AI systems for both defense of national security and forms of offensive cyberattacks, investing in both the most effective and cost-effective technologies have become crucial for maintaining national safety and infrastructure, Lee explained, but priorities for securing private sector contracts can become muddied if deals are based too closely on preexisting social ties.

“If that procurement is based upon relationships rather than merits and strengths of technology, that puts us at risk,” he added. “As AI companies take on national security risks, we need clearer rules on oversight and conflict interest, so I think there is some governance concern.”

OpenAI said all parties are aware of post-employment restrictions and will comply.

The relationship between OpenAI and the Trump administration grew closer in February, when OpenAI signed a new deal with the Pentagon to deploy its AI models in the agency’s secure networks. Earlier that month, Hegseth issued an ultimatum to OpenAI rival Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, demanding the company allow unrestricted use of its AI, which has safety guardrails against the use of the technology for mass domestic surveillance and autonomous weaponry—but Anthropic refused to remove the restrictions. Trump then asked federal agencies to stop using Anthropic’s products, and Hegseth designated the company a national security “supply chain risk,” the first time the U.S. has ever used the designation for an American company.

OpenAI’s subsequent deal with the Pentagon still set limits on how the government can use its technology, but allowed for the deployment of its AI models inside the Pentagon’s secure networks under an “all lawful use” clause, offering broader usage of the technology within legal confines.

Experts warned the deal left space for legal loopholes—like whether large-scale analysis of Americans’ data, which is legal, is different from mass surveillance.

“Right now, under U.S. law, it’s lawful for government authorities to buy up commercially available information from data brokers and other third parties,” Samir Jain, vice president of policy at the Center for Democracy & Technology, told Fortune earlier this year. “If you buy up massive amounts of data and allow AI to analyze it, you may end up, in effect, engaging in mass surveillance of Americans through that process. It’s not currently restricted by law or prohibited by law.”

In a blog post updated in March, OpenAI noted language it added to the deal with the Department of Defense, including that in accordance with the Fourth Amendment of the Constitution, the National Security Act of 1947, and other applicable laws, its AI system would not be intentionally used for domestic surveillance. It also noted the Pentagon understands limitations to prohibit deliberate tracking of U.S. persons or nationals, including through the procurement or use of personal information from commercial third parties.

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5507. Wall Street is bracing for a fresh wave of tariffs, Iran action (and potentially a government shutdown) after the midterms

Though analysts have been wrong before, many observers expect the Democrats to claw back some political power in this week’s midterm elections. Despite that, Wall Street is expecting President Trump to double down on some of his less popular policies, following the vote.At the time of writing, Harvard University’s polling gives a 96% chance that the Democrats take the House, and a 78% likelihood of the Democrats taking both the House and the Senate.Goldman Sachs, for example, wrote to clients this morning that it expects President Trump to increase tariffs in the event the Democrats secure greater congressional influence. Economists Alec Phillips and Abhay Duggirala reasoned that “Democrats have indicated they would seek to reverse some of President Trump’s tariffs, but we expect this to have a limited effect since the reversals would likely be focused on a few countries (e.g., Canada) or products.”“We expect President Trump to announce new tariff increases after the election that would more than offset those reductions, likely resulting in a rise in the US effective tariff rate of a little under 2pp.”

Tariffs will also likely become an increasingly important revenue source in the coming months. The conflict in the Middle East, for example, is proving costly, and sits against a backdrop of $40 trillion in national debt with calls from budget hawks to reduce deficits to 3% of GDP from its current 6%.

But any efforts to reduce these deficits will likely get bogged down in a more divided government, according to ING’s James Smith. He wrote to clients that fiscal gridlock will likely push attention back to trade policy and how to squeeze more revenue out of import relationships.

“Remember tariffs?” Smith wrote. “After the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s emergency tariffs, temporary 10% blanket rates ultimately gave way to a more permanent structure under Section 301. The issue has since slipped remarkably far down the agenda.”

The White House’s course of action in the Middle East, post-midterms, remains an unanswered question. As UBS’s Paul Donovan described it, the president may become more aggressive in the Gulf war “once freed from the pursuit of popularity.”

According to a Pew Research study last month, just 14% of voters said they strongly approve of President Trump’s handling of the military conflict with Iran, with a further 20% said they “somewhat” approve. With voters disenchanted, Trump’s only remaining motivations for the conflict lie in national security and his personal legacy.

“Where markets will want to focus is on the Republican reaction to the results,” said Donovan. “Does the Republican Party divide over MAGA-related issues, and does President Trump escalate hostilities in the Gulf war with wider economic consequences at home and abroad?”

More broadly, the cost of paying for the action settles into longer-term divisions about the future of government spending. Recent reports on the costs of the Iran war now come to $47 billion, with the conflict initially outlined as a matter of weeks now stretching into months.

“Republicans will likely attempt to pass a reconciliation bill along party lines in the coming weeks that could add substantially to defense spending and potentially address the debt limit, which will have to be dealt with before the late summer/fall of next year,” Deutsche Bank wrote to clients on Friday. “Recall, also, that federal government funding runs out on December 11 which will require bipartisan support for a continuing resolution to prevent a shutdown.”

Trump signed the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act on Sept. 2, which funded federal agencies through a 72-day window to Dec. 11.

#5506. Madrona Prize goes to UW research on agents that shrink AI models to run on small chips

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 3:13 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 11:53 am

A University of Washington project that uses AI agents to squeeze AI models onto tiny devices — such as a solar-powered camera that spots elk in the wild — won the Madrona Prize at the Allen School’s annual Research Showcase on Thursday.

Seattle venture capital firm Madrona has awarded the prize since 2006 to Allen School student projects that combine strong research with commercial potential. The winners were chosen from among the student posters presented at the evening event on the UW campus.

Zhihan Zhang, a PhD student in the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, presented the winning project. It tests whether AI agents can do a job that experts now do by hand: shrinking AI models and tuning device software to run on small, low-power chips with tight limits on memory, power and heat.

In the team’s tests, leading AI models failed at the task without feedback from real hardware. The team built a system that let the agent load its work onto real hardware, measure the results and try again. With that feedback, the agent beat human experts within seven rounds.

The researchers used the approach on two real-world projects: an elk-detection camera trap, which needed its vision model shrunk by 250 times, and a wearable device that records children’s speech for child development research.

The team released its benchmark, called Embedded Arena, as open-source code. Allen School faculty members Shwetak Patel, Vikram Iyer, Natasha Jaques and Kurtis Heimerl also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Alexander Metzger, Jiuyang Lyu, Chun-Cheng Chang, Jiayi Shao, Yujia Liu, Emmanuel Azuh Mensah, Edward Wang and Gregory D. Abowd.

The People’s Choice award went to Keisuke Kamahori for VibeSys, a project that uses AI agents to write custom software for a specific chip and task, then keep improving it, instead of relying on general-purpose tools built for common setups.

Its first application, VibeServe, writes the behind-the-scenes software that takes requests from users and runs them through an AI model. On Amazon’s Trainium2 chips, the software it built handled up to 2.7 times as much work as an existing system. Shihang (Vic) Li and Allen School faculty members Simon Peter and Baris Kasikci also worked on the project.

The first runner-up for the Madrona Prize, Tanush Yadav, presented VideoNet, a test of how well AI models recognize specific actions in video, such as a particular bouldering move or a type of surgical stitch. It covers more than 1,000 actions across 38 fields.

Leading AI models struggle with it compared to ordinary people. Shown three examples, people improved their accuracy by about 14 percentage points, while AI models improved by about 3 percentage points.

Allen School faculty members Ali Farhadi, Hanna Hajishirzi and Ranjay Krishna, and former Allen School faculty member Yejin Choi, now at Stanford University, also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan and Rohun Tripathi.

The second runner-up, Henry Wong, presented work on securing benchtop DNA synthesizers, machines that let users print synthetic DNA.

His project focuses on protecting the screening software meant to stop someone from printing a dangerous pathogen, and concludes that even perfectly secure hardware wouldn’t fully solve the problem.

Allen School faculty member Jeff Nivala and former Allen School faculty member Tadayoshi Kohno, now at Georgetown University, also worked on the project.

All of the presenters are PhD students in the Allen School.

Correction: An earlier version of this story misidentified Sethu Raman of Madrona in the lead photo caption.
