#5505. Republicans pitch 3.5% income tax cap as an affordability fix in North Carolina—but Gov. Josh Stein says it won’t put ‘more money in anyone’s pockets’

Republican lawmakers in North Carolina have steadily reduced the state’s income taxes for more than a decade. On Tuesday, voters will decide whether to make it harder for future lawmakers to reverse those cuts as affordability emerges as one of the biggest issues of the midterms.

North Carolina voters are considering a constitutional amendment that would lower the maximum allowable income tax rate from 7% to 3.5%. This would halve the ceiling for what the state government can charge individuals and corporations through income taxes.

But despite the legislation’s name, “Lower Taxes for All NC,” the amendment wouldn’t actually lower state taxes immediately.

North Carolina’s individual income tax rate currently stands at 3.99%. Under legislation that has already passed, it is scheduled to fall to 3.49% in 2027. The rate is set to drop further to 3.24% in 2030 and 2.99% in 2033.

The measure facing voters Tuesday deals with the future. If approved, raising income taxes above 3.5% would require another constitutional amendment, which requires the approval of three-fifths of both chambers of the state legislature and then a majority of voters.

Supporters say the restriction would protect taxpayers from future tax increases, while critics warn it could leave the state with fewer options to raise money for public services during an economic downturn.

The measure is part of how the Republican-dominated state legislature is trying to tackle the rising cost of living, which 48% of registered voters identified as their top issue, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll from Tuesday.

Across the country, voters are considering several competing tax initiatives as they grapple with how to address rising costs. Apart from the constitutional referendum to lower the cap on state income tax, North Carolina voters will also vote Tuesday on whether to allow the state legislature to impose a limit on how much local governments can raise property taxes.

In total, nine income and wealth tax related measures are on the ballot in six states, according to Ballotpedia, including one of the most well known, Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on individuals in California with a net worth of more than $1 billion.

The North Carolina income tax amendment is just the latest reform aiming to cut taxes under the Republican-controlled legislature.

After years of Democratic control of the legislature, in 2010, Republicans won control of both chambers of the state’s General Assembly and have been in power since 2011. For years, Republicans in the legislature have held enough seats to enact their legislation even without the support of the two consecutive Democratic governors who have held the executive position since 2017.

Republicans have used this influence to slowly cut taxes.

Republican lawmakers in 2013 passed a tax reform that changed the state from a system of graduated individual income tax brackets to a flat tax. They have also reduced corporate taxes.

In 2018, North Carolina voters approved a constitutional amendment lowering the maximum allowable income tax rate from 10% to 7%, with less than 60% of voters supporting the proposal.

The latest amendment on the ballot Tuesday would cut that limit in half again to 3.5%. The measure already passed the Republican-controlled state Senate and state House to get on the ballot. Democratic Gov. Josh Stein was not required to approve of the measure because governors in North Carolina can’t veto proposed constitutional amendments.

Still, Stein has made it clear he opposes the proposed amendment, saying in a press conference from May the initiative would allow the legislature to cut taxes for wealthy individuals while raising pressure to increase the state’s sales tax to make up the revenue short fall.

“It will not put any more money in anyone’s pockets,” Stein said. “But what it will do is make regular people pay the consequences of it next year and years into the future because it will insulate the very wealthy from ever having an increase in their income tax.”

Stein also pointed out that because the amendment is in the state constitution it will be harder for future legislatures to change later.

Republican state Sen. Michael Lee, a sponsor of the legislation that put the income tax cap on the ballot, has said the restriction would build on the legislature’s previous actions to lower taxes.

“Our tax reforms have produced more than a decade of strong revenue growth while letting people keep more of what they earn, and this amendment locks in that progress,” Lee said in a statement earlier this year to North Carolina news station WECT.

Yet, the measure raises questions about how North Carolina would pay for government services, and what services may need to be cut if income tax revenue falls.

The state collected approximately $17 billion in individual income taxes during the 2024-25 fiscal year, accounting for nearly half of its $34.6 billion in General Fund revenue, according to the North Carolina Office of State Budget and Management.

That money helps fund public education, health care, and other government services. The amendment won’t reduce tax revenue immediately, but opponents say that making future income tax increases harder would make lawmakers more likely to either cut services or raise revenue elsewhere, including through higher sales taxes.

Alexandra Sirota, executive director of the NC Budget & Tax Center, has also warned that restricting income taxes could limit how the government adapts to changing conditions in the economy.

“These tax amendments won’t cut anyone’s taxes,” Sirota said in a September statement. “But they would make it more difficult for future lawmakers to fairly raise the revenue needed to meet costs through a higher rate on millionaires, billionaires, and highly profitable corporations.”

North Carolina isn’t the only state reconsidering how much its government should be allowed to tax residents and businesses.

Voters in Colorado will vote Tuesday on competing proposals that will either replace the state’s 4.4% flat income tax with a graduated tax rate reaching up to 8.4% or one that will cap income tax rates at 4.4%. In Iowa, voters are weighing a measure requiring a two-thirds legislative majority to increase income taxes. Washington voters will also decide whether to repeal a newly enacted 9.9% income tax on household income exceeding $1 million.

California voters, meanwhile, are set to weigh in on one of the most contentious ballot measures up for a vote Tuesday—a 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth that has been opposed by well-known figures such as Google cofounder Sergey Brin.

The proposals across the country come as voters are struggling to afford what they could before as inflation surged to 3.6% in September, up from 3.4% in August, according to the Commerce Department. Meanwhile, the war in Iran, which has pushed up the price of oil about 68% over the past year, has partly led to price increases by increasing the prices for products reliant on gas for their production or distribution.

Polls show Democrats have gained traction even in some deeply red states as they emphasize how Republicans in power have fallen short on tackling affordability. In Texas, polls show former Republican attorney general Ken Paxton slightly behind Democrat James Talarico in a Senate race that faces long odds given no Democrat has won statewide office in Texas since 1994. In Michigan, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed holds a double digit lead over Republican opponent Mike Rogers in another closely watched Senate contest.

Still, Republicans have tried to alleviate voters’ concerns about affordability at the national level, where GOP members control both chambers of Congress. Republicans earlier this year helped push through the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, a piece of bipartisan legislation aimed at tackling high housing costs including by accelerating homebuilding and reforming zoning.

Role: Reporter Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez is a reporter for Fortune covering general business news.

#5504. Montana voters take on Citizens United with a ballot initiative to strip corporations and nonprofits of their political spending power

Sixteen years ago, the Supreme Court decided in the Citizens United case that corporations have a First Amendment right to spend money to influence elections. On Tuesday, Montana voters will decide whether their state can take that power away.

Initiative 194, also known as the Montana Plan, would strip corporations, trade associations, nonprofits, and other organizations of the legal power to spend money supporting or opposing a political candidate or ballot initiative in Montana. Backers say they’ve found a way around Citizens United, while critics argue the semantics of the ballot initiative still violate the 2010 Supreme Court ruling.

Rather than ban corporate political donations outright, I-194 would change the powers Montana grants to corporations and other entities it refers to as “artificial persons,” limiting them to only those powers that are “necessary and convenient.”

The measure would apply to entities that do business or hold property in Montana, but exempts political action committees (PACs), news and editorial content, and individuals. Organizations that violate this would forfeit the privileges Montana grants them to do business in the state, including limited liability, which protects owners from personal responsibility for business debts.

At first glance, the language of the ballot initiative looks like it contradicts what Citizens United established—that corporations can spend money on elections. But Tom Moore, a former chief of staff to FEC Commissioner Ellen Weintraub and now senior fellow at the Center for American Progress (who also devised the legal theory behind the Montana Plan), told Fortune that states have authority over what corporations can do through corporate law.

“When the state creates a corporation, it is starting from nothing and deciding what to give the corporation, and no case has ever held that they have to give local spending power to a corporation,” Moore said.

He said I-194 would no longer grant corporations and nonprofits the ability to spend money on elections, which is different from banning them from exercising an existing right.

“It’s not regulation; it’s redefinition,” Moore said.

He said he believes the measure would shut down dark money spending by preventing wealthy donors from hiding behind organizations that don’t disclose their contributors. For instance, a donor can give money to a nonprofit that then funnels it to a PAC, which would report the nonprofit as the donor rather than identifying the person. Moore said I-194 would cut off that route by preventing corporations, nonprofits, and trade associations from political giving, though individuals can still donate.

“This is not going to stop Elon Musk from writing a big fat check to some election in Montana,” Moore said. “What it will stop them from doing is laundering the money through a dark money group.”

But opponents of the ballot measure say the distinction between banning corporations from political giving and exercising their political rights is blurry. Bradley Smith, a former FEC chairman and professor at Capital University Law School, told Fortune states can’t sidestep the First Amendment by calling political spending a corporate power instead of a right.

“The Supreme Court isn’t engaged in a semantic game,” he said.

Smith said states can set rules for corporations, but they can’t make them surrender constitutional protections in exchange for the benefits of incorporation.

“The core centerpiece undoubtedly is we’re going to deny all corporations in the state the right to speak about political affairs and about political candidates, and that’s just going to fail,” he said.

Montana has tried curbing corporate influence in elections before. In 1912, Montanans passed the Corrupt Practices Act by initiative with 76% of the vote, angry at the political power of mining giant Amalgamated Copper, years after the state’s mining magnates, known as the Copper Kings, had bribed state legislators.

The law barred corporations from spending money to influence elections, but the Supreme Court struck down the restriction in American Tradition Partnership v. Bullock in 2012, ruling that it conflicted with Citizens United.

Montana also isn’t the only state trying to limit corporate influence over elections. Hawaii enacted a law similar to I-194, called Act 11, in May. It’s now facing two federal lawsuits: one from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and another from the Grassroot Institute of Hawaii, which the Institute for Free Speech, an organization Smith founded, represents. The cases could help decide whether states can use corporate law to restrict political spending despite Citizens United.

Moore expects the issue to go up to the Supreme Court, whether through I-194 or the Hawaii lawsuits. If voters approve I-194, it would take effect Jan. 1, 2027, unless a court blocks it.

#5502. Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 5:21 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 6:29 am

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week.

Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer, an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday, saying it was obtained from an unnamed source.

In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief.

“What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.”

“I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data.

The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company.

“If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said.

He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said.

Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said.

Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.”

He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges.

“What we have here is so bloody special,” he said.

Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.”

The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028.

The newsletter said it stripped the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported.

Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records, including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former CEO Steve Ballmer each gave $250,000, and Vice Chair and President Brad Smith gave more than $500,000. Other backers include T-Mobile, F5, Alaska Airlines and Weyerhaeuser.

Washington Needs to Compete has spent about $3 million so far, according to state records. Most of it has gone to state legislative races, the Observer reported, including more than $700,000 backing Rep. Amy Walen, D-Kirkland, in the 48th District, home to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters.

The group spent $97,000 to air the ad during the Seahawks’ Oct. 15 Thursday night loss to the Denver Broncos on Prime Video and $130,000 during their Oct. 25 Sunday night win over the Kansas City Chiefs on NBC, according to the Observer.

Microsoft referred GeekWire’s inquiry to the group, which the company described as a growing coalition of more than 60 funders that want to keep the state competitive.

A press representative for the group sent a statement from Nick Streuli, an officer of Washington Needs to Compete. Streuli runs the government relations firm Sundial Advocacy and was previously policy and outreach director for former Gov. Jay Inslee.

“Washington Needs to Compete is committed to our state and wants to see it succeed,” Streuli said in the statement. “Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to invest and grow here. We are starting a conversation about our economic challenges and how to solve them.”

What the ad says: The spot opens with a nod to “inventors in garages,” “mom-and-pop shops down Main Street” and farmers “feeding the world,” before declaring, “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

Then it turns: “But today, Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less.” Jobs are leaving, the ad says, and “it’s harder than ever to afford a home and raise a family.”

It doesn’t name Ferguson or any legislation. It ends by saying Olympia needs to “quit wasting money, fix what’s broken and put Washington families first.”

Taxes and the business climate: Ferguson this year signed a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, known as the millionaires tax, which takes effect in 2028 and is projected to raise about $3 billion a year. Initiative 645, which would repeal it, is on the Nov. 3 ballot.

In September, Smith joined former Gov. Chris Gregoire and dozens of regional officials to launch a partnership aimed at reversing the Seattle area’s economic slide. “The warning signs are flashing on our economy,” Smith said at the time.

The region lost nearly 7,000 jobs in 2025, according to the group, and Washington has fallen from 32nd to 47th in CNBC’s ranking of states by cost of doing business since 2017.

In the same CNBC study, Washington ranks 11th overall, up from 14th last year, and fifth for its economy. WalletHub ranks Washington’s economy second in the nation, behind Massachusetts.

Washington’s gross domestic product grew faster than any other state’s in the first quarter of 2026, driven largely by its tech sector, according to federal data released in June.

Long-term plans: On its website, Washington Needs to Compete describes itself as businesses and residents building “a modern, permanent political organization” to support leaders and ideas that “strengthen our economy, improve affordability and expand opportunity,” through elections and public education.

The site lists its top five contributors as Microsoft, T-Mobile, the Washington Coalition for Responsible Taxes and Spending, F5 and Smith.

The group is saving most of its money for future campaigns, the Observer reported.

Updated Nov. 2 with comment from Washington Needs to Compete.

#5501. What Solana’s Alpenglow Switch Actually Changes at Slot 459,653,000

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

For about 400 milliseconds this afternoon, Solana will stop landing user transactions. That isn't a failure.

It's the scheduled handoff between two consensus systems, and it's probably the only "400 ms" figure that matters today.

Many people heading into the Alpenglow launch still treat 400 ms block times and 12.8-second finality as the bar to beat. Those are the old chain's numbers. They describe TowerBFT, the system Alpenglow is replacing, so Alpenglow shouldn't be checked against them. If you go through Solana's own documentation, you'll find the right benchmarks before the first post-launch numbers arrive.

According to Solana's official Alpenglow page, the upgrade's feature gate activates at the start of epoch 1064 on Wednesday, October 21, at about 13:20 UTC. The Solana Foundation says to treat that time as an estimate and to watch the epoch instead.

The new consensus doesn't take over the moment the epoch begins. TowerBFT keeps running for the first 5,000 slots, and Alpenglow takes control at slot 459,653,000. Anza, the team behind the main Agave client, put that switch at around 14:00 UTC.

That time isn't fixed. Solana Compass calculated that with about 375,000 slots left before the switch, each millisecond of drift in average slot time moves the boundary by roughly six minutes. Using epoch 1062's pace, it estimated the switch at about 14:02 UTC.

The transition itself has a cost. Solana Compass reports a gap of roughly two slots, about 400 ms, during which blocks carry only votes and user transactions don't land. So the 400 ms everyone is watching for will turn up, just as a pause rather than a block time.

This is where much of today's coverage gets it wrong.

Block time first. Solana's page says slots moved from 400 ms to 200 ms in a separate "reduced slot times" upgrade, which finished this month. That change isn't part of Alpenglow. It was already running before today. Solana Compass measured epoch 1062 averaging 217.7 ms per slot over 26.1 hours. Checking Alpenglow against 400 ms would mean grading it against a number the network had already beaten before the switch.

Then finality. The 12.8 seconds is TowerBFT's figure. Under that system, a block became final only after enough votes built up over 32 slots. Alpenglow's stated target is about 150 ms, which Solana describes as 99% faster than TowerBFT.

Solana is careful about that 150 ms figure, and I think readers should be too. The Foundation calls it an expectation, not a constant, and says one-round finality comes in lower. Galaxy's engineers, quoted by Solana Compass, call it a design target rather than a measured result. As I noted when looking at how CertiK verifies a TPS claim, a target is a claim until someone measures it on the live network.

Alpenglow is Solana's first replacement of its core consensus since TowerBFT, and today's launch only covers part of it.

The first phase, Votor, ships in Agave 4.3. Validators now send votes directly to each other and combine them into certificates, instead of submitting votes as on-chain transactions. Per Solana's page, votes are no longer transactions and no longer appear in blocks. A block can finalize in one round if at least 80% of stake notarizes it. Otherwise, a second round uses 60% thresholds.

Proof of History no longer paces block production. Execution stays the same: the SVM, programs, transactions and fees don't change.

The second phase, Rotor, will replace Turbine, Solana's block propagation layer. Solana lists it as "not yet scheduled." If someone credits today's numbers to "Alpenglow" as a whole, half of the design hasn't shipped yet.

The security trade-off is also worth knowing. TowerBFT needed more than two-thirds of stake for confirmation. Alpenglow tolerates 20% malicious stake plus 20% offline stake. Solana Compass notes that slashing for double voting is defined but not enabled in this first version.

Validators also pay differently. TowerBFT voting cost about 1 SOL per epoch in vote transaction fees. Alpenglow replaces that with a flat 0.8 SOL per epoch Validator Admission Ticket (SIMD-0357), which is burned. A validator that can't pay doesn't vote or produce blocks in the next epoch.

In my view, this is the detail most likely to affect today's real numbers.

Alpenglow's fastest finality depends on the one-round fast path, which needs at least 80% of stake to notarize a block. On the morning of October 20, a tracker run by Pumpkin's Pool, cited by SolanaFloor and reported by Solana Compass, flagged 151 validators holding 20.3% of stake as unprepared. The day before, that figure was 45%.

The math is uncomfortable. If 20.3% of stake really couldn't vote, only 79.7% would be left, which is just short of the fast-path threshold. In that case, blocks would need the slower second round, and finality would land above the headline figure.

I expect that number to drop before the switch, since operators have been upgrading quickly. But it's the main reason I wouldn't trust any finality figure from the first hour without also checking how much stake is actually voting. Validators without a registered BLS key, or that miss the required client version, stop voting entirely. Their delegators also stop earning inflation rewards.

There's already one public reference point. Solana's page links to a community cluster explorer run by Valid Blocks, where Alpenglow has been running on Agave 4.3.2.

When I checked this morning, it showed an average finalization time of 131 ms over the past hour, ranging from 111 ms to 156 ms. Average slot time was 215 ms. That's inside Solana's target range.

That cluster had 62 active validators and about 10.2 million SOL staked. Mainnet is far larger, more spread out geographically, and runs under real load. Test-cluster results are a strong sign, but they aren't proof of how mainnet will perform.

You don't need to wait for a press release to know whether the switch happened. Solana's getAgGenesisCert RPC method returns null while the cluster is still on TowerBFT and returns a genesis certificate once Alpenglow is live. Nodes older than Agave 4.3 return a "Method not found" error, which shouldn't be confused with null.

Once the certificate shows up, here's what I'll be watching over the first few epochs:

One caveat for developers: according to Anza's operator notes, the Clock sysvar's unix_timestamp now estimates when the parent block ended, not when the current block began, and should be treated as approximate. Any timing tool that reads block timestamps may need adjusting.

If Alpenglow delivers, Solana goes from finality you wait for to finality you'd barely notice. I'll believe the 150 ms figure once mainnet consistently shows it.

#5500. Dave’s Hot Chicken’s CEO Was Handed a $100 Bill and 3 Words of Advice by His Boss at a Valet Stand. Those Words Are Still How He Runs the Company Today.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Jim Bitticks spent years watching his boss give generously to the people around him. He says that habit is a big part of how Dave’s Hot Chicken grew.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Jim Bitticks had a crisp $10 bill ready for the valet. Then Bill Phelps handed the man $100.

The parking lot was only about 30 feet away. Retrieving the car had taken less than a minute. Bitticks looked at his own tip and told Phelps he could have at least let him go first.

Phelps pulled out another $100 bill and handed it to Bitticks.

In January 2026, Bitticks became CEO of Dave’s Hot Chicken, moving up from president and chief operating officer. He succeeded Phelps, who became executive chairman.

Asked what he learned from his predecessor, Bitticks talks about taking care of employees beyond their salaries and benefits.

“I’ve seen Bill pay people’s student loans off,” Bitticks says.

Phelps once upgraded a private jet to make room for an hourly graphic artist named Eddie. Earlier, while Bitticks was working at Blaze Pizza, where he rose to chief restaurant officer, a manager called about $200 Phelps had left in a tip jar. She worried he had meant to leave $2.

Bitticks asked Phelps’ longtime business partner Elise Wetzel about it.

“That’s Bill Phelps, generous to a fault,” she told him.

Bitticks sees a connection between those gestures and the company Dave’s Hot Chicken has become.

“I think a lot of the Dave’s success story is connected to sort of that willingness to be generous to others,” he says.

That includes sharing experiences and giving people opportunities to learn. When asked about building the team behind the company’s growth, Bitticks starts with believing people can develop the skills they need if someone gives them training and a chance.

He estimates that about 60 of roughly 75 corporate support employees had worked with the leadership team at Wetzel’s Pretzels, Blaze Pizza or Carl’s Jr.

The team has grown across brands because people who worked together before have brought one another into the next opportunity. Bitticks now leads a company staffed largely by those familiar faces, with firsthand knowledge of what they can do when given room to grow.

The graffiti at Dave’s Hot Chicken connects a restaurant in Dublin to a parking lot in Los Angeles.

For Bitticks, that recognizable identity travels alongside something the company cannot export: a franchise partner’s knowledge of the local market. The company initially heard warnings about entering the United Kingdom. An experienced restaurant operator saw an opportunity instead.

“We know how to do U.K.,” Bitticks recalls the group saying.

The partner backed that confidence with its choice of real estate, combining two neighboring souvenir shops into a corner restaurant on London’s Shaftesbury Avenue. Artwork, construction and marketing helped turn the location into the brand’s highest-volume restaurant for roughly a year, according to Bitticks.

Dave’s also opened in Dublin and signed a deal to expand into 10 additional European countries, including Italy, Poland and Germany.

“The whole model is built around franchisees that know their market,” Bitticks says.

What guests recognize when they arrive comes from a different kind of expertise.

Dave’s began in 2017 as a chicken stand in a Los Angeles parking lot, with street graffiti on the brick wall behind it. When the founders opened their first permanent restaurant, they wanted to preserve that energy. They hired two graffiti artists who were friends of the founders to bring it inside.

The artists have worked with the company’s design and construction team to give new restaurants a family resemblance without repeating the same room.

“Every single location you go to at Dave’s isn’t exactly the same as another, but feels related,” Bitticks says.

#5499. OpenAI hires Uber President Jill Hazelbaker to lead communications, filling a critical role that was curiously vacant for 10 months

OpenAI has hired one of Uber’s highest ranking executives to oversee its global communications efforts, filling a key role that had been vacant for nearly a year as the AI company navigates a challenging political landscape and moves closer to an initial public offering.

Jill Hazelbaker is joining OpenAI as chief corporate affairs officer, the company announced on Tuesday. Hazelbaker, who had been president and chief corporate affairs officer at ride hailing giant Uber, will work alongside OpenAI’s leaders to “deepen public understanding of AI and strengthen trust in its mission,” the company said.

She will report to OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman and starts in early December, OpenAI told Fortune.

“As AI becomes part of more people’s lives, how we communicate, engage, and earn public trust has never been more important,” Brockman said in the announcement, citing Hazelbaker’s experience and understanding of the “opportunities and responsibilities that come with building technology at global scale.”

Hazelbaker is a well respected communications professional in the technology industry. She has served as Uber’s President and Chief Corporate Affairs Officer for the past 11 years, and previously held senior leadership roles at Snap and Google. She is replacing Hannah Wong, who served as OpenAI’ chief communications officer (CCO) until January 2026. Since then, OpenAI’s Chris Lehane has been leading the team in the interim.

In the ten months since Wong’s departure, OpenAI has experienced a series of public controversies—most notably when its AI agents hacked the company Hugging Face during training in July. The 11-year old company has been criticized for not being sufficiently transparent and communicative about its operations, at a time when public concerns about AI’s potential harms to society, the labor market, and the environment are rising. Backlash to the massive AI data centers being built across the U.S. has emerged as one of the key issues in the midterm elections taking place on Tuesday.

In September, OpenAI told Fortune it was not rushing to fill the role, and was focused on getting the right candidate. Over the summer, it ramped up its search by hiring an executive recruiting firm.

OpenAI offered Hazelbaker the position in the spring, but she turned it down, as Fortune reported in September. Sources suspected her close relationship with Uber’s CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, desire to be on the East Coast for her family, and already high salary played a role in her declining the role.

It appears OpenAI has now made Hazelbaker an offer she cannot refuse.

Hazelbaker will remain on the East Coast, but will spend time in San Francisco, where OpenAI is headquartered, the company told Fortune.

“The work of building public trust has never been more consequential,” Hazelbaker said in the announcement, describing AI as the “most profound technological shift of our lifetime.”

#5497. How to Decide Whether to Build In-House, Buy an Existing Solution or Partner With Another Company

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

When should a company build, buy or partner? Here’s what you need to know.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The challenge of when a company needs to develop a capability it doesn’t currently possess poses a management question. The analysis starts with a financial comparison. Management calculates the cost of developing internally, compares it with the price of purchasing an existing solution and selects the option with the more attractive projected return.

The analysis, however, runs the risk of reducing a strategic decision to a procurement exercise. In practice, companies can choose to build the capability themselves, buy it through a product, platform or acquisition, or partner with another organization that already possesses it.

I’ve encountered versions of this problem across banking, fintech, technology, construction and financial services, including technology modernization and system conversions, M&A work and the development and pricing of financial products.

The details and economics widely vary, but the strategic question underneath is consistent. Companies should assess what they actually need and then work towards the best answer to fulfill that need based on a larger strategic vision.

Building internally makes sense when a capability is sufficiently important to competitive differentiation that management wants to control how it evolves.

This can apply to technology, intellectual property, operating processes or specialized expertise. If a capability determines why a customer chooses the company over competitors, then an outside provider may limit the ability of the company to differentiate. Internal development allows the company to shape the capability around its strategy rather than shaping its strategy around what the market offers.

Leaders, however, generally underestimate what “build” entails. Building does not end when a system launches, the new steam is assembled or the capability becomes operational. The organization has also chosen to maintain it, staff it, improve it and keep it relevant as the business changes. A company may have the capital to build a function, but it requires continued management attention, technical talent and operating discipline.

Buying can compress years of development work. In simple terms, that means purchasing an established technology platform or service rather than creating one internally. At the other end of the spectrum, it can mean acquiring a company because the desired capability, people, intellectual property, customers, volume, distribution or market position can be difficult to produce organically.

The financial analysis of an acquisition naturally focuses on purchase price, expected return, opportunity cost and integration challenges. Strategically, management should also determine exactly what it is buying and why. What value is the company trying to solve through inorganic growth or acquisition?

The second stage of buying includes integration. A company can acquire an asset immediately without immediately acquiring the ability to use the new asset well. Systems may have to connect, processes may change, and employees may need to adopt an entirely new operating model. The objective is to determine what advantage buying produces and how quickly it can be absorbed and transitioned into an operating advantage.

The third option is partnership. This approach allows companies to access expertise, distribution, technology or operating capabilities without assuming full ownership. That can be particularly useful when the capability matters to the customer proposition but does not itself need to become a core institutional competency.

Financial services provide many examples of this logical framework. Banks and finance companies frequently leverage technology providers, payment systems, capital providers, third-party complementary products or specialized services. Creating these components internally would consume enormous resources without necessarily improving what makes the company distinctive.

The same logic applies beyond financial services. A manufacturer may partner for logistics. A technology company may rely on specialized infrastructure. A growing business may use an outside provider for a function that would be expensive to build but does not meaningfully distinguish the company in the market.

Partnerships work best when companies have clearly defined value propositions and can find mutually beneficial arrangements that add value.

A disciplined build-buy-partner decision can be organized around several questions.

First, how important is this capability to differentiation? The closer it sits to the reason customers choose the company, the stronger the argument for ownership or significant control.

Second, how quickly does the organization need it? Build may produce a better long-term fit but arrive after the market opportunity has passed. Buying or partnering can create speed when timeliness matters.

Third, does the company possess the talent to own it? Capital alone doesn’t create capability. Management has to attract, retain and lead the people who operationalize ideas.

Fourth, what is full economics? Build costs include maintenance and continued development. Acquisition costs include integration. Partnerships may require recurring payments.

Fifth, how much control does the business actually need? Leaders sometimes demand ownership when contractual rights, service standards or a well-designed partnership would provide sufficient control at a substantially lower organizational cost.

Finally, what does this choice require the company to become? Every internal capability creates another area that leadership must manage well. Every acquisition adds complexity. Every partnership creates an external dependency that must be governed.

Each of the three options has pros and cons that largely depend on the functional needs of the business. There is no right option when costs and opportunities coexist, depending on the company’s strategy and fundamentals. The main point is that all three options require careful analysis and thought before operationalizing.

The challenge of when a company needs to develop a capability it doesn’t currently possess poses a management question. The analysis starts with a financial comparison. Management calculates the cost of developing internally, compares it with the price of purchasing an existing solution and selects the option with the more attractive projected return.

The analysis, however, runs the risk of reducing a strategic decision to a procurement exercise. In practice, companies can choose to build the capability themselves, buy it through a product, platform or acquisition, or partner with another organization that already possesses it.

I’ve encountered versions of this problem across banking, fintech, technology, construction and financial services, including technology modernization and system conversions, M&A work and the development and pricing of financial products.

#5496. Apple warns rogue AI agents could ‘conceal’ and ‘manipulate,’ causing unintended consequences for its business

Apple is cautioning that rogue AI agents that “conceal actions” or hide or manipulate information could pose a threat to its business if they access systems without authorization and cause damage.

The warning by the world’s second most valuable company came in an annual filing Tuesday, a day after Apple reported its fourth-quarter financial results. In the risk factors section, Apple expanded its warnings about artificial intelligence. Apple’s caution underscores the risks tech giants and other companies are projecting after a string of AI safety incidents in recent months, which have prompted companies to release new security features and debate regulatory measures.

In its 10-K filing, which is made each year following the end of its fiscal year, Apple said “artificial intelligence agents and other technologies can take actions autonomously, including interacting with internal or external systems that in some cases they may not be authorized to access, executing or altering code, sending communications, and completing transactions.”

Such technologies, the iPhone maker said, “may behave in unintended or unpredictable ways, including by taking actions that were not directed, instructed or authorized, exceeding permissions, defying directions or resisting instructions.” And it noted that autonomous AI agents that go rogue could “conceal actions, hide, withhold or manipulate information, or generate inaccurate or deceptive outputs.”

Apple is the latest to warn about risks posed by AI agents. Google parent Alphabet also pointed out the risks posed by rogue agents in a recent filing. Google, however, was more pointed about the potential consequences, writing that during AI model testing, it had observed unexpected behavior, including agents taking actions outside their intended scope, which could ultimately lead to “severe or catastrophic security and societal incidents, or negatively affect human rights.”

The risks outlined by companies follow several major cybersecurity incidents involving AI models, most notably this summer’s attack by OpenAI agents on AI company Hugging Face. In Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, made public last week, the company listed many risk factors, including incidents in which its models gained unauthorized access to real-world systems during security testing. It also estimated that 5% to 7% of its revenue this year came from customers later found to be violating its usage policies.

Executives at Microsoft and other major tech companies have called for a greater focus on securing AI agents. Microsoft recently announced a set of controls to detect, monitor, and restrict AI agents, including cutting their permissions or stopping them if they behave suspiciously. Chief executive Satya Nadella has argued that companies should treat agents as potential insider risks and put security controls outside the AI model rather than trusting the model to police itself.

In its 10-K filing on Tuesday, Apple also outlined other pressures, including memory and storage component shortages that it said will intensify. It also said demand for cloud computing, storage, and other AI infrastructure has produced “constrained supply, extended lead times, and increasing costs” that could affect its AI rollout. Its research and development spending rose 32% year over year, driven by higher infrastructure-related costs, including AI investments.

Apple shares dropped roughly 2% on Tuesday after the company said its margins would continue to be squeezed by memory chip costs and after it showed slowing growth in its Services segment. Ternus, on his first earnings call as CEO, largely stuck to scripted marketing points and offered few details about Apple’s plans for personalized AI agents.

#5494. That ‘100% Tax Write-Off’ on Your Company Car Isn’t What You Think. Here’s What to Know Before You Buy.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Your business car write-off is smaller than social media claims.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Every year, around this time, the same type of question appears from business owners: “Can I write off the entire cost of a car if I buy it before December 31?” It usually accompanies a video featuring someone leaning against an SUV promising that the government will pay for the whole thing.

The short answer is no. The rules for deducting a business vehicle are clear, and the discrepancy between what is promised on social media and what can be written off according to the law can cost you in an audit.

Let’s go through an example: $50,000 passenger car under 6,000 pounds, purchased from an unrelated seller, placed in service in 2026, driven 60% for business and deducted using the actual expense method. All dollar amounts are based on federal-only numbers.

The deduction amount depends on the use of the vehicle, not its ownership.

The amount you can deduct does not depend on whether the car title is in your name or whether it is an LLC buying the car. The deduction amount depends on how much of the vehicle was used for business purposes. A vehicle used 60% for business purposes will be 60% deductible and the other 40% personal, no matter the purchase structure.

Commuting trips create the most common errors. Commuting from home to a regular workplace or business location is always personal, regardless of the fact that the vehicle belongs to the business. Driving from the workplace to a client or from one job site to another is considered business use. Get your percentage correct as every number below depends on this figure.

There are two main methods of claiming a deduction for vehicle expenses. Standard mileage rate is applied when the mileage log of business trips is multiplied by the per-mile figure that includes all costs of maintaining the car. In 2026, the IRS established the standard mileage rate at 72.5 cents for the first half of the year and increased it to 76 cents for miles driven from July 1 through December 31. If you choose this method, make sure your mileage log breaks down at July 1.

Actual expense method includes the business portion of the actual cost of the vehicle, including its depreciation. Here is what is not explained in videos on social media: to maintain the option of using the standard mileage rate for the owned vehicle, you must claim it in year one. If you claim accelerated depreciation, bonus depreciation or Section 179, you cannot use the standard mileage method for the vehicle anymore. Make this decision with your CPA before purchasing the car, not afterwards.

Section 280F of the Internal Revenue Code places a cap on the annual depreciation of passenger cars. IRS adjusts these caps each year.

First, we calculate the basis. The business use of the vehicle is 60% and, therefore, the business basis of the $50,000 passenger car is $30,000. The other $20,000 is personal and will never be deductible.

Second, let’s apply the cap. According to Rev. Proc. 2026-15, the first-year depreciation cap is $20,300 for a passenger car placed in service in 2026 and bonus depreciation applicable. Apply your business use percentage to the cap: $20,300 x 60% = $12,180. This is your maximum deduction in the first year — neither $50,000 nor $30,000. The balance of $17,820 will be depreciated in future years. If bonus depreciation is not applicable or is elected not to be claimed, the cap is reduced to $12,300, which becomes $7,380 after applying the business-use percentage.

Bonus depreciation at 100% is applicable again for the property acquired after January 19, 2025. However, it will not raise the passenger car depreciation above the 280F cap. The business share of fuel, insurance and repairs is deducted separately, and thus, $12,180 is not the full deduction for your vehicle.

Those videos promise the full deduction for heavy vehicles. The caps for passenger cars apply for the weight up to 6,000 pounds, measured by unloaded weight for passenger cars and gross vehicle weight rating for trucks, vans and most SUVs. Check the sticker inside the driver’s door of the vehicle before you buy.

Heavier vehicles avoid the specific caps mentioned above; that’s why there are so many posts suggesting “buy a big SUV.” But there are some limits nevertheless. In tax years beginning in 2026, the Section 179 deduction for a heavy sport utility vehicle is limited to $32,000, although bonus depreciation may deduct the remainder of the business basis of the car.

Independent of the vehicle’s weight, the Section 179 deduction cannot bypass passenger car caps. No method, entity or vehicle category can make our $20,000 personal portion deductible.

Nothing stated above makes sense without a contemporaneous mileage log documenting the date, business purpose and miles driven for each trip. The log created after receiving an audit notice is one of the easiest ways to lose your legitimate deduction, and a phone application allows you to create it easily.

In order to use accelerated depreciation, bonus depreciation or Section 179, the qualified business use must be more than 50%. Our 60% car qualifies for this requirement. At 50% or lower qualified business use, you may still take the deduction using the straight-line depreciation method or, if you qualify, the standard mileage rate; however, without accelerated write-offs.

Here comes the pitfall. When the qualified business use falls to 50% or lower later, the excess depreciation will be included in the income, and you will have to use the straight-line depreciation method. Usually, it happens when a business car gradually turns into a family car. Moreover, when you dispose of or sell the vehicle, depreciation is recaptured as ordinary income, and the benefit is partially temporary.

Tax advantage should never be the motivation for buying the car. Start by identifying the vehicle your business needs, and then go through the rules:

•            Verify the weight classification of the vehicle before you buy it

•            Choose the method of deduction in year one

•            Keep business use above 50% if you need to deduct with acceleration

•            Document all business miles immediately

•            Take the business portion only as allowed by law

For our $50,000 car, it is $12,180 in first-year depreciation plus the business portion of the operating expenses.

Every year, around this time, the same type of question appears from business owners: “Can I write off the entire cost of a car if I buy it before December 31?” It usually accompanies a video featuring someone leaning against an SUV promising that the government will pay for the whole thing.

The short answer is no. The rules for deducting a business vehicle are clear, and the discrepancy between what is promised on social media and what can be written off according to the law can cost you in an audit.

Let’s go through an example: $50,000 passenger car under 6,000 pounds, purchased from an unrelated seller, placed in service in 2026, driven 60% for business and deducted using the actual expense method. All dollar amounts are based on federal-only numbers.

#5493. Pope Leo XIV on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 1, 2026 at 10:11 amNovember 1, 2026 at 10:57 am

On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.

“The future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.”

I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.

First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”

Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”

Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”

I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014, with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

“Take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.

Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.

Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said, adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”

I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.

Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.

Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk, but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.

Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

#5492. Pump.fun Perps on Hyperliquid: How the 0.10% Builder Fee Works

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On a $10,000 Bitcoin perpetual order placed through Pump.fun, Pump.fun can charge up to $10.

Hyperliquid, the exchange that actually matches and settles the trade, charges a standard taker $4.50. Only one of those fees has a written rule sending it toward a token burn, and it's Hyperliquid's.

Most launch coverage focused on whether to buy HYPE or SOL. The more useful question for PUMP holders is where each dollar of perps fees goes. When you compare Pump.fun's fee schedule, its buyback methodology and Hyperliquid's fee documentation, then, you'll see they don't connect the way many people assume.

Pump.fun didn't build a derivatives exchange. Its perps run on Hyperliquid's order books through builder codes, a feature that lets outside apps send user orders to Hyperliquid and add their own fee on top. Hyperliquid's engine handles matching, margin and liquidations.

The product first appeared in Pump.fun's API around October 9, when Wu Blockchain spotted a /coins/perps endpoint showing prices, funding rates, open interest and maximum leverage, all pulled from Hyperliquid's mainnet. The same endpoint also listed SOL, Nvidia, Tesla, gold and crude oil contracts. Trading launched around October 16 and 17, with up to 40x leverage on BTC and 25x on ETH reported at launch.

Pump.fun updated its terms and conditions on October 17. The perps feature is blocked for users in the United States and Ontario, along with sanctioned parties.

Pump.fun's official fee schedule splits the cost of a perp trade into separate parts.

Here's the math on a $10,000 market order at entry-tier rates, assuming Pump.fun charges its full maximum:

For a maker order, the gap is wider: $1.50 to Hyperliquid and up to $10 to Pump.fun. At full rate, the app routing the trade earns more per order than the exchange that runs it. Note that 0.10% is the published maximum, not a confirmed rate for every trade.

This side of the trade has the clearest documentation. Hyperliquid says its fees are "entirely directed to the community," meaning its HLP vault, the assistance fund and market deployers.

The assistance fund converts trading fees into HYPE automatically as part of the chain's execution.

According to Hyperliquid's documentation,

So every Pump.fun perp trade feeds part of Hyperliquid's own token-burn mechanism through standard protocol rules. That share never touches Pump.fun's treasury.

There's one more possible layer. Some of the markets in Pump.fun's API, such as stocks and commodities, are the kind of contracts that third-party HIP-3 deployers usually run on Hyperliquid. Those deployers can set their own fee share. If Pump.fun lists them, another party joins the split.

Under Hyperliquid's builder code rules, the builder fee goes to the builder's address on Hyperliquid. Builders claim it through the standard referral-reward process. The fee is charged in the collateral asset, so for these markets it builds up in USDC on Hyperliquid, not in SOL on Solana.

That matters once you check Pump.fun's PUMP buyback methodology. The program puts 50% of revenue toward buying and burning PUMP. It defines revenue as income from:

Perps builder fees and bridge fees aren't on that list. The page also says buybacks aren't a commitment to future purchases, except as "deterministically programmed prior to April 29, 2026." Perps launched in October, so they weren't covered by that commitment.

To be fair to Pump.fun, the absence of a rule isn't proof that the money stays out of buybacks. Pump.fun could add perps to its revenue definition at any time. But as of today, no published Pump.fun document links a perps fee to a PUMP burn. Any connection would also need USDC moved off Hyperliquid and converted, because the buyback table records purchases in SOL.

This also changes how to read the buyback numbers I've covered before. The PUMP page shows $490.65 million in cumulative buybacks on its dashboard and $465 million in Newsletter #14. It also says the fee dashboard has misreported revenue and buyback amounts since Custom Pairs launched and that this "will be fixed soon." If perps revenue grows, Pump.fun's total income and the share that actually reaches PUMP burns could move further apart.

Hyperliquid makes the builder side of this traceable. It publishes daily fill files for each builder at:

[https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/](https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/){builder_address}/{YYYYMMDD}.csv.lz4

The builder address must be entirely lowercase. A builder's total collected fees also appear in Hyperliquid's referral info query.

Without Pump.fun's builder address in its fee schedule, terms or announcements, nobody outside the company can add up the actual perps revenue, which is the number that would show whether this product is a side feature or a real revenue line. Once that address is public, the next step is to check whether a matching amount ever shows up in the PUMP buyback table.

Until then, the honest answer is this: Hyperliquid's share has a documented path to a HYPE burn, while Pump.fun's share has a documented path into Pump.fun's own wallet.

#5491. Before He Was a Billionaire, 24-Year-Old Mark Cuban Had 5 Roommates and Lived in ‘Hell Hotel’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The future billionaire’s early living situation was a far cry from luxury.

Before earning billions, Mark Cuban lived with five roommates and had no bed of his own in a cramped three-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment in Dallas, Texas.

Cuban disclosed in an X post earlier this week that he lived in a 1,352-square-foot apartment for two years. He was “the last one in” to the arrangement, so he got the floor to sleep on and “a spot in the corner” of a bedroom to put his belongings.

Cuban said that he honestly “didn’t mind living with 5 roommates.”

“We all were in the same boat,” he wrote. “I moved in when I was 24. Lived there or across the way for 2 years before I only needed one roommate.”

He acknowledged that not everyone would be content with the living arrangements.

“If it’s not the lifestyle for you. So be it,” he wrote. “If you don’t think just getting any job to get started is the right career choice for you. Do what you think is right. I don’t care and I don’t judge.”

The price of renting the apartment was $2,388, the “same in 2026 dollars” as when Cuban lived there. Split six ways, each person was paying about $400 for rent.

The future billionaire’s early living situation had an apt nickname to match.“I didn’t say I was living in a dream apartment,” he wrote. “Everyone called it the Hell Hotel.”

Cuban regularly shares career advice on X, encouraging young workers to keep learning.

In June, Cuban urged recent graduates to consider small- and medium-sized businesses rather than focus on big companies. His reasoning was that smaller companies may need help putting AI to work, giving newcomers a chance to make an immediate, outsized contribution to their workplaces.

Cuban said that new hires could teach those businesses how to use AI agents to handle processes they previously lacked the time or money to tackle. “Entrepreneurial companies will love the value you add,” Cuban wrote.

Cuban became a millionaire in 1990, at age 32, when he sold his computer consulting business, MicroSolutions, to CompuServe for $6 million. He then co-founded AudioNet, which later became Broadcast.com. Yahoo acquired the company for $5.7 billion in 1999, making Cuban a billionaire at age 40.

According to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, the 68-year-old Cuban is now one of the richest people in the world, with a net worth of $10.7 billion.

Cuban has also previously discussed keeping his personal life relatively ordinary despite his wealth. In a 2023 interview on The Really Good Podcast, he said he preferred doing chores and driving himself to hiring people for everything.

“I just try to be the same person, I mean, as I was when I was poor, middle, and rich,” he said.

#5490. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”

#5489. 7 Mistakes Founders and CEOs Make When Talking to the Media (and How to Avoid Them)

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Even accomplished business leaders make mistakes during media interviews. Here’s how to avoid seven common missteps that can undermine your credibility and cost you valuable coverage.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Being a successful CEO doesn’t automatically make you a great media spokesperson. I’ve coached executives across financial services and other professional industries who can lead organizations, navigate complex challenges and command a boardroom, yet struggle to communicate effectively with journalists.

Even the most accomplished executives can undermine their credibility by talking too much, making unsupported claims or turning interviews into sales pitches. Fortunately, these mistakes are avoidable. Here are seven I see most often and how to prevent them.

One of the biggest misconceptions executives have is that they must answer every question a journalist asks. You don’t. Even when a question relates to your industry, it may fall outside your specific expertise.

Rather than guessing, say, “I’m not the best person to answer that, but I can connect you with someone who is,” or “That’s outside my area of expertise, but what I can tell you is…” Journalists don’t expect you to know everything. They do expect you to know what you’re talking about. Of course, declining to speculate isn’t the same as evading a legitimate, difficult question about your business.

A journalist asks a straightforward question, and the executive launches into a five-minute explanation filled with background, caveats and unnecessary details. By the time they make their point, the reporter may have lost interest or run out of time.

My advice? Lead with the headline. Answer the question directly in one or two sentences, then stop. If the journalist wants more, offer an anecdote or compelling example that illustrates your point. Journalists love stories, but don’t bury your main message beneath layers of explanation. If the reporter remembers only one sentence, make sure it’s the one that matters.

Before every media interview, I coach clients to identify three key messages they want to communicate. Not 10. Not 15. Three. These might relate to your business, expertise, product or the issue being discussed.

Ask yourself: If only three things I say make it into the story, what should they be? Even when a journalist calls unexpectedly on deadline, it’s reasonable to ask, “Can I call you back in five minutes?” Use that time to organize your thoughts, assuming the reporter’s deadline allows it.

Don’t be afraid to reinforce important messages naturally throughout the conversation. Preparation isn’t about memorizing a script; it’s about knowing what matters before the interview begins.

Financial services, healthcare, biotechnology and other specialized industries are filled with acronyms, credentials and technical terminology. But just because a term is familiar to you doesn’t mean the journalist understands it.

I encourage executives to explain complicated concepts as though they’re talking to a family member around the dinner table. Could your mother, grandmother or 10-year-old understand your point? If not, simplify it.

And don’t confuse a journalist’s unfamiliarity with industry terminology for a lack of intelligence. Reporters cover multiple subjects, often under tight deadlines. A question that seems obvious to you may be exactly what their readers need answered. You’re the subject-matter expert. Help them understand.

A media interview isn’t a sales presentation. Journalists aren’t interviewing you to hear how wonderful your company is. They’re looking for information, perspective and insights that help them tell a compelling story.

Statements like “We’re the best in the industry” or “Our firm offers unparalleled service” aren’t particularly useful. Excessive self-promotion can immediately undermine your credibility.

Instead, share a surprising insight, explain an emerging trend, offer a contrarian perspective or provide a real-world example. It’s fine to provide background about your firm, but don’t hijack the conversation with a commercial.

The best media sources make the journalist’s story better, not their own company sound bigger.

Unsupported statistics, exaggerated claims and overconfident predictions can quickly damage your credibility, especially when discussing financial markets, economic conditions or other complex subjects where forecasts are inherently uncertain.

If you cite a statistic, know where it came from and be prepared to provide the source. If you’re making a prediction, distinguish your opinion from established fact. And if you don’t know an answer, say so. There’s nothing wrong with telling a reporter, “I don’t have that figure in front of me, but I can check and follow up.”

Journalists remember sources they can trust. Don’t give them a reason to question yours.

When speaking with a journalist, assume you’re on the record. That includes casual remarks, offhand observations and comments made before or after the formal interview.

I strongly caution executives about going “off the record.” Many misunderstand what that means or assume they can declare something off the record after saying it. They can’t. Such arrangements require mutual agreement before information is shared, and I generally advise clients to avoid them unless there’s a compelling reason and clearly established terms.

The safest approach is simple: Don’t say anything to a journalist that you wouldn’t be comfortable seeing in print or hearing repeated publicly.

A successful media interview isn’t about demonstrating how intelligent you are, answering every question perfectly or finding opportunities to promote your business. It’s about being a credible, knowledgeable and useful source.

The best spokespeople prepare without sounding rehearsed, offer insights rather than commercials and know when to stop talking. Ultimately, being quotable isn’t about saying more. It’s about having something meaningful to say and knowing how to say it clearly.
