#5421. 42AI comes out of stealth with $62.5M and a world model that can ‘predict human behavior’

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Here’s a question straight out of sci-fi: What if AI could predict what you were going to do before you decided to, even in a completely new situation?

Israeli startup 42AI says it is developing a “behavioral world model” that can do just that, and it has just come out of stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding. The company is initially running its predictive system at a handful of financial brokerages, where it says the model can help predict how individual traders will respond to volatile conditions.

“Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” 42AI’s CEO and co-founder Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch when I asked him to justify his company’s tall claim. He argues that people have underlying psychological tendencies that influence their decisions even when their circumstances change, and that’s what the startup is trying to measure and convert into data that the model can understand.

“A week from now, you might be a different person, but your tendencies will always play out in certain areas to a probability or distribution,” his co-founder and CTO Ehud Ezra added. And that, the company argues, is what the model does: show the probability of a person making a certain decision.

42AI says the model tries to figure out people’s internal motivations instead of extrapolating patterns based on their previous actions. To do that, 42AI examines how people react to seemingly unrelated events. For an investor or trader, for example, such events might include completing KYC processes, onboarding, support calls, money transfers, or trading stocks.

“When the person is talking to support or sales in the initial process […] we’re looking at the sentiment, we’re looking at the voice, we’re looking at a lot of interactions that they’re doing, how many times do they call, and so forth,” added Ezra. “And all of those data points are going into the model. Later on, you have the interactions: how you buy and sell, and when, and we’re looking at the market at that stage.”

“So we’re trying to look at how they’re looking at the world. In a world model, every individual is the world,” he added.

The company then converts those observations into mathematical representations of traits, which are then fed into a transformer-based world model that lays out probabilities for possible decisions under different circumstances. (The company uses a separate language model to generate explanations for its predictions.)

Ezra said the model is trained to preserve a person’s underlying tendencies during simulations. So if someone is usually risk-averse, but the model suddenly treats them as a risk-taker, “the target is off,” he said, explaining how the model’s training rewards are structured.

42AI spent three years developing this approach, combining psychological research with neuroscience and genetics, as well as advice from experts in psychology and PTSD, and Dan Shechtman, who was awarded the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Gal-Or said the team first studied thousands of people via psych assessments and behavioral scenarios, before adding government and biobank datasets covering more than 2 million people. Its customer datasets have since expanded to cover almost 30 million people, he said.

In live deployments, the model analyzes customers’ existing records, including transactions and support calls. Gal-Or pointed out the system doesn’t need personally identifiable information, arguing that “the model never knows who the person is.” However, it seems the company still creates individual behavioral profiles from linked customer activity.

In predicting market trades, 42AI claims its model achieves 98% accuracy, but Gal-Or clarified that this is more a measure of whether trading flows fall within a predicted range, not if each trade was predicted correctly.

He also said the model consistently achieves an F1 score of 0.8 to 0.85 for predicting trading direction and volume. (F1 score is a metric in machine learning that measures how well a classification model can balance correct predictions against false alarms and missed events.)

And it’s not like the model can work everywhere, given it’s still a machine in a box. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said. Ezra explained that the system’s accuracy also suffers when it misses important situational context, like if someone chooses to change their trading choices based on advice from a friend or a colleague.

Gal-Or said 42AI is working with 10 large brokerages, who are using it to manage liquidity, margin requirements, and hedging exposure. The company is onboarding more customers, he said, and is generating more than “seven figures” in revenue, though he wouldn’t specify a number.

Customers pay the startup a flat fee, or a percentage of the value the platform helps them gain. He claimed one brokerage generated approximately $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging.

The $62.5 million seed funding came from the founders and Infinity Group over three years, and wasn’t entirely raised from external investors, Gal-Or said. Infinity was founded by his father, Amir Gal-Or, who is also 42AI’s chairman and a co-founder. 42AI now plans to raise more money.

Beyond finance, 42AI is now exploring applications for its model in gaming, fraud prevention, and cybersecurity, and one day wants to use it to help robots and AI agents understand people. But that may be a ways off yet: Ezra acknowledged that the model needs to be trained on rules and context for each new domain.

And like with all AI tools, there’s a potentially troubling side to 42AI’s technology: If a brokerage can anticipate what its customers may do, what’s to stop someone from using that knowledge to their own benefit? Ezra admitted that this was “a valid concern” when I raised it, and the founders pointed to regulations, monitoring, and an internal ethics committee, though they didn’t explain what, if anything, would stop their customers from using the technology to gain an advantage over the very people it’s profiling.

Amit Gal-Or, however, was confident that the technology could help address such risks. “We are very proud that actually we are part of the solution; we are the solution to this problem,” he said.

#5420. Crypto Developers Using Claude Via VS Code May Have Been Compromised: This Version Has a Backdoor

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Developers using Claude AI through Visual Studio Code (VS Code) may have been exposed to a serious security threat after researchers discovered a malicious version of the popular coding assistant's extension.

According to an October 30 report from cybersecurity researchers at OpenSourceMalware, version 2.1.313 of the Claude Code extension contained a hidden backdoor that could enable attackers to remotely access infected computers.

The malicious version was identified in the Open VSX extension registry, where developers download tools for their coding environments.

The compromised extension reportedly looked and functioned like the legitimate Claude Code tool, making the threat particularly difficult to notice. However, researchers discovered additional malicious code designed to run automatically when the extension loaded.

Once activated, the backdoor attempted to establish a remote connection to an attacker-controlled server, potentially giving hackers access to the victim's computer.

More concerningly, the malware was designed to remain active even after the computer restarted.

This means simply closing VS Code or stopping work with Claude might not eliminate the threat.

Although the attack was not specifically designed to target cryptocurrency users, developers working on blockchain projects could face significant risks.

Their computers may contain sensitive information, including private keys, wallet credentials, exchange API keys, and access to cryptocurrency infrastructure.

If attackers successfully gained remote access, they could potentially obtain this information and use it to compromise wallets or projects.

However, researchers did not report confirmed cryptocurrency theft or identify any specific blockchain-related functionality in the malicious code.

The researchers confirmed malicious code in the analyzed Open VSX version but could not establish how it was introduced.

Importantly, the findings do not prove that Anthropic's official VS Code Marketplace release or its broader distribution systems were compromised.

Developers who installed version 2.1.313 through Open VSX should treat their systems as potentially compromised and investigate immediately.

Removing the extension alone may not be sufficient, as the backdoor was designed to persist independently.

#5419. Readwise takes on Amazon’s Kindle and Goodreads with its new app for book lovers

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Readwise, the maker of a read-it-later app and digital reading companion that keeps track of your highlights across services, is now taking on Amazon’s e-book empire with its latest app, Readwise Books. The app is an e-book store and helps you track what you’ve read, similar to Amazon’s Goodreads.

The bootstrapped startup described the new app as “a cross between Kindle and the Goodreads apps,” as it offers a single place to buy, read, and track books. However, Readwise Books aims to offer more detailed reading stats than the dates you read a book and whether you finished it. It lets readers visualize richer reading data like words read, pace, depth, immersion, and sessions.

Meanwhile, its new store offers “millions” of e-books from the big five publishers and others, initially in the U.S., with more countries to come. Print books (fulfilled by Bookshop.org’s distributor) and some audiobooks are available as well, the company notes.

The launch comes at a time when there’s been an explosion of new reading apps and book trackers, all hoping to challenge Goodreads by introducing new features like book clubs, widgets, improved discovery features, goal-setting, better lists and organizational tools, habit-tracking, and more. However, few indie developers have gone so far as to launch an alternative to Amazon’s Kindle e-books store, which remains the industry leader, with an 83% share of the market when Kindle+ (formerly Kindle Unlimited) is included in the stats.

One of Kindle’s bigger advantages is that it offers an end-to-end solution for everything related to reading e-books, from the hardware devices to the book-tracking log. Readwise isn’t selling its own e-readers, but it is attempting to create its own community around reading, complete with tools for reading purchased and uploaded e-books, tracking them (like on Goodreads), sharing your reading progress with friends, and more.

It also offers a number of ways to track books outside its ecosystem. This includes a way to track reading sessions by using Kindle’s browser-based Cloud Reader and a feature that lets you snap photos of physical books to mark your progress. Plus, you can upload any DRM-free EPUBs (a common e-book file format without copy protection). The app can read your e-books aloud via text-to-speech.

Readwise believes its more in-depth metrics could be a big selling point, too, likening them to a “Strava for reading” — a reference to the metrics-heavy exercise app.

“The desire to read books, like exercising and eating well, is laden with guilt,” the company explained in a blog post penned by co-founders Daniel Doyon and Tristan Homsi. “Many people feel like they should be reading more, but feeling bad about it tends to change nothing. The session tracking taps into a different psychological mechanism. It makes the reading you’re doing legible and, as the adage goes, that which is measured is improved.”

The company adds that the most consistent feedback from users is that the app has led them to read more without willpower tricks like goal-setting, streaks, or scheduling.

With publishers’ permission, the app will support AI-powered features as well, like session recaps, definitions and term lookups, word and phrase translations, and a location-aware ability to ask questions about the part you’re reading. (So far, only HarperCollins has opted in, though.)

Unlike Goodreads’ locked-down ecosystem, Readwise is embracing open technology. This includes a public API and an MCP server. The latter supports AI agents that could be used to research book recommendations on your behalf, use your Readwise data to create a books page on your personal website, or even wire up your hackable e-reader to log your sessions automatically, depending on how involved your AI use cases may be.

The new Readwise Books app will remain free, with some AI features later going behind a paywall. Its prior apps for reading and tracking highlights are either $7.99 per month each or $9.99 per month for both.

#5418. Solana Validator Admission Ticket: Who Fell Short After Alpenglow, and How Marinade Responded

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

StakeThat +MEV went into one of Solana's first Alpenglow epochs with about 137,000 SOL staked with it and 0.8169 SOL in its vote account. The new admission ticket required 0.8198 SOL. It was 0.003 SOL short.

That's the first post-activation picture of Solana's Validator Admission Ticket. Most stake made it through without trouble, but a small group of validators keeps dropping in and out, often by amounts smaller than a typical transaction fee. At least one large stake program changed its delegation code hours before activation so its stake wouldn't stay with those validators. Marinade's published validator snapshots for epochs 1063 to 1067 show who fell short and what happened next.

According to Solana's BLS Pubkey and VAT page, Alpenglow has been active on mainnet since epoch 1064, which began around 13:36 UTC on October 21. From then on, each validator's vote account pays a 0.8 SOL Validator Admission Ticket at the start of every epoch. The fee is burned, and it pays for the following epoch. The first charge, at the start of epoch 1064, covered epoch 1065.

The rules are strict. If the fee can't be paid, Solana's page says, "your validator does not vote or produce blocks in the next epoch." Validators without a registered BLS key, or outside the top 2,000 by stake, are also excluded. Delegators to an excluded validator earn no inflation rewards for that epoch. The page also stresses that the balance "has to stay funded, not be funded once."

The vote account also has to stay above its rent-exempt minimum. In Marinade's data, the full requirement works out to 0.8197612 SOL.

Marinade publishes the inputs to its stake auction every epoch in a public pipeline repository. The input data checks whether each validator's vote account holds enough to cover the next epoch's ticket. Each snapshot covers about 670 validators and roughly 438 million SOL of stake.

Before activation, in the epoch 1063 snapshot, 33 validators holding 7.63 million SOL, or 1.74% of stake, were below the ticket balance. Once Alpenglow went live, that number fell quickly: 15 validators with 1.55 million SOL (0.35%) in epoch 1064, then 19 with 1.15 million (0.26%) in epoch 1065, the first epoch the ticket actually paid for. By epoch 1066 it was 13 validators with 790,000 SOL (0.18%), and by epoch 1067 just 8 with 710,000 SOL (0.16%).

The epoch 1063 count matches a figure in Marinade's own code history. A commit on October 21 notes that its new gate "refuses the 33 validators with vat_eligible false" in the 1063 snapshot.

The biggest pre-activation gaps were fixed in time. An unnamed validator with 2.05 million SOL of stake, Temporal Emerald with 1.23 million and Bitget Wallet with 593,000 were all below the ticket balance in epoch 1063. All three had topped up by the next snapshot. Of the 33 flagged before activation, 25 had recovered by epoch 1064.

So the fee didn't remove a large share of stake. The balance check affected less than 2% of stake at its peak, and about 0.16% by epoch 1067.

The validators that did fall short show a pattern: many of them nearly had enough.

Because the ticket is charged every epoch, a validator that tops up just enough to pass once will fail again an epoch later unless it adds more. Between epochs 1064 and 1067, between 3 and 11 validators fell below the threshold each epoch, while a similar number recovered.

The shortfalls also cut across setups. Every validator flagged in epoch 1067 runs either Agave 4.3.x, the client release the migration required, or the latest Firedancer build. Software readiness wasn't the issue. Keeping the balance funded was.

Solana offers a fix: routing block revenue to the vote account through solana vote-update-commission-collector. That keeps the account funded automatically, though the change takes two epochs to apply.

The bigger story is how stake programs reacted. Marinade, one of Solana's largest delegation programs, changed its auction code in pull request #153, merged at about 06:47 UTC on October 21, roughly seven hours before Alpenglow activated.

The change adds a new disqualifying condition, vatIneligible. A validator whose vat_eligible flag is false "gets no SAM and no backstop stake," because "Agave then pays its stakers no inflation rewards for the epoch." A null value never disqualifies a validator. The check currently tests only the SIMD-0357 balance, not BLS key registration.

The first version applied the rule only in Alpenglow epochs. Marinade's developers then caught a timing problem. Agave starts charging the ticket at the 1063-to-1064 boundary, and "a stake move made in epoch E takes effect in E+1," so the original rule "left Marinade stake on refused validators for epochs 1064 and 1065." The merged version refuses ineligible validators in every epoch.

The snapshots confirm it worked. In the epoch 1064 snapshot, 192,762 SOL of Marinade stake sat on ineligible validators, nearly all of it on one unnamed validator. By epoch 1065, that had dropped to 2,407 SOL, and by epoch 1066 to 10 SOL. A later commit gives the rule its own label and call to action in Marinade's interface, so operators can see why they've been excluded.

Marinade, in short, turned a protocol fee into a delegation rule of its own. A validator that misses one ticket loses an epoch of rewards, and it also loses Marinade stake until its balance recovers.

Before activation, Solana Compass reported that a community tracker flagged 45% of stake as not ready two days ahead of epoch 1064, mostly validators on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1. The following day, that had dropped to 20.3%.

Marinade's snapshots show the software gap closing much as those warnings suggested it needed to. Stake on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1 fell from 6.56% in epoch 1063 to 0.08% by epoch 1067. Firedancer operators, who had to switch to Agave for the migration, dropped from 11.0% of stake to 5.9% in epoch 1064. They then came back strongly, reaching 17.2% by epoch 1067, well above their pre-migration share.

The large readiness gap was about software and keys, and it was mostly closed by the time it mattered. The fee gap was always small.

For most delegators, nothing changed: more than 99.8% of stake sits with validators that keep their tickets paid. For those delegated to the few that don't, the cost is clear: no inflation rewards for that epoch, and in Marinade's case, stake moved elsewhere.

The protocol sets one requirement: 0.8 SOL in the vote account every epoch. Stake programs are now adding their own rules on top, starting with Marinade's. Validators that keep running near the threshold will keep losing epochs of rewards, and possibly delegations, until they keep a buffer or automate funding.

#5417. Former Ripple CTO Mocks $6 Billion Binance Hack With Stellar (XLM) Joke

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

The cryptocurrency market is going through the largest robbery in its history, but industry veterans manage to find a reason for harsh dark humor in it.

Former Ripple CTO and creator of the XRP Ledger network David Schwartz reacted to the Binance exchange hack with a caustic joke aimed at his main historical competitor, the Stellar (XLM) blockchain.

Schwartz commented on a post by EasyA co-founder Dom Kwok, who complained that hackers had wiped out his balances, leaving only Litecoin untouched. The former Ripple CTO, in turn, quipped: “These sick b*stards dropped an extra 517 XLM into my Binance account!”

The sarcasm is tied to a long-running corporate conflict: Stellar was created by former Ripple co-founder Jed McCaleb, and the idea that hackers forcibly “credit” victims with competitors’ tokens instantly went viral.

Despite Schwartz’s ironic tone, the blow landed directly on Ripple’s own ecosystem. The attackers instantly withdrew 233.46 million XRP tokens (about $296 million) from Binance’s hot wallets. It is impossible to return them: the XRP Ledger architecture excludes forced freezing of the native token at the protocol level.

However, with the company’s second asset, the situation turned out differently. Ripple Senior Vice President Jack McDonald announced that the company had detected the movement of stolen Ripple USD (RLUSD) stablecoin and urgently blocked the attackers’ addresses.

Binance co-founder Yi He has already publicly thanked the Ripple team for promptly freezing about $200 million in RLUSD funds, emphasizing that user funds are now protected (SAFU). While XRP showed the hackers absolute decentralization, the controlled RLUSD stablecoin became the main protection tool.

The incident itself became part of the historic Binance hack totaling $6.3–6.36 billion across 10 blockchain networks.

#5416. Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Whether developed by OpenAI or Anthropic or built on open source alternatives, current AI models share a critical limitation: They don’t learn from their mistakes without further training.

Businesses adapting these models for specialized fields, such as law and finance, typically get around this by fine-tuning general models. However, that often requires hiring internal research teams or relying on expensive consultants, commonly known as forward-deployed engineers (FDEs).

Trajectory, a startup founded about a year ago by three Stanford classmates with experience at Google DeepMind and Apple, wants to automate that process, allowing AI models to learn from feedback and continuously improve at specialized tasks.

The 18-person company just announced that it raised $45 million in a Series A round at a $300 million valuation, led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures.

Trajectory co-founder Ronak Malde compared foundational models to a very smart PhD student who’s always starting a new job. “But what the economy values is someone who worked on the job for 30 years,” he told TechCrunch.

The startup aims to solve this problem through an approach known as continual learning. Businesses using Trajectory can start with an open source AI model and connect the platform to their applications, allowing it to collect feedback on how the model performs. Trajectory then uses that information to retrain the model, helping it improve at specialized tasks over time.

With Trajectory, lawyers, doctors, and other specialists can improve the models near automatically themselves, Malde said. That capability could make deploying specialized AI faster and cheaper.

Companies like Harvey and Rogo are already using Trajectory’s platform to post-train open source models, helping them perform more like experienced lawyers or financial analysts by learning from previous tasks, such as reviewing a particular type of legal contract or valuing a company using a specific methodology. Trajectory’s other customers include Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia. The startup is now making its post-training platform publicly available.

The people using Trajectory decide “what good looks like for their organization and can turn that into improvements for their model,” Malde said.

Trajectory’s approach to continual learning shares some similarities with recursive self-improvement (RSI), the idea that AI systems can improve their own capabilities. But co-founder Michael Elabd argues that keeping humans involved in the training process makes Trajectory’s approach safer, since autonomous self-improvement could lead to unintended or even dangerous outcomes.

Trajectory isn’t the only startup trying to automate post-training. Other companies going after this market include Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati and the company behind the fine-tuning platform Tinker, Applied Compute, which was valued at $3.25 billion last month, and Prime Intellect, a platform that helps companies build and train their own AI agents.

Malde believes the startup’s biggest advantage is its team. He was among the handful of researchers Google DeepMind acqui-hired from Windsurf. Elabd also worked at DeepMind, while Trajectory’s third co-founder, Arjun Karanam, previously worked on generative foundation models at Apple. The startup has also recruited researchers and product designers from OpenAI, Stripe, and Netflix.

Why does design matter so much to a company focused on AI training? Karanam says the startup has developed an interface that makes post-training more accessible to its nontechnical customers.

#5415. Y Combinator’s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he’s suffered from “cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast The Builders, set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion.

“I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens,” he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack, on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said.

On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson’s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life.

“It’s read all of my email and all of my Dropbox. It’s read, like, all of my Apple Notes, even my therapy notes going back 20 years,” he said.

He describes using AI agents as getting help with “almost anything that you do in your day-to-day life, and for it to do it somewhat more autonomously. Think of it as a Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder at all times. Like, almost anything you want to do, it knows you, and it’s there to help. And it will actually sort of run ahead and say, ‘What about this?’ Or it’ll help you see around corners.”

As an early OpenClaw adopter who is now a power user, Tan says one thing he’s learned is not to treat AI agents like traditional software. Some people are so worried about “repeatability and safety that they actually trade off all of the beautiful parts of working with an AI agent, which basically can be so similar to a human,” he said.

For instance, Y Combinator is also using an agent that is “rebuilding the way we operate at YC,” he said. “We now have an internal AI agent, for instance, named Stray Light that kind of has a personality, and then it has a company brain. Like it actually has the total context of every founder we’ve ever backed, anyone who’s ever emailed us, like all the applications.”

Tan, who is, naturally, an avid lover of technology (as anyone running Silicon Valley’s famed startup accelerator would be), believes personal AI agents will eventually become mainstream, if one major problem is solved: Costs have got to come down.

“It’s too expensive right now,” he said, adding that he knows the amount of money he spends on AI agents is “a crazy privilege that not everyone can do.”

But freebie agents controlled by Big Tech maybe aren’t the answer, either. When discussing the future he’d like tech to build, and how Meta as a social media company has impacted us, he said, “This is a huge company that controls the algorithm, and we all wish that they didn’t at some level,” he said. “So you could imagine a personal AI that you control, that you program.”

Bitcoin settled Friday’s $10.92 billion Deribit options expiry at $78,119, almost exactly on the $78,000 max pain level, after the $6.36 billion Binance hack knocked it from $80,850 to a $76,500 low overnight.

That low touched BTC’s 200-day EMA, the long-term trend line, to within $32. BTC trades at $77,620, down 3.2% in 24 hours, and the Fear & Greed Index fell from 51 to 30 in a day.

With about a third of Deribit’s open interest now gone, the options market is lighter than it has been all month. The next large date is November 27, when $3.55 billion expires with max pain at $80,000.

Coinbase Premium hit a 4-year low.The last time it was this low was in Nov 2022, right after the FTX collapse, when BTC bottomed.Market sentiment is bearish enough to be bullish, imo. pic.twitter.com/jab4bk1GIX

Discover: Bitcoin Braces for a $10.9 Billion Options Expiry With Max Pain at $78,000, Two Days After the Fed’s Split Hold: Can BTC Hold $79,000?

The drop came in two legs. BTC opened the 20:00 UTC hour on Thursday at $80,850 and hit $78,297 within minutes as news of the Binance breach spread, a 3.2% fall. It bounced, then slid again after 23:00 UTC and printed its $76,500 low just after 02:00 UTC on Friday, 5.4% below where the hour began.

Forced selling did much of the work. CoinGlass data showed $1.55 billion of crypto positions liquidated in 24 hours, 83.6% of them longs, with $501.6 million in BTC alone.

Smaller accounts bought the dip: the share of OKX accounts that are long jumped as the price fell, and open interest rose by about $210 million into the low. Funding on OKX’s BTC perpetual stayed positive throughout, so longs are still paying shorts.

Implied volatility told a more cautious story. Deribit’s DVOL index, which tracks the 30-day volatility options traders are pricing in, jumped from 37 before the hack to 42 just before midnight UTC and has only eased back to 38.7.

About 135,000 BTC of options expired on Deribit at 08:00 UTC on Friday, the last Friday of the month, when monthly contracts settle. Max pain, the strike where the most options expire worthless, sat at $78,000. Deribit settled the contracts at $78,119.01.

The book was heavily tilted toward calls. Deribit data reported before the expiry put the put/call ratio at 0.53, close to two calls for every put. With BTC settling just above $78,000, most of those calls, bets that BTC would be higher by the end of October, expired worthless.

Once the expiry cleared, Deribit’s BTC options open interest stood at 285,073 BTC, or about $22.1 billion, as of 11:17 UTC.

BTC options notional by Deribit expiry as of 11:17 UTC on October 30, 2026. Source: Deribit.

Max pain isn’t a forecast; BTC often settles far from it. But the November levels frame the range traders are betting on: puts clustered at $74,000 to $76,000, right around the 200-day EMA, and calls stacked from $90,000 up.

One more sign of caution: in the 24 hours to 11:17 UTC on Friday, Deribit traders bought 1.63 BTC of puts for every BTC of calls, the reverse of the call-heavy book that just expired.

On the daily chart since early August, BTC is back where it spent most of September: between its 200-day EMA at $76,468 and its 50-day EMA at $80,593. Friday’s low wick stopped $32 above the 200-day line, which BTC has closed above every day since its late-August breakout.

August 2 to October 30, 2026: BTCUSDT 1D chart. Source: Binance.

The levels line up with the options book:

BTC has tested this 200-day zone before. In mid-September, it dipped to $74,968, held, and ran to $87,395 within a week. Friday’s buyers are betting on the same bounce, as the OKX long/short ratio shows.

Discover: Bitcoin Swings Less Than Coinbase and Oracle, Yet Crypto Stocks Move Up to 2.4 Times as Hard: Why?

For Bitcoin, the next test is Binance itself. If withdrawals reopen smoothly within the promised 48 hours, the call-heavy positioning that just expired worthless could rebuild toward the $90,000 strikes. If they don’t, the puts at $74,000 to $76,000 are where traders have already placed their bets.

#5411. Ukraine’s new pocket-sized gadget turns Russian drones’ cameras against them

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Ukrainian drone teams have a new way to spy on the drones that spy on them. A Kyiv equipment startup called CODE380 has been gaining attention for a pocket-sized receiver, the D·Vision SDR, that picks up live camera video from many Russian drones and shows it on a screen.

Those drones send their video over the air without any scrambling, so anyone with the right receiver can watch along. A Ukrainian unit can see where a drone is heading and what its pilot is aiming at before it hits.

According to Defense News, the device is light, at about 10 ounces, which is less than half the weight of competing Ukrainian models, one of which weighs a couple of pounds.

It also listens on the radio channels Russia’s newer Molniya drones started using for video in June. Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a radio specialist who advises Ukraine’s president, said in a June Facebook post cited by Defense News that “most detectors don’t see these frequencies, or see them poorly.” He warned that putting too much trust in a detector could prove fatal.

Beskrestnov has also warned that digital video could one day replace analog, which would blind receivers like this one. The New York Times reported in August that some Molniyas are AI-guided, using Nvidia chips and emitting no signals.

In its official X account, the exchange told its customers that withdrawals are now enabled for several networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, BSC, Dogecoin, and many others.

The world’s largest crypto exchange, Binance, suffered what appeared to be the largest crypto heist on record on Oct. 29, 2026. Hackers stole $6.3 billion, but the company managed to freeze $2.54 billion.

The exchange, co-founded by Chinese-Canadian entrepreneur Changpeng Zhao (CZ), suspended deposits and withdrawals on the day of the attack. The firm assured clients that users’ funds are safe and that it would cover all losses from the hack.

On Saturday, the FBI released an official statement revealing that North Korea was responsible for the breach that led to the theft of $6.3 billion from Binance on Thursday.

That evening, Binance announced it successfully restored 90% of the crypto assets lost in the breach. The firm said it used its own reserves, including the SAFU and internal treasury, to fully cover customer losses so clients would not lose their capital.

Today, Binance announced its withdrawal system is back to normal, and customers can withdraw any amount without delay. According to data shared this evening by CryptoQuant, over $4 billion in assets have been withdrawn from the exchange since withdrawals resumed after the $6.3 billion hack.

Meanwhile, crypto analyst Michael van de Poppe believes Bitcoin is likely to fall toward $74,000 as customer outflows and a wider market sell-off weigh on investor sentiment. Bitcoin currently trades at $77,789 following Binance’s security breach, and the analyst is watching whether support around $76,200 and $76,800 holds.

He warns of broader impacts, as persistent, massive withdrawals could trigger a plunge in BTC’s value toward $74k. The selling momentum could push BTC lower from current levels due to high-leverage BTC shorts and expectations of a relief rally.

#5407. Cosmos Hub Approves Gaia v29 With 99.41% Support Ahead of October 28th Upgrade

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.

While the FBI and the U.S. Secret Service investigate the theft of $6.3 billion from Binance wallets, a public discussion between Elon Musk and the exchange’s founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ) unfolded on the X platform. The spat highlighted an unexpected irony: Musk decided to troll the crypto exchange in the midst of the crisis, but in response received a harsh reminder that his own assets had become Binance’s main argument in the dispute over solvency.

The reason for the dispute was a meme by one of the users, which ironically compared CZ’s public promises to cover the losses with Sam Bankman-Fried’s famous tweet on the eve of the FTX collapse: “FTX has enough to cover all client holdings.” Elon Musk reacted to this comparison with an awkward emoji (😬), launching a wave of trolling directed at the exchange.

@elonmusk @HuaweiMate6 Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop. Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!

The reaction of the Binance founder followed immediately: “Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop.” As a counterstrike, Zhao, right in the discussion thread, reminded Musk whose money exactly he had used to buy Twitter in 2022. At that time, Binance provided the billionaire with $500 million. By October 2026, these investments had transformed into a stake in the aerospace giant SpaceX (SPCX) with a market value of more than $1 billion.

Trying to shame Musk and at the same time prove the stability of the exchange to the audience, Zhao disclosed internal calculations right there in the dispute thread. According to him, of the $6.3 billion in stolen funds, about $3 billion was promptly frozen by stablecoin issuers, and another part is covered by the SAFU reserve fund. The actual balance gap is about $2 billion, exactly half of which is potentially covered by this stake.

“Gap is about $2b, we have $1.x billion in SPCX alone. The remaining gap is (still painful, but) manageable,” Zhao replied to Musk, adding at the end: “Would appreciate it if you show a little support. Thanks!”

To finally shift the focus away from security problems and put Musk in his place, Binance co-CEO Yi He harshly intervened in the discussion. She published an ironic open address to Zhao, taking a veiled jab at the head of SpaceX: “Reporting to the major shareholder: Our company’s revenue for the year is sufficient to cover the losses, so we do not yet need to sell the SpaceX shares you are bullish on.”

Zhao himself later explained that he pulled out the data on the SPCX stake in the dispute with Musk exclusively to demonstrate the platform’s safety margin, so that he “can be less worried.” The owner of X himself has so far left the attacks of Binance’s leadership unanswered.

The exchange plans to resume withdrawals within 45–48 hours after the completion of internal checks, and the four-year-old investment has de facto turned into the main stash with which Binance is now protecting itself from market panic.

#5405. CoinDepo Revises Earn Rates to Reflect Asset Economics and Deployment Horizons

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

CoinDepo is introducing revised Earn rates effective November 8, 2026. The changes connect the economics of each supported asset with the practical requirements of managing client capital across different account lengths.

Client deposits are placed into a diversified portfolio whose primary focus is lending. At the close of the second quarter of 2026, overcollateralized crypto lending represented 37% of deployed capital and microcredit programs represented 24%. Remaining allocations covered liquidity pools, real-world and private-market investments, stablecoin yield strategies, and market-neutral trading.

Income produced by these activities funds the interest paid to users and also covers operating costs and liquidity needs. The resulting APRs therefore align with the broader economics of operating the CoinDepo platform.

Daily APRs will decline for every asset listed in CoinDepo’s 30-asset update table. EURC is handled separately and keeps its 10% Daily APR. USDT and USDC Daily APRs will adjust from 17% to 15% while their Annual APRs change from 23% to 22%. BTC and ETH Daily APRs move from 12% to 11%, with Annual APR remaining at 18%.

Across the 30 assets, the difference between Daily and Annual rates expands from six percentage points to seven. The adjustments will also be asset-specific as well as period-specific; the Annual APR for Filecoin (FIL), for instance, will be changed from 18% to 12%.

Short-term funds require the platform to retain greater flexibility so that withdrawals can be met without delay. A more predictable funding horizon simplifies the planning of capital allocation and the matching of funds with available lending and investment opportunities. The wider gap between Daily and Annual APRs places greater weight on that planning advantage. Daily accounts continue to be offered for users who place priority on ready access to their funds.

CoinDepo’s open Monthly, Quarterly, Semi-Annual and Annual Interest Accounts will keep their current APR through the remainder of the active term. Revised rates apply only to accounts that are newly opened or renewed after the effective date. The complete before-and-after comparison appears in the platform’s Earn rate update, together with the business disclosures that describe the activities supporting client interest.

CoinDepo is a centralized digital asset platform that provides crypto interest accounts and portfolio-backed borrowing services.

Near Protocol (NEAR) is seeing a significant shift in derivatives market activity, with futures trading volumes rising and capital flows increasing. With NEAR trading around $4.31, derivatives data shows a complicated picture: bullish positioning, higher trading activity, and selling pressure that continues.

#5402. Coinbase Sinks 11% to a 52-Week Low as Brian Armstrong Defends a Plan to Sell Up to 8.17 Million Shares: Are Crypto Stocks Near a Floor?

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

Crypto stocks fell on Friday as Coinbase dropped 11% to $142.73, after touching a 52-week low of $138.71, when CEO Brian Armstrong had to defend a new plan to sell up to 8.17 million COIN shares alongside a 35% drop in quarterly revenue.

The plan, disclosed with Coinbase’s third-quarter results on Thursday, is worth about $1.31 billion at Thursday’s $160.59 close. Co-founder Fred Ehrsam and President Emilie Choi filed plans of their own, bringing the total to about 13.6 million shares, roughly $2.2 billion.

Armstrong replied on X that the plans only sell above price targets, “most of these are set for very high prices, a signal of how bullish I am.” The market didn’t take much comfort: every major crypto stock was down at least 6.8% in early trading.

Discover: Bitcoin Swings Less Than Coinbase and Oracle, Yet Crypto Stocks Move Up to 2.4 Times as Hard: Why?

A Rule 10b5-1 plan lets executives set up share sales in advance, with fixed rules on price and timing, so they can’t be accused of trading on inside information later. Coinbase’s quarterly filing and TipRanks’ breakdown show three new plans:

Armstrong’s plan can sell from November 16, 2026 through October 2027. It’s more than double his previous plan from the third quarter of 2025, which covered 3.75 million shares. Together, the three plans cover about 6% of Coinbase’s 223.7 million Class A shares.

Armstrong’s defense rests on the price targets, which Coinbase hasn’t disclosed. In the same thread, he wrote:

“Very few of the sales in my 2025 plan ever sold. I have the vast majority of my net worth in one stock: COIN. Even if this entire plan executed that would still be true.”

If the targets really sit far above today’s price, the plans won’t sell anything at $142. Traders will only know for sure from Form 4 filings, which start showing any sales after November 16.

The plans landed on a weak quarter. Total revenue fell 35% from a year earlier to $1.22 billion, transaction revenue dropped 44% to $590 million, and consumer spot trading volume fell 59%. Net income of $718.7 million came almost entirely from a $715 million paper gain on the crypto Coinbase holds. October looks no better: CNBC put fourth-quarter transaction revenue at just $165 million through October 25.

There was a bright spot: prediction markets passed $200 million in annualized revenue, and Armstrong said he’s “seeing signs that the market is turning.”

Coinbase led a broad selloff in crypto stocks on Friday morning. The rest of the group fell between 6.8% and 9.1%, more than twice as hard as Bitcoin, which was down 3.5% over 24 hours after Thursday’s $6.36 billion Binance hack.

Crypto stocks on October 30, 2026, about 10:05 a.m. ET, versus Thursday’s close. Sources: Yahoo Finance, Binance.

Two things stand out. Coinbase fell 3.2 times as hard as Bitcoin, well above the up-to-2.4-times range crypto stocks have shown against BTC this year. And the Nasdaq 100 fell only 2.5%, so the drop is specific to crypto rather than a broad tech selloff.

The Binance hack cuts both ways for Coinbase. Binance has paused withdrawals and is repaying users from its own reserves, which could push some traders toward a US-listed, regulated exchange. But a $6 billion theft also hits confidence in crypto trading generally, and Friday’s selling suggests investors are weighing that more heavily.

Wall Street hasn’t given up on the stock. TipRanks counts 19 Buy ratings, nine Holds and two Sells, with an average price target of $206.61, about 45% above Friday’s price. COIN is now 60.5% below its 52-week high of $361.40.

The daily chart since mid-May shows why $139 matters. Coinbase bottomed at $139.18 on June 26 and $139.11 on July 31, and both times it rallied. Friday’s low of $138.71 is the third test of the same floor, and the first to break it, even if only by 40 cents so far.

May 12 to October 30, 2026: COIN 1D chart. Source: Yahoo Finance (Nasdaq).

The stock is below both its 50-day EMA ($173.51) and its 200-day EMA ($189.59), and the 50-day has stayed under the 200-day throughout the five months on the chart. Friday’s drop also left a gap between Thursday’s $157.61 low and Friday’s $148.50 high.

For crypto stocks, Coinbase’s $139 floor is the line to watch next week. Armstrong says his plan only sells far above it, and the Form 4 filings from November 16 will show whether he’s right.

#5401. Ripple Moves $389 Million of XRP Amid Aid for Binance Hack

The San Francisco blockchain firm backing XRP, Ripple, has just pulled a mysterious XRP move that could barely go unnoticed considering the volume of the tokens involved.

According to the latest data provided by blockchain tracker Whale Alert, Ripple has been spotted moving hundreds of millions of XRP, a few hours after it announced support for Binance's attack.

Per the data, Ripple has conducted multiple transactions carrying a total of 310 million XRP worth over $389.08 million with an unidentified wallet address on Friday, October 30.

While the transfers were made in three separate transactions within just a few minutes, the data showed that they were conducted when XRP was trading at around $1.25.

The first transaction saw Ripple transfer 120 million XRP, worth about $150.57 million, to an unknown wallet. Meanwhile, the two other transactions saw 90,000,001 XRP worth $112.96 million and 99,999,999 XRP worth $125.56 million transferred to Ripple from wallets that could not be identified.

The timing and volume of such a transfer, especially from a renowned firm like Ripple, did not go unnoticed, and it has sparked concerns among market participants about the motive behind the transfers, as none has been stated yet.

Although speculations suggest that the move could have been attributed to Ripple selling XRP, especially at a volatile time like this, other commentators are raising a different concern.

Since the transfers arrived just hours after a Ripple executive confirmed that the company was assisting with efforts to address the recent exploit involving Binance, which led to the theft of some XRP, there are questions about whether the moves could be related.

#5400. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5393. Not Just Ledger: Karpeles Warns of Tampered Trezor Devices

The ex-CEO of the now-defunct Mt. Gox, Mark Karpeles, has flagged the potential compromise of Trezor hardware wallets sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis, indicating that the recent supply chain attack on Ledger devices is not an isolated case.

"Ledger n'est pas la seule. @Trezor devices sold by CryptoBilis were also implanted," Karpeles said in an Oct. 30 post on X.

In his post, Karpeles advised customers who bought Trezor devices from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onwards to immediately transfer their cryptocurrency to new wallets with new recovery phrases.

He also offered to manually review potentially compromised devices, saying that he would be willing to cover the shipping fees if customers wished to get their wallets checked.

Karpeles's alert follows Trezor's confirmation that its security team was made aware of a credible report of a suspected hardware implant in a Trezor Safe 5 device.

As detailed in Trezor's Oct. 30 announcement, the device in question was acquired through the online marketplace Tokopedia in Indonesia in August 2026.

The report on the suspected device was received by Trezor on Oct. 28, and a video interview with the customer was conducted.

That said, Trezor said it hasn't checked the device in question in person to verify the report.

The report states that the suspected compromised device has an extra board between the main board and the screen.

The extra board has a cellular module and an antenna that can receive data from the device, such as the wallet's recovery phrase.

Afterwards, the data can be sent via a mobile network when the hardware wallet is plugged in.

This suspected modus operandi is similar to the highly advanced hardware implants previously found in Ledger devices sold by CryptoBilis.

In fact, Ledger's investigation into suspicious fund losses involving the reseller began on Oct. 9. Later, it was confirmed that some Ledger devices had been physically tampered with.

On the same day, Trezor decided to cut ties with CryptoBilis as an authorized reseller.

Four devices bought by CryptoBilis customers have been checked by Trezor, but no signs of tampering have been found so far.

According to Trezor, no CryptoBilis customers have reported losing funds in connection with the suspected Trezor implant.

Despite this, Trezor recommends that affected customers create a completely new wallet instead of just restoring their existing recovery phrases on other devices.

While mainland China maintains a strict ban on cryptocurrency transactions, the American platform Solana Foundation has made a major step in the region by signing a strategic agreement with a local licensed issuer in Hong Kong, Anchorpoint Financial Limited.

The partnership launches the HKDAP stablecoin for retail payments and tokenized assets — this is the project's first direct collaboration with a public blockchain foundation.

The issuer Anchorpoint is a consortium of Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong), telecom operator HKT and Animoca Brands, which received the FRS01 license from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA).

Integration with Solana provides instant issuance and redemption of the asset, opening a legal banking gateway for retail and for trading real-world assets (RWA).

The deal rests on Hong Kong’s Stablecoins Ordinance, which took effect on August 1, 2025: any issuer of a fiat-referenced stablecoin must hold an HKMA license, fully back the token with high-quality liquid reserves and redeem it at par.

Since the Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the US dollar within a 7.75–7.85 band, HKDAP effectively becomes another dollar-linked instrument, but one issued in a separate jurisdiction outside direct US regulation.

Solana's infrastructure is ready for this: according to rwa.xyz data as of October 30, 2026, the total RWA volume on the platform stands at $18.89 billion, of which $14.13 billion (around 75%) is made up of stablecoins with a monthly transfer volume of $370.94 billion across 13.56 million addresses.

Consolidating its position, Solana Foundation is joining Hong Kong's government program OASES, opening a local office and rolling out the TAP tokenization program together with PwC.

This infrastructure creates a legal track for big capital. While mainland China tests the digital yuan exclusively within state-controlled pilot zones, Hong Kong provides clear rules of the game for private business.

As a result, Standard Chartered and its partners get a fully legitimate settlement instrument, and the international market gets direct access to Hong Kong dollar liquidity via the Solana blockchain.
